all.title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
institutions: Institute of Operations Research and Analytics
Institute of Real Estate and Urban Studies
all.abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the construction of a new measure of human-perceived difficulty rating for each knapsack instance, we found evidence that players who were assigned to instances with a higher difficulty rating in the past tended to perform better on future attempts. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: S. Agarwal’s research is supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore, under its Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic [Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022] and the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. J. Goh’s research is supported by a Startup [Grant R-314-000-110-133] and a 2021 Humanities and Social Sciences Faculty Research Fellowship from the National University of Singapore. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.00747 .

all.title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
all.abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. Sulaeman acknowledge research support from Sustainable and Green Finance Institute [Grant WBS A-0006413-00-00]. Y. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72402239] and China Scholarship Council. all.title: LLM time machines: Valuing digital goods over time
all.abstract: Digital goods generate substantial consumer welfare, but their valuations are difficult to estimate because many are free to consumers. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can reconstruct these valuations over time using incentive-compatible binary choice experiments. We benchmark predictions against eight waves of representative US survey data collected between 2016 and 2024. Calibrating GPT-4-Turbo on one year, we find that it approximates the magnitude and temporal patterns of median human valuations in other years. Newer models do not necessarily improve predictions, tending to favor monetary compensation. Our findings suggest opportunities and limitations for longitudinal valuations using LLMs.

all.title: Fintech Expansion
all.abstract: I study credit market outcomes with different competing lending technologies: a fintech lender that learns from data and can seize on-platform sales, and a banking sector that relies on physical collateral. Despite flexible information acquisition technology, endogenous fintech learning is surprisingly coarse, with a single threshold that screens out low-quality borrowers. As fintech lending technology improves, better enforcement harms, while better information technology benefits traditional banking sector profits. Big data technology enables the fintech to leverage data from its early-stage operations in unbanked markets to develop predictive models that support expansion into wealthier markets. (JEL G21, L13, L52, O33, O36)

all.title: Optimal Incentive Design for Decentralized Dynamic Matching Markets
institutions: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
all.abstract: In decentralized dynamic matching markets, agents can benefit from sharing resources, but they will collaborate only if properly incentivized. Motivated by applications such as multihospital kidney exchanges and job-hunting markets, this paper proposes novel monetary and nonmonetary mechanisms to incentivize collaboration in such decentralized dynamic markets. We study a model in which multiple self-interested agents manage local multiway dynamic matching problems. Jobs of different types arrive stochastically at each agent, expire after a limited time, and yield rewards when matched. An agent’s job backlog and actions are the agent’s private information, and each agent aims to maximize its long-run average matching reward. We design simple mechanisms that incentivize agents to submit all jobs upon arrival, thereby enabling centralized matching. Our first mechanism, the marginal-value (MV) mechanism, reimburses agents based on the MV of their submitted jobs. This can be implemented in a nonmonetary way by randomly selecting an agent (with a specified probability) to perform a match and collect the associated matching reward. We show that under the MV mechanism, full job submission constitutes an approximate Nash equilibrium—that is, the gain from unilateral deviation vanishes as the number of agents grows. To further eliminate incentives for deviation, we propose a refined mechanism, the MV-plus-credit (MVC) mechanism, and show that, when the number of agents exceeds a constant threshold, full job submission constitutes a stronger oblivious equilibrium. Numerical experiments based on kidney exchange data demonstrate that the gains from deviation under our mechanisms are small even in moderately sized markets. This paper was accepted by Peng Sun, optimization and decision analytics. Funding: J. Zhang is partly supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) [Grant 72394361] and the Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Mathematical Foundations for Artificial Intelligence [2023B1212010001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01346 .

all.title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
institutions: Center for Economic and Policy Research
all.abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: K. J. Mitchener thanks the Ciocca Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation at Santa Clara University for funding this research (Grant 2024-CIOG11). Any views expressed in this paper exclusively represent those of the authors and do not reflect the official viewpoint of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, the European Central Bank, or the Eurosystem. all.title: Mobile Location-Based Recommendation Systems and Local Businesses: Evidence from the Restaurant Industry
institutions: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology
all.abstract: When looking for a place to eat, how much do recommendations on your smartphone influence your choice? Can they help restaurants tucked away on side streets thrive in an age of algorithmic recommendations? We studied the launch of a location-based recommendation feature on South Korea’s largest search platform, tracking 16,720 restaurants over eight months. We find that visibility matters, but its benefits are uneven. Restaurants tucked away on side streets, far from subway stops, attracted the most additional attention when recommended by the algorithm. Yet this advantage did not translate into greater intentions to visit. Making a restaurant easier to discover did not necessarily overcome the inconvenience of reaching it. Digital information helped bridge this online-to-offline friction. Hard-to-reach restaurants with stronger online reputations and richer information, including customer reviews, photos, and menus, were better able to turn attention into visit intentions. For small businesses, visibility creates opportunities, but credible information helps turn attention into potential customers. For platforms and policymakers, location-based recommendations can bring overlooked businesses into view, but realizing their potential requires making reliable information readily available to consumers.

all.title: Impact of Data Privacy Regulations on Recommender Systems Performance
institutions: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
all.abstract: Data protection regulations like GDPR and CCPA let consumers delete personal data or opt out of collection, but companies struggle to understand how these practices affect their recommendation systems. This matters because recommendations drive substantial revenue; according to industry reports, Netflix’s system saves more than $1 billion annually, and personalized suggestions generate 35% of Amazon purchases. We analyzed how different data privacy practices impact recommendation accuracy using large-scale simulations with real-world data. A critical finding: Context matters enormously. For services where user preferences are more stable (e.g., streaming platforms), opting out barely affects recommendation quality while deleting data cuts performance dramatically. However, for platforms where preferences and needs can change frequently (e.g., e-commerce), deleting old data can actually improve recommendations while opting out severely harms them. For policymakers, this means one-size-fits-all regulations may be counterproductive. For companies, we demonstrate that data privacy practices can be redesigned: users can protect their most revealing data while maintaining close-to-optimal recommendation quality. This challenges the tradeoff between privacy and personalization, showing both could be achievable through smarter design. Companies should offer context-appropriate privacy options; regulators should recognize different platforms need different approaches.

all.title: The investment attraction effect of financial technology: evidence from China
all.abstract: Frontier technologies, such as artificial intelligence, when deeply integrated with traditional finance, give rise to financial technology (Fintech), which continuously influences cross-regional capital flows. We examine the development of Fintech in Chinese prefecture-level cities, using data on cross-regional investments by A-share listed firms, and empirically analyze the attraction effect and mechanisms of Fintech development. The results indicate that Fintech has a significant investment attraction effect, which can attract nonlocal firms to invest locally. Mechanism tests show that Fintech attracts nonlocal firms’ investment by reducing firms’ financing and business costs, while also improving cities’ innovation levels and entrepreneurial vitality. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the investment attraction effect of Fintech is more significant when the investment destination is a core city, has a high level of human capital, possesses high-speed rail connections, and is located in the same province as the firms’ registration. Additionally, if the firm’s CEO is from the investment destination, or if the firm has a higher level of diversification, the attraction of Fintech to the firm’s cross-regional investment is significantly enhanced. Further analysis demonstrates that after Fintech attracts investment from nonlocal firms, it not only enhances firms’ market value but also promotes income growth for local residents.

all.title: The Workplace GenAI Usage Divide: A Genetics-Informed Cognitive and Metacognitive Account
all.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly deployed in organizations, yet employees differ substantially and persistently in how frequently and intensively they use it. This workplace “usage divide” raises a fundamental but underexplored question: Why do employees differ systematically in their use of GenAI, even under common formal access? We argue that this divide reflects a broader challenge for IS research: explaining the use of systems that are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and general-purpose yet uneven and evolving in their capabilities. In workplaces where employees remain accountable for task performance, these properties make the use of GenAI not a routine adoption decision but a judgment process in which employees assess the system’s credibility and determine where task-relevant expertise lies. Drawing on molecular genetics and metacognition research, we theorize that genetic propensity, indexed by the educational attainment polygenic score (PGS)—an aggregate genetic index associated with educational attainment—helps account for systematic variation in these judgments and, ultimately, persistent differences in workplace GenAI use. Specifically, we develop a parsimonious two-pathway model linking educational attainment PGS to GenAI use: a cognitive pathway involving formal educational attainment and perceptions of GenAI credibility, and a metacognitive pathway involving strategic mindset and metaknowledge of where task-relevant expertise lies. We test our model using a multisource dataset combining primary genetic data, survey measures, and 21 months of objective usage logs. The results show that educational attainment PGS, a broad distal genetic index, is associated with both GenAI use frequency and interaction intensity and provide theory-consistent evidence for the proposed pathways. Overall, our study offers a micro-foundational account of the persistent GenAI usage divide and advances IS theory on the use of probabilistic, general-purpose systems in the workplace.

all.title: Understanding the Prompting Effects of Chain-of-Thought on Human Collaboration with Generative AI
all.abstract: It is well established that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves model performance in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). Far less understood is whether presenting CoT reasoning in AI-enabled interfaces enhances users’ perceived trust in GenAI’s competence in performing tasks. Drawing on the Heuristic-Systematic Model, we develop a theoretical framework in which CoT presence and quality trigger either heuristic perceptions of transparency or systematic perceptions of diagnosticity and germane cognitive load, with distinct mechanisms across task-difficulty conditions. Across a series of online experiments, we identify two key findings. First, high-quality CoT consistently enhances perceived trust in GenAI’s ability to generate correct outputs, regardless of task difficulty. Notably, under high-difficulty conditions, users’ trust in GenAI is primarily driven by the greater germane cognitive load perceived from high-quality CoT, whereas under low-difficulty conditions, trust is primarily driven by perceived transparency or diagnosticity. Second, low-quality CoT reduces users’ competence trust in GenAI that generates incorrect outputs only under low-difficulty conditions and only when users engage in careful processing, operating through perceived diagnosticity. Yet, under high-difficulty conditions, low-quality CoT amplifies trust via perceived transparency. By disentangling the cognitive pathways through which CoT shapes competence trust in GenAI and by identifying task difficulty as a critical boundary condition, these findings deepen our understanding of transparent reasoning in AI interfaces and offer valuable insights for deploying CoT in GenAI systems.

all.title: PNC bets on hospitality to counter AI disruption
all.abstract: A PNC branch executive is counting on the lender’s hospitality focus being even more advantageous amid the proliferation of artificial intelligence. PNC has zeroed in on the friendliness concept in recent years, from hiring branch staff from the hospitality industry to walking customers to their cars under an umbrella on rainy days. Jeff Martinez said the hours he invests in employee training geared toward providing a warm and welcoming experience at the bank’s locations will “be worth 10x a year from now.” Bank customers becoming increasingly comfortable with help from generative AI are likely to do initial research through that channel, said Martinez, the Pittsburgh-based bank’s head of branch distribution and sales management. But Martinez is confident customers will want to connect with bank employees during consequential moments in their financial lives, even if it’s to reinforce what they already heard from a large language model, he said. Jeff Martinez Permission granted by PNC “That is an art form married with science, that I think in ‘27 is going to be worth more than in ‘26,” Martinez said in a recent interview. By 2030, people will seek out human guidance amid the rise of AI-generated advice, he predicted, and PNC’s efforts to prioritize hospitality will pay dividends. Banks are eager to play up their human side in the battle against generative AI, and doing so will be essential to maintain customer relationships, said Udi Ziv, the CEO of fintech Personetics . all.title: Data silos threaten banks’ competitive edge in AI
all.abstract: Dive Brief: Artificial intelligence is disrupting banks’ business models, prompting a race to reap the benefits before the window of opportunity closes, according to a McKinsey & Co. report published last week . Nearly three in four consumers using AI for banking turn to OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude or Google’s Gemini for banking tasks, almost double the amount who use a bank’s chatbot, the report found. The trend highlights a quickly fading grace period, as consumers across demographics embrace AI faster than previous technology waves, according to McKinsey. As banks pour investment dollars into AI efforts, “speed could determine how much value the bank keeps, and unlike in past technology cycles, a late start may not offer chances to catch up, depending on how the profits get reinvested,” the report said. Dive Insight: As banks seek to strike a balance between accelerating AI use and maintaining operations and security, they’re also contending with digital technology challenges. Thousands of customers from JPMorgan Chase, among other firms, reported issues accessing their online accounts Monday . While navigating traditional technology challenges, data readiness continues to be an issue for chief information officers on their AI journeys. Nearly half o f banking executives ranked data readiness as their top AI obstacle, McKinsey found. all.title: Banking disruption resolved after thousands report access issues
all.abstract: JPMorgan Chase has resolved a “technical issue” that caused transactions to take longer than usual to complete for much of Monday. A spokesperson for the nation’s largest bank confirmed to Bloomberg that transactions were processing normally by Monday evening, after JPMorgan customers reported an uptick in errors accessing the bank’s services. The spike began roughly around 10 a.m. Eastern time Monday, according to Downdetector . Service disruption appeared to multiply around noon and reach a peak of nearly 4,700 reported errors at 2 p.m., the website indicated. But disruption wasn’t contained to JPMorgan. Customers of Bank of America , Wells Fargo , U.S. Bank – and, to a lesser degree, PNC , Capital One and Truist – also reported errors, generally cresting between 2 and 3 p.m. Monday, according to Downdetector. “JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related,” the bank posted on X at roughly 3 p.m. Monday. “Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue. Customers still have access to their accounts and funds.” One commonality among the seven biggest banks experiencing an uptick in service disruption Monday is that they’re all co-owners of Zelle, the peer-to-peer payment platform. all.title: Building trust in an AI-driven banking landscape
all.abstract: As people turn to AI for money guidance, institutions can keep those conversations grounded in trusted relationships. Josh DeTar discusses building useful AI with accuracy, transparency and human judgment. Trust has always been fundamental to banking. Why does it feel especially consequential for banks and credit unions today? TD Bank found 55% of Americans had used AI to manage finances, up from 10% a year earlier, though only 18% trust AI to recommend on its own. OpenAI says more than 200 million people ask ChatGPT money questions monthly. Institutions already hold the data and trust people want. Ceding that conversation to AI Assistants can cost them business and erode public perception over time. Credit unions have long differentiated themselves through relationships and community. How can institutions preserve that advantage as more member interactions move into digital channels? AI could leave a credit union holding the deposit while another service holds the relationship. Local trust matters: 35% cite community involvement as a reason to switch institutions, RivalMind found. But even though locality matters, convenience often wins. But if you pair community connection with AI-enabled tools that make everyday tasks easy, you've got a winning combination. As AI becomes part of how consumers seek advice, make decisions and manage their money, how might it change the relationship between a financial institution and the people it serves? all.title: CSI arms community lenders for commercial banking fight
all.abstract: Recent acquisitions that core provider CSI has made are aimed at helping its community bank clients better compete in commercial banking, where they’re facing more pressure, the company’s CEO said. “Bigger banks are coming into some of the smaller communities, for sure, going after small business, which is part of our message to the banks: they also have to be aggressive about leveraging the technology,” said Nancy Langer, CSI’s president and CEO, said during an interview at last month’s Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. “All of our banks, they get it,” she said. CSI, which competes with larger rivals Fiserv, FIS and Jack Henry, provides financial software and technology for community banks. The Paducah, Kentucky-based company’s customer base ranges from de novos to banks with about $20 billion in assets, Langer said. Serving commercial banking needs is essential for community banks to remain competitive with regional and super-regional lenders, who are racing to serve small businesses . And commercial business is a top driver of margin and growth for small banks, Langer said. Nancy Langer Permission granted by CSI Local lenders will always get commercial real estate loans but may not be able to retain deposits, especially as a business grows, she said. all.title: The MoneyPot Live: Your AI Is Ready. Is Your Data? What Financial Services Needs to Get Right
all.abstract: Recorded live at Money2020 USA, host Dhanum Nursigadoo sits down with Chad Primakow, AI and Data Leader at Everpure, to unpack what it really takes for banks and fintechs to move AI from pilot projects into trusted, real-world production. Drawing on his experience in financial services and data management, Chad breaks down why so many financial institutions underestimate their data challenges, from dark data and data rot to not having a clear picture of what data they have. The conversation covers: -Why more data isn’t always better, and what a sweetener in coffee has to do with it -Why AI pilots fail to scale, and the warning sign most teams miss -How AI agents change the risk equation, and what an agent won’t do unless you tell it to Ready to see where your own organization stands? all.abstract: The MoneyPot heads to Riyadh for Money20/20 Middle East, where host Scarlett Sieber, Money20/20's Global Chief Strategy and Growth Officer, sits down with Oliver Hughes, Head of International at TBC Bank Group. Oliver's career reads like a tour through some of the world's most dynamic and often overlooked markets, from a decade at Visa to fifteen years building Tinkoff from the ground up as the original fintech, and now to TBC, where he is spearheading the bank's bold expansion into new geographies. In this conversation, Oliver unpacks the leadership lessons that shaped him, the power of extreme customer centricity paired with deep analytics, and why having mathematicians on a finance team is non negotiable for building a true data driven organization. The discussion dives into TBC's entry into Uzbekistan, a greenfield banking build with its own tech stack and license, and the strategic logic behind TBC's majority stake acquisition in OLX Uzbekistan, a move that signals how digital banks are expanding beyond core financial services into adjacent ecosystems. Oliver also shares how TBC is deploying AI, including its own speech tech stack and conversational assistant Lola, across efficiency, revenue generation, and customer experience use cases, and offers a grounded, hype free take on where financial services are really heading over the next few years. all.title: Finovate Awards finalist VantageScore: Their mission to provide accurate credit scoring for everyone
all.abstract: In this episode of the Finovate podcast, host Greg Palmer sits down with Rikard Bandebo, Chief Strategy Officer and Chief Economist at VantageScore, a finalist in this year's Finovate Awards financial inclusion category. VantageScore, now 20 years old and originally founded as a joint venture between the three major credit bureaus in 2006, has grown into the most used credit score in the United States. The conversation opens with a broader look at the state of consumer credit health, where Rikard shares encouraging news: delinquency rates, which had been climbing steadily since January 2022 in the wake of pandemic-era stimulus and forbearance programs, have finally stabilized and in some cases are beginning to decline across all credit tiers. He attributes this shift to households acclimating to higher prices and borrowing costs, along with a boost from outsized tax refunds earlier in the year that appears to have had lasting positive effects. The discussion then turns to what sets VantageScore apart from legacy credit scoring models. Rikard explains that VantageScore 4, the most widely used version and now accepted in the mortgage industry, leverages 400% more data than legacy mortgage scores by incorporating rent and utility payment history, 24 months of trended credit behavior rather than a single snapshot, and consumer permissioned open banking data through VantageScore 4+. all.title: FinovateFall Best of Show winner Neural Payments on bringing payments to the masses
all.abstract: Host Greg Palmer wraps up our series spotlighting the FinovateFall 2026 Best of Show winners with a conversation featuring Mick Oppy, founder and CEO of Neural Payments. Drawing on over a decade of payments experience, including leading issuing product for a large US processor, Mick explains why he started Neural Payments: to close the gap between the pace of change in the industry and the ability of banks and credit unions to keep up. The company's mission is to bring payments to the masses in a way that works smoothly for both consumers and the back office teams who support them. At the heart of Neural Payments is its “any to any” payment capability, letting users send money to anyone, anywhere, instantly, without worrying about which payment rail is used behind the scenes. The experience is embedded directly into a financial institution's existing mobile banking app, so there is no new wallet or separate registration required. all.title: “Generate” the Future of Work Through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
institutions: University of Science and Technology of China
all.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping online labor markets in ways that go beyond simple job displacement. Using evidence from a leading freelance platform around the release of ChatGPT, this study shows that demand falls sharply in markets whose tasks closely match large language model capabilities. Labor supply also declines, but less than demand, leaving remaining freelancers to compete more intensely for fewer jobs. The study also identifies an important adaptive response: Some freelancers shift toward programming-intensive work as generative AI lowers the human-capital barrier to coding. These transitions are not evenly distributed. Higher-skilled freelancers are more likely to make the shift and to preserve or improve their earning efficiency, whereas less-skilled workers face greater risk of being left behind. The findings suggest that platforms and policymakers should treat AI not only as an automation shock but also as a force that redirects labor supply. Effective responses include real-time information about changing demand, targeted reskilling support, and training that builds workers’ capacity to learn and use new AI tools strategically.

all.title: Screening, Investment Incentives, and the Welfare Trade-Offs of Privacy
institutions: École Supérieure des Sciences Économiques et Commerciales
all.abstract: This paper studies how information disclosure affects investment incentives and contracting efficiency. We analyze a class of principal-agent models in which information helps the principal screen the agent but also facilitates surplus appropriation, thereby weakening the agent’s incentive to invest before contracting. Efficient privacy regimes balance these two forces. Along the frontier of efficient information policies, more privacy is associated with stronger investment incentives and higher agent payoff. We characterize conditions under which full privacy, full disclosure, or intermediate privacy is efficient. The results provide guidance for intellectual property and innovation policy by identifying when additional privacy fosters or hinders economic efficiency and innovation. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01507 .

all.title: Is low-carbon transition risk affecting the market and credit ratings equally? Evidence for European companies
institutions: Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia
all.abstract: This paper assesses the relationship between credit risk and different climate variables under a system of equations tested using seemingly unrelated regression. When considering both total emissions and Scope 1 emissions only, carbon intensity is found to be relevant to both the rating level credit risk and the market-implied distance-to-default. However, only the rating level credit risk has grown in importance since the Paris Agreement. With respect to mitigation variables, our findings indicate that the setting of emission targets is relevant in a similar way for both market and rating measures and that the Paris Agreement has had no impact. Furthermore, carbon pricing, a strategy that emerged after the Paris Agreement, was found to be significant for both market and rating agency measures. This finding suggests that markets and rating agencies do not value the same mitigation strategies more highly after the Paris Agreement, but they do value their greater definition and sophistication more highly. Overall, the results indicate that, after the Paris Agreement, rating agencies attribute greater importance to emissions in determining the distance-to-default, while the market assigns greater importance to carbon pricing strategies than the rating agencies do.

all.title: Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce
institutions: University of International Business and Economics
all.abstract: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

all.title: Gatekeepers and Kingmakers: Do Superplatforms Distort Digital Competition?
institutions: The University of Texas at Dallas
all.abstract: The rising dominance of superplatforms raises concerns about conflicts of interest and externalities on innovation, because they act as both marketplace gatekeepers and strategic investors. Studying Google’s dual role via Google Ventures (GV) and the Android marketplace, we find Google-backed startups receive 115% more reviews, 12% higher ratings, and 77% fewer bug complaints than their iOS counterparts—despite no major app updates. These gains are consistent with selective review removal and platform promotion. Using a difference-in-differences approach with iOS versions as controls, we isolate treatment from selection effects. Our findings challenge platform neutrality and highlight subtle mechanisms of competitive distortion. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The Online Appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03354 .

all.abstract: Hi, I’m Flavia, an Expert in Model Design and AI Risks at ING, with a background spanning academia and banking. I work at the intersection of responsible AI strategy, model design and risk methodologies, bringing scientific thinking and design thinking together to turn complex questions into practical solutions. I’m passionate about research and see it as a key enabler of thought leadership, advocacy and responsible innovation. My interests include emerging risks, methods and education. A key part of my work is translating complex regulatory and technical topics into practical methodologies, best-practice guidance and learnings tailored to different audiences, helping people better understand risks and their broader impact (ex. EU AI Act). Algorithmic transparency is a key element to build trustworthy classification models to support decision making . But what happens when people change their behaviour in response to transparent systems ? When people understand how a classification system works, for example, they may adapt their actions and learn from others in their network. Our research shows that these behavioural responses can influence accuracy, fairness, and operational costs. all.title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
all.abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Evidence from firms’ biodiversity dependencies suggests that physical biodiversity risks are also priced in the bond market. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07660 .

all.title: Sample Range as Subjective Variability and Implications for Experience-Based Decision Making
all.abstract: Variance and standard deviation are common metrics of statistical variability in the management and decision-making literature. In everyday contexts, however, information about sample range prevails. Range is arguably easier to comprehend and compute than variance, yet it often yields equivalent judgments about variability. Hence, we reason that decision makers often rely on range to judge variability. We test this hypothesis across four behavioral experiments (total n = 1,093). When comparing the variability of two number sets, decision makers predominantly based their judgments on sample range rather than sample variance when the two metrics disagree (experiment 1). Sample range tends to increase with sample size, whereas sample variance does not. Consistent with the range as variability hypothesis, decision makers perceived distributions as more variable after observing larger samples (experiment 2). This perceived variability, in turn, influenced risky decisions, as larger sample sizes led to decreased valuations of uncertain rewards for risk-averse decision makers (experiment 3). In further support of the hypothesis, when asked to mentally simulate new samples from a previously experienced distribution, participants generated more numbers within the observed range and fewer numbers outside of it than the true distribution implies (experiment 4). To model the data, we propose a “cognitive fence” idea as a potential psychological explanation for how experience shapes subjective variability. We conclude by discussing implications for research on overconfidence, distributional learning, risk perception, and communication. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05050 .

all.title: Proximity-Based Delivery Policies: Efficiency, Coverage, and Fairness
all.abstract: The growing demand for rapid food and grocery delivery has prompted many restaurants and retailers to develop their own on-demand delivery services. Although hiring additional couriers can expand delivery capacity, it is often prohibitively costly. As a cost-effective alternative, we propose a proximity-based delivery (PBD) policy that prioritizes the delivery of orders from customers located closer to the vendor, in contrast to the traditional first-come-first-served (FCFS) approach. We show that PBD can substantially reduce average delivery delays without requiring additional couriers; however, it may raise fairness concerns, because distant customers experience longer wait times, potentially shrinking market coverage and exacerbating service disparities. To address this issue, we introduce an incentive-compatible PBD (IP) policy, where nearby customers are incentivized to pay for priority, whereas distant customers receive compensation to offset longer delays. We demonstrate that this mechanism can restore fairness to levels comparable to FCFS while preserving efficiency, expanding market demand, and enhancing consumer surplus, particularly in moderately dense markets with moderately delay-sensitive customers. We further show that vendors can enhance these benefits through optimal pricing and benefit from less extreme staffing adjustments due to a “pull-to-center” effect. Our findings highlight the operational, economic, and ethical dimensions of proximity-based delivery, and offer a practical framework for balancing speed, profitability, consumer welfare, and equity. Finally, we conduct a mini case study using empirical data to demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Funding: Z. Wang acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72322017]. Y. Li acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72132007]. Q. Zhang acknowledges support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 724B2024]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02206 .

all.title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
all.abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08298 .

all.title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
institutions: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
all.abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06826 .

all.title: Determinants of Norm Compliance: Moral Similarity and Group Identification
all.abstract: What determines whether someone complies with a social norm? The social identity approach offers a mechanism for norm compliance: A person who feels similar to a group identifies more with that group and, in turn, complies with the group’s norms. Using an experiment, we test whether similarity in values increases identification and adherence to a group rule. To do so, we varied the similarity/dissimilarity between the values of an individual and members of a social group and measured group identification and rule compliance. We find that moral similarity in progressivism increases group identification, and group identification can increase compliance with rules from the social group. However, our results also suggest that this relationship can be disrupted. Because of our design and empirically verified in our study, social norms do not differ between treatments. As a consequence, observed behavior changes are attributable to increased group norm sensitivity and not changes in group norms. We advance the study of social identity by testing a causal pathway between group identification, group norm sensitivity, and behavior change. Our contribution to the management literature is to extend the empirical rationale, and cautionary notes, for investing in value-alignment between individuals and organizations. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors thank the Max Planck Institute for Research on Collective Goods and the University of Michigan School of Information for financial support. They also gratefully acknowledge support from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under Germany’s Excellence Strategy (EXC 2126/2 – 390838866), and from the Center for Social and Economic Behavior at the University of Cologne. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08000 .

all.title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
all.abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01302 .

all.title: Campaigns That Click: Unleashing the Power of Push Notifications on Mobile Apps
all.abstract: Push notifications can do more than promote a single merchant: They can redirect attention across an entire mobile marketplace. Drawing on more than 200 campaigns, 60 million user-campaign observations, and two controlled experiments, this study shows that notifications substantially increase same-day engagement with advertised merchants while also generating meaningful spillovers to other merchants within and across categories. Effectiveness varies by merchant, user, message design, and delivery timing. Notifications tend to work especially well for less prominent merchants, newer users, Android users, deeper discounts, urgency cues, and carefully timed delivery. However, repeated exposure produces diminishing returns and can eventually reduce engagement as annoyance and attentional overload increase. For platform managers, the findings support managing notifications as a portfolio rather than evaluating campaigns in isolation: targeting, message design, timing, cross-merchant benefits, and cumulative frequency should be optimized jointly. Platforms should also incorporate spillover value into campaign pricing, performance reporting, and merchant communication. For policymakers and platform-governance leaders, the results underscore the importance of meaningful consent, frequency controls, and transparent notification practices that protect user attention while preserving the economic benefits of timely, relevant mobile communication.

all.title: Effortful vs. Opportunistic Consumption of Discretionary Time: How Time-Reporting Decisions Influence Extra-Role Effort
all.abstract: Employees often work under incomplete contracts, performing both contracted in-role tasks and valuable but noncontracted extra-role activities. Once employees have completed in-role tasks, discretionary time remains, which they may allocate to extra-role activities or consume opportunistically. This study examines how managers’ time-reporting decisions, as a less intrusive form of control, affect subordinates’ effort-allocation decisions. I propose two opposing predictions. First, managers’ control implementations may signal distrust, resulting in more opportunism and thus less extra-role effort. Second, I identify value signaling as a novel theoretical mechanism through which time-reporting decisions may increase extra-role effort. The main experiment manipulated two factors: the type of time report (aggregated versus disaggregated) and its implementation source (managerial choice versus random assignment) to isolate signaling effects from monitoring effects. Results reveal that when managers choose not to implement disaggregated time reporting—that is, reports that make discretionary time salient—subordinates significantly reduce their extra-role effort. Structural equation modeling shows that value signaling outweighs distrust signaling in driving employees’ effort-allocation decisions. In contrast, when the time-reporting format is randomly assigned, effort remains unchanged, underscoring the signaling role of managerial choice. An additional online experiment shows directionally consistent results with the main experiment. These findings reveal a hidden cost of not controlling and contribute to the literature on incomplete contracts, slack resources, and input-based controls in modern work contexts. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding: This work was supported by the Bijzonder Onderzoeksfonds UGent [Grant BOF/STA/202009/047]. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00955 .

all.title: Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
all.abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In all cases, the whiplash effect persists, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our findings. Finally, we use the prediction from our theoretical model as a feature and apply machine learning techniques to predict the time that vessels spend in Shanghai Port after a typhoon disruption and show that using the predictor derived from our theoretical model, alongside all relevant vessel and voyage attributes as raw features, significantly reduces prediction errors by roughly 10%–30% on average compared with not using it. This paper was accepted by Elena Katok, operations management. Funding: This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada [Grant RGPIN-2021-04295]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05427 .

all.title: Connectors and Influencers
institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique
Groupe d'Analyse et de Théorie Economique Lyon St Etienne
all.abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by H2020 Future and Emerging Technologies [IBSEN Contract 662725]; the Keynes Fund, University of Cambridge; and the Creative-Pioneering Researchers Program, Seoul National University. S. Goyal acknowledges financial support from the Center of Behavioural Institutional Design and Tamkeen [New York University Abu Dhabi Research Institute Award CG005]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07308 .

all.title: Online Review Generation in the Digital Age: A Meta-Analytic Study of Online Review Behavior
all.abstract: A large body of literature on online review generation has investigated various antecedents to online review characteristics. However, the mixed and even contradictory findings in this domain have hampered a clear understanding of consumers’ online review behavior for both researchers and practitioners, thereby complicating actionable strategies. To address this issue, we conduct a comprehensive meta-analysis of 154 independent samples from 152 empirical papers, synthesizing the relationships between 28 antecedent factors and 12 review features, which we categorize into rating-based (evaluative) and non-rating (expressive) dimensions. Our results indicate that rating attributes are dominantly driven by stable reviewer tendencies and market-level reputation cues, whereas non-rating features—such as text length and image inclusion—are primarily influenced by reviewer social embeddedness and platform engagement. Crucially, we identify that inconsistencies in prior literature can be explained by critical boundary conditions, including platform type (business-hosted vs. third-party), goods type (service vs. tangible), and cultural background (Asia vs. North America). By distinguishing between evaluative and expressive review components, our study reconciles mixed findings and uncovers underlying mechanisms such as expectation-based evaluation and self-presentation. The findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for empirical model specification and offer actionable insights for retailers and platforms to optimize reputation management and system design. Ultimately, our work offers a holistic framework for understanding online review behavior and proposes a rich agenda for future research in the digital marketplace.

all.title: Dicas para comprar com segurança na Black Friday
all.abstract: A Black Friday é um dos momentos mais aguardados por quem deseja economizar nas compras ou aproveitar descontos. Mas o volume de tentativas de golpes aplicados por criminosos poderá também aumentar nessa época do ano. ​ ​ Para isso, eles usam frequentemente a engenharia social, técnica que consiste em manipular o consumidor a fim de obter informações sensíveis, transferências de valores ou dados bancários. ​ É por isso que, mesmo com a empolgação, vale redobrar os cuidados nas compras online ou em lojas físicas. Se a oferta tem preços irreais ou há pressão para fechar negócio imediatamente, pare, pense e desconfie. A urgência pode te prejudicar nessas horas. ​ ​ Quem traz as dicas para você se proteger ao fazer compras é o Raphael Mielle, diretor de Serviços e Segurança da Febraban. ​ #Febraban #BlackFriday #Economia ​ ​
