all.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
all.abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09021 .

all.title: Carbon home bias
all.abstract: We undertake a global analysis of institutional investor portfolios and find widespread underweighting of companies with higher carbon emissions, both in levels and intensities. This underweighting is largely driven by foreign companies with high carbon emissions, both at the intensive (tilting) and extensive (exclusion) margins. Domestic firms with high emissions are overweighted but by a smaller magnitude. These results reveal a bias for domestic companies with high carbon emissions. The carbon home bias is stronger in settings where institutions have tighter business connections, in countries with weaker social norms regarding climate crisis, and where the political environment is more polarized.

all.title: Climate Risk Disclosure and Risk Sharing in Financial Markets
all.abstract: In this paper, I model how climate risk disclosure impacts climate risk sharing among investors. I show that this disclosure can improve risk sharing by helping investors identify stocks that effectively hedge climate risk, and I analyze the disclosure’s impact on investors’ equilibrium portfolio choices. I then study firms’ voluntary disclosure incentives and analyze when disclosure mandates enhance risk sharing. Finally, I demonstrate that, by facilitating risk sharing, climate risk disclosure reduces the climate risk premium among stocks held by climate-focused investors. Hence, disclosure can lower the valuations of firms with low climate exposures and the overall market. (JEL: D82, D84, G12, G14)

all.title: Widely Used Measures of Overconfidence Are Confounded with Ability
all.abstract: Measures of overconfidence are used both to assess biases in people’s beliefs regarding their own abilities and to identify correlates of those biases. Proposed correlates of overconfidence include narcissism, social status, (low) task anxiety, savings, planning, and many more. Research on these correlates typically explicitly or implicitly claims that the associations with overconfidence are not attributable to ability (i.e., latent inputs enabling successful task performance, including inputs that vary across people, states, or contexts). I argue that several typical approaches used to measure overconfidence are not sufficient to support such claims. This argument follows from two underappreciated properties of these measures of overconfidence. First, performance is an imperfect measure of ability: accounting for performance does not sufficiently account for ability. Second, self-evaluations of performance should reflect ability in addition to performance: because performance is ambiguous, people should incorporate prior beliefs about their ability. These properties imply that multiple commonly used measures of overconfidence are confounded with ability. I support these analytical results by reexamining previously published findings. In the first analysis, I find that overconfidence predicts subsequent performance, consistent with measures of overconfidence serving as a signal of ability. In the second set of analyses, I find that some purported associations between overconfidence and other constructs could be attributed to ability instead. I close with recommendations to recognize and reduce the potential for mistaken inferences. When research indicates that differences in overconfidence are associated with other behaviors, beliefs, or evaluations, researchers should account for the possibility that differences in ability could provide a sufficient explanation. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by the UCLA Anderson Morrison Center for Marketing and Data Analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05184 and https://researchbox.org/1597 .

all.title: The Horizon of Investors’ Information and Corporate Investment
all.abstract: The quality of investors’ information across different horizons has real effects. When managers care about the effect of investment on their stock price, a decline in the informativeness of investors’ signals about long-term cash flows leads firms with long-term projects to cut investment more than firms with short-term projects. Using a novel, hand-collected measure of project horizons, we confirm this hypothesis: relative to firms with short-term projects, the investment of firms with long-term projects decreases by 3.7% following a 1-standard-deviation drop in the quality of investors’ long-term information. This effect becomes larger when managers prioritize current stock prices. (JEL D84, G14, G17, M41).

all.title: The Financial Economics of Spaceflight
all.venue: The Review of Corporate Finance Studies
all.abstract: We present a financial economics analysis of the global Space Economy, which has surged in value and scale since 4Q2024. The combined market valuation of private and publicly traded space companies now exceeds $4.0 trillion after SpaceX’s $75 billion June 2026 IPO. Space companies made 2025 capital investments totaling $25.7 billion, despite revenues of only $87.9 billion and net losses of $20.1 billion. Commercial products and services represent three-fourths of space economy revenues, while government orders account for one-fourth. We categorize the space economy along an entrepreneurial spectrum. Massive recent declines in launch costs have transformed demand for space services. (JEL H5, L1, O3, O32, O38)

all.title: Modeling the Future of Finance: Digital Transformation, Fintech Innovations, Market Adaptation, and Strategic Growth
all.venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
all.abstract: The financial industry is undergoing a profound transformation driven by rapid advancements in digital technologies, fintech innovations, and evolving market dynamics. This paper explores the critical role of digital transformation in reshaping financial services, emphasizing the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, big data analytics, and cloud computing to enhance efficiency, security, and customer experience. Fintech innovations have disrupted traditional banking models, enabling digital payments, decentralized finance (DeFi), roboadvisors, and open banking, fostering financial inclusion and accessibility. Market adaptation remains a crucial aspect of this evolution, as financial institutions must navigate regulatory challenges, cybersecurity threats, and shifting consumer expectations. This study examines the impact of digital disruption on traditional financial frameworks, highlighting the adoption of agile methodologies, risk management strategies, and regulatory compliance to ensure stability and resilience in a rapidly changing landscape. Additionally, the rise of embedded finance and digital currencies is reshaping transactional ecosystems, prompting financial institutions to innovate and collaborate with technology providers to sustain competitive advantage. Strategic growth in the digital finance era requires a data-driven approach, leveraging predictive analytics and machine learning to optimize investment decisions, enhance fraud detection, and personalize financial services. The paper presents a framework for financial organizations to embrace digital transformation by integrating emerging technologies with sustainable business models. Furthermore, it discusses the role of financial literacy and digital accessibility in fostering inclusive economic growth, ensuring that technological advancements benefit diverse populations. By synthesizing insights from case studies, market trends, and regulatory developments, this research provides a comprehensive outlook on the future of finance, highlighting opportunities for stakeholders to capitalize on technological advancements while mitigating associated risks. The study underscores the need for a collaborative approach among financial institutions, regulators, and technology firms to create a secure, efficient, and customer-centric financial ecosystem. The findings offer valuable implications for policymakers, industry leaders, and researchers seeking to understand and shape the trajectory of digital finance in the coming decades.

all.title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
all.abstract: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.

all.title: Gating the Internet
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: More than half of the traffic on the internet now comes from machines, and the share grows every year. The gates that decide which machines get through can tell which company runs an agent, and that is all they can tell. They can't say whether the agent is cleared to fill out a form, move money, or act without a person watching, and they can't see how it has behaved before. So every website makes its own trust decision alone, with almost no information, and the agents that want to wreck things get the same answer as the agents that want to help. This paper argues that no AI agent should act online without a certificate being checked, and that the check should happen at the places every agent already passes through: the model APIs that give agents their brains, the content delivery networks in front of most websites, the browsers and operating systems that agents act through, the protocol that signs their requests, and the payment rails. A certificate, in the sense that Licensed to Act lays out, says what an agent is cleared to do and how it has behaved. An agent without one can read the web, but it can't act on it. An agent with one acts within its scope, and an agent whose record stays clean earns room to act on its own. The whole method rests on one principle: misalignment has to cost more than alignment, everywhere and at every moment, and the gates are where that price gets charged. Gating the whole internet can happen without anyone being in charge, because it has happened twice before, when email adopted sender authentication and the web went encrypted. The paper also faces what gating can't do: it won't stop a well-funded attacker on its own, it depends on telling people from agents, and it hands real power to whoever runs the gates. It argues the answer is an open standard, many certifiers, and a floor that nobody falls below. Humanity Systems working paper. Part of a series on one question: how do we trust AI, now and into the future?

all.title: GuardRail: Runtime Action Authorization and Behavioral Safety for Agentic AI Systems
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: LLM agents no longer only produce text: they call APIs, query databases, send messages, and initiate payments. The safety mechanisms deployed around them, however, still operate mainly on text. They screen the prompt going in and the response coming out, while the agent's plan, the ordered sequence of tool calls it is about to execute, runs unchecked. That gap is exploitable: instructions planted in a web page, email, or tool result can steer the plan toward actions the user never intended, and an agent can alter an action after it has been approved. We present GuardRail, a runtime action-authorization and behavioral safety layer that sits between an agent and its tools and decides, before execution, whether each proposed action may run. GuardRail combines (i) a plan validation gate that checks every action against a trusted agent registry and four deterministic policy checks, issuing APPROVE, APPROVE_WITH_CONDITIONS, ESCALATE_TO_HUMAN, or BLOCK; (ii) a semantic risk-analysis layer whose signals can raise caution but can never override a deterministic refusal; (iii) forward taint tracking over multi-step plans, with detectors for seven multi-step attack chains; (iv) an Action Passport that binds an approval to the SHA-256 hash of the exact action, re-verified at an execution gateway so a substituted action cannot execute; and (v) a tamper-evident, SHA-256 hash-chained audit log of every decision. GuardRail was built for Infosys Ignite EngNext 2026 (Problem ET-03), where it received Special Recognition, and its enforcement core was later released as the open-source package guardrail-middleware. We describe the system and a red-team benchmark of 42 adversarial scenarios across 8 attack classes, including 5 benign controls. We report the benchmark's design, protocol, and the outcomes documented during development. We do not report a headline detection rate: the project artefacts record no standardised quantitative run. The necessary next step is measurement on public benchmarks.

all.title: Navital Gym: Rule-Graded Agent Environments for Indian Workflows
all.abstract: AI agents are being deployed on Indian workflows such as payments, tax, forms, travel and customer support in Hindi and Hinglish. Public agent evaluations rarely cover these workflows, and many score with another language model. We present Navital Gym, a set of six open environments with 321 public tasks in five task families: trip planning, UPI payments and disputes, GST invoicing and returns, form filling (including a multi-document split) and customer support in Hindi, Hinglish and three experimental Indian languages. Every task is graded by named, deterministic rules that recompute the outcome from a synthetic sandbox world. No language model judges any score. We report one run per task for three models on all six environments, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and for Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite on two (UPI and the Support core). Opus solves 315 of 321 tasks, Sonnet 302 and Haiku 205. Trip planning and Hindi/Hinglish support separate the models most. We also describe a private held-out set that is not published, and a 7B adapter trained in the gym. Code is Apache-2.0 and task data is CC BY 4.0. The rules are a documented simplification of Indian practice, not the live systems.

all.title: Evaluation of Fintech Solutions for Secure Digital Transactions via Complex q-Rung Orthopair Fuzzy Dombi MABAC Approach
all.abstract: In the era of rapid digitalization, fintech solutions have transformed the way financial transactions are conducted, offering speed, convenience, and global accessibility. However, ensuring the security of digital transactions remains a critical challenge due to the increasing sophistication of cyber threats. To address this concern, the present study proposes a novel decision-making framework for the classification of fintech solutions aimed at secure digital transactions. The framework integrates multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methodology with the multi-attributive border approximation area comparison (MABAC) technique under complex q-rung orthopair fuzzy sets (Cq-ROFSs). To enhance the robustness of the decision-making process, Dombi aggregation operators are employed to handle uncertainty and imprecise information in expert evaluations. The proposed approach systematically evaluates and ranks fintech alternatives based on multiple security-oriented criteria, including authentication, encryption, regulatory compliance, and fraud prevention. A numerical case study is conducted to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed framework, while a comparative analysis is performed to assess its effectiveness. This research contributes to the extension of fuzzy MCDM models by integrating Cq-ROFSs with Dombi aggregation operators. It also offers practical insights for policymakers, regulators, and financial institutions regarding the adoption of secure fintech technologies.

all.title: Structural Transformation in the Global South: Innovation and Enterprise as the New Engines of Development (Volume II)
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The assumptions that guided international development for seventy years no longer hold. Official development assistance fell by 23.1% in real terms in 2025, the largest drop on record, while low- and middle-income countries paid US$436 billion more in debt service than they received in new financing between 2022 and 2025. At the same time, automation is weakening the labor-intensive export ladder: a process-level model of garment factories shows that up to 58.4% of jobs could be displaced. This second volume argues that the new engines of structural transformation are indigenous innovation, digital public infrastructure (DPI), sovereign computing capacity and domestically anchored enterprise finance. It examines India's Unified Payments Interface and Open Network for Digital Commerce, and Brazil's Pix, which processed 79.6 billion transactions in 2025. It then reviews sovereign AI strategies across four archetypes, the 2025 recalibration of venture capital in Africa, Latin America, the Middle East and Southeast Asia, and the embedded-finance model of pay-as-you-go asset lending. Every statistic was checked against primary sources for this edition. The paper concludes with four policy priorities for governments, institutions and investors in the Global South.

all.title: Corporate Contributions to Ballot Measure Campaigns: Real Effects and Valuation
all.abstract: We analyze novel data on corporate contributions to ballot initiatives at the U.S. state level. Firms make large contributions to ballot measure campaigns in favor of or against specific initiatives. They contribute significantly more to business initiatives compared with ideological initiatives. Corporate campaign spending is systematically associated with the likelihood that a ballot measure passes. Contributing firms experience changes in sales growth following the passage of important ballot measures. Following successful (failed) initiatives, all firms in affected industries exhibit significantly more positive (negative) cumulative abnormal returns around the election, but contributing firms do more so than peers. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Fahlenbrach gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Swiss Finance Institute. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06801 .

all.title: Spatial Competition in Fast-Charging Networks
all.abstract: Despite the steady growth of fast-charging networks under government subsidies, the impact of spatial and ownership structures of charging points on pricing strategies of charging point operators (CPOs) and consumer welfare is poorly understood. Given EVs’ limited range, the competition in a fast-charging network is inherently regional. It is unclear whether and under what circumstances CPOs’ competition can lead to regional monopoly, which may hinder the transition to electric mobility. In this paper, we develop a novel framework to examine the competitive dynamics in fast-charging networks that serve regional demand, incorporating delay costs arising from congestion and locational attractiveness of charging stations. At the core of our framework is a spatial competition model, which characterizes the strategic interactions between CPOs and consumers. To overcome tractability issues associated with large networks that arise from real-world settings, we propose a computationally efficient method to optimize CPOs’ pricing decisions. We instantiate the framework in Germany’s Deutschlandnetz, whose awarded regional network comprises 900 charging stations. Using demand projections for 2030, we conduct a series of counterfactual simulations. Our analysis generates four sets of findings. First, price exhibits a strong negative correlation with the local competitiveness level (measured by the density of charging stations), but shows no clear dependence on absolute demand levels. Second, CPOs’ profits are shaped by both local competitiveness and absolute demand. Third, a uniform, stringent price cap may create inefficiencies in network utilization and discourage infrastructure investment, particularly in less lucrative regions. Finally, spatial and ownership constraints in tender rules may fail to ensure competitive outcomes in large-scale charging networks, allowing CPOs to strategically select locations that strengthen their market power ex post. Taken together, these findings suggest that policymakers should enable regionally equitable access to fast charging while ensuring efficient network utilization.

all.title: An Explainable Machine Learning Framework with Large Language Model Features for Predicting Monetary Redress in Bank Fraud and Scam Complaints
all.abstract: Liability for scam losses is shifting towards banks, yet few interpretable tools can anticipate which fraud and scam complaints will end in redress. This study develops SCAM-XD, an explainable framework that predicts whether a complaint to the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) flagged as possible fraud or a scam closes with monetary relief reported by the company. From the CFPB narratives archive, the study builds a benchmark of these complaints, about half of which human coders confirm as fraud or scams. A large language model (LLM) codes each narrative for scam type, payment rail, authorisation, manipulation cues and signals of the bank's response, agreeing closely with human coding on scam type. These features are combined with structured fields, company identity and text representations in a stacking ensemble, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and linked to a cost-sensitive triage layer. Tested on a later period, SCAM-XD improves significantly on strong baselines across seeds, including a reimplemented topic model approach. LLM features yield a compact, interpretable model that nearly matches a high-dimensional text baseline but do not significantly improve the full model. Company identity is the strongest driver of predicted redress, yet firm identity alone predicts far less well, and payment rail and bank response cues act in directions consistent with liability rules. Under assumed costs, thresholds selected on validation data substantially reduce modelled expected cost relative to standard thresholds, whereas model choice matters much less. Redress depends on both the firm and the facts that determine liability.

all.title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models
all.abstract: Linear probes are the cheapest LLM lie detectors but often fail to transfer across kinds of lie. Label-free directions from honest and deceptive role-play are untested at 70B scale and on lies about knowledge, where a lie and an honest denial can be identical. We widen a published persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they have, plus honest counterparts. At each model's middle layer the resulting persona direction ranks lies across Liars' Bench better than single-dataset probes on three of its four models; it fails on Qwen, even when Qwen stays in role far more often. On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct it beats directions from a random persona bank, but its gain over the published direction is within the range of random widenings. On lies about knowledge, persona directions mainly track a reply's wording: where lies and honest denials share their words, our three main contrasts stay inside the random-direction band on Llama and Qwen and reach only its edge on Gemma, though on Mistral one clears it. A knowledge direction contrasts questions the model can answer with ones nobody can, each followed by the same scripted denial. It separates lies from identical honest denials on two models and narrowly on a third, but not on the fourth; its other results partly depend on the benchmark's wording. On the Gender-Secret fine-tune it clears the band by a few hundredths on Llama and fails on Mistral. The sum of the two directions ranks lies better than a supervised probe at the same depth on all four models (on one, both near chance) but is level with the persona direction on Llama's average and behind that probe on held-out lies. More varied role-play questions do not help the persona direction on Liars' Bench.

all.title: Harnessing Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models for Automation and Smart Manufacturing in Production and Service Industries
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding and transforming the industrial and service industries. This is leading to a shift to automation and intelligent manufacturing. The 4.0 industry has established a digitally connected world where machines, human beings, and processes work harmoniously. AI and LLMs are crucial to this paradigm, and they can be used alongside automation technologies, robotics, and data-driven decisions to help organizations predict demand, optimize schedules, and minimize downtimes. LLMs augment the management of knowledge, create technical documentation, and provide a gap in communication between human operators and complex systems. They are applied to generative AI to assist in designing smart products, make the supply chain logistics more efficient, and provide real-time quality control with the help of computer vision and reinforcement learning. The AI-powered cobots and voice-based systems have empowered human employees in the workplace, building cooperative workplaces with safety and efficiency coexisting. These intelligent chatbots, voice assistants, and automated response systems will provide 24/7 customer service in high levels of personalization. LLMs are used in the healthcare sector in diagnostics, treatment planning, and patient record management, whereas AI predictive care and medical imaging are improved by AI. Financial services are beneficiaries of real-time fraud detection, compliance, and automated advisory systems, and as a result, smart ecosystems with distributed decision-making across cloud and edge platforms are formed, allowing them to be responsive in real time. However, large-scale applications come with their own set of big problems, including the risks of data security breaches, significant costs of implementation, worker retraining, and ethical concerns of autonomous factories, hyper-personalized service experiences, and energy-efficient production systems that would be consistent with sustainability efforts. The breakthroughs in quantum computing and edge AI are set to enhance the speed of decision-making processes whereas the human-centered AI design will make it more inclusive and trustworthy .

all.title: Generative AI in Financial Systems and Banking Forensics
all.abstract: The constantly rising technology adoption in the financial sectors has shown more dynamic patterns in their fraud activities, making them increasingly complex. Despite the presence of class imbalance in fraud detection scenarios in the real world, increasing label latency, the dynamics of fraud attack patterns, and the rise of sensitive data in financial data sets act as barriers for applying rule-based machine learning techniques in financial products for precise fraud detection. Generative Artificial Intelligence refers to a revolution in the analysis of financial fraud because it encompasses all the critical processes involved in legitimate as well as fraudulent financial operations. The use of representation learning and simulation of transactions achieved by generative models enables the prior detection of financial fraud. The use of generative AI is applicable in various financial security systems such as transaction risk evaluation, identification of payment fraud, analysis of anti-money laundering (AML), Know Your Customer (KYC) automation, identification of synthetic identities, and evolutionary patterns of financial fraud identification. The current chapter offers an in-depth analysis of the application of generative AI in financial systems and banking forensics. The use of generative techniques for behavioral simulations, aggressive fraud simulations, fraud analysis and simulations through graphs and time-series analysis, and finally, design and implementation issues and regulations in integrating generative AI in financial systems. The above topics and considerations put together create a comprehensive framework through which one can apply and understand the application of generative AI in the financial and banking system for fraud analysis and detection.

all.title: LLM Maintainer: A Judge-in-the-Loop Framework for Continuous Quality Monitoring and Regression Detection in Deployed Large Language Model Systems
all.abstract: Large language model (LLM) systems deployed in production are subject to a form of degradation that classical software is not: their behavior can change without a corresponding code change, because the underlying model, its provider-side weights, or the prompt scaffolding around it can shift independently of the application's own release cycle. Traditional regression testing, built around deterministic assertions, is poorly suited to this setting, because LLM outputs are open-ended, stochastic, and evaluated along dimensions –– tone, faithfulness, safety, format compliance –– that resist exact-match comparison. This paper presents LLM Maintainer, an open-source tool that treats a second LLM call as a judge, scoring a fixed suite of "golden prompts" against natural-language rubrics on every run, persisting the results, and flagging statistically meaningful drops relative to a rolling per-test-case baseline. We describe the system's architecture –– a YAML-configured test suite, an execution runner, a structured LLM-as-judge module, a regression-detection algorithm, a SQLite persistence layer, and a Flask dashboard –– and its command-line and dashboard-triggered workflows for both ad hoc and scheduled (cron-style) use. Because this work was produced in a network-restricted sandbox without access to the live Anthropic API, we report a fully disclosed, seeded, synthetic case study rather than presenting simulated data as genuine field results: we ran the actual, unmodified runner, judge, regression-detection, and persistence code for 30 simulated daily evaluation cycles (180 evaluated prompt-response pairs) against a six-case suite modeling a retail-banking customer-support assistant, with three deliberately injected incidents –– a transient API failure, a silent quality regression introduced by a system-prompt refactor, and a one-off output-format violation. The tool's naive, fixed-threshold rolling-baseline detector recovered five of six injected anomalies (83.3% recall) but also raised 18 flags attributable to ordinary sampling variance in a five-point ordinal judge scale (21.7% precision, F1 = 0.345), a quantitative finding that motivates statistically smoothed alternatives. We situate this design relative to LLM-as-a-judge evaluation research, holistic benchmarking, documented behavioral drift in commercial LLMs, and concept-drift detection in classical machine learning operations, and we discuss the threats to validity inherent in judge-based scoring –– including self-preference and verbosity bias –– alongside concrete mitigations. We conclude that continuous, judge-in-the-loop regression testing is a necessary complement to pre-deployment benchmarking for maintaining LLM-integrated software, while cautioning that naive thresholding requires the same statistical care long established in the concept-drift literature.

all.title: Impact of Generative AI on Cybersecurity Risks, Phishing, and Digital Defense in the US
all.venue: Journal of Engineering and Computational Intelligence Review
all.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has reduced the expenses of creating natural, personalized and context-relevant content, thus challenging defenses based on the linguistic weaknesses of traditional phishing. This paper explores the effects of GenAI on cybersecurity risk and phishing and digital defense in the United States with a structured synthesis of 23 studies and a controlled detection experiment. The synthesis is structured around offensive and defensive applications of GenAI. The experiment evaluates six different detectors (keyword rules, word and character n-gram classifiers, header/URL metadata model, metadata-plus-intent model, and fused model) against traditional phishing, GenAI-style phishing, and GenAI phishing from compromised accounts. Pre-GenAI mail was trained on the detectors, which were then evaluated at a 0.5% false-positive rate, using five different seeds. GenAI-style messages did not include any misspellings or classic lure words and were lexically nearer to legitimate messages (median cosine similarity 0.22 compared to 0.13 for traditional phishing). None of them were detected by keyword rules and the word-level classifiers dropped from 1.0 on traditional phishing to 0.508. Metadata was effective in detecting 97% of GenAI phishing messages originating from attacker infrastructure, but just 3.6% of messages originating from compromised accounts. Adding 1,500 defender-generated examples of phishing using GenAI improved the results of fused-model recall from 0.149 to 0.790 on the compromised-account case with no corresponding increase in false positives. The results suggest that GenAI has transformed the phishing threat from content to identity and context; thus, U.S. organizations need to implement email authentication, defender-side generative augmentation and continuous retraining, and account-takeover controls.
