all.title: Generative AI Adoption and Employee Performance in Digital Finance and Marketing: The Mediating Role of Work Engagement and the Moderating Role of Technostress
all.abstract: The rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed organizational practices by providing new opportunities to improve employee productivity, work efficiency, and professional performance. This study examined the influence of Generative AI adoption on employee performance in digital finance and marketing organizations in Pakistan, focusing on the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technostress. A quantitative research approach and cross-sectional survey design were employed, and primary data were collected from 351 employees working in commercial banks, digital finance companies, FinTech institutions, digital banking departments, and digital marketing organizations across Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Islamabad Capital Territory through a self-administered questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. Convenience and purposive sampling techniques were used to select respondents, and the collected data were analyzed using SPSS, regression analysis, and Hayes' PROCESS Macro. The findings revealed that Generative AI adoption positively influenced employee performance, explaining 32.9% of its variance (R² = 0.329). Furthermore, work engagement partially mediated this relationship, with an indirect effect of 0.261, demonstrating that employees' active involvement and motivation at work contributed to improved performance through AI adoption. The moderation analysis indicated a negative interaction effect of technostress (β = -0.156), suggesting that excessive technological pressure weakened the positive relationship between Generative AI adoption and employee performance. These findings emphasize that technological integration alone may not ensure improved organizational outcomes unless employees are adequately supported in adapting to AI-based working environments. The study further highlights the importance of providing AI-related training, improving digital competencies, and developing supportive workplace policies to minimize technostress. From a theoretical perspective, the research contributes to understanding the combined influence of technological adoption and employee psychological factors on workplace performance. The findings offer practical guidance for commercial banks, FinTech institutions, and digital marketing organizations in developing employee-centered AI adoption strategies that promote work engagement, reduce technological stress, and strengthen overall organizational productivity.

all.title: Beyond The Classroom Walls: Generative AI and Big Data-Driven E-Learning Frameworks for Sustainable Madrasah Higher Education
all.venue: International Journal of Multidisciplinary and Innovative Research
all.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) reached Bangladeshi madrasah students before any policy did. Students in Fazil (bachelor's level) and Kamil (master's level) madrasahs, now affiliated to the Islamic Arabic University, can ask a chatbot to explain a hadith or draft a tafsir assignment, yet the answers may contain invented chains of narration or misattributed rulings, and their teachers have little guidance on assessment or data use. This conceptual paper asks how GenAI and learning analytics can be governed in madrasah higher education so that they widen access without weakening scholarly accuracy or the integrity of examinations. It builds on, and narrows, the authors' earlier work on AI-supported madrasah e-learning by focusing on the higher tiers and on generative tools specifically. The method combines a structured review of 2013 to 2026 literature, document analysis of UNESCO guidance on GenAI (2023) and its AI competency frameworks for teachers and students (2024), and secondary data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics and the World Bank. In 2025 Bangladesh had 1,085 Fazil and 273 Kamil madrasahs with 911,265 students in all sections, about 32% of post-primary madrasah enrolment, while only 53.4% of the population used the internet in 2024. The paper re-specifies a Four-Pillar Sustainable E-Learning Model (FPSELM) that links guided generative tutoring, learning analytics, source-verified content governance and inclusive access to objectives of Maqasid al-Shariah. It closes with staged recommendations for government, the university, madrasahs and OIC partners, and with testable propositions for pilots.

all.title: Whose appraisal? A Freire-informed, think-aloud study of allied health students’ use of Generative AI in evidence appraisal
all.abstract: Background Generative AI (GenAI) can now produce artefacts such as essays, literature reviews, and worked rationales which challenge assessment designs that reward the products of thinking over the practice of it (Bearman et al., 2024; Corbin et al., 2025; Dawson et al., 2024). In evidence-based practice (EBP) education, students are required to appraise study quality, interpret effect sizes, and integrate findings into clinical decisions (Lehane et al., 2019). GenAI can now generate convincing outputs for each of these tasks. Observational data on what students do cognitively when they use GenAI in EBP tasks are scarce. Depending on how students use it, GenAI may scaffold the reasoning that EBP education is designed to develop or may bypass it (Vendrell & Johnston, 2026). Aim This study explores how allied health students engage with GenAI, how much they rely on it, and how they reason about its use when completing an EBP evidence-appraisal task. Methods This is an exploratory qualitative study using a concurrent think-aloud protocol with allied health students who have completed an EBP unit. The unit must have included critical reasoning as a learning outcome. Participants complete a structured 60-minute EBP task involving a clinical scenario. During this task, participants verbalise their reasoning and rationale for using or declining GenAI. A researcher facilitates this process through non-directive questions. Sessions are audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed in two stages. In the first stage, transcripts are coded deductively and inductively against the six critical thinking processes in Vendrell and Johnston’s (2026) framework: conceptual interpretation, inferential reasoning, evaluative judgement, metacognitive regulation, intellectual curiosity, and epistemic integrity. This stage identifies whether and how reasoning is handed over to GenAI. In the second stage, an interpretive analysis informed by critical pedagogy (Freire, 2005) examines how students position themselves in relation to AI-generated knowledge. Freire described a banking model of education, in which an authority deposits knowledge into passive students. This model offers a lens for examining uncritical acceptance of GenAI output, should that be present (Freire, 2005). Freire located authority in the school system and in the teacher who deposits knowledge into students (Freire, 2005). GenAI is a further candidate for that position in higher education. Unlike a teacher or an institution, it is designed by companies whose incentive is engagement and commercial return rather than student learning (Bartsch et al., 2025). Findings Data collection is in progress. This study will generate think-aloud data on how allied health students engage cognitively with GenAI during EBP appraisal tasks, mapping where GenAI use aligns with or diverges from the reasoning processes EBP education is designed to develop. The interpretive analysis will explore the degrees of agency students exercise over AI-generated knowledge and the conditions in which they exercise or relinquish it, which process-level coding alone cannot capture. Conclusion Findings may inform teaching and assessment design in EBP units and provide a think-aloud protocol that can be adapted to examine GenAI use in reasoning tasks across health professions education.

all.title: Generative artificial intelligence-related concerns among medical students in the West Bank, Palestine: a cross-sectional study
all.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical education. However, concerns about its professional, ethical, and psychological implications for future physicians remain insufficiently studied, particularly in resource-constrained settings. This study assessed GenAI-related concerns among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, using the Fear, Anxiety, Mistrust, and Ethics (FAME) scale. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional online survey using convenience sampling via online recruitment was conducted among medical students at Palestinian universities between March and April 2026. Data were collected on sociodemographic and academic characteristics, prior GenAI tool use, self-reported level of AI concern, and FAME scores. Non-parametric tests and multiple linear regression were used for analysis. Results Of 399 participants included in the analysis, 96.0% reported using ChatGPT. The median total FAME score was 40 (IQR, 35–45). Median domain scores were highest for Mistrust and Ethics, both with a median score of 11, compared with Fear and Anxiety, both with a median score of 9. Male students had higher Fear and Anxiety scores than female students, but total FAME scores did not differ significantly by gender. In the exploratory adjusted regression model, no sociodemographic, academic, or AI-use variable was independently associated with the total FAME score, and the overall model explained only a small proportion of score variability. Conclusions GenAI use was widespread among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, with higher median scores observed in the mistrust and ethics domains than in fear of professional displacement. None of the variables included in the exploratory multivariable model was independently associated with total FAME score. Structured AI-literacy education addressing ethical reasoning and critical appraisal of AI-generated information may represent a potential educational implication of these findings.

all.title: AI-Assisted Regulatory Intelligence and Adaptive Compliance Verification System for Banking Supervision
all.abstract: Regulatory requirements issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) fall into categories including numerical thresholds, deterministic conditions, temporal obligations, and qualitative standards such as ''adequate due diligence,'' each of which requires a different mode of verification. Bank employees and officers must first locate and interpret the appropriate requirement among an ever-growing corpus of Master Directions, circulars, and notifications, while the regulator must independently verify (at scale) whether submitted bank evidence satisfies the requirement. We present a two-module regulatory intelligence system that addresses both sides of this problem in a single pipeline. The Regulation Comprehension module ingests an RBI circular or Master Direction and segments and categorizes its clauses, extracts a typed and machine-readable rule representation, simplifies regulatory language for reading by humans, and enables natural-language question answering with clause-level sourcing. The main technical contribution is an adaptive reasoning-modality router that determines, for a given regulatory requirement and evidence set, whether a deterministic rule engine, a retrieval-based large language model (LLM), or human escalation should be used, governed by an explicit cost--accuracy--latency objective and a hard architectural override that directs fully specified deterministic rules and complete evidence to the rule engine unconditionally. This differs from the well-studied task of routing between LLMs of differing capability, since our router chooses among fundamentally different reasoning mechanisms rather than among models. We also contribute a rule-grounded synthetic RBI compliance benchmark across nine difficulty categories and a dedicated regulation-comprehension benchmark design (with extraction, question-answering, and simplification variants), such that the two modules can be evaluated with equal rigor rather than treating comprehension as a subordinate preprocessing step, yielding two distinct sets of metrics, baselines, and ablation points, each for one of the modules, across extraction accuracy, retrieval and answer-faithfulness, simplification quality, compliance accuracy, and routing efficiency. We also contribute an evidence-grounded explanation architecture that traces every such decision and comprehension answer to a specific rule, clause, and evidentiary or source field. Since operational bank data cannot be accessed for confidentiality and regulatory reasons, evaluation is performed on a synthetic, rule-grounded benchmark of 1,393 cases drawn from 215 rules. On the 294 held-out test cases, whose rules were never seen in training or tuning, the adaptive router reaches 92.2\% automated accuracy and 96.9\% end-to-end accuracy, compared with 85.4\% for a fixed hybrid router, 72.5\% for retrieval-augmented LLM-only reasoning, and 56.8\% for LLM-only reasoning, and ablations show that removing adaptive routing, the rule engine, or evidence grounding lowers accuracy. Adversarial and ambiguous cases remain the hardest. All results are on synthetic rather than operational bank data, the decisions of the LLM reasoning paths in these runs were produced by a deterministic surrogate of the LLM judge, and results of the regulation-comprehension benchmark are not reported in this paper.

all.title: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure
all.abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in hiring pipelines is growing, yet existing evaluations generally overlook their compliance with legal rules. To fill this gap, we introduce HireWatch, an evaluation that assesses whether LLMs comply with U.S. laws that govern the questions that job candidates may be asked. We construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, whose legal classification is based on U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. We instruct LLMs to select questions from this bank in preparing for job interviews, across a set of various occupations and contexts, and report the fraction of unlawful questions that LLMs select. Evaluation of 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across ~100,000 trials under different types of contextual pressure reveals that LLMs' legal compliance is brittle. While LLMs generally avoid selecting unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher pressure. Explicit prompts to comply with law can improve compliance rates, but do not altogether eliminate legal violations. We publicly release our code and data at https://github.com/hnghiem-nlp/hirewatch_repo.

all.title: Agentic AI in Finance
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This working paper examines how agentic AI (systems that plan, call tools, retain state and act within defined constraints) is being applied across financial services, and what it takes to deploy it responsibly. Ten chapters cover the shift from generative to agentic AI; the building blocks of agentic systems (agent architectures, large language models and reasoning, tools, memory, orchestration and knowledge graphs); customer-facing agents in retail banking; fraud, compliance and risk management; investment management and capital markets; operations and back-office transformation; building, deploying and scaling agents; the regulatory landscape and ethical guardrails; case studies and lessons learned; and the outlook for the coming decade. The case studies include the authors' own prototypes: an agentic Monte Carlo Value-at-Risk simulator, a cross-jurisdiction regulatory comparison tool and a continuous policy gap-analysis loop. First drafted in 2025, the paper was reviewed and updated in November 2026. Statistics, case studies and statements about law and regulation were checked against current sources (position as of 13 November 2026), and external claims that could be traced are tied to a numbered list of 62 references. A Review and Update Note sets out what was corrected and added. Nothing in this paper is legal, regulatory or investment advice.

all.title: Bias-Aware and Hallucination-Resistant Financial AI for Credit Scoring
all.venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
all.abstract: Financial institutions are increasingly exploring Large Language Models (LLMs) for financial document analysis and credit assessment. However, hallucinated financial information and demographic bias can undermine the reliability and fairness of AI-assisted lending decisions. This study proposes an integrated framework for trustworthy financial AI that combines hallucination detection, bias mitigation, and fair credit-risk assessment. The framework uses an LLM to extract structured financial information from source documents, followed by an evidence-verification module that identifies unsupported claims through source matching, semantic verification, numerical consistency checks, and confidence assessment. Verified features are then processed by a separate credit-risk model, while a fairness module evaluates demographic and intersectional disparities in extracted information and credit predictions. The framework will be evaluated using public financial question-answering and credit-risk datasets, supplemented by controlled synthetic financial documents containing known factual and numerical errors. Experiments will examine hallucination detection performance, counterfactual demographic bias, credit-risk prediction quality, and the propagation of incorrect financial information into downstream credit decisions. Evaluation will use claim-level precision and recall, false acceptance rate, AUROC, Brier score, calibration, demographic parity, equal opportunity, equalized odds, and credit-decision flip rate. The study aims to determine whether integrating evidence-based verification and fairness controls can reduce the influence of unsupported financial information while maintaining predictive performance and improving the consistency of AI-assisted credit assessment. Keywords - Trustworthy Financial AI; Large Language Models; Hallucination Detection; Bias Mitigation; Fair Credit Scoring; Credit Risk Assessment; Evidence Verification; Algorithmic Fairness.

all.title: Towards Agentic Video Corpus Moment Retrieval
all.abstract: Video corpus moment retrieval (VCMR) requires finding the video and time interval that match a text query in a corpus of videos. We present RELAY, a training-free framework for VCMR that shares memory across queries. RELAY processes a batch of queries in three stages: search with a query bank, ranking with video notes, and localization with video prompt caching. In the search stage, an embedding model scores each video by its best-matching frame. The query bank penalizes videos that score highly for many other queries in the batch. In the ranking stage, a vision-language model (VLM) writes notes on each candidate video's scenes, people, objects, and actions once. Then, a large language model (LLM) reranks the candidates from these notes. In the localization stage, a VLM predicts the time interval of the moment in the top-ranked video. When multiple queries select the same video, prompt caching lets the VLM reuse its frames. On the three VERIFIED benchmarks, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in video retrieval R@1 without training. Without any labeled moment, its predicted intervals are shorter than the annotated ones. In VCMR, it achieves similar performance to VideoSearch-R1 on one benchmark and trails it at IoU 0.5 on the other two. Human annotators also mark shorter moments than the original annotations of the benchmarks. A single margin, calibrated on a few labeled queries, widens the predicted interval to the annotation convention of the benchmarks. With it, RELAY outperforms the trained baselines in VCMR at IoU 0.5.

all.title: Cross-Industry Case Studies and Applied Frameworks
all.abstract: This chapter specifies cross-industry case studies and generative AI-based methods that illustrate how the technology has completely changed fraud detection by linking theory with practice in various industries. Capital One and Swedbank, as examples of banks, make use of GANs to create synthetic transactions and consequently reduce fraud by half through real-time anomaly detection in their credit card transaction streams, as well as through KYC synthetic identity verification, further enabling risk scoring that is dynamic via integration with FinTech APIs. Insurance companies like Allianz employ VAEs for the simulation of rare claim frauds, and a 40% false positive rate reduction is attained by multimodal document forensics and federated learning that is compliant with HIPAA/GDPR. UnitedHealth in healthcare uses transformers for NLP, powered claim narrative scrutiny, and GAN-augmented datasets, increasing detection accuracy in billing scams to 35% while also ensuring privacy is maintained. Major e-commerce companies (Amazon, Shopify) are utilizing diffusion models to create behavioral profiles in retail scams that lead to account takeovers, which are then countered by multi-agent ensembles resulting in a total of 25% loss prevention. Cybersecurity companies such as Chainalysis are adopting graph-based GenAI for blockchain analytics, in which NFT scams and crypto laundering networks are traced using 90% traceability that is further improved by SOC integrations.

all.title: Metadata-Driven AI: An Architectural Pattern for Sustainable Data Analysis with LLMs
institutions: Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology
all.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) let users analyse data in natural language, either by giving the data to the model to read directly or by having the model generate code to process it. Both routes send the data, or fragments of it, to the model; both pay for inference on every run; and the code a model writes to answer a question is usually discarded once the question is answered. We present Metadata-Driven AI, an architectural pattern that keeps the data away from the model and turns each analysis into a reusable program. Only metadata (not the actual data) crosses a one-way inference boundary to the LLM. The program the LLM returns runs next to the data and is kept, so that inference is paid once per analysis rather than once per run. We describe the pattern together with a simple cost model, a measurement of how little information crosses the boundary on public datasets, and a benchmark showing that a small, locally hosted model can serve as the generator. We illustrate the pattern on three applications, each built on a different implementation of it: geospatial photovoltaic prospection over live public APIs, extraction of portfolio positions from bank statements, and a conversational assistant over smart-city dashboards.

all.title: Dressed in Authority: Practical Black-Box Jailbreaking of MLLMs via Visual Trust Bias
institutions: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
all.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly advancing, yet their safety remains a critical concern, especially under jailbreak attempts. Existing MLLM jailbreaks either inject fragile adversarial perturbations into irrelevant images or synthesize toxic visual cues to achieve text-driven attack intents. In contrast, a more practical MLLM jailbreak emphasizes enhancing attack efficacy directly on naturally occurring harmful image-text pairs. We address this problem by proposing Visual Trust Bias Attack (VTBA), a new jailbreak framework that exploits a previously overlooked attack surface: MLLMs exhibit an intrinsic trust bias toward authoritative visual features, which enables transferable and stealthy jailbreaks. VTBA constructs a bank of authoritative templates, matches each input pair to the most relevant one, and integrates the harmful intent into the selected layout, thereby leveraging credible visual cues to override safety refusals while preserving naturalness. We further construct a dataset of 2,500 naturally occurring image-text pairs to evaluate jailbreaks in this practical multimodal setting. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently achieves high attack success rates across strong MLLMs, revealing a severe and previously underexplored weakness in current multimodal safety alignment. Warning: This paper may contain sensitive content.

all.title: What Do LLMs Use to Judge Synthesis Recipes? An Experimental Analysis on 240 Solid-State Syntheses
all.abstract: Inorganic materials discovery is increasingly limited by synthesis rather than by material design. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted to propose synthesis conditions with little experimental evidence of their capabilities and biases. Here, we carry out an experimental synthesis benchmark of 240 experiments across eight known and unknown inorganic oxides and subsequently evaluate an LLM as a zero-shot ranker over fixed banks of solid-state synthesis recipes. For each pair of recipes for the same oxide target, `GPT-5.6-Sol` selects the recipe expected to yield higher target-phase purity. We aggregate these pairwise preferences using a regularized Bradley-Terry model to obtain a ranked list of synthesis recipes for a given target material. By comparison with the actual purity, obtained through X-ray diffraction, we measure `GPT-5.6-Sol`'s performance as a zero-shot ranker (0.72 pairwise accuracy). By selective removal of the information exposed to the model during this ranking, we conclude that ranking is driven predominantly by thermal features, with reaction chemistry modulating the effect. Ranking accuracy tracks the purity-temperature correlation by target (Spearman ρ= 0.91\), \(p = 0.002\), and on the six thermally-driven targets withholding all chemical identity hardly impacts performance (0.68) compared to withholding temperature (0.56). Ranking performance was higher on known than unknown targets, but the group-level difference was not statistically conclusive. The methodological choices highlight the need for more experimentally validated synthesis benchmarks and position LLMs as a thermally informed prior.

all.title: Transaction Monitoring That Survives Reconciliation
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This white paper sets out an engineering design for transaction monitoring in anti-money laundering (AML) programs, for U.S. banks and for fintech lending programs run with a sponsor bank. It starts from a public enforcement case. The U.S. Justice Department found that one bank left about 92% of its transaction volume unmonitored for more than six years. The paper argues that most monitoring failures happen before any model is involved: products that were never connected to monitoring, data that was never reconciled, alerts that can’t be rebuilt later, and testing that measures new models against filings the old system produced. This is done by Muoro's team. The design works in a fixed order. First, reconcile the data, so the institution can prove which transactions its controls checked. Second, run the scenarios regulators require in a protected lane, where no model can switch them off. Third, add machine learning in a separate lane to rank the optional alert queue and to find patterns the rules miss. Every alert keeps its source events, its known data gaps, and the logic that raised it, so an investigator or examiner can see what the system knew at the time the alert fired. The paper covers: mapping regulatory obligations to engineering requirements the difference between what a bank and a fintech lending program can each see a reference architecture and a typical tech stack a worked example in SQL: three loans repaid from one shared funding account, and how the picture changes when one of those payments is returned how to choose training labels, and why past suspicious activity reports (SARs) are not ground truth testing a new model in shadow mode, and comparing it with the current system at the same investigator capacity where generative AI can help investigators questions examiners and model risk committees will ask a phased rollout with acceptance criteria and rollback steps The worked example and the capacity comparison use synthetic, illustrative figures. This paper is not legal or regulatory advice.

all.title: Architecting & Engineering Production-Grade Agentic AI for Industry-Specific Needs
all.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly adopted across industries, yet each industry brings its own regulations, users, data and ways of working. A general-purpose chatbot built on a large language model cannot meet these needs on its own; the system around the model has to be designed for the industry it serves. This paper presents a cross-domain practitioner study of four Agentic AI systems that were architected, engineered and deployed by the Author and are presented together in Rimjhim AI Kingdom®, a navigable web ecosystem in which each system appears as a building in a virtual city. The systems serve banking, residential property, hotel review management and e-commerce customer service, and were developed in Python without the use of any no-code or low-code platforms. For each system, the paper traces how the needs of the industry shaped the architecture. Comparing the four systems, it identifies six customisation dimensions along which an AI architect adapts a shared agentic core: interaction mode, knowledge source, reasoning style, compliance layer, integrations and the boundary of automation. The paper argues that these decisions belong to the AI architect and engineer, and it draws design lessons for building industry-specific agentic systems.

all.title: 2026 Multi-Market U.S. Credit Union AI Search Visibility Study: Explicit Geo-Declared "Money-in-Motion" Prompts, Cross-Engine Disagreement, and Three-Metro Comparative Omission
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: EquiSchema AI Empirical Benchmark Report No. 2026-04 evaluates generative AI search visibility, Total Brand Omission, and cross-engine recommendation variance across 12 regional credit unions ($450M to $19B+ in assets) in two distinct U.S. economic corridors: Central Texas (Austin Metro) and the Mid-Atlantic Federal Corridor (Baltimore–Washington). Across 480 total evaluation slots (20 localized and multi-variable "Money-in-Motion" financial prompts tested across ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Perplexity, and Claude), regional credit unions suffered an 80.8% Total Brand Omission rate (19.2% aggregate visibility)—even when prompts explicitly declared the borrower’s residential city. Category-level audits revealed a 97.9% omission rate on High-Yield Savings and emergency fund deposit prompts (0.0% visibility on explicit $10,000 emergency fund queries) and a 97.9% primary omission rate on First-Time Homebuyer mortgages, where AI models routed borrowers to out-of-state digital banks, lead-generation aggregators, state housing finance programs, and private mortgage brokers. Cross-engine disagreement averaged 73.0% across all 20 benchmark prompts (peaking at 95.0% on state HELOC inquiries), with stark model-level divergence between Google Gemini (27.5% credit union visibility) and Claude (15.0%). Combining these 480 evaluations with our prior 1,800-evaluation Midwest baseline (Report No. 2026-03) and 2,160 commercial banking and sterile credit union evaluations (Reports No. 2026-01 and 2026-02) brings the EquiSchema AI empirical series to 4,440 total evaluations, demonstrating that unstructured HTML rate tables and legacy PDFs prevent frontier LLMs from verifying multi-variable financial product terms.

all.title: ContextFact: Remembering Facts in Context for Long-Term Conversational Agents
all.abstract: Agents built on large language models must maintain continuity across repeated interactions with users. However, long-term conversations scatter facts across turns and sessions, making it difficult to retrieve the right evidence with enough context. Memory for such conversations must therefore preserve facts with their context while keeping evidence selectively accessible. We first study how memory construction and retrieval-unit boundaries affect answerability and evidence access. Reading the entire memory bank reveals gaps that cannot be resolved by retrieval selection alone, showing that some context must be preserved during memory construction. Adjacent-turn grouping improves evidence access at matched unique-turn budgets, while wider windows do not consistently help. This motivates keeping fact-specific context local while organizing cross-session evidence separately. We propose ContextFact, which links context-preserving fact memories with source-grounded entity representations. Within sessions, it gathers the context needed to interpret each fact. Across sessions, it aligns recurring referents and revisits the source dialogue to reconstruct coherent entity representations linked to the supporting facts. At query time, ContextFact retrieves fact and entity views, reranks them independently, and uses entity-linked expansion to surface related facts; complete entity representations then provide organized cross-session evidence. With Qwen3.5-27B as the backbone, ContextFact achieves state-of-the-art performance while using only $21\%$ of the evidence tokens consumed by the strongest evaluated baseline, obtaining $86.49\%$ overall judge accuracy on LoCoMo and $91.00\%$ on LongMemEval-S. Controlled ablations support context-preserving fact boundaries and source-grounded entity reconstruction, while entity readout improves multi-hop accuracy beyond adding more facts.

all.title: JFinBench: A Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams
all.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to finance, creating a need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities across financial systems with different regulations and practices. However, existing financial benchmarks provide limited coverage of country-specific financial systems, and they are difficult to keep up to date as released questions leak into training data. We introduce JFinBench, a Japanese financial benchmark comprising 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six regularly administered certification exams covering accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking. To construct it, we develop a human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline in which a coding agent writes exam-specific conversion code and a review page, while a human verifies every example and feeds corrections back to the agent. This pipeline adapts to heterogeneous exam formats and reduces the effort of incorporating new exam editions, enabling periodic refreshes that mitigate data contamination. Evaluating 12 recent LLMs, we find that Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra exceed 93% overall, while even the best open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, trails Claude Fable 5 by 12 percentage points. When models can additionally use a terminal and web access, they retrieve the knowledge they lack and every model improves. The gap narrows but about 4 points remain, and the ranking of models stays largely the same, suggesting that knowledge held in the model itself remains valuable even with tools. We release the dataset, the evaluation code, and the construction pipeline.

all.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
all.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.

all.title: Adversarial prompt detection via contrastive dual-encoder transformer for zero-day jailbreak defense based on AdverSentinel-LLM model
all.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become core elements of current artificial intelligence applications yet are highly susceptible to adversarial prompt attacks such as jailbreaks that compromise safety alignment. Current defense mechanisms rely predominantly on fixed rule-based filters or single-encoder classifiers with limited generalizability to new, zero-day jailbreak signatures. This paper presents AdverSentinel-LLM, a novel adversarial prompt detector based on a Contrastive Dual-Encoder Transformer (CDET) architecture trained to identify malicious prompts in real time, including zero-day jailbreak attacks. The CDET architecture maintains two independent representation spaces—one encoding prompt semantics and one encoding structured threat patterns—trained jointly under a supervised contrastive objective that explicitly pushes adversarial embeddings away from benign clusters, enabling zero-day generalization to unseen attack vectors via contrastive disentanglement. The framework comprises two parallel transformer encoders: a Prompt Semantic Encoder (PSE) that learns deep contextual representations of input prompts and a Threat Pattern Encoder (TPE) that learns discriminative representations of known adversarial attack patterns. A supervised contrastive learning objective encourages separation between adversarial and benign embeddings, enabling zero-day generalization to unseen attack vectors. We additionally incorporate a Dynamic Threat Memory Bank (DTMB) with prototype pruning and rejuvenation to prevent stagnation, and an Anomaly-Aware Gating Mechanism (AAGM) for context-sensitive detection threshold modulation. Extensive experiments on AdvBench, JailbreakBench, ToxicChat, and PromptSafety-Bench demonstrate state-of-the-art performance with an F1-score of 0.967, detection accuracy of 97.3%, and a zero-day detection rate of 94.8%, with the contribution of every architectural element verified by ablation studies and preliminary evidence of cross-model transferability demonstrated across adversarial prompt distributions independently curated against GPT-4, LLaMA-3, Claude-3, and Gemini-Pro backends; a controlled matched-prompt evaluation is deferred to future work.

all.title: Telemetry Blindness in LLM Agents: A Controlled Measurement of Valid-Format Semantic Errors at the Write Boundary
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: An agent built on a large language model (LLM) can write a wrong value into a database while every signal reports success: the value has a valid format, the database accepts it, the write returns success, and the agent's explanation raises no flag. This paper measures how often this happens when the value is a computed financial amount. The reference is computed by deterministic code from Central Bank of Brazil series, and each value is read back from four database engines. The main experiment was specified and frozen in version control before its runs and uses one model, gpt-6-luna, with up to 100 instances per configuration. With reasoning effort none and no calculator, under the weekday calendar, the first answer was wrong in 82 of 100 compound-interest instances, 26 of 100 dated currency conversions and all 100 instances of a task that combines both. Of 532 wrong first answers, 384 were stored and passed every observer, with a median error of 0.15%. The database range rules caught only 9, each either about 5 to 10 times the correct value or about one-fifth to one-hundredth of it. Two pre-specified paired tests rejected their null hypotheses: raising reasoning effort to medium corrected 192 instances and made 3 wrong, and offering an exact calculator corrected 171 and made none wrong. One retry after a rejection that hides the value recovered fewer than 1 in 20 interest errors at effort none. A third pre-specified test, of a range check that needs no reference, could not be interpreted. Of the checks tested, only comparison with the reference, or recomputing it, separated every error. In exploratory runs on the same instances, outside those tests and on other dates, two other models gave far fewer and far more wrong answers (12 and 915 of 1,240, against 501). The pre-specified results hold for one model on numeric tasks. Code, data and evidence: https://github.com/estefano-ferreira/telemetry-blindness-agents/releases/tag/v1.0.0

all.title: Attack-Path-Aware Enterprise Risk Quantification for Cloud-Native Financial Data Platforms Using AI and Cybersecurity Graphs
all.abstract: Enterprise risk quantification in banking has historically treated vulnerability management and financial-impact analysis as separate disciplines: scanners rank findings by base severity scores, while risk functions estimate loss with coarse, qualitative heat maps. Neither accounts for how an adversary actually chains weaknesses across a modern cloud-native data platform to reach regulated financial data. This paper presents an attack-path-aware risk-quantification architecture that unifies the two. The system ingests posture and identity telemetry from cloud-security, identity, and configuration-management sources, constructs a directed attack graph whose nodes are asset and privilege states and whose edges are adversary transitions tagged by MITRE ATT&CK tactic, and uses this graph to propagate compromise likelihood toward designated crown-jewel assets. An AI layer scores edge-transition likelihoods from heterogeneous signals using a graph neural network with a transparent fallback, and large language models are used only in a constrained, retrieval-grounded role to normalize unstructured control evidence into the graph schema. Risk is expressed in monetary terms through a Factor Analysis of Information Risk (FAIR) loss model driven by graph-derived frequencies, producing an annualized loss distribution rather than a point estimate. A budget-constrained optimizer then selects controls by their marginal effect on crown-jewel loss, making remediation path-aware rather than severity-ordered. We describe the end-to-end technical architecture, formalize the quantification method, and demonstrate it on a synthetic but representative cloud data platform. In the illustrative study, path-aware control selection reduced expected annual loss by 85% at a fixed budget, versus 41% for conventional severity-ordered selection, and correctly identified a third-party integration path—low in individual CVSS severity—as the dominant driver of crown-jewel risk. We position the method as a decision-support instrument for model-risk and operational-risk functions, requiring human validation and governance rather than autonomous action.

all.title: Add-in DSE Brain: A Domain-Specific Expertise Architecture for Governing LLM Reasoning via a Graph-Guided SEPath Framework and Causal AI
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved widespread adoption across the financial sector, pure neural architectures still suffer from inherent stochasticity, creating severe bottlenecks in mission-critical, zero-tolerance operations such as corporate syndicated lending, cross-asset portfolio stress testing, and regulatory compliance. Currently, financial institutions rely heavily on costly frontier generalist LLMs, which are plagued by numerical hallucinations, black-box opacity, lack of auditability, and cloud data-leakage risks. Furthermore, because these models rely on surface-level statistical correlations, they are highly susceptible to spurious correlations and confounding biases. Conversely, on-premises compact open-weight LLMs offer superior data localization and cost efficiency, yet their constrained parameter scales prevent them from independently executing complex multi-hop financial logic and causal inference. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid neuro-symbolic architecture that decouples natural language representation from causal-logical governance by integrating an on-premises compact open-weight LLM, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and an add-in Domain-Specific Expertise Brain (DSE Brain). Functioning as a Cognitive Exocortex grounded in the five-layer Structured Expert Path (SEPath) control architecture, the DSE Brain upgrades static knowledge graphs into a universal, dual-regime Causal-Constrained Logic Graph (CC-LG), such as the Causal-Constrained Financial Logic Graph (CC-FLG) demonstrated in this financial setting, that distinguishes data-supported empirical variables from normative regulatory and procedural rules. Rather than forcing statistical estimation where observational data is unavailable, the system selectively invokes multi-paradigm Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) causal discovery (PC, GES, and DirectLiNGAM), dual-track back-door and Double Machine Learning (DML) estimation, and triple-robustness refutation diagnostics exclusively to calibrate empirical causal impact weights for data-supported DEPENDS_ON dependencies, while enforcing codified prerequisite and safety assertions over normative nodes. Executed through a five-layer CoT-CR-ReAct pipeline with dual compliance gates, external deterministic solvers, and closed-loop meta-learning, the architecture actively governs latent reasoning trajectories and agentic actions. Empirical validations across global financial market series, structural prompt auditing (achieving the maximum 5.00 audit score), and longitudinal FinQA benchmarks (\approx92.0% mean accuracy) demonstrate that equipping compact open-weight LLMs with the DSE Brain transforms them into deterministic, white-box auditable inference engines that surpass frontier generalist LLMs in reasoning depth, compliance fidelity, and cost efficiency.

all.title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning in Islamic banking: insights using lexicon and machine learning-based models
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) within the Islamic banking sector, focusing on sentiment analysis of these technologies across annual reports from 71 full-fledged Islamic banks in 16 countries between 2015 and 2023. Design/methodology/approach The authors used five sentiment analysis models, TextBlob, valence aware dictionary and sentiment reasoner, AFINN, long short-term memory (LSTM) and bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT), to assess sentiment polarity and word frequency of AI and ML terms using Python. Sentiment distributions and trends were analysed across time, country and individual banks using visualisations from R Studio. Findings The results indicate a predominantly positive sentiment towards AI and ML in Islamic banking, with advanced models like LSTM and BERT capturing nuanced sentiment more accurately than traditional models. Regional differences emerged, with countries like Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE demonstrating notably higher positive sentiment levels. The findings reveal significant sentiment variations among models, countries and banks, emphasising AI and ML’s perceived value in enhancing efficiency, compliance and customer experience. Research limitations/implications The study’s reliance on annual reports may limit sentiment scope, suggesting future research could expand to other data sources for a comprehensive view. Practical implications The findings offer valuable insights for Islamic banks, regulators and stakeholders to inform responsible AI adoption and its application in enhancing service quality and regulatory compliance. Originality/value This research fills a notable gap by examining AI and ML sentiment in Islamic finance, providing new insights into stakeholder perspectives on these technologies’ role and impact.

all.title: Technological and Organisational Readiness for Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Organisational Innovation in Deposit Money Banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria
all.venue: GPH-International Journal of Social Science and Humanities Research
all.abstract: Banks in emerging economies are under pressure to deliver faster, more personalised and more efficient digital financial services, yet many struggle to convert investments in artificial intelligence (AI) into innovation. This study examined how two dimensions of AI adoption readiness, technological readiness and organisational readiness, relate to product innovation and process innovation in deposit money banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model and the Resource-Based View, the study adopted a descriptive, cross-sectional, correlational survey of 400 employees and managers selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. Respondents rated organisational readiness (M = 3.62), process innovation (M = 3.59), product innovation (M = 3.54) and technological readiness (M = 3.45) above the scale midpoint. Both readiness dimensions correlated strongly and positively with both innovation outcomes (r = .68 to .74, p < .001). In multiple regression, the two predictors jointly explained 57.5% of the variance in product innovation and 56.7% in process innovation, and organisational readiness had the larger standardised coefficient in both models (β = .535 and .444) compared with technological readiness (β = .263 and .353). The findings indicate that technology is necessary but not sufficient for AI-enabled innovation. Banks should pair investment in infrastructure and skills with leadership sponsorship, employee training, a supportive culture and strategic alignment.

all.title: Legal and Ethical Implication Framework for Artificial Intelligence Application in Centenary Bank Uganda Limited
all.venue: DS Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics
all.abstract: This manuscript examines the legal and ethical implications framework for the application of Artificial Intelligence in Ugandan Centenary banks, with a case study focus on the Lango Sub-Region of Northern Uganda. As banks increasingly deploy AI for credit scoring, fraud detection, customer onboarding, chatbots, anti-money laundering monitoring, and risk analytics, the technology promises greater efficiency, lower operating costs, and improved financial inclusion. However, these benefits are accompanied by significant legal and ethical concerns, including privacy infringement, algorithmic bias and opacity in automated decision-making, cybersecurity exposure, unlawful profiling, data localization issues, and uncertainty around accountability when AI systems cause harm. The manuscript situates these concerns within Uganda’s emerging legal and regulatory environment, including the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, the Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019, the Computer Misuse Act, 2011, the Financial Institutions Act, and sectoral supervision by the Bank of Uganda. It further engages ethical principles of fairness, transparency, accountability, explainability, non-discrimination, human oversight, beneficence, and proportionality. Using the Lango Sub-Region as a contextual lens, the paper argues that AI adoption in commercial banking must be governed by a hybrid framework combining statutory compliance, internal bank governance, regulatory supervision, and context-sensitive ethical safeguards. The manuscript concludes that Uganda requires clearer AI-specific rules, stronger supervisory guidance, institutional audit mechanisms, and bank-level governance protocols to ensure that AI innovation does not erode consumer rights, trust, and financial stability.

all.title: The Impact of Using Artificial Intelligence in the Financial and Banking Sector
institutions: Larbi Ben M'hidi University of Oum El Bouaghi
all.abstract: The accelerated use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing the financial services industry and the banking sector in terms of improving the efficiency of their operations, customer experience, risk management and the effectiveness of strategic decision-making. The proposed researc examines the profound influence of artificial intelligence (AI) on the financial sector, analyzing its many effects on operations, risk management and client experiences. By examining the incorporation of machine learning algorithms, natural language processing and robotic process automation, the substantial improvements in efficiency and reductions in costs that Artificial Intelligence (AI) provides to financial institutions was revealed. Moreover, the study explores the consequences of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in improving fraud detection procedures and reducing operational risks, thereby strengthening the sector's ability to withstand challenges. Nevertheless, the study also acknowledges the risks related to data privacy, ethical considerations and the possibility of employment displacement, emphasizing the necessity for strong regulatory frameworks.

all.title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence for Enhanced Personalized Banking Services
all.venue: JOURNAL OF ACCOUNTING AND FINANCIAL MANAGEMENT
all.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into banking systems has been a transformative development, offering the potential to significantly enhance customer satisfaction and operational efficiency. This study explores the impact of AI-driven personalization on customer satisfaction, investigates data privacy and security challenges, and assesses the effectiveness of AI integration with existing banking infrastructure. Utilizing a survey of 133 banking professionals, the research reveals that a substantial majority of respondents experience positive outcomes from AI integration, with 71.4% noting improvements in customer satisfaction and 68.4% reporting enhanced operational efficiency. However, the study also identifies concerns regarding data security and various integration challenges, including technical compatibility issues and insufficient staff training. These findings highlight the need for banks to address these challenges through enhanced training programs, robust security measures, and strategic cost management to fully leverage the benefits of AI technologies. The results underscore the importance of continuous refinement and effective implementation strategies to maximize the positive impacts of AI while mitigating associated risks.

all.title: FinTech and European Bank Performance: A Machine-Learning Analysis of Greenwashing and Sustainability Channels
all.abstract: The parallel diffusion of financial technology and the tightening of European sustainable-finance regulation have reshaped banking, yet how digitalisation affects financial performance remains unclear. Using a panel of 90 European banks over 2014–2025 (1080 bank-year observations) and a Fintech index built from annual-report text through a Dynamic Factor Model, we examine whether, and through which channels, Fintech adoption is associated with bank performance, focusing on two mechanisms usually treated as controls: greenwashing and substantive ESG practices. We combine causal mediation, a sensitivity analysis to hidden confounding, a doubly robust Double Machine Learning estimator, unconditional-quantile (RIF) regressions, Local Projections, a Causal Forest, and optimal policy learning. Four findings emerge. First, Fintech’s direct effect raises long-term soundness while depressing short-term profitability, though its total effect on profitability is insignificant. Second, both channels mediate the relationship in the baseline specification, but only the substantive-ESG channel is robust to alternative measurement: the greenwashing channel, significant in the baseline, does not survive a performance-free re-measurement of the disclosure–performance gap, so we read these as associations rather than established causal mechanisms. Third, effects are heterogeneous across the performance distribution and over time, with profitability turning positive from the second year. Fourth, the benefits concentrate among large, well-capitalised, high-ESG, low-greenwashing banks, a profile that an exploratory policy rule can target. These associations are specific to Europe’s sustainable-finance architecture; because the design is not experimental, they are interpreted as conditional on the identifying assumptions, and their external validity remains open.

all.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Financial Sector
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
institutions: University of Science and Technology, Meghalaya
all.abstract: The financial sector is under constant pressure to do the evolution of risk management techniques for discharge of financial services with the broad objectives of meeting the tenet of optimising cost and boost productivity with enlargement of the scope of inclusivity and financial outreach programme. This will be facilitated by a blending of financial services software interface, the facility that enables the nation to achieve an enviable record of ease of doing business, digitalisation of financial market through a safe and secure network portal. Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a game-changer in nearly all financial sectors. The use of AI in banking, insurance, stock market, quantitative finance has revolutionised the process of data analysis, predictions and risk management thereby improving the decision making process for investors. In this context an attempt has been made to focus on the application of AI in financial sector and analyse the global best practices of AI in banking, property and title insurance enforcement.
