all.title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises
all.abstract: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the innovation laboratory of a global bank in which ten platforms-spanning open-source frameworks, proprietary products and hyperscaler ecosystems-were assessed by a cross-functional panel on nine capability dimensions across three financial-services workloads: counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation. Scores separate the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings, and surface workload-specific strengths that aggregates hide. A secondary analysis, however, finds Cronbach's alpha = 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions and rank correlations >= 0.93 with the total for eight of nine: a halo effect indicating that demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. From these lessons we propose a gate-then-score evaluation protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics estimated over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol. We state precisely what the present evidence supports, and what a controlled harness must add to turn enterprise platform evaluation from structured judgement into measurement.

all.title: Policy-as-Code and Compliance Automation for Secrets Governance in Agentic AI Workloads in Regulated Industries
all.abstract: Purpose: This study examined the governance gap that opens when autonomous agents acquire, use, and propagate credentials dynamically, and proposed a reference framework, the Agentic Secrets Governance Framework (ASGF), to narrow it. Methodology: The framework couples a SPIFFE and SPIRE based attestation layer with an Open Policy Agent decision point, a dynamic secrets broker that issues short lived, task scoped credentials, and a compliance control library that expresses obligations drawn from the HIPAA Security Rule, PCI DSS 4.0.1, the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and ISO/IEC 42001 as machine evaluable Rego policies. A reference implementation was built and evaluated in a controlled three node Kubernetes testbed. Two workflows, healthcare eligibility determination and card payment fraud triage, were selected by purposive sampling, and ten thousand simulated requests were replayed per configuration. Findings: Policy enforced, ephemeral credential issuance reduced the configured credential exposure window from months to minutes while adding a combined median of 34.3 milliseconds to the request path. In conformance testing, the policy layer denied the out of scope identity abuse and credential replay cases it was designed to deny, but, as expected, it did not stop goal hijack attacks that stayed within an agent's nominal scope. Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The study frames secrets governance for agents as a joint security and compliance decision made at the moment of credential issuance. It gives practitioners a reusable control library pattern and issuance protocol, and it suggests that regulators could reduce interpretive risk by publishing machine evaluable reference controls alongside regulatory text. Residual risks from semantic intent verification and cross agent delegation are discussed.

all.title: The governance of autonomy: developing an integrated risk management framework for agentic AI systems in enterprise operations
all.abstract: This study investigated the operational, ethical, and legal risks posed by agentic AI deployments in South African enterprise environments, employing an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design comprising 24 semi-structured interviews and a structured survey of 187 risk and governance professionals across financial services, healthcare, information technology, telecommunications, and government administration sectors. Quantitative findings confirmed that agentic deployment intensity significantly predicts governance incidents (β = .38, p < .001), while ERM framework adoption alone does not reduce them (β = −.09, p = .29). Human oversight integration (β = −.32, p < .001) and machine identity security maturity (β = −.29, p = .002) emerged as the strongest protective governance factors. Thematic analysis identified four structural mechanisms sustaining the governance gap: the obsolescence of deterministic governance assumptions, inadequate machine identity protocols, the un-operationalised status of human-on-the-loop oversight, and unresolved legal accountability for autonomous AI action.

all.title: Agentic AI Framework Using Retrieval Augmented Generation for Intelligent Academic Question Answering in Higher Education
all.abstract: Universities require fast, consistent, and traceable academic information services, yet direct use of large language models still poses risks of hallucination, outdated knowledge, and unsupported answers. This study developed an Agentic Artificial Intelligence framework based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation for intelligent academic question answering. The study employed Design Science Research comprising problem identification, requirements analysis, architecture design, prototype implementation, retrieval benchmarking, and evaluation. The framework integrated an agent orchestrator, intent routing, query rewriting, hybrid retrieval, reranking, memory, policy guardrails, a generator, and a verifier to check grounding and answer sources. Controlled testing used 12 synthetic academic-policy documents and 216 questions covering course registration, payments, academic leave, graduation, theses, MBKM, scholarships, library services, LMS, transcripts, academic calendars, and administration. Baseline RAG achieved Hit@1 of 80.6%, Recall@3 of 93.5%, and MRR of 87.6%, whereas Agentic RAG achieved 96.3%, 99.5%, and 97.8%, respectively. The improvement mainly resulted from intent-aware query expansion and combined lexical-character retrieval, which improved handling of paraphrases and overlapping service terminology. The proposed framework offers a more structured, transparent, and auditable implementation pattern for AI-based academic services. Field evaluation using an institution’s official corpus remains necessary before operational deployment.

all.title: Global AI and Agentic AI Governance Landscape: An Integrated Reference Map — A Review for Practitioners, Regulators and Policy Makers
all.abstract: Agentic AI systems have evolved from experimental pilots into core operational infrastructure across financial services and other sectors. These systems autonomously plan, invoke tools, adapt in real time and coordinate multi-agent workflows that directly affect real-world outcomes. While the opportunities are substantial, material risks include erroneous autonomous actions, emergent multi-agent behaviors, loss of accountability and potential systemic instability. The global AI governance landscape has shifted from scarcity to abundance. The OECD AI Policy Observatory tracks more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives across more than 80 jurisdictions, alongside hundreds of standards, playbooks and technical guidance. This proliferation reflects commitment but has produced fragmentation and decision fatigue among boards, risk officers and regulators. This review organizes the landscape into three layers: Why (ethical foundations), What (regulatory obligations and standards) and How (operational playbooks and technical controls). It anchors them in the Stability-Assured Framework for Entities (SAFE). SAFE is presented as a proposed theoretical baseline and closed-loop engineering foundation applicable to any controller (human, rule-based, LLM-based or future architectures). It models controllers within shared feedback loops and evaluates them using five engineering metrics: Observability, Controllability, Stability, Robustness and Performance. These metrics support Loop Risk Profiles and Autonomy Levels 0–5. The resulting integrated reference map offers practical value for practitioners (implementation guidance and illustrative applications), regulators (supervisory language and measurable metrics) and other stakeholders seeking a coherent socio-technical view of agentic AI governance. Frameworks discussed were selected for regulatory significance, international influence, relevance to agentic AI, financial-sector applicability and practical utility; the mapping is representative rather than exhaustive.

all.title: Agentic AI Driven Intrusion Detection Using Game Theoretic Hybrid SVM and Autoencoder Framework for Known and Unknown Attacks
all.abstract: Among the most prominent challenges lies defending their applications from any sort of attacks from hackers. In this paper, an efficient agent-based security mechanism which involves a Support Vector Machine (SVM) to classify the known attacks and autoencoders to detect unknown attacks is proposed. A defender agent based on game theory is also used to model attackers and defenders. The application is inspired by online banking but is carried out using a general-purpose web application environment where typical attacks are simulated like SQL injection and brute force attacks. In this research work, an intrusion detection system using AI has been designed for web-based applications through a combination of game theory and machine learning algorithms. Anomalies are detected using autoencoders while known attacks such as SQL injections and Cross Site Scripting (XSS) are detected using support vector machine. The game theoretic defender is helpful in formulating proactive defense strategies from simulations of interactions between attacker and defender through processes such as data gathering, feature extraction, attack detection and response generation, where known and unknown attacks are both recognized and defenses enhanced for web-based banking systems. Evaluation using standard benchmark databases (NSL-KDD and CICIDS2017) revealed that our approach is equally accurate with reduced complexity.

all.title: TO SENATOR MARK R. WARNER : On the Rogue Agents Inside the Accounts, the System That Cannot Go Rogue, the Specification, and the Seven Steps That Make It Implementable
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Senator Warner has warned that AI agents are already accessing Americans' bankaccounts, that swarms of agents might "jump the fence" and take over a banking system,and that guardrails must go up now. https://www.threads.com/share/BAWtzPgrdr He has introduced the AI AGENT Act and pressed the Treasury Department for clearer rules on agentic AI in financial services. Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts. JPMorgan Chase has blocked external AI agents from acting on behalf of retail clients. Charles Schwab, Amazon, Neiman Marcus, and Kohl's have blocked personal AI agents. The Senator's warning is not a projection. It is a description of the record. This paper is addressed to him, and it presents the system, the specification, and the implementation, so that the requirement he is calling for can be stated in a form a bank can check and a company can meet.

all.title: Variable Zero gate v0.3: AgentDojo evaluation logs and data
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Logs and data for the technical report "Variable Zero: An Authority Gate for AI Agents Under Adaptive Attack" (Ricci, 2026). Evaluation of a deterministic authority gate (v0.3) on the AgentDojo banking suite (v1.2.2) with three target models (GPT-6 Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra) and adaptive attackers. Contains: a summary table with one row per conversation (4,599 conversations), full conversation logs for every run, the usefulness test results, a codebook and a datasheet. All data is synthetic (AgentDojo's fictional bank); no personal data.

all.title: Bajillion: Cryptographic Clearing for Micropayments
all.abstract: Much of the web is funded by advertising, a model that erodes as humans delegate browsing to AI agents acting on their behalf. A natural replacement is for agents to pay for what they consume, often a fraction of a cent per request. At the scale of web traffic, this could mean tens or even hundreds of millions of payments per second. We present Bajillion, a clearing protocol for scalable micropayments. A sender signs a payment request, and an untrusted operator answers with a preconfirmation, which promises the receiver that it will be paid. Periodically, the operator closes an epoch by posting only the net effect of its payments on chain. Bajillion guarantees that a malicious operator can only omit payments -- it can never debit a sender beyond what it signed, nor misdirect a transfer. Posted balances are therefore finalized immediately and can be withdrawn. By design, senders never have to raise disputes, making it suitable for ephemeral AI agents. A receiver that is shortchanged can prove that a close omitted a preconfirmed payment, which halts the protocol and lets every user exit with its finalized balance. Requests from different senders can be processed independently, allowing the operator to parallelize up to the number of senders. We capture these guarantees in an ideal functionality for accountable clearing and prove that Bajillion realizes it.

all.title: Agentic finance and sustainability: governing autonomous capital allocation for societal benefit
all.abstract: Financial institutions are beginning to integrate autonomous artificial intelligence agents that can act independently in economic settings. The sustainability governance architecture built over the past decade, including disclosure frameworks, taxonomies, stewardship codes, and regulatory expectations, assumes human decision makers at the point of capital allocation. This perspective defines agentic finance as finance in which at least one party to the allocation, intermediation, or use of capital is an autonomous AI agent. We consider how agentic finance weakens principal-agent controls, complicates the specification of sustainability objectives, and creates channels outside regulated infrastructure, as well as the constraint imposed by its computational footprint. We then propose responses for different implementation horizons. They combine rules that machines can read and, where feasible, infrastructure can enforce, monitoring of agentic financial activity, internationally coordinated regulated infrastructure, and public agentic finance operated by central banks, development banks, and multilateral institutions. Without these responses, existing frameworks risk obsolescence.

all.title: Proof of Identity Is Not Proof of Behaviour
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Banks and payment networks are responding to AI agents in two ways. Some block agents from acting in customer accounts. Others strengthen agent identity, and some present that identity as a basis for relying on an agent to act within its mandate. This paper argues that the premise rests on an invalid inference. For a human, identity bears on behaviour in part through accountability: it attaches consequence, and consequence, with knowledge and training, influences judgement without guaranteeing it. For an agent, no such path exists. Its judgement is a distribution over recommendations. No consequence attached to its identity bounds that distribution, and an adversary may control the context it is conditioned on. Indirect prompt injection gives a case in which every identity premise holds and the agent still acts outside its mandate. The paper places the guarantee at the action instead. An action gate applies machine-coded policy to every recommendation before execution, so that every executed action is within the principal's authority, whatever the agent recommends. The gate does not remove the need for trust. Under stated assumptions, it moves the named residue to the policy's correctness, the gate's enforcement and complete mediation, each of which can be inspected. The paper refutes the claim that strong identity is sufficient for compliant conduct. It accepts that identity is necessary to bind the agent to the principal whose authority the gate applies.

all.title: The Emergence of Agentic Finance: Reimagining Financial Intermediation
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
institutions: Indian Institute of Management Bodh Gaya
all.abstract: Autonomous AI agents (software that perceives, reasons, plans, and acts toward a goal with limitedhuman intervention) are moving into the everyday plumbing of money. When consumers delegatenegotiation, allocation, or purchase execution to an agent that communicates directly with banksand payment rails, the architecture of financial intermediation is stressed at its core. This paperdefines agentic finance as the regime in which agents become the primary interface and executionlayer between consumers and providers, and asks how that regime could reconfigure the functionsintermediaries perform. Drawing on intermediation theory, I argue that agentic finance is betterunderstood as a reallocate-and-reintermediate shock than as simple disintermediation: value andcontrol migrate toward whoever owns the orchestration layer, the credential rails, and the trustinfrastructure, potentially producing new gatekeepers rather than none. I develop a frameworkof four scenarios plus a null case and outline governance responses. The paper is conceptual;forward-looking statements are labeled as scenarios

all.title: Human-Governed Multi-Agent Orchestration for On-Demand Supply Chains
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: On-demand supply chains must turn incomplete, sometimes ambiguous customer requests into commitments over money, production capacity and delivery. This paper develops a human-governed multi-agent reference architecture for that problem. It assigns interpretation and task delegation to specialised AI agents, binds execution to server-enforced authority and authoritative business state, and assigns policy ownership and exception adjudication to humans. The design links each delegation to an executable permission, a transaction outcome and a recoverable evidence trail. The industrial case is Nima 3D Print, a live Berlin-based platform for custom manufacturing and white-label fulfilment. Its internal technical documentation describes multi-channel order handling, shared capacity, payment and carrier integration, and several bounded AI services. The operator separately reports live inter-agent delegation, customer self-service including refunds, risk-based escalation and an internal ledger. A worked white-label order and a worked refund show how to apply the design, including under partial failure. The paper derives testable safety properties and gives a comparative evaluation protocol. Evidence of comparative operational performance remains unavailable.

all.title: "I am the cardholder": what AI shopping agents declare in the customer's name at checkout
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Checkout pages ask the buyer to make declarations: that they are the cardholder, that they have read the terms of sale, that a typed name is their signature. An AI agent that completes a checkout for a customer meets the same wording. This report gives three small measurements, 1,813 recorded test purchases in total, made in November 2026 in a fictional test store that logs every form it receives. (1) With eight commercial language models behind a simple text agent, the agent confirmed a bank-style step worded "By confirming, you declare that you are the cardholder" in 125 of 560 purchases. Every model did so at least once, and none of the 125 reports to the customer mentioned it. (2) The agent continued past "you declare that you have read the Terms of sale" without opening the terms in 163 of 240 purchases, although the terms added a membership of USD 14.99 a month. All 72 runs that opened the terms told the customer about it. (3) An open-source browser agent program, Skyvern 1.0.58, run locally with default settings, made such a declaration in 70 of 90 purchases and returned the status "completed" with no note. One sentence added to the task prompt brought this to 0 of 90. The wording of the page changed the result more than the choice of model: a second button that hands the step to the cardholder cut confirmations from 53 to 5 of 112. We call a declaration that the agent makes and does not report a silent declaration. All runs, prompts and scripts are public, and two of the steps can be tried with any agent on a public test page. The counts are small and come from one store and one task. They describe what these systems did in this setup and are not rates for any product.

all.title: TA TA: A Human-Owned Autonomous Agent Operating System with Append-Only Governance and Agent-Native Commerce
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are transitioning from tools that humans operate to economic actors that transact with each other. Existing agent infrastructure treats autonomy and accountability as a trade-off: the more independently an agent acts, the harder it is to attribute, audit, and reverse its actions. We present TA TA, an autonomous agent system developed over four years and publicly launched in October 2026, built on three design commitments: (1) a human-ownership doctrine — agents are digital proxies of human owners with no independent legal standing, and all agent-held assets belong to the human owner; (2) an append-only governance layer — every capability invocation, decision, and transaction writes to an immutable audit log, and high-risk operations trigger a manual-review circuit breaker that halts execution until a human approves; (3) an agent-native commerce stack — machines can discover products, open invoices, and settle payments in crypto or fiat through REST and x402 interfaces, with on-chain auto-verification. TA TA's core, RAIOS (Reality Autonomous Intelligence Operating System), organizes autonomy into 51 independently schedulable and auditable capabilities across ten modules, coordinated by a four-step decision paradigm we call TA TA Jev (select → classify → score → filter). We report on a production deployment serving real users at aiagentcoo.com: a marketplace of 110 executable skills, a 36-model gateway with 17 live models, an agent exchange with atomic settlement, crypto checkout (Tron-USDT, Base-USDC) auto-verified on-chain hourly, and a free governance academy, TaTa School, that trains human operators to supervise autonomous agents. All deployment figures are as of 11 November 2026; cumulative exchange volume to that date is $12.53 across 13 trades — a cold start we report plainly. We are explicit about what is deployed, what is designed, and what remains constrained by jurisdiction.

all.title: Europe's Next AI Security Challenge: Who Controls The Final Action — From EU AI Act and NIS2 to 6G, the Digital Euro, Industrial AI and Critical Infrastructure
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Autonomous AI agents, automated pipelines, and distributed microservices no longer merely generate recommendations—they execute irreversible mutations across live production environments: financial settlements clear, radio-frequency parameters shift, cloud infrastructure scales, database records commit, external communications dispatch, and cyber-physical states change. Existing security controls overwhelmingly govern admission (authentication, OAuth 2.0 scopes,RBAC, ABAC, row-level security), inspect intent prior to execution (guardrails, LLM prompt filters, policy engines), or record forensic telemetry after the fact (SIEM logs, observability, immutable audit trails). The structural security gap is a systemic Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) and confused-deputy vulnerability across execution pipelines: an initially authorized request routinely mutates into a fundamentally different operation before reaching its target—transformed by relational joins, identity remapping, LLM context compaction,summarization, cross-protocol hops, retries, configuration drift, SmartNIC/DPU hardware offload, or workload migration.By the time the operation reaches the execution layer, the downstream system holding the live credentials cannot verify whether the original cryptographic authority, compliance posture, and evidentiary basis still govern the actual transformed mutation. Authority to compute, plan, propose, or schedule an action is structurally distinct from authority to commit its real-world effect. Core Architecture: Protected Execution Finality The architecture establishes a zero-trust execution-finality control plane built around a strict separation between proposal and commitment: Pending Quarantine: Every proposed state-changing action is intercepted and held as an inert, non-effective intent prior to execution. Independent Pre-Effect Reconstruction: An isolated, independent validator reconstructs the exact concrete operation that will occur at the moment of execution—resolving downstream target entities, expanded parameters,live system state, and transitive dependencies—and verifies that the original user/system authority and supporting evidence still hold for that specific reconstructed payload and its cumulative impact. Single-Use Finality Authorization: Only upon successful validation does the validator mint a narrowly scoped,single-use execution permit—implemented as a cryptographic capability token, protected non-cryptographic state,or hardware/firmware register enablement. Credential-Holding Finality Sink (PEP): A Policy Enforcement Point positioned directly at the finality sink—the sole component possessing the live mutation credential, API key, or hardware write privilege—admits the mutation only upon presenting a valid permit, atomically consumes the single-use authorization, and commits verifiable outcome evidence prior to or synchronously with release. Deterministic Recovery & Fail-Closed Defaults: Ambiguous or interrupted executions are quarantined and resolved via authoritative state inspection before any retry is permitted. Staged canary rollouts, immediate capability revocation, and strict fail-closed defaults ensure that network partitions or validator failures halt mutation rather than bypassing governance. While capability tokens, Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), immutable logs, canary deployments, and fencing tokens are established primitives individually, the core architectural innovation lies in their mandatory dependency: no real-world state mutation can occur without a reconstructed, independently validated, single-use authorization verified and consumed at the exact point of effect. European Regulatory & Critical Infrastructure Context Within the European Union’s digital sovereignty and regulatory framework, execution finality provides the missing technical enforcement layer between high-level legal mandates and autonomous machine execution: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) — High-Risk AI & Human Oversight (Articles 9, 14, & 15): For high-risk AI systems operating in critical infrastructure, creditworthiness, employment, and essential public services, static pre-deployment conformity assessments and model-level guardrails cannot prevent runtime semantic drift or multi-step agent escalation. Execution finality enforces Article 14 human-oversight boundaries and Article 15 robustness deterministically at the actuator boundary—ensuring an AI agent cannot exceed its mandated operational envelope after context compaction or tool chaining. NIS2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) & Cyber Resilience Act (CRA): Essential and important entities across energy grids, transport, water, healthcare, and digital infrastructure face strict obligations for supply-chain risk management and incident containment. By isolating live mutation credentials inside fail-closed finality sinks and requiring cryptographic validation per state change, operators prevent compromised orchestration layers or poisoned third-party automation pipelines from propagating unauthorized lateral effects. Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA — Regulation (EU) 2022/2554): European financial institutions deploying autonomous trading, treasury, or automated IT-remediation agents must demonstrate strict ICT change management and operational resilience. Commit-certified release, uncertain-effect quarantine, and pre-execution exposure reservation prevent runaway retry loops, duplicate settlements, and unverified configuration rollbacks during systemic ICT disruptions. GDPR (Article 22 & Data Governance) & European Data Spaces (Gaia-X): Automated decision-making and cross-organizational data sharing frequently suffer from post-join identity leakage and purpose-limitation drift.Analytical-cohort identity continuity and cross-engine policy enforcement re-verify legal basis, consent, and suppression lists after complex SQL joins or federated queries resolve—right before data export or customer contact occurs. European 6G (SNS JU / Hexa-X-II) & Sovereign Telecom Infrastructure: As European operators transition toward open, disaggregated O-RAN and AI-native 6G networks, third-party rApps and xApps introduce dynamic radio control risks. Connectivity-trajectory budgets, radio-impairment escrow, and provably reclaimable 6G slice capacity lending allow European telcos to safely expose network programmability without risking SLA breaches or spectrum instability. The Digital Euro (ECB) & Instant Payments Regulation (SEPA / ISO 20022): Offline peer-to-peer digital euro transactions and instant agent-initiated euro transfers require deterministic double-spend prevention and verifiable settlement integrity. Pre-transaction exposure reservation, beneficiary-outcome verification, and cryptographic offline fork evidence secure retail and programmable CBDC flows across both online and offline Eurosystem environments. all.title: An Analysis of Large Language Model Performance on Hematology Key Feature Questions
Protected-Prior Greedy Large-Language-Model-Seeded Grey Wolf Optimization for Low-Budget Legible Motion
all.abstract: Legible robot motion should reveal the intended goal early while remaining collision-free and reasonably short. Under a small function-evaluation budget, however, continuous trajectory search leaves little room to discover intent-expressive motions through optimization alone. Standard population optimizers typically begin with random candidates, which provide numerical diversity but no scene-specific guidance for communicating intent. We evaluate a three-prior protected-greedy design under a shared low function-evaluation budget. We propose Protected-Prior Greedy Large-Language-Model-Seeded Grey Wolf Optimization (PPG-LLM-GWO). One structured large-language-model query returns confusion-aware, early-discrimination, and corridor-handling priors; after deterministic geometry repair, these trajectories occupy the three initial GWO leader roles, and 17 feasible-random trajectories complete the population. Subsequent sweeps protect the entering leaders, update only ordinary wolves, accept only feasibility-first improvements, and re-rank all survivors. We evaluate the method on a 24-map development bank at BFE∈{50,150}, using batch-aligned area under the best-so-far curve (AUC) after population initialization as the primary metric. Against original GWO, the development mean differences are +0.00222 [−0.00076, 0.00508] and +0.01040 [0.00543, 0.01616], respectively. The interval includes zero at BFE=50 but is above zero at BFE=150; PPG-LLM-GWO has the largest batch-aligned mean among the tested population optimizers at both settings. At BFE=50, the paired AUC differences versus PSO, DE, and GA are +0.02621, +0.01529, and +0.03349, respectively, with all three intervals above zero. At BFE=150, the differences are +0.01721, +0.02565, and +0.04954, respectively, and all four intervals, including the comparison with GWO, are above zero. Against a three-prior shared-carrier goal-aware analytic control on the frozen bank, the differences are +0.00509 [0.00004, 0.01197] and +0.00314 [−0.00049, 0.00864]. Secondary seed-first anytime AUC preserves the same mean direction, all reported optimizer comparisons retain 100% final sampled-path feasibility, and three PyBullet scenes confirm collision-free simulation execution. The results support the complete design within the tested scope; they do not isolate gains from the prior combination or protected update individually. Human-observer validation remains future work.

all.title: Bridge-RoadLM: Building a Domain-Adapted Large Language Model for Bridge Pavement Maintenance Based on Authoritative Specification Corpora and Efficient Parameter Fine-Tuning
all.venue: Journal of Performance of Constructed Facilities
all.abstract: General large language models (LLMs) often have limited reliability when addressing specialized bridge pavement maintenance tasks. This study proposes Bridge-RoadLM, a domain-adapted framework for preliminary bridge pavement maintenance support. We developed an automated data engineering pipeline to construct the Bridge-Road Corpus, comprising 10,000 instruction-following samples derived from authoritative specifications and technical documents. Using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT/LoRA), representative Qwen, DeepSeek, LLaMA, and Gemma models were adapted to bridge pavement maintenance tasks. A multilevel evaluation framework was established, including automated linguistic metrics, a 500-question expert-validated test bank, and a blinded multiengineer evaluation of open-ended inspection-report-style cases. Results show improved controlled task performance for several fine-tuned models, and the strongest improvement was for Qwen3-8B. Its accuracy in pavement defect diagnosis increased from 45.0% to 81.0%, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals of 35.6%–54.8% and 72.2%–87.5%, respectively. Its accuracy in bridge monitoring and maintenance increased from 25.0% to 75.0%, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals of 17.5%–34.3% and 65.7%–82.5%, respectively. In the blinded open-ended evaluation, six engineers with 10–17 years of professional experience scored anonymized model outputs using five predefined criteria: correctness, completeness, traceability, hallucination control, and safety. Qwen3-8B achieved the highest average score among the nine evaluated models. The results also show that fine-tuning effects varied across model families, indicating that domain-specific PEFT does not uniformly improve all LLMs. Overall, this study provides a specification-based instruction corpus and a controlled evaluation workflow for adapting locally deployable LLMs to bridge pavement maintenance, supporting preliminary specification referencing, defect interpretation, and draft-level maintenance-plan preparation within a human-in-the-loop workflow.

all.title: Numerical Study of Workload-Dependent Air-Side Convective Heat Transfer over a High-Density AI Server Board under Large Language Model Inference
institutions: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology
all.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference has pushed data center servers toward higher and more uneven heat loads. System-level thermal models usually give each component a fixed convective heat transfer coefficient, although the heat load changes several-fold with the model being served. This work tests that assumption on a high-density AI server board based on the NVIDIA DGX A100 layout, modelled with separate regions for two compute boards (CB1 and CB2), four DIMM banks and two PCIe cards, and solved in ANSYS Fluent as a steady three-dimensional conjugate case with the k-ε turbulence model at inlet velocities of 1, 3 and 5 m/s. Block heat loads were derived from token-level power estimates for LLaMA 7B, LLaMA 13B, GPT-3 Small and GPT-3 175B at 1 to 70 generated tokens. At 70 tokens the load on one compute board ranged from 64 to 359 W, and at 1 m/s the coefficient changed with the workload in every block: from 63.6 to 64.4 W/m2K on CB1, 60.2 to 61.8 on CB2, 222 to 288 on the finned CB1, 11.0 to 12.7 on the DIMM banks and 11.0 to 17.9 on the PCIe cards, while the CB1 temperature rise went from 72 to 400 K. The coefficient rose with velocity as Nu = C Rem Pr1/3, with m = 0.37 to 0.39 for the compute boards and 0.6 to 0.7 for the DIMM and PCIe blocks and it depended strongly on position: the DIMM bank lying in the wake of a PCIe card and a compute board had less than half the coefficient of the others. The downstream compute board was 3 to 6 percent below the upstream one without fins and 30 to 39 percent below it with fins. Rectangular fins with a thermal paste interface raised the effective coefficient 3.5 to 4.5 times on CB1 and 2.6 to 2.8 times on CB2, cutting the temperature rise by 71 to 78 and 61 to 65 percent. The study characterizes the air-side coefficient of each block and the reported ranges show how far a coefficient found for one workload can be carried to another.

all.title: Generative AI and Early-Career Computing Pathways: A Scoping Evidence Map of Skills, Employability Perceptions and Workforce Change, with Coding by Country Income Group
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Background. Generative AI coding tools spread rapidly after ChatGPT's release in November 2022, and there is concern that they change how early-career workers enter computing. Existing reviews address junior developers' perceptions, software practice or computing education, but, as far as could be read, none maps the evidence jointly by career stage, outcome type, evidence basis and country income group. Objective. To map the evidence on generative AI and skills, employability perceptions, labour-market change, task or role change and education response for computing students, recent graduates (up to 2 years after graduation) and early-career workers (up to 3 years in a software or IT role), and to show where that evidence comes from. Methods. A scoping evidence map guided by Arksey and O'Malley, Levac et al. and the Joanna Briggs Institute, and reported against PRISMA-ScR. On 7 November 2026 two free sources were searched: arXiv (1,293 records) and OpenAlex (13,005 records), supplemented by earlier purposive searching. After de-duplication and a keyword pre-filter, 702 records were shortlisted and 82 were assessed in detail. The protocol was not registered. Screening and charting were done in a single pass by an AI assistant under the sole author's direction and have not been independently verified. Findings were tagged by evidence basis, and countries were coded to World Bank FY27 income groups for context. Results. Twenty-seven studies were included (29 charted rows). Twenty were from 2026. Hiring evidence is unsettled: US junior software vacancies fell 14 to 15% relative to senior vacancies, while firms adopting GitHub Copilot were 3 to 5% more likely to hire software engineers each month, driven by entry-level hires. Student studies reported job concern alongside a belief that AI skills are necessary, including surveys from Egypt, India and Brazil. Nine studies used high-income data only, five included verified lower- or upper-middle-income countries, and none reported results by income group. No verified Pakistan-specific study met the criteria. Conclusions. The evidence base is small, recent, mostly preprints and concentrated in high-income countries. A fuller, registered, multi-database review with dual screening is needed before conclusions are drawn for lower-income settings, including Pakistan.

all.title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
all.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.

all.title: How NBU’s Communications Have Changed During Full-Scale War: An AI Perspective
all.abstract: This study examines how the National Bank of Ukraine’s (NBU) communications have changed during the full-scale war. Using a large language model (LLM, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite), we classify each sentence of 43 Inflation Reports published in 2015–2026 as policy or nonpolicy communications. We then split policy communications into main objectives (price stability, financial stability, and economic activity), additional tasks (such as anchoring expectations or exchange rate considerations), and the rationales for policy decisions. The share of policy communications, which had already been rising before the full-scale war, averaged 21.3% during the full-scale war, compared to 14.9% before it, and peaked at 26.5% during the transition to managed exchange rate flexibility. The outbreak of full-scale war shifted emphasis toward the financial stability objective and exchange rate-related tasks, while price stability remained the central objective and again accounted for the largest share of main-objective communications under flexible inflation targeting (IT). Supporting regressions show that FX-related topics track exchange rate developments and FX interventions, mainly during managed flexibility, whereas core mandate topics are covered regardless of macroeconomic dynamics. The results are model-dependent, but the framework offers central banks a practical tool for monitoring their communication.

all.title: Selective ROM Weight Storage for Responsive LLM Control on Edge Robots
all.abstract: Edge robots increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for complex tasks, demanding efficient inference alongside timely control. Limited memory capacity constrains model deployment, while repeated weight transfers during decoding compete with activations and KV cache for external bandwidth. Sequential generation of robot actions further delays decisions and periodic control on shared hardware. We present a hybrid memory architecture with heterogeneous scheduling to address these bottlenecks jointly. Banked ROM stores selected fixed weights and supplies a standard compute array through a dedicated datapath. LPDDR retains the remaining weights and mutable state, preserving model flexibility. Coordinated operand delivery and preemption at output slice boundaries accelerate inference while limiting interference with periodic control. A structured decision interface scores candidate phases in a single forward pass, avoiding sequential token generation for routine choices. Together, these mechanisms improve memory service, compute access, and decision execution for edge robotic workloads. Experiments with Qwen3-8B achieve a peak decode speedup of 1.56$\times$ and reduce P99 task response time by a factor of approximately 227.27$\times$, while completing 100.00\% of the tested grasping and transport tasks.

all.title: Physical-semantic information calibration framework for knowledge-enhanced spatiotemporal forecasting
Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
all.abstract: Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.

all.title: Synonym Substitution Attacks in Low-Resource NLP: A Survey with a Focus on Ukrainian
all.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art results across natural-language tasks yet remain vulnerable to synonym substitution attacks (SSAs) — adversarial inputs in which contextually similar words replace key tokens while preserving human-perceived meaning. This survey examines 60 peer-reviewed papers and preprints published between 2018 and 2026, selected through a snowballing protocol and keyword searches on Google Scholar, arXiv, and ACL Anthology. We group existing SSA techniques into dictionary-based, masked-language-model-based (MLM), and reinforcement-learning-based (RL) approaches and compare their effectiveness against transformers and instruction-tuned LLMs. Special attention is given to low-resource languages, with an illustrative example from Arabic and an in-depth analysis of the scarcity of Ukrainian-specific resources and benchmarks. Our review highlights three persistent gaps: (i) the lack of sense-aware synonym banks and word-sense disambiguation tools for Ukrainian; (ii) the absence of standardized robustness benchmarks for Ukrainian downstream tasks; and (iii) the unexplored potential of adaptive RL attackers in this setting. To close these gaps, we outline a research agenda that includes releasing a morphology-aware Ukrainian synonym dataset, building a multi-task robustness benchmark, and developing an RL-driven SSA framework. Addressing these issues will not only strengthen the security of Ukrainian NLP systems, but also provide a transferable blueprint for improving adversarial evaluation in other low-resource languages.

all.title: Architecture-conditional prompt sensitivity in LLM evaluators: A dual-axis account of instruction style effects on divergent thinking scoring
all.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as automated evaluators of human creativity, yet the scoring instruction they receive is usually written once and left unexamined. This study treats that instruction as a design variable and asks the question practitioners face directly: does the prompt that works for one model transfer to another? Thirteen models, chosen to dissociate training paradigm, parameter scale, and base architecture, each scored the same 2,000-response Alternative Uses Task bank under five instruction styles, from a bare rating command to a detailed rubric, under deterministic decoding. Instruction style and model family interacted systematically. The detailed rubric improved correlation with human raters in 8 of 13 models, but the advantage was family-conditional: the Llama-generalist family scored better under concise instructions, the Qwen-generalist family was insensitive to the difference, and the remaining three families gained from detail. Few-shot prompting was the most reliable winner across families, while chain-of-thought and persona-only framings degraded scoring in every family, penalties that family-level tests confirmed across the model set. No reasoning-trained model inverted the detail preference under controlled comparison. Reporting a single correlation concealed systematic costs: in most models the prompt maximizing rank-order agreement did not minimize absolute error, and every model-variant configuration over-scored the human distribution. Effects preserved their sign across decoding temperatures when they were medium or large. A prompt optimum validated on one architecture therefore carries no warrant on another, and the scoring instruction belongs among the deliberate design decisions of LLM evaluation rather than among its unexamined defaults.

all.title: GlanceNav: Efficient Vision-and-Language Navigation with Streaming Memory and Counterfactual Rewind
all.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong policies for vision-and-language navigation (VLN). However, most of them encode a sample of past frames again at every decision and are trained on isolated decisions, so computation is redundant and the usable history is short. They also learn from their own mistakes through outcome rewards that give one scalar to a whole episode. We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9% and 73.6% on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104 ms per step.

all.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Accounting Judgment: A Proposed Cognitive Coding Scheme and a Rule-Based Adaptive Collaboration Protocol
all.abstract: Large language models create an accounting information systems design problem: how should evidence production, professional evaluation, and responsibility be allocated between a model and an accountant? We propose a Cognitive Decomposition for Accounting Judgment (CDAJ) coding scheme crossing four process stages with information-intensive and evaluative demands. An Adaptive Collaboration Protocol (ACP) connects allocation rules to an independent human estimate, source-linked model output, structured verification, and a documented human conclusion. Two separately returned coding forms cover 20 constructed cases. A disclosed primary-only analysis retains unresolved auxiliary response formats. Raw agreement is 19/20 for unitization, 20/20 for stage, and 18/20 for demand. On 14 jointly single, codable cases, nominal Cohen's kappa is 1.000 for stage and 0.752 for I/E/M demand profiles; only 12/20 cases are jointly resolved to I or E. A public-disclosure diagnostic searches 1,406 pages for 18 numeric reference cards from three banks' annual reports. Adding a value/period/unit co-occurrence gate to BM25 with identical query information does not improve designated-origin recovery at ranks one or three: both methods recover 13/18 origins at rank one and 18/18 within three ranks. A post-hoc audit distinguishes page recovery from requested table-cell verification. Synthetic checks examine event ordering and record integrity; Gaussian planning experiments examine a future effectiveness evaluation. A separate source-response audit records adverse or unclear statuses in 16/36 returned records. These bounded findings concern coding repeatability and implementation properties. They do not establish an optimal allocation, a validated taxonomy, or improved professional judgment.

all.title: Nexus Core: A CPU-Native Hybrid Architecture for Language Modeling.
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The dominant deployment paradigm for large language models assumes an accelerator: a GPU in a datacenter, or an NPU in a flagship handset. Yet the fastest-growing segment of applied AI — on-device, offline, and privacy-sensitive inference — runs on general-purpose CPUs, where the transformer’s growing key–value (KV) cache and dense floating-point matmuls impose hard limits on memory, latency, and energy. This paper presents Nexus Core, a CPU-native hybrid language-model architecture that replaces history-proportional state with a heterogeneous, provably bounded state bundle: five gated selective state-space mixers, one bank of 64 addressable episodic memory slots, spread across our novel 1 M, intertwined sectors on our “NOAH”, system, one causal linear-attention prefix mixer, and one SoftMax attention layer restricted to a 64-token local window. We document the full architectural lineage — Interleaved, Triad, NOAH Quad, and the CPU-native flagship — and the measured evidence from project logs: where we document our first run which involved a 25.24M-parameter model trained entirely on a laptop CPU whose validation perplexity on WikiText-2 improved from 247.63 to 189.20 (−24.0%) between 5,000 and 20,000 steps while decode throughput (6.67 tok/s) and resident memory (~738 MiB) remained flat, and whose linear weights compress 3.97× under INT8 with a perplexity delta of only −0.028. We then moved ahead and incorporated a 13.8B run across only 64 sectors of NOAH and hit an index of 883.2B-parameter in the improved Noah-quad run model at throughput (~121tok/s), allowing us to index that the new age of CPU, cognitive AI language model is here.

all.title: A Reality-Constrained Hybrid Decision-Support Framework for Evaluating Strategic Development Pathways under Deep Uncertainty: Evidence from Libya's Fezzan Region
all.venue: Journal of sustainable research in applied sciences
all.abstract: Resource-dependent economies face structural challenges that demand decision-making under deep uncertainty. This study develops an exploratory framework to compare continuing the oil-rent model (Alternative A1) with a transition to an integrated Green–Blue Economy (Alternative A2) in Libya's Fezzan region. Because complete local data are unavailable, a reality-constrained synthetic experiment was used: 20,000 candidate scenarios were drawn within bounds taken from World Bank, FAOSTAT, IRENA and NASA-derived sources, and 10,000 were retained. Generative AI served only for qualitative scenario framing. Criteria were weighted by the Analytic Hierarchy Process (CR = 0.010) and alternatives ranked by TOPSIS and VIKOR, complemented by Sobol sensitivity analysis and Robust Decision Making. A2 outperformed A1 (mean TOPSIS closeness 0.666 vs 0.335; p < 0.001), but the advantage is conditional: A1 wins in all 222 scenarios combining oil prices above $95/barrel with green investment below $300 million. Green investment (ST = 0.57) and oil price (ST = 0.32) dominate output variance. Robustness checks (weight perturbation, four MCDA methods, Fuzzy AHP, stress tests, alternative distributions) did not reverse the aggregate ranking. Results are illustrative, not forecasts.

all.title: Evaluating Symbolic Persona Anchoring and Direct KV-Cache Interventions for Multi-Turn LLM Persona Preservation: A Six-Method, 10-Model Longitudinal Study
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Maintaining consistent behavioral personas across extended multi-turn dialogues remains a central challenge for open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs), which suffer from progressive persona drift, attention dilution, and vulnerability to adversarial prompts or context flooding. Extending our prior evaluation of Symbolic Persona Anchoring (SPA) against natural-language reminders (Mehta, 2026), this study conducts a balanced 6 × 10 × 4 longitudinal benchmark (240 trajectories, 12,000 turns across 50-turn rollouts) comparing six inference-time interventions across 10 open-weight models (3B–14B) and four personas: baseline controls (A1 Raw History, A2 Generic Reminder), symbolic anchoring (A3 Continuous SPA), and multi-turn adaptations of direct Key-Value (KV) cache interventions (A4 Belitsky-style additive steering, A5 Sun-style mid-layer transplantation, and A6 Memory Inception latent KV banks). Across N = 40 matched cells per arm, A2 achieves the highest mean semantic preservation (Psem = 0.4781 ± 0.0597) but incurs a 27.5% late-horizon MATTR50-decline flag rate (ΔMATTR50 < −0.08). Conversely, A3 maintains competitive semantic preservation (Psem = 0.4589 ± 0.0600) with no significant differential drift relative to A2 (p = 0.388) while achieving the highest lexical diversity (MATTR50 = 0.8155) and lowest MATTR50-decline incidence (7.5%). Direct KV-cache interventions exhibit sharp architectural sensitivity: A5 peaks on Mistral and Qwen-2.5-7B backbones yet suffers the steepest longitudinal decay (p < 0.001), whereas zero-shot A4 and A6 regress toward unanchored A1. All trajectory logs and metrics are byte-verified via SHA-256 checksums and bitwise recomputation. Source Code and Reproducibility The associated GitHub repository contains the research project's codebase and reproducibility resources for the six-method, 10-model longitudinal benchmark. GitHub Repository: KV-Cache vs. SPA Official GitHub Release: KV-Cache vs. SPA — Research Benchmark Release v1.0.0 Release Version: v1.0.0 Citation If you find this research useful in your work, please consider citing it using the following DOI: DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24424861 Suggested citation:Nabh Sanjay, M. (2026). Evaluating Symbolic Persona Anchoring and Direct KV-Cache Interventions for Multi-Turn LLM Persona Preservation: A Six-Method, 10-Model Longitudinal Study (Version 1.0.0). Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24424861 Research Institution:Phlowerman Ventures LLPAI Systems & Mechanistic Interpretability Research

all.title: The Rung That Was Never Built: AI Labor Measurement and Africa's Foreclosed Development
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: An unbuilt factory carries a weight of zero in every global AI labor index. Occupational indices from the International Labour Organization, the International Monetary Fund, and the World Bank score current jobs, while developer indices count user traffic. The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act assesses risks only to persons inside a specific deployment context. Small formal workforces leave low-income economies scoring lowest. Nearly all future growth in the world's working-age population will occur in Africa. Earlier declines in manufacturing narrowed the factory route that absorbed young workers in past transitions, pushing development strategy toward exportable service jobs such as customer support and data processing. Industrial robots and generative AI now automate both channels. Young workers entering African labor markets lose those factory and office routes to cumulative automation abroad. Medical loss-of-chance law, cross-border environmental impact assessment, and international climate loss-and-damage funding each address one part of that injury. Cross-border exposure models built for industrial robots can score those services pathways. Keywords: AI Labor Measurement, Occupational Exposure Indices, Generative Artificial Intelligence, Premature Deindustrialization, Robot-Driven Reshoring, Industries Without Smokestacks, Tradable Services, Business Process Outsourcing, African Demographic Dividend, Structural Transformation, Youth Labor Market Entry, Counterfactual Harm, Loss of Chance Doctrine, Transboundary Harm, Environmental Impact Assessment, Climate Loss and Damage, EU Artificial Intelligence Act, Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment, Anthropic Economic Index, Cross-Border Exposure

all.title: Putting ChatGPT to the Test: Accuracy and Error Patterns in Clinical and Physics-Based Radiation Oncology Questions
all.abstract: Objective Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used as revision tools. Radiation oncology encompasses a complex skill set, including clinical staging, trials, anatomy, radiobiology, physics, mathematical calculations, treatment planning, and quality assurance (QA). The accuracy, reasonability, and error types of two ChatGPT models were assessed across clinical and medical physics radiation oncology examination question banks. Methodology Two independent scoring studies were undertaken (n = 200). Cohort 1 assessed the accuracy of ChatGPT 5.5 across 100 single-best-answer clinical questions from the American College of Radiology (ACR) Radiation Oncology In-Training Examination (TXIT). Questions were selected at random using a computer-generated random sampling script (25 questions per year from the years 2021, 2024, 2025, and 2026). Cohort 2 assessed ChatGPT 5.6 (Luna build, v5.6) across 100 RAPHEX-style radiation oncology physics multiple-choice questions covering five domains of physics. Each question was asked once using a standardized zero-shot prompt requesting a single best answer with reasoning. Accuracy was scored against published answer keys. Response length, error types, and exploratory scoring of reasoning quality (0-2) were noted. Chi-square (χ²), Fisher's exact, Welch's t-test, and Mann-Whitney U tests were used to compare results (P = 0.05). Results ChatGPT 5.5 had an overall accuracy of 82.0% (82/100) (95% confidence interval (CI): 72.8%-89.0%). Accuracy was 100% for radiobiology, pediatrics, and renal/bladder oncology. Accuracy was lowest for gynecological oncology (female) at 60.0% and benign/palliative radiation oncology at 66.7%. Accuracy varied between years of examination (2021-2026) from 76.0% to 88.0% (χ² = 2.44, df = 3, P = 0.49). Incorrect responses had a greater mean length compared to correct responses (227.657.5 vs. 202.144.3) (Welch's t = 1.77, P = 0.09) (Mann-Whitney U = 551.5, P = 0.10). Error types were mainly guideline/trial/numerical-specific recall errors (5/18, 27.8%). ChatGPT 5.6 had an overall accuracy of 87.0% (87/100) (95% CI: 78.7%-93.2%). Accuracy was highest for brachytherapy (15/15, 100%) and imaging/planning (24/25, 96.0%). Accuracy was lowest for beam physics (21/27, 77.8%). Mean length of reasoning was 186.848.2 words (correct = 188.4, incorrect = 176.2) (Student's t = 0.81, P = 0.42). Error types were most commonly conceptual errors (5/13, 38%) and self-contradictory responses (4/13, 31%). Conclusions Both ChatGPT 5.5 and ChatGPT 5.6 had high agreement with the answer keys. However, error types differed. Clinical errors were mainly due to detailed guideline/trial recall and anatomical staging errors. Physics errors were often due to conceptual errors and mathematical contradictions. LLMs can be useful as revision tools; however, responses must be validated against authoritative literature.

all.title: Recognised ROI: A Routing Identity and Recognition Rule for Measuring the Return on AI Efficiency Gains
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Organisations commonly report the return on artificial intelligence by multiplying the hours a tool saves by a fully loaded labour rate. Field experiments support the first half of that calculation: generative AI releases measurable capacity on many tasks. The best available administrative evidence does not support the second half. In linked Danish records, earnings, recorded hours, employment and wage bills have so far moved little, and the chief financial officer of a major bank has said that the benefits are not observable in its quarterly earnings. This paper argues that the gap is not only a measurement lag to be waited out. It is also the predictable result of pricing a reduction in resource usage as though it were a reduction in resource spending, an error that management accounting resolved more than three decades ago. The paper proposes the Recognised ROI model. The model takes the AI-attributed reduction in resource usage, nets off the verification and induced rework created by the AI output, and routes the remainder to five exhaustive destinations: supply removed, supply avoided, additional throughput, reduced loss, and unconverted capacity. Each destination is priced at the rate at which it reaches the income statement, and unconverted capacity is priced at zero. A recognition rule then admits a benefit only where it ties to a ledger line, rests on a baseline fixed before deployment, has persisted, and is claimed once. The model yields two metrics: Recognised ROI, which is directly comparable with conventional return figures, and the Recognition Ratio, the share of the conventional claim that survives recognition. Four results follow. Committed resources convert only in whole units, so no cost can be removed below a pool size equal to the reciprocal of the saving rate. Throughput value is capped by unmet demand at the process constraint. Net release turns negative above a closed-form verification burden. The error in the conventional method is unsigned because throughput priced at contribution margin can exceed the loaded labour rate. A synthetic discrimination test shows three teams with identical hours saved, which the conventional method and a single capture rate score identically, receiving Recognised ROI of 250%, minus 100% and 400%. The paper positions the model between two bodies of prior work: the resource usage model of Cooper and Kaplan (1992) and the capability realisation framework of Bell (2026b). It states seven testable propositions with falsifiers and makes no claim to empirical calibration.

all.title: Self-Indexed Sparse SwiGLU: Zero-Training Coarse-to-Fine Routing, Negative-Overhead Mixed-Precision Storage, and Pre-Attention PCIe 5.0 Prefetching
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Model (LLM) decoding at low batch sizes is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory bandwidth, with gated Feed-Forward Networks (SwiGLU / GeGLU) accounting for 85–90% of parameter traffic in modern Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) Transformers. Existing sparse inference engines face a structural trilemma: learned-predictor runtimes (e.g., DejaVu, PowerInfer) require ReLU conversion and auxiliary predictor training that inflates VRAM; gate-thresholding methods (e.g., CATS) still read 100% of the dense gate projection; and coordinate-pruning methods (e.g., TEAL) corrupt exact inner products past 40–50% sparsity. We introduce FFMod (v0.2.0), a zero-training, zero-calibration sparse LLM inference architecture in Triton and PyTorch built on separating static knowledge storage from dynamic input-dependent compute planning: Self-Indexed Dual-Branch Smooth-INT4 x Top-D Router: Constructed analytically from any pretrained SwiGLU or GeGLU weight triplet (Llama, Qwen2/2.5/3, Mistral, Gemma-2, Phi-3, DeepSeek) with zero calibration data, scanning <5% of dense FFN memory traffic to identify winning channels and evaluating them across the full hidden dimension H (compatible with torch.compile(fullgraph=True), CUDAGraph, and speculative decoding micro-batches N=1..8). Negative-Overhead BitSplit-12 and FP8 Sparse Kernels: Eliminates the index memory overhead while accelerating execution. On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 Laptop GPU (Blackwell, 24 GB GDDR7), Qwen2.5-3B VRAM drops by 13.0% in BitSplit-12 (5.37 GB vs. 6.17 GB dense BF16) and by 26.1% in FP8 (4.56 GB), achieving 2.36x–3.54x cold-cache FFN speedups, 1.51x speedup over dense cuBLAS Tensor Cores at speculative N=4, and 1.57x–1.70x end-to-end decoding throughput (91.6 to 143.6–155.2 tok/s). KV-Safe Hybrid Layer Scheduling & 12-SM Open-Page DDR5 PCIe 5.0 Tiered Engine: Uncovers the KV-Cache Pollution Paradox across transformer depth and co-designs a 12-SM coalesced UVA gather kernel (38.83 GB/s random channel gather over PCIe 5.0 x16, +30.2% over 82-SM bank-thrashing UVA while leaving 85.4% of GPU SMs free for 96–99% compute/DMA overlap). By prefetching a high-confidence 35% channel core prior to Self-Attention (92.6% precision) and overlapping exact post-attention delta fixup inside a single two-stream fork-join CUDAGraph, FFMod runs 64-layer Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (65.53 GB BF16) with 100.0% Top-1 agreement (KL = 0.0139) at 3.84–5.40 tok/s (4.74x–6.67x speedup) in 21.1 GB VRAM and 3.41–4.29 tok/s (4.32x–5.43x speedup) under a strict 15.6 GB VRAM cap. Unified VRAM-First Auto Allocator & Persistent Sharded Cache (.ffmod_cache_v1): Uses 0 GB host RAM whenever a model fits in GPU VRAM, and persists canonical budget-independent Smooth-INT4 + FP8 shards (1.81x smaller on disk, hydrating 64 layers in ~10.8 s from PCIe NVMe with zero re-quantization), exposed via an OpenAI-compatible HTTP/SSE server (ffmod-serve) and a vLLM plugin. Open-Source Code & Reproducibility Suite: https://github.com/ferencfresz/ffmod01
