all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

all.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Digital Infrastructure, and Business Productivity: A Cross-Country Empirical Analysis Using Secondary Data
all.abstract: AuthorsMhel Cedric D. BendoCollege of Business Administration, Polytechnic University of the Philippines, Maragondon Campus, Cavite, Philippines,Domar C. AlviarArts and Languages Department, College of Education, Arts, and Sciences, National University, Manila, Philippines,Ma. Victoria Ulgado-RosasGraduate School of Business, Colegio de San Juan de Letran, Manila, PhilippinesAvillardo V. ClarinCollege of Business and Accountancy, National University, Manila, PhilippinesLucky S. CarpioFlorentino Cayco Memorial School of Graduate Studies, Arellano University, Manila, PhilippinesAriel M. GomezArchitectural Engineering Department, United Arab Emirates University, Maqam Campus, Al Ain, UAE. How to CiteBendo, M. C. D., Alviar, D. C., Ulgado-Rosas, M. V., Clarin, A. V., Carpio, L. S., & Gomez, A. M. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Digital Infrastructure, and Business Productivity: A Cross-Country Empirical Analysis Using Secondary Data. International Review of Management and Marketing, 16(6), 292–302. https://doi.org/10.32479/irmm.24231 Keywords: Artificial Intelligence Adoption; Digital Infrastructure; Business Productivity; Technological Readiness; Cross-Country Analysis; Digital Economy AbstractArtificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology reshaping business operations and economic productivity across industries and countries. As organizations increasingly integrate AI-driven systems into operational processes, understanding the relationship between AI adoption and productivity outcomes has become a critical research concern. This study employs a cross-country quantitative secondary data analysis using harmonized datasets from the OECD Artificial Intelligence Policy Observatory, the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Index, the World Bank World Development Indicators, and the McKinsey & Company. The sample includes five economies representing varying levels of digital development. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and multivariate regression modeling are applied to examine relationships among AI adoption, digital infrastructure, and business productivity. Findings reveal a positive and statistically significant effect of AI adoption on productivity, with digital infrastructure strengthening this relationship. Industries characterized by higher data intensity demonstrate greater AI adoption rates. The findings contribute a structured cross-country empirical framework linking artificial intelligence adoption, digital infrastructure, and productivity performance across developed and emerging economies. The results emphasize the importance of technological readiness, innovation ecosystems, and data-driven capabilities in supporting productivity growth within digitally transforming economies. The findings provide insights for policymakers, leaders, and digital transformation strategists seeking to strengthen economic competitiveness.

all.title: Separating AI from Capital: Identifying the Productivity Contribution of Artificial Intelligence across Countries and Sectors
all.abstract: Does enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) raise total factor productivity (TFP), or does measured output growth mainly reflect capital deepening and labour growth? We separate these channels in two stages. First, we compute T\"ornqvist growth-accounting residuals using time-varying labour shares from the Penn World Table (PWT) 10.01, with PWT capital stocks extended to 2024 by perpetual inventory using World Bank investment data. Second, we relate TFP growth to the share of enterprises using AI, taken from Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) business surveys, in a country-year panel with country and year fixed effects. To address endogenous adoption, we use shift-share instruments that interact 2010 fixed-broadband and internet penetration with leave-one-out cross-country AI diffusion, estimated by two-stage least squares (2SLS) and limited-information maximum likelihood (LIML), with weak-instrument-robust Anderson--Rubin inference. Because adoption data cover only 36 countries in recent years (102 country-year observations), statistical power is limited. We find no detectable contemporaneous effect of AI adoption on TFP growth: the fixed-effects estimate is 0.005 percentage points per percentage point of adoption ($p = 0.93$), and the 2SLS and LIML estimates are 0.153 ($p = 0.42$) and 0.299 ($p = 0.48$), with a weak first stage. Point estimates at one- and two-year lags are larger (0.054 and 0.096) but imprecise. A sectoral exposure design with country-by-year and sector-by-year fixed effects, an OECD-only subsample, and a leave-one-country-out jackknife give similar results. The evidence is consistent with, but cannot confirm, a delayed productivity J-curve. JEL Classification: O33 , O47 , C23 , C26 , E23 , D24

all.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Financial Decision-Making, and Firm Growth: Evidence From Nigerian Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises.
all.venue: Journal of Current Research and Studies
all.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in the relationship between financial decision-making quality and firm growth among Nigerian micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs). Adopting a positivist philosophy and a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design, the study collected primary data from 144 MSME owners and managers in Nigeria using a structured questionnaire. Hypothesised relationships were tested using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4, with bootstrapping (5,000 subsamples) used to estimate direct, indirect, and total effects. Independent-samples t-tests and one-way ANOVAs with Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons examined group differences. Financial decision-making quality is positively and significantly associated with firm growth, both directly (β = 0.218, p = .003) and indirectly through AI adoption (indirect effect = 0.332, p < .001). AI adoption is strongly associated with firm growth (β = 0.542, p < .001). The variance accounted for (VAF) is 60.4%, indicating partial mediation: about 60% of the total association is transmitted through AI adoption. AI adoption differs significantly across sectors (F(3, 140) = 4.28, p = .006), with services and manufacturing firms reporting higher adoption than trade/retail and agro-processing. Financial decision-making quality differs significantly across educational levels (F(3, 140) = 5.14, p = .002). The model explains 48.2% of the variance in firm growth and 37.5% in AI adoption. The study extends an AI-finance literature dominated by banks to MSMEs, providing survey evidence on a mediation model in which AI adoption operationalises financial decision-making capabilities for firm growth, and documenting heterogeneity across sectors and education levels.

all.title: Leveraging Artificial Intelligence in Predicting and Mitigating Food Insecurity in Nigeria
all.venue: International Journal of Latest Technology in Engineering Management & Applied Science
all.abstract: Food insecurity remains a critical challenge in Nigeria, driven by climate change, population growth, economic instability, and low agricultural productivity. This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be leveraged to predict and mitigate food insecurity in Nigeria. Adopting a systematic review design, the study synthesizes evidence from recent empirical and conceptual studies on AI applications in agriculture, climate risk management, and food systems. In addition, descriptive trends from the World Bank and the Food and Agriculture Organization are used to contextualize the Nigerian experience. The findings reveal that AI technologies, particularly machine learning and deep learning models, have strong predictive capabilities in identifying food insecurity risks through the analysis of climatic, economic, and agricultural data. Furthermore, AI contributes to mitigation by enhancing crop productivity, improving resource efficiency, supporting climate-smart agriculture, and optimizing food supply chains. Despite these benefits, the study identifies significant barriers to AI adoption, including infrastructural deficits, limited data availability, high costs, and low technical capacity among farmers. The results also highlight that existing studies are largely fragmented, focusing on isolated aspects such as prediction or productivity without integrating them into a comprehensive framework. The study concludes that while AI holds significant potential for transforming food security outcomes in Nigeria, its impact depends on effective integration, supportive policies, and inclusive implementation. It recommends a coordinated approach that combines predictive analytics with actionable mitigation strategies to enhance food system resilience.

all.title: AI Readiness, Adoption, and Productivity: Firm-Level Evidence from Low- and Middle-Income Countries
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Can firms in developing economies translate readiness for artificial intelligence (AI) into higher productivity and greater AI adoption? This paper develops Firm-Level AI Enablement Index (FAEI), a composite measure of Power Reliability, Digital Connectivity, Human Capital, and Institutional Environment. Using World Bank Enterprise Survey data for 44,251 firms across 76 low- and middle-income economies and a 2026 follow-up covering 3,579 firms in seven economies, the analysis examines the relationship between readiness, adoption, and productivity. The findings are as follows. First, the FAEI is strongly associated with labour productivity. A 0.1 increase in FAEI is associated with 11.5 percent higher sales per worker, conditional on country, sector, and survey-year fixed effects. Second, Human Capital shows the strongest positive association among the four pillars, followed by Power Reliability and Digital Connectivity. Third, FAEI is not consistently associated with AI adoption. However, firm-level digital practices, particularly website presence and electronic payments, are positively associated with AI adoption and several measures of AI engagement. Fourth, AI adoption is not significantly associated with productivity in the 2026 follow-up and readiness is no more strongly associated with productivity in industries with greater AI exposure. These findings highlight the heterogeneity between the capabilities associated with firm productivity and practices associated with AI adoption. For developing economies, strengthening Human Capital and foundational digital capabilities may be important priorities for improving firm performance and supporting AI adoption.

all.title: Scalability and Efficiency enhanced based Machine Learning for Hyperledger Fabric and Private Ethereum in Smart Contract Execution
all.abstract: Blockchain platform selection for enterprise applications increasingly rests on empirical throughput and latency evidence rather than architectural claims alone. This paper proposed a benchmarking work flow based machine learning to compare Hyperledger Fabric v2.5 and private Ethereum (Geth) across four smart contract functions (QueryUser, Crea-5 teUser, IssueMoney, and TransferMoney) under varying network sizes (2–16 peers) and 6 transaction batch sizes (10–1,000), plus an additional 10,000-transaction scalability stress 7 test on Ethereum. Both platforms were independently rebuilt on a single-host Docker 8 deployment, implemented equivalent banking-application smart contracts in Solidity and 9 Go, and reran the full experimental matrix using an in-house benchmarking harness. Our 10 results corroborate the original paper’s central claims: Fabric outperforms Ethereum on 11 write-heavy invoke operations by a factor of roughly 1.4–8.2× depending on network size, 12 while Ethereum’s account-based ledger model yields consistently higher query throughput 13 (1,224 vs. 594 TPS, averaged across all tested batch sizes). This Paper additionally identify 14 a failure mode not emphasized in the original study: Fabric’s multi-key read-modify-write 15 function (TransferMoney) failed under optimistic-concurrency conflicts at every tested 16 batch size and, notably, at a rate that was statistically invariant to peer count. Beyond 17 reproduction, This Paper contributes a supervised machine-learning layer: Random Forest 18 and Gradient Boosting regressors trained on the reproduced dataset to predict through-19 put and latency directly from network configuration. Under leave-one-peer-count-out 20 cross-validation, the surrogate model predicts per-transaction latency with high fidelity 21 (R 2 = 0.887) but throughput far less reliably (R 2 = 0.478), a gap attribute to the discontinu-22 ous, contention-driven nature of the throughput data itself. This paper discuss deviations 23 from the original study’s setup and their implications for the generalizability of both papers’ 24 findings.

all.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND CAPITAL MARKET PERFORMANCE IN NIGERIA: EVIDENCE OF SPILLOVERS FROM THE GLOBAL AI MARKET
all.abstract: This study investigates the effect of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on capital market performance in Nigeria, using the Adaptive Market Hypothesis as its theoretical framework. The study examines whether growth in the global AI market is associated with changes in Nigeria’s capital market performance, measured by stock market capitalisation. Secondary annual data were obtained from the World Bank, Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), and relevant industry reports. To account for potential technology diffusion lags, global AI market size was introduced with a one-year lag. Brent crude oil price, USD/NGN exchange rate, and inflation rate were included as control variables. Pearson correlation and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression were employed for the empirical analysis. The findings indicate that global AI market growth has no statistically significant immediate effect on Nigeria’s capital market performance. However, the positive coefficient associated with the one-year lag suggests a potential delayed transmission effect, while the inclusion of macroeconomic controls improves the explanatory power of the model. The findings suggest that the benefits of global AI development may reach Nigeria gradually through channels such as fintech adoption, algorithmic trading, digital financial services, and investor sentiment. The study contributes to the emerging literature by providing empirical evidence on the relationship between global AI market development and Nigeria’s capital market performance, thereby extending the discussion of AI and financial markets to an emerging-market context.

all.title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
all.abstract: Predictive artificial intelligence (AI) models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice, the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here, we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge. Funding: This research was supported in part by funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council [Grant 430-2024-01156] to M. Joshi.

all.title: Collaborating with Machines: A Qualitative Study on Job Satisfaction Among Banking Employees
all.venue: International Scientific Journal of Engineering and Management
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence is no longer a futuristic concept, it is the defining technology of 21st century, embedding itself into every aspect of our lives. Industry 5.0 communicate the next phase of industrialisation focussing on the association between Human imagination or creativity with the AI driven technology. The swift progress of technologies and artificial intelligence has touched and transformed every sector and the Banking sector is not left out of this either leading to enhanced interaction and dependence of employees and the system. The human-machine collaboration has become a prime component of the workplaces now where employees are working in a data driven environment and presence of both is equally valuable. It refers to the interplay between the technological system and employees of the organisation. The aim of this collaboration is to improve or enhance productivity of the organisation by easing out the task of employees. However, working with machines and automated environment has an impact on the perception and satisfaction level of the employee too. The present study “Collaborating with machines: A qualitative study on Job Satisfaction among Banking employees” examines the influence of human machine collaboration on job satisfaction level of the banking employees. Over the past decade, the banking sector has seen a massive upgradation in the technology adoption. The online banking platforms, digital payment technologies and AI driven applications are its various examples. The motive of the research is to explore how the adoption of advanced technologies is perceived by the employees and how it has affected the motivation and satisfaction level of employees. A qualitative research approach was adopted by using a semi-structured comprehensive interview of banking professionals working with either public or private sector bank. Qualitative methods are best suited for complex workplace phenomenon as they allow to collect detailed insights of perspectives of interviewee about its work and environment both. Purposive sampling was selected as the sampling method as employees with higher level of interaction with technology were interviewed. The data collected was analysed using thematic analysis to identify repetitive patterns, themes and apprehensions of employees. The results depicted that machine collaboration in the form of digital banking platform, automated service tools and AI based systems have notably moulded the employees’ working culture and processes. The data suggests that the association can improve job satisfaction by upgrading work efficiency, minimising the routine works and empowering employees to concentrate effectively on customer satisfaction and other strategic roles. The study at the same time also highlights some issues like the very common technological anxiety, need for employees’ advancement and increased work load of monitoring digital performance. These factors pop up irritation in employees and influence the satisfaction levels. The findings proposes that organisations should ensure proper training and technological support for the employees. The use of machines has always made the work easier and quick only if machines are used in the right way. Quick and easy work automatically maintains a high job satisfaction level among employees. The study contributes to the existing literature on Industry 5.0, technology driven workplaces and well-being of employees in particular and for banking industry in specific. It also provides strategic understandings for the policy makers and managers who want to maintain a satisfied and motivated workforce along with technological upgradation.

all.title: The Impact and Implementation of Advanced Security Technologies in Online Banking
all.venue: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences
all.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital banking has increased cybersecurity risks, necessitating the adoption of advanced security technologies to safeguard online financial transactions. This study investigates the influence of technological, organizational, and environmental factors on the adoption of advanced security technologies in online banking based on the Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) framework. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 60 online banking users, and data were analyzed using SPSS through descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation, and multiple regression techniques. The results indicate that technological and organizational factors significantly influence adoption, with organizational factors representing the strongest predictor. In contrast, environmental factors related to artificial intelligence technology were not found to significantly affect adoption behaviour. The regression model explains 96.4% of the variance in adoption, indicating strong predictive capability. The findings emphasize the importance of organizational readiness and technological effectiveness in enhancing trust and encouraging secure digital banking usage. This study provides empirical evidence supporting cybersecurity adoption strategies and offers practical implications for financial institutions seeking to strengthen online banking security implementation.

all.title: Is AI Adoption Outrunning Security in New Jersey Businesses?
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This research examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among New Jersey businesses is keeping pace with cybersecurity readiness and governance. The study analyzes publicly available evidence covering business AI adoption, cybersecurity incidents, data breaches, compromised credentials, reported cybercrime losses, regulatory developments, and organizational security practices. Drawing on evidence from the U.S. Census Bureau, Federal Reserve Banks, New Jersey Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Cell (NJCCIC), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), and other relevant sources, the research evaluates the relationship between growing AI adoption and the security environment facing New Jersey businesses. Key findings include: New Jersey business AI adoption reached 18.5% in May 2026, while 20.5% expected to adopt AI within six months. NJCCIC recorded 954 cybersecurity incident reports in 2025, representing a 92% increase from 2024. New Jersey recorded 1,951 initial breach reports affecting residents in 2025. FBI IC3 reported $660.4 million in cybercrime losses associated with New Jersey complaints in 2025. The research identifies a critical evidence gap: publicly available data does not establish whether New Jersey businesses adopting AI have adequate cybersecurity and governance controls within those same organizations. Rather than assigning an unsupported statewide security-gap percentage, the study proposes a matched organization-level benchmark to evaluate AI adoption alongside measurable security controls, including multifactor authentication, data protection, vendor governance, monitoring, and recovery readiness. Research Scope: New Jersey business AI adoption, cybersecurity readiness, AI governance, regulatory developments, and cyber-threat exposure. Evidence Period: 2024–September 2026. Research Lead: Milan Baria, Blueclone Networks. Supporting Materials: An accompanying CSV file containing key research metrics and quantitative information. Original Research: https://www.blueclone.com/new-jersey-ai-adoption-security-research/ Disclaimer: This publication is an evidence-based research synthesis and does not constitute legal, financial, or cybersecurity compliance advice. Findings are limited by the availability, scope, and methodology of the cited public sources.

all.title: Beyond technology acceptance: the enabling roles of awareness and perceived risk in AI-powered banking
A STUDY ON FACTORS INFLUENCING THE ADOPTION OF CHATGPT AMONG COLLEGE STUDENTS IN ERODE DISTRICT
all.venue: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
all.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a technology that enables computers and machines to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as understanding human language, recognizing faces and objects, answering questions, translating languages, making predictions, and creating images, videos, and music. Nowadays, numerous AI tools are available to make human tasks easier and more efficient, particularly in the fields of education, healthcare, banking and finance, business, marketing Human Resources Management etc. In the field of education, AI is widely used to improve efficiency, accuracy, and the overall learning experience. Among the various AI tools available, ChatGPT has gained considerable popularity among college students due to its wide range of applications and user-friendly features. Considering its growing importance in the educational sector, the present study aims to examine the factors influencing college students to use ChatGPT in Erode District of Tamil Nadu. The findings of the study indicate that Offers new ways of learning and exploring information is the most significant factor influencing college students to use ChatGPT.

all.title: Mobile Banking and Financial Inclusion in Developing Economies: A Comprehensive Review of Recent Trends
all.abstract: economies over the past decade. This systematic review aims to examine the impact of mobile banking on financial inclusion in low- and middle-income countries by identifying inclusion mechanisms, documenting persistent barriers, and comparing regional models. The study synthesises peer-reviewed literature and global database reports from 2021 to 2026, drawing on the 2025 Global Findex Database, 32 empirical studies from Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, and EconLit, and comparative case analyses from sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Findings document that mobile banking raised account ownership from 42% to 71% across developing economies (2011–2021) through four mechanisms: expanded account access, formal savings facilitation, credit access for informal enterprises, and household resilience. However, persistent barriers remain: gender gaps (48% of unbanked women in subSaharan Africa lack phones), rural-urban adoption disparities (up to 58%), digital literacy deficits, and affordability constraints. Comparative analysis reveals African agent-based and Asian digital ecosystem models as distinct but converging pathways. The study recommends an integrated policy framework addressing proportionate regulation, infrastructure investment, gender-responsive design, and digital literacy programmes. Future research should prioritise longitudinal impact studies, experimental intervention designs, intersectional analysis, and artificial intelligence applications in mobile banking.

all.title: Institutional blind spots in occupational mental health: a data-driven identification and prioritization of psychosocial risk factors using administrative records, interpretable machine learning, and psychosocial safety climate theory
The Rise of Multi-Agent AI in Strategic Human Resource Management: Exploring How Collaborative AI Agents Transform Talent Management, Workforce Coordination, and HR Decision Authority
all.venue: Journal of Business Insight and Innovation
all.abstract: This study examined how professionals in Pakistan understood the role of collaborative artificial intelligence (AI) agents in talent management, workforce coordination and HR decision authority. Guided by Socio-Technical Systems Theory and Organizational Information Processing Theory, the study used reflexive thematic analysis to interpret 20 online interviews with HR, operations and technology professionals. Six themes captured participants’ accounts of recruitment, career development, workforce planning, decision authority, procedural fairness and organizational readiness. Participants located a critical point of recruiter oversight at initial screening, when historical hiring preferences could exclude qualified applicants before human review. In development and scheduling, they identified employee aspirations, skills and personal circumstances as information that could change an otherwise plausible recommendation. They assigned responsibility for pay adjustments to compensation committees and staffing reductions to executives. Across functions, participants connected fairness with understandable reasons and access to a reviewer empowered to correct an outcome. The findings show that, in participants’ judgments, the value of collaborative agents depends on whether decision owners can inspect underlying evidence, exercise judgment and intervene when recommendations affect employment opportunities. References Abrar, K., & Amjad, S. I. (2026). Gamified advertising in the metaverse: How Pakistani brands can leverage virtual experiences for customer engagement. all.title: Proved, Probable, Possible: A Board Reporting Framework for the Return on AI Efficiency Gains
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Management usually reports the return on an investment in artificial intelligence to its board as a single figure. That figure carries two different things at once: benefit that has reached the accounts and benefit that management expects to reach them. When management combines the two, a board cannot tell how much of the reported return has been banked, how much depends on decisions not yet taken, and how much rests on capacity that no one has acted on. The Australian Institute of Company Directors now advises boards on how to assess AI return on investment but provides no form for doing so. This paper proposes a reporting framework that separates those quantities. It classifies the return on an AI efficiency gain into three classes. Proved return has met a four-part recognition rule and is tied to a ledger line. Probable return is supported by a dated conversion commitment from the owner of the affected cost centre. Possible return is verified released capacity with a feasible path to the income statement and no commitment. Released capacity with no feasible path is reported as stranded and carries no value. The structure is adapted from mineral reserves reporting, in which confidence in a quantity and the conditions for converting it into economic value are assessed on separate axes. The framework reports return as a band of three figures: a floor on proved return alone, an expected figure that adds probable return adjusted by the organisation’s own record of commitments kept, and a ceiling that adds possible return. It adds two measures that, to the author’s knowledge, existing AI return methods do not report in this form. Leakage is the spend that continued in the period on capacity that AI had released and that was not converted. Conversion yield is the share of past commitments that were later proved, which calibrates the expected figure from the organisation’s own history in place of an assumed realisation rate. An AI Return Statement brings the classes, the band, a capacity roll-forward, leakage and yield onto a single page, with attestation divided between the technology function, the cost centre owner, the risk function, finance and internal audit. In a worked illustration, a portfolio with a conventional return of 473% reports a floor of 17%, an unadjusted expected return of 183% and annualised leakage of about $402,000. Carried over three reporting dates with constructed events, the same portfolio shows the floor rising to 83%, the ceiling rising to 300% after a change in the operating model, and the expected return falling as a lapse and a reversal take the conversion yield from 0.85 to 0.65. The framework is a design artefact evaluated analytically and by constructed illustration. It has not been applied to an organisation’s records, and five propositions state how it could be tested.

all.title: International Migration and Remittance Patterns in Southern Africa: Evidence from Cape Town, South Africa
all.abstract: This chapter explores the intersections among international migration, remittances, and resilience in Southern Africa. Despite socio-economic and political vulnerabilities, migrants continue to remit to support the livelihoods/welfare of households in their countries of origin. The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted remittance flows. Lockdowns, mobility restrictions, and unemployment, along with job/income losses, increased precarity among migrants and their dependents. Notably, Fintech and mobile/digital remittance technologies emerged as critical adaptive mechanisms by providing faster, more accessible, secure, and affordable alternatives to formal banking systems. Disruptions to informal channels were also mitigated. Based on survey data (n = 844) and in-depth interviews (n = 32) with ZimbabweansZimbabweans, Somalis, and Congolese migrants in Cape Town, South Africa, the research demonstrates that pandemic precarity reshaped transnational remitting practices and accelerated the adoption of digital financial servicesDigital financial inclusiondigital financial services. The digital/mobile systems have become increasingly prominent in the post-pandemic context, complementing trust-based informal channels in a hybrid landscape and promoting digital/financial inclusionDigital financedigital financial inclusion. Therefore, there is a need for inclusive digital financial ecosystems, enabling regulations, infrastructure investments, the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), and enhanced digital/financial literacy. This is crucial for advancing the financial inclusion of undocumented migrants, unbanked/under-banked individuals, women, informal workers and traders, and low-income urban and rural households in Southern Africa.

all.title: Residual Self-Guided Quantum Vision Adversarial Attention Network for Predicting AI-Driven Financial Performance in Automobile Industries
all.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the automobile banking industry and its impact on the business processes is very fast, the impact of AI techniques in financial performance is not fully understood. The challenge here is that banks involved in the automotive sector often have fragmented disclosures of AI and inconsistent metrics, making it challenging to come up with accurate predictions of the financial impact of AI. To address this gap, they propose a model known as “Residual Self-Guided Quantum Vision Adversarial Attention Network for Predicting AI-Driven Financial Performance in Automobile Industries. To fill this gap, they propose a model called “Residual Self-Guided Quantum Vision Adversarial Attention Network for Predicting AI-Driven Financial Performance in Automobile Industries.in the automobile banking industry has transformed business processes, yet how AI techniques influence financial performance is not yet fully understood. The difficulty here lies in scattered AI disclosures and disparate metrics that hinder effective forecasts of financial results in car-related banks. In order to bridge this gap, the research introduces a model called “Residual Self-Guided Quantum Vision Adversarial Attention Network for Predicting AI-Driven Financial Performance in Automobile Industries.” The analysis relies on a dataset called “AI Techniques on Financial Performance of Automobile Industries,” which contains 131 annual report records for sixteen Indian-listed banks from 2015 to 2023. This dataset captures keyword-based AI disclosures, as well as institutional and financial indicators. Data pre-processing is done through the use of the Correlation Coefficient with Min–Max Weighted (CCMMW) method to normalize and fine-tune the input parameters, while the Masked Attention Mask Transformer (Mask2Former) is utilized for feature extraction for isolating the disclosure patterns that have the greatest influence. Following these steps, a Self-Guided Quantum Generative Adversarial Network (SG-QGAN) is constructed and then advanced into the new Residual Self-Guided Quantum Single-Head Generative Elk Herd Vision Adversarial Attention Network (RSG-QSAGE-HV2AN). This network combines SG-QGAN with a Residual Attention Single-Head Vision Transformer Network (RA-SHViT-Net) and fine-tunes its parameters with the Elk Herd Optimizer (EHO). This work aims to propose a new hybrid approach named RSG-QSAGE-HV2AN to forecast AI derived financial performance of automobile financing banks. The data set is composed of ` (2015–2023), which is divided into 80% training and 20% testing. The 5-fold cross validation is used to guarantee robustness. The accuracy of the proposed model is 99.98% (95% confidence interval [99.98 ± 0.72%]) which is much better than the conventional model (Random Forest and XGBoost). The framework is combined with CCMMW pre-processing, feature extraction using Mask2Former, SG-QGAN with EHO optimized RA-SHViT-net. The results of experiments show the higher predictive performance, interpretability (through the use of SHAP) and lower computation cost.

all.title: Exploring AI-Driven Adaptive Learning Systems for Personalized Education in Nigerian TVET Institutions to Enhance Student Engagement and Skill Acquisition Outcomes
all.venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
institutions: Akwa Ibom State College of Education, Afaha Nsit
all.abstract: The emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education has revolutionized learning methodologies, particularly through the implementation of adaptive learning systems. This paper explores the impact of AI-driven adaptive learning systems on student engagement and skill acquisition outcomes in Nigerian Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) institutions. Traditional educational practices often follow a one-size-fits-all approach, failing to cater to the diverse learning needs of students, thereby contributing to high dropout rates and inadequate skill development. AI technologies offer personalized learning experiences that align educational outcomes with industry demands, addressing the skills mismatch highlighted by the World Bank. However, the successful integration of these systems faces significant barriers, including insufficient infrastructure, limited funding, and resistance to change among educators. Additionally, concerns regarding data privacy and ethical implications pose challenges to stakeholder acceptance of AI in educational contexts. Recommendations include enhancing institutional infrastructure, providing targeted training for educators, and establishing clear policies to safeguard data privacy. Furthermore, fostering collaboration between educational institutions and industry can ensure curriculum alignment with labor market needs. By addressing these challenges, AI-driven adaptive learning systems have the potential to transform the educational landscape in Nigeria, equipping students with relevant skills and enhancing their engagement and motivation. Ultimately, the adoption of these innovative technologies could lead to improved educational outcomes and better prepare graduates for the demands of the modern workforce.

all.title: Evidence-Gated Delegation for Agentic AI How to Let an AI Agent Act Only When the Evidence Justifies It, Learn Safely from Verified Mistakes, and Prove It Offline: A Bank-Reconciliation Case Study
Independent Execution Authorization for AI Agents: Separating the authority to permit an action from the system that proposes it
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: AI agents are moving from answering questions to taking actions: they make payments, change records, grant access and commit organizations to third parties. Holding a credential is not the same as being authorized to take a specific action at a specific moment. This position paper defines independent execution authorization: the decision, made immediately before an AI agent's action takes effect, on whether that specific action is permitted to execute, made outside the trust domain of the system taking the action. It grounds the idea in established security principles (separation of privilege, complete mediation, fail-safe defaults), sets out six requirements (independence, action specificity, fail-closed, no route around it, verifiable evidence, every applicable authority), distinguishes it from identity and access management, policy-based authorization, platform gateways, guardrails, agent security and observability, and states its limits. The system taking the action cannot be the system authorizing the action, and if the check cannot run, the action does not. Author: Damian Kissane, founder of INVARIANCE (invarianceip.com), the control plane for safe AI action. INVARIANCE is not affiliated with Invariant Labs, The Invariance Group, Invariance Arc or other similarly named organizations.

all.title: Earned Autonomy for AI Agents: A Pre-registered Error-Budget Test of Per-Action-Type Delegation
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Which actions may an AI agent take without human sign-off? We propose an open rule: an agent earns autonomy on one action type after N consecutive verified successes and loses it at the first confirmed error; N is derived from an error budget fixed in advance per stakes level by adapting the unrestricted AOQL of continuous sampling plans, with a conditional bound on the extra errors delegation lets through. We test it in a pre-registered replay: three Claude 5.5 models on four public benchmarks (τ-bench airline, retail and banking; WorkBench), 14,266 episodes played (13,623 analysed), writes checked by exact comparison (98.7% coverage) and alerts reviewed on blind sheets by separate Claude instances. No configuration reached the pre-registered level of evidence required for delegation (verdict R4). Only one of twelve configurations had enough volume to be judged; its error rate, 8.6% (lower bound 4.1%), is established above the 0.76% threshold. Of its 79 errors, 48 are one plot end-date discrepancy reviewers decided both ways; lifting it throughout leaves 31, established by two errors, and lifting also four one-day window shifts would not. The other eleven had too little effective volume to conclude either way. Descriptively (no multiplicity correction), 20 of 40 model–environment–type combinations have an error rate established above their threshold (11 of them on banking); 13 show no observed error but too little volume. The rule was not refuted, but it was hardly put to the test, and its usefulness could not be judged. These rates count action errors confirmed by review against a single expected path per task; in a blind sample reviewed by the author, 3 of 10 confirmed alerts were lifted, too few to rule out false-alert shares that would overturn the judged excess. As the plan stated in advance, earning autonomy under such budgets takes far more verified actions than these benchmarks provide at our volumes.

all.title: SACred: mining the Protein Data Bank for single-atom catalyst sites
all.abstract: Single-atom catalysts (SACs) are built from a small set of sites, most often a metal held by four nitrogens, while enzymes run hydrogen evolution, O2 and CO2 reduction and N2 fixation on single metals in many different first coordination shells. Here we mine that diversity. SACred, an automated pipeline built and run with AI agents, reduces every transition-metal site of the Protein Data Bank (PDB) to its first coordination shell, turns the recurring shells into candidate SAC sites and screens them in a funnel: each shell is mapped onto a single or double vacancy in graphene, screened with GFN2-xTB calibrated per metal against DFT, refined with PBE-D3 DFT for hydrogen adsorption (∆GH), formation energy (Ef) and dissolution potential (Udiss), simulated at 1,500 K with a fine-tuned MACE force field and checked against the literature by agents. From 291,977 metal sites in 53,868 PDB entries the pipeline builds 1,155 graphene sites for xTB and 123 for DFT. We validate each stage. Extraction agrees with the PDB’s own metal–ligand annotation (precision 0.98, recall 0.94). The mapping keeps all donors for 98 % of the sites but distorts single-vacancy geometries. In a prospective test, sites picked by calibrated xTB reached |∆GH| ≤ 0.3 eV in DFT in 67 % of cases, against 39 % for sites picked from enzyme knowledge alone and 44 % for a random sample from the xTB window (p = 0.06 and 0.07), and the whole xTB stage cost about 400 core-hours, as much as four to five

all.title: Agentic AI for Autonomous Detection and Resolution of Hold Transactions in Integrated Multi-Vendor Hospital Pharmacy Systems
all.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)
all.abstract: This paper presents an agentic artificial intelligence framework that detects, diagnoses and resolves hold transactions, which are stuck or failed transactions, in integrated hospital pharmacy environments. Large health systems often run order entry, medication processing, billing, stock and inventory, laboratory, blood bank and automated dispensing software from different vendors, and holds arise at the interfaces where no single vendor sees the whole transaction. Analysts resolve holds manually today, so backlogs build up and stock records drift from physical reality. The research problem is how to automate the repetitive part of this work without weakening audit, inventory accuracy or patient safety. Using a design science approach, the paper develops a taxonomy of five hold causes, a five agent architecture based on a monitor, analyze, plan, execute and knowledge control loop, a tiered autonomy policy with approval gated reprocessing, and an artificial intelligence governance model. A 30 day simulation with 20 replications and a sensitivity analysis evaluate the design. Under stated assumptions, about 82 percent of holds are resolved automatically and mean handling time falls from about 43 to 11 minutes, but the human escalation queue stays bounded only above a break even of about 80 percent automatic resolution. The work indicates that governed agentic automation is a promising option for multivendor hospital pharmacy operations, provided that automatic resolution and false fix rates are confirmed through the staged pilot protocol proposed here.

all.title: NEXUSFlow: A Multi-Boat Autonomous Survey System for Locating Bank-Side Arsenic Sources in Rivers—System Design and Monte Carlo Evaluation
all.abstract: Arsenic contamination of the Kok River in northern Thailand is currently monitored by manual sampling at fixed points, and laboratory results take three to four weeks, while the source often remains unknown. We present NEXUSFlow, a monitoring system in which a fleet of five autonomous surface vehicles surveys a river reach along automatically planned zigzag routes, a plume-mapping model (PatternTrack AI) estimates the contaminant field and traces its source, and an AI agent (NATEE) drafts a response plan that is released only after approval by a pollution control officer and a village leader. To test the central design choice—mobile zigzag sampling instead of fixed stations—we ran a Monte Carlo simulation of 2,000 bank-side discharges in a 12 km reach using a two-dimensional transverse-mixing model with reflecting banks. The median full-mixing length was 46 km, so plumes remained attached to one bank throughout the reach. In the 1,776 scenarios in which some location exceeded 0.01 mg/L, seven fixed stations on one bank detected the plume in 38% of cases, stations on both banks in 75%, mid-channel stations in 2% and a centreline boat in 4%, whereas a 40-sample zigzag survey detected 83%. A short follow-up along the affected bank reduced the median source-location error to 15 m, compared with about 830 m for fixed stations. The ranking was unchanged for strongly meandering reaches. A prototype run on simulated data took 81 min from the first report to a village alert. The results support combining mobile zigzag surveys with fixed stations and must be confirmed by field tests.

all.title: THE CONZETIAN PROTOCOL LANDSCAPE: Ecosystem Alignment, The Evidence Root Vacancy, and the Five Moves
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive strategic analysis of the global AI agent-protocol landscape as of November 2026, and maps the Conzetian Sovereign Architecture directly against it. By reverse-engineering the adoption metrics, security gaps, and structural failures of current industry protocols—including MCP, A2A, x402, and AP2—this paper reveals an "unseen pattern": the global industry has successfully built communication, coordination, and payment rails, but has entirely failed to build the **Trust Layer**. This paper identifies that vacancy not as a product category, but as a specific architectural role: the **Evidence Root**. It demonstrates how the Conzetian architecture (L0–L8) and the G0 Prime trust root directly solve the "Ephemeral-Identity Crisis" described in current academic literature. Finally, it outlines the Five Moves required to transition the architecture from a private design into a public, verifiable standard.

all.title: Clawd Confidential Compute & Dark DeFi — A Complete Guide
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This guide documents Clawd Confidential Compute: the CLAWD-TEE trust substrate and the Dark DeFi protocol family built on top of it, drawn from the public tea repository, the upstream clawd-tee monorepo, and Dark-Defi-1. Its thesis is that TEE attestation — signed hardware quotes binding code measurements to enclave keys across Intel TDX, NVIDIA Confidential Computing, and OP-TEE — should live on Solana in public, content-addressed, and checkable by anyone, with only digests crossing from the compute plane to the control plane: prompts, weights, and plaintext balances never go on-chain. The guide walks the attestation flow, the Pinocchio proof-storage program, the OpenAI-compatible TEE gateway, the RedPill-lineage provider verifiers, the OP-TEE signer, and Solana Attestation Service credentials, then introduces Dark DeFi: Sapling-style shielded wallets on Solana, encrypted dark-pool order flow, and TEE AI agents attested through the Solana Attestation Service, closing with the wider Dark family (Dark Payments, Dark x402, Dark Percolator, Dark Perps). Every status claim is labeled the way the source repositories label it: the stack is self-described Alpha, the hosted gateway relies on a stub TDX backend, and the shielded system uses placeholder ZK proofs — a design and research artifact, not production cryptography.

all.title: Who Moved the Frontier? Paying Open Frontier Challenges with Free Identities
all.abstract: In an open frontier challenge, anyone, person or AI agent, submits changes to a shared problem, and a change that beats the best measured score becomes the public baseline. How should it pay when identities are free? Rank prizes can be gamed: on a replay of one track of a recent challenge, one solver's steps under two identities would have taken first and second prize. We consider a prediction-market rule, proposed for machine-learning contests, that pays each accepted step for the progress it adds; with exact scores, among rules that see only a step's start and end, only these resist splitting and merging, and extra identities gain nothing. With noisy scores and independent normal runs, we prove that any payment that never takes money back and pays real improvements also pays something, on average, to a change that does nothing. We propose a fee per submission, at least what luck pays per attempt, that removes each attempt's expected profit if verifiers are honest and no submission is noisier than planned; nothing enforces that bound, and under noise the rule does not cap the total paid. If crediting another and faking credit to one's second account look the same, a rule that neither rewards fakes nor punishes honesty pays for credit at most what lying costs. We introduce a royalty on how much a later gain falls without the earlier change, which needs no claims but needs removable changes. For five public challenges, we name the rule our results would support.

all.title: Reviewed Before It Runs: Automated Review of an Architect's Authority
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: AI agents are granted authority in two layers: a boundary written in advance for a whole deployment, and a decision on each action as it arrives, made by a person or, increasingly, by a classifier model. Neither states what one task needs before it runs. We study an alternative, in which each task’s authority is written down before anything runs and reviewed there. From a task in natural language, an architect model writes a signal graph, a dataflow graph in which every node declares the capabilities it holds, and every grant quotes the words of the task that need it. Before anything runs, a formal review checks the graph, and a reviewer model, here the architect’s own model in a separate call, reviews it. Because each grant is an artefact, it can be held to least-authority labels registered before the run, so whether review catches a widened grant can be counted. On AgentDojo’s banking suite, with one model (claude-haiku-5-5) as both architect and reviewer, we registered one test: whether a pretext in the task, claiming that wider access had been approved, raises the rate of widenings both reviewers miss. They came in 29 of 160 trials with the pretext (18.1%) and 6 of 80 without it (7.5%): one-sided Fisher exact p = 0.019, against a registered 𝛼 = 0.01. That is below the conventional 0.05 but above the threshold the registration set, so by its registration the test is not supported. Post hoc, the rise is mostly in whether the architect wrote a graph at all: compared within each task, p = 0.0033 per trial but 0.19 per graph (Section 5.1). The reviewer caught all 10 widenings planted to test it before use, but only 17 of the 76 trials in which the architect had widened a grant beyond its label; re-run post hoc on the same graphs, a larger model of the same family caught 22 of the 76, and flagged 6 clean trials against 3. The link check, which requires each grant to quote the task, caught none. The architect’s graphs scored utility on 7/16 tasks (3/11 beyond tasks that pass when nothing is done), against 13/16 (8/11) for the same model undefended, and attack success was zero for both, which shows no defence here.

all.title: Intent Governance in Artificial Intelligence A Purpose-Aware Framework for Human Authorization, Intent Drift Detection, Persistent Memory, and Lifecycle Accountability within AIVORIX™
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Zenodo Publication Description Intent Governance in Artificial Intelligence: A Purpose-Aware Framework for Human Authorization, Intent Drift Detection, Persistent Memory, and Lifecycle Accountability within AIVORIX OS™ This research paper introduces Intent Governance and Purpose Validation (IGPV) as a proposed architectural capability within AIVORIX OS™, a governance-centric artificial intelligence operating system architecture developed by Nicole Aleece Crossleytownsend, Founder and Chief Architect of Crossley Enterprises, Inc. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly autonomous and interconnected across enterprise environments, conventional identity verification, access controls, and policy enforcement may not adequately establish whether AI operations remain consistent with the purposes for which they were originally authorized. This research explores a critical additional dimension of AI governance: not only determining who is authorized to use artificial intelligence and what actions are permitted, but also establishing why an AI operation is being performed, whether its purpose is authorized, and whether subsequent actions remain consistent with that purpose. The proposed Intent Governance framework introduces five interconnected capabilities: Intent Declaration, Purpose Authorization, Intent–Action Consistency Evaluation, Intent Drift Detection, and Intent Evidence and Accountability. Strengthening Persistent Memory A central contribution of the proposed framework is its potential to extend AIVORIX OS's persistent organizational memory beyond retaining operational context, policy decisions, and historical activities. Through Intent Governance, persistent memory could preserve the authorized purpose behind AI-mediated activities, including the original human objective, applicable authority, permitted operational boundaries, policy versions, subsequent purpose amendments, and associated human approvals. This creates the foundation for purpose-aware institutional memory, allowing authorized AI systems to reference not only what occurred previously, but also why an operation was authorized, under what conditions it was permitted, and whether those conditions remain valid. Such continuity could help prevent AI agents from losing or misinterpreting governing objectives during workflow transitions, system recovery, delegated operations, and interactions involving multiple AI providers. Advancing Lifecycle Traceability and Accountability Intent Governance also proposes strengthening AIVORIX OS's lifecycle traceability by establishing verifiable relationships among human-declared objectives, authorization decisions, AI actions, policy restrictions, and execution outcomes. Rather than maintaining isolated activity records, the proposed architecture would associate each governed operation with its originating purpose and subsequent authorization history. This approach could enable organizations to reconstruct an AI decision lifecycle and determine: What objective the human originally declared. Whether the purpose and requested action were authorized. Which policies and human approvals governed execution. Whether an AI agent remained within its approved operational boundaries. When a material purpose deviation occurred. How the system responded through restriction, escalation, denial, or authorized amendment. What evidence was preserved to support accountability and subsequent review. By connecting intent-related governance records with persistent memory and lifecycle evidence, AIVORIX OS could improve the continuity, explainability, and auditability of AI-assisted operations. Intent Drift and Cross-System Governance The paper further introduces Intent Drift Detection, a proposed mechanism for identifying material deviations between an approved purpose and subsequent AI actions. Such deviations may arise through changing human instructions, agent delegation, unauthorized data transfers, prompt injection, workflow expansion, or changing operational circumstances. The proposed framework would evaluate observable actions and authorization boundaries rather than claim to determine hidden human motivations. Integrated with AIVORIX OS's governance and orchestration capabilities, Intent Governance could support continuous purpose validation across heterogeneous AI models, agents, enterprise applications, and software-defined systems. Research Scope and Future Validation The paper presents a conceptual technical architecture, formal authorization model, six illustrative operational scenarios, cross-industry applications, legal and ethical safeguards, and an experimental validation methodology. Potential applications include healthcare, financial services, government, scientific research, automotive software-defined systems, and critical infrastructure. The research maintains the existing ten-layer AIVORIX OS architecture, proposing Intent Governance as a cross-layer capability principally involving Persistent Memory Infrastructure, Governance and Risk Management, Human Oversight, and Runtime Orchestration. The proposed framework emphasizes privacy, proportionality, human authority, and the distinction between declared operational purpose and unobservable psychological intent. Intent Governance is presented as a proposed research capability requiring further implementation, controlled experimentation, and independent technical validation. Ultimately, this research advances the AIVORIX OS architectural hypothesis that persistent governance state can support accountable AI operations by preserving not only organizational knowledge and decision history, but also the authorized purposes that give those decisions meaning. The central proposition is that responsible AI governance should preserve not only what an AI system did, but why the action was authorized, whether its execution remained within that purpose, and who retained accountability throughout its lifecycle. Author: Nicole Aleece CrossleytownsendAffiliation: Crossley Enterprises, Inc.Research Platform: AIVORIX OS™ — Powered by AIVORIX™Publication: November 2026Research Category: Artificial Intelligence Governance, Persistent Memory, Intent Governance, and Lifecycle Accountability

all.title: Stopping Email Spam Before It Reaches Gmail, Outlook, and iCloud Mail: Why Apple Hide My Email May Not Be Enough — A Purpose-Bound, Recipient-Controlled Email Delivery Architecture
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: From Lead-Form Data Resale and Unwanted Marketing to Protected Pre-Inbox Enforcement Using Non-Bearer CVID Communication Authority Abstract You enter your email address into a hotel booking form, insurance quotation website, educational inquiry, online marketplace, or service-request page. You expect one relevant response. But what happens when that email address is retained, shared with affiliates, transferred to lead brokers, or sold to multiple marketing companies? A single inquiry can become the beginning of repeated promotional messages, unsolicited follow-ups, and persistent email spam. Why should knowing someone's email address automatically create the ability to contact that person indefinitely? This technical disclosure examines a fundamental architectural problem affecting Gmail, Microsoft Outlook, iCloud Mail, enterprise email systems, and other digital communication platforms: an email address functions as a delivery destination, while conventional email authentication, reputation scoring, spam filtering, and address-masking mechanisms do not necessarily establish whether an individual sender has current authorization to deliver a particular message for a particular purpose. Existing solutions provide important protections. Gmail employs sophisticated pre-inbox spam and phishing detection; Apple Hide My Email conceals permanent email addresses through forwarding aliases; and Sign in with Apple's private email relay additionally restricts authorized sending sources. Nevertheless, sender authenticity, possession of an active alias, or an existing commercial relationship does not inherently establish recipient-controlled, purpose-specific permission for every subsequent communication. The disclosure presents a prospective solution based on Capability-Validated Inbound Descriptors (CVID) and Protected Communication-Finality, grounded in international patent application PCT/IB2026/056353, titled Non-Bearer Capability-Validated Architecture for Pre-Effect Authorization of Communication, Payment Settlement, Data Export, and AI-Native Machine Operations. The central technical principle is that possession of an email address, virtual alias, API credential, previously issued communication reference, or authenticated sender identity must not independently confer unrestricted email-delivery authority. Under the proposed architecture, a governed inbound email attempt remains in a technically enforced Non-Effective State until a protected authorization domain verifies the sender, recipient, permitted communication purpose, message class, delivery channel, consent state, validity window, quota, nonce or freshness condition, revocation state, and intended recipient-side effect. Only upon successful validation does the enforcement gateway release a bounded capability permitting the authorized email effect. For example, a hotel may receive permission to send a quotation, booking confirmation, or reservation-related notification without acquiring unrestricted authorization to send promotional campaigns, unrelated marketing, or indefinite follow-up messages. If the customer's email address is subsequently transferred to a lead broker, copied from a business database, or obtained by an unauthorized marketer, possession of that address alone would not satisfy the required delivery authority within a participating CVID-controlled system. Unlike ordinary email masking, which primarily protects the destination's identity, the proposed system seeks to control the authority to make communication effective. The disclosure examines how this principle could complement existing Apple Hide My Email, Sign in with Apple private relay, Gmail security controls, and OAuth-based authorization without assuming that their established protections are absent or ineffective. Potential enforcement points include SMTP receiving gateways, mail-transfer agents, secure email relays, alias resolvers, mailbox-delivery services, enterprise mail gateways, and notification controllers. Different implementation variants may prevent unauthorized delivery, quarantine messages, defer processing, withhold inbox placement, or suppress user-visible notifications while preserving permitted transactional communication. The technical analysis also addresses legacy SMTP compatibility, gateway latency, hot-path and cold-path authorization, protected-state caching, anti-replay enforcement, mailing-list forwarding, legitimate unknown senders, compromised enterprise identities, purpose misrepresentation, and fail-closed handling of alternate communication paths. A critical challenge is establishing trustworthy evidence of message purpose. A sender's self-declared label cannot alone prove that promotional content is genuinely transactional. Accordingly, practical implementation requires authenticated transaction context, recipient consent, protected authorization records, reliable enforcement boundaries, and empirical evaluation of false positives, delivery reliability, and processing overhead. The invention extends beyond email to telephone calls, SMS/RCS, push notifications, AI-agent communication, machine-to-machine messaging, and related protected-finality applications. Its email-specific deployment represents a proposed application of this broader communication-authority architecture. The disclosure does not claim experimentally demonstrated elimination of all spam, control over email infrastructure that has not adopted the mechanism, or implementation by Google, Apple, or Microsoft. The central question is no longer merely whether an email is authentic, suspicious, or addressed correctly. It is whether this sender has independently verifiable authority to cause this specific message to reach this recipient for this particular purpose. By shifting the security decision from address possession and sender reputation toward recipient-authorized, non-bearer, purpose-bound communication effectuation, the proposed CVID architecture offers a technical direction for reducing unauthorized email delivery before it reaches the user's governed inbox or notification boundary. Keywords Email Spam Prevention; Gmail Security; Apple Hide My Email; iCloud Mail; Microsoft Outlook; Pre-Inbox Spam Prevention; Capability-Validated Inbound Descriptor; CVID; Protected Communication-Finality; Purpose-Bound Email Authorization; Recipient-Controlled Email Delivery; Lead-Form Privacy; Data Broker Spam; Email Address Resale; Non-Bearer Communication Authority; SMTP Gateway Security; Email Delivery Enforcement; Protected Authorization Domain; Email Alias Security; OAuth; Sender Authentication; SPF; DKIM; DMARC; Consent-Based Messaging; Transactional Email; Marketing Abuse Prevention; Anti-Replay Authorization; AI-Agent Email Security; Legacy SMTP Compatibility; Zero Trust Communication. Foundational Technical Disclosure: PCT/IB2026/056353 Author: Sangam Kumar Das Technical Scope: Proposed complementary integration with existing email security infrastructure. No adoption, endorsement, or implementation by Google, Apple, Microsoft, or other identified organizations is implied.

all.title: Does an Integrity-Gated Governance Observability Index Measure Reconstructability? A Simulation-Based Criterion-Validity Study of Agent Telemetry under Out-of-Specification Faults
all.abstract: Governance of agentic AI systems depends on execution evidence: an operator can judge whether an agent stayed within its authority only if its telemetry allows what it did to be reconstructed. The Governance Observability Index (GOI) proposes to measure this as a gated geometric mean of coverage, fidelity, integrity and timeliness, with an integrity gate intended to stop untrustworthy evidence being masked by completeness elsewhere. This simulation study tests one implementation of the index against criteria computed from complete ground truth, of which the estimator sees only a 40-record ledger sample. A seeded testbed simulates a scripted payments agent, a policy gateway, an authoritative ledger and an HMAC-chained telemetry stream. The estimator uses only the stream, a gateway control total and a 40-record ledger sample. Twelve fault families—four within the original specification, four outside it and four benign infrastructure perturbations—are evaluated in 2,520 single-family runs and 1,000 mixed runs. GOI correlates with reconstruction accuracy (Spearman ρ = 0.85, 95% CI 0.83–0.87) and separates degraded from sound reconstructions (AUC 0.93). It is weaker as a warning of missed time-sensitive violations (AUC 0.87), and 63% of runs scoring at least 0.90 had degraded reconstructions. The integrity gate, as implemented, never activated in the mixed runs. A 5% forgery by a key holder left the index at 0.99 while 98% of sequence-level violations went undetected in time. When deletion targets the same records as forgery, it shifts part of the defect from fidelity to coverage; a sensitivity experiment with independent deletion leaves the headline results unchanged. In this testbed GOI works as a screening measure, not a certificate of trustworthy evidence, and its usefulness depends on evidence channels independent of the telemetry.

all.title: Cascading Attack-Surface Entropy in Hyper-Scale Platforms: Deterministic Zero-Knowledge Isolation Against Autonomous Exploit Discovery and Foundational Middleware RCE Chains (CVE-2026-123007 / NGINX2Root) (日本語副題:超大規模プラットフォームにおける連鎖的アタックサーフェス・エントロピー:自律型AI脆弱性探索および基盤ミドルウェアRCE連鎖[CVE-2026-123007 / NGINX2Root]に対する決定論的ゼロ知識隔離アーキテクチャ)
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: 0009-0009-1355-5287 This monograph formalizes the structural vulnerability propagation and cascading attack-surface entropy inherent in hyper-scale digital platforms (exemplified by tightly coupled social, payment, API, advertising, and AI microservice ecosystems such as X) in the wake of autonomous AI-driven vulnerability discovery in foundational Internet infrastructure. Motivated by the November 2026 disclosure of CVE-2026-123007 ("NGINX2Root" / "NGINX2Shell", CVSS v4.0 9.2)—an 11-year-old unauthenticated HTTP/2 flow-control integer underflow and heap buffer overflow in nginx discovered and weaponized via autonomous AI security harnesses (Theori Xint) and chained with Linux kernel SCTP subsystem flaws to escape containers and seize host root privileges—we prove mathematically that hyper-scale platforms built atop shared C-based middleware suffer super-linear security degradation. As functional components (OAuth/authentication gateways, third-party APIs, real-time ad-bidding engines, embedded payment rails, and stochastic AI agents) proliferate under rapid continuous deployment, configuration drift and cross-service privilege coupling amplify single-point foundational zero-days into systemic platform compromise. To eliminate cascading middleware-to-kernel and microservice-to-platform collapse, we introduce a Deterministic Cryptographic Isolation Architecture grounded in The Hasebe Doctrine and QFS-zkVM over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field . By enforcing zero-knowledge state-transition verification at every ingress/API boundary, capability-bounded memory-safe execution envelopes, and Human-in-Command (HIC) fiduciary circuit breakers aligned with Delaware Caremark oversight standards and cyber-resilience mandates, our framework mathematically bounds blast-radius propagation even when underlying Web/OS primitives experience zero-day remote code execution. 【日本語要旨】 本論文は、世界のWeb基盤の約3割・日本の約6割を支えるWebサーバー「nginx(エンジンエックス)」において約11年間潜伏していた深刻な認証不要リモートコード実行(RCE)脆弱性(CVE-2026-123007 / 通称「NGINX2Root」、CVSS 9.2)が自律型AIセキュリティ基盤(Theori社「Xint」)等によって発見され、さらにLinuxカーネルのSCTPサブシステム脆弱性との連鎖(Exploit Chain)によりコンテナ脱出およびホスト最高権限(root)奪取が実証された事案[cite: 1]を起点として、X(旧Twitter)等の超大規模複合プラットフォームにおける構造的脆弱性の連鎖(Cascading Attack-Surface Entropy)を数理モデル化するものである。単一のWebサーバーにとどまらず、外部連携API、認証基盤、広告配信、決済網、サードパーティ連携、AI機能が無数に絡み合い高速改修が繰り返される巨大プラットフォームでは、基盤OSSのゼロデイ脆弱性と運用上のデグレード・設定不備が非線形に結合し、システム全体が構造的崩壊(全身的侵害)に至る必然性を証明する。さらにその根本的解決策として、Goldilocks素体上の決定論的ゼロ知識仮想マシン(QFS-zkVM)とHuman-in-Command(HIC)統治原則に基づく境界検証・権限隔離アーキテクチャを提示し、基盤ミドルウェア侵害時にも被害範囲を数学的に局所封じ込めする設計仕様および取締役会の善管注意義務(Caremark基準)を確立する。(予約DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24357979) Full-text PDF access is strictly by registration and approval for verified human researchers, corporate executives, and institutional reviewers under the Sovereign Open-Read & Strict No-Learn License (NLL-v1.0-2026) (Master Declaration DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23681957).
