all.abstract: This study examines the roles of perceived risk and service trust in fintech adoption among rural shopkeepers in India and develops a necessity-driven adoption framework for institutionally constrained settings. Drawing on TAM, TPB, Institutional Theory, and the capability approach, it distinguishes perceived risk as an adoption trigger and service trust as a post-adoption sustainer. Using survey data from 274 shopkeepers and PLS-SEM, the results show that perceived risk positively influences both intention and actual usage, acting as a behavioral driver under institutional voids. In contrast, service trust is more important for sustaining long-term engagement than for initial adoption. Trust also weakens the effect of perceived risk on behavioral intention, reducing reliance on necessity-driven adoption. The study introduces a risk-inversion mechanism, showing that perceived risk can encourage adoption in constrained environments. Practical implications suggest that fintech providers should focus on trustbuilding and retention strategies, while policymakers should combine digitalization with digital literacy to ensure meaningful financial inclusion.

all.title: CONSUMER AWARENESS, ADOPTION PATTERNS AND DETERMINANTS OF GREEN FINTECH ADOPTION INTENTION: EVIDENCE FROM SELECTED SMART CITIES OF UTTAR PRADESH
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

all.title: Too Old to Benefit From FinTech? An Exploratory Study on Older Adults' Access to and Adoption of Robo‐Advice
all.abstract: Robo‐advice has the potential to provide affordable financial advice to assist older adults with building and managing retirement income. Yet robo‐advice uptake among those aged 60 to 80 years is low, and little is known about how they engage with robo‐advice. Our study examines the drivers and barriers to robo‐advice access and adoption among older adults, and provides practical recommendations for industry and policymakers. Drawing on qualitative surveys and interviews with academic and industry experts familiar with the Australian financial advice landscape. We identify six core themes and their possible interrelationships, which likely affect older adults' access and adoption: robo‐advice design, digital and financial capabilities, trust, psychological comfort, regulatory deficiencies, and social influence. In integrating our findings with the technology acceptance and financial planning literature, we construct a conceptual framework that responds to calls for more comprehensive explanations of consumer behavior toward robo‐advice.

all.title: EXPLORING PERCEIVED CHALLENGES HINDERING GREEN FINTECH ADOPTION AMONG CONSUMERS IN SELECTED SMART CITIES OF UTTAR PRADESH
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

all.title: Factors influencing FinTech adoption in the agrarian sector of developing economies: bridging technology, finance and policy for sustainable development
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the factors influencing financial technology (FinTech) adoption among Indian farmers by extending the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), with behavioral intention as a mediating mechanism. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 461 farmers across nine districts of Uttar Pradesh, India. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling and multigroup analysis. Findings Facilitating conditions and habit significantly influence behavioral intention, which strongly drives actual FinTech adoption. Behavioral intention mediates these relationships. Multigroup analysis shows that the behavioral intention–adoption relationship remains stable across gender, age and farm size, although demographic characteristics influence antecedent effects. Practical implications Policymakers, financial institutions and FinTech providers should develop intention-focused, demographically sensitive strategies emphasizing digital literacy, accessibility and enabling infrastructure. Social implications Greater FinTech adoption can reduce rural financial exclusion, strengthen economic resilience and support inclusive rural development, contributing to the Sustainable Development Goals. Originality/value This study extends UTAUT by demonstrating how behavioral intention translates enabling conditions and habitual technology use into actual FinTech adoption among farmers.

all.title: Impact of Fintech Adoption, Green Innovation, and Organizational Financial Literacy on Sustainable Performance of SMEs Through Circular Economy Practices
all.abstract: The world is facing an alarming challenge of environmental threats due to overproduction and overconsumption of scarce resources. Manufacturing SMEs are considered the backbone of this problem. SMEs are also considered key actors in promoting a circular economy and sustainable performance (SP). This study aims to investigate the direct impact of fintech adoption (FA), green innovation (GI), access to finance (AF), and organizational financial literacy (OFL) on the sustainable performance (SP) of SMEs operating in Pakistan. The study further aims to investigate the indirect relationship via circular economy practices (CEP) between independent and dependent variables. The researcher dispensed closed‐ended structured questionnaires to managers and owners of SMEs in Pakistan. The researcher employed a non‐probability, purposive sampling technique to select respondents. Eight hypotheses were formulated to test the study's model. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modelling (SEM) in Smart‐PLS were used for data analysis. Seven out of eight hypotheses were accepted after making an empirical analysis. The results reveal that SMEs following CEP tend to enjoy both competitive advantage and environmental benefits. The study also reveals that financially enlightened managerial staff are inclined to make informed and environmentally friendly decisions. The study has theoretical implications for the Natural Resource Based View (NRBV) theory. The study also guides SME owners and managers to adopt technology 14.0 (fintech) along with CEP to achieve sustainable performance (SP). It also guides policy regulators to prioritize SMEs for CEP to achieve environmental benefits. SMEs are adopting modern world concepts to ensure their survival and growth in the industry. At the same time, they're under pressure from stakeholders due to their environmental effects. The study aims to assess the impact of modern world concepts (FA, GI) in conjunction with the circular economy (CEP) to achieve both competitive and environmental benefits.

all.title: Role of Financial Technology (FinTech) in Transforming Indian Banking Sector
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Indian banking has seen more change in the last decade compared to the previous three. Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar-based identity checks, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and app-first lenders have altogether rewritten the ways that ordinary people pay, save and borrow. This paper is a qualitative narrative review of the literature on FinTech and banking. It draws on sixteen sources: ten works on FinTech, financial inclusion and bank-technology relationships, and six papers from Indian management and accounting research that touch on technology, change and organisational performance. The paper is organised by theme: payments and inclusion, competition between banks and FinTechs, the shift from competition to collaboration, risk and regulation, and the internal organisational side of digital change. The main argument is that FinTech has not so much replaced Indian banks as forced them to rebuild their front ends, their risk models and their culture. The gains in access and convenience are real, but so are the unevenness, the data risks and the regulatory gaps. Because the evidence is mixed and often comes from outside India, the conclusions here are tentative.

all.title: The Fintech Productivity Paradox in Islamic and Conventional Banking: Evidence from Bangladesh
all.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology (IJISRT)
all.abstract: In this study, the impact of fintech on the profitability of Islamic and conventional listed commercial banks in Bangladesh has been examined. Based on the annual report data of 36 listed banks, from 2019 to 2024, a composite Fintech Adoption Index (FAI) is created that is derived from six standardized indexes: IT investment intensity, ATM/CRM density, agent banking density, internet banking density, mobile application availability, and technology disclosure. Two-way fixedeffects and random-effects panel regressions (using Hausman test) are used to estimate the relationship between the Fintech Index and Return on Assets (ROA) and Return on Equity (ROE), then a mediation analysis is conducted on the Cost-toIncome Ratio (CIR) as a transmission channel, and a moderation analysis is conducted by adding an Islamic bank dummy and Fintech Index.

all.title: Toward inclusive FinTech: insights from indigenous communities in the chittagong hill tracts
all.venue: Journal of Banking and Financial Technology
institutions: Ahsanullah University of Science and Technology

all.title: Green Fintech Strategies for Circular Plastic-Recycling Supply Chains in an Emerging Economy
all.abstract: Bangladesh recycles only about 31% of its roughly 977,000 tons of annual plastic waste through formal channels, and recyclers face limited working capital and weak traceability of recovered materials. This study examines whether green fintech adoption strategies (GFASs), measured as a higher-order capability and adoption-readiness construct (reported use, readiness, perceived usefulness and acceptance), are associated with circular plastic-recycling supply chain performance (CPRSCP) and whether supply chain digital transparency (SCDT) mediates this association. We hypothesize that GFAS is positively associated with SCDT (H1), SCDT with CPRSCP (H2), and GFAS with CPRSCP directly (H3), and that SCDT mediates the GFAS–CPRSCP association (H4). Cross-sectional survey data from 472 respondents in recycling and fintech-integrated organizations in Bangladesh’s three main plastic-recycling clusters were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling. GFAS was positively associated with SCDT (β = 0.59; p < 0.001), and GFAS was also directly associated with CPRSCP (β = 0.17; p = 0.026). The indirect association via SCDT was significant (standardized β = 0.30; unstandardized B = 0.306; 95% BC bootstrap CI: [0.202, 0.452]), consistent with partial mediation. Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, the findings are interpreted as associations, not causal effects. This study extends dynamic capabilities theory by positioning digital transparency as a proposed link between fintech capabilities and circular supply chain outcomes and offers policy suggestions for digitally enabled plastic circularity.

all.title: The digital transformation of Islamic consumerism: a bibliometric mapping of ethical marketing in Islamic fintech
all.venue: Journal of Islamic accounting and business research
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to map the intellectual and thematic structure of research on the digital transformation of Islamic consumerism and ethical marketing in Islamic fintech, using the theory of planned behaviour (TPB) as an interpretive scaffold and situating findings within the Sustainable Development Goal 2030 agenda. Design/methodology/approach Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 1,020 documents were retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science and analysed using bibliometric performance analysis and science mapping (VOSviewer; Biblioshiny/R), encompassing co-word clustering, strategic thematic mapping and co-citation network analysis. Findings Publication output grew from three documents in 2019 to more than 400 in 2025 and is concentrated in a small number of Muslim-majority economies in Southeast Asia and the Gulf. Thematic mapping reveals a dominant motor theme around “AI–sustainable development–finance”, a niche theme around “trust–religiosity” and a fragmented basic theme around “fintech–sustainability–Islamic finance”. A dual-layer antecedent architecture is identified: generic digital adoption drivers form the first layer, whereas Islamic-specific antecedents, such as perceived Sharīʿah compliance, religiosity, Sharīʿah financial literacy and maqāṣid orientation, function as direct determinants, moderators and constraints on adoption. Research limitations/implications Findings are limited to English-language, Scopus- and WoS-indexed documents and exclude regional journals and non-English Islamic fintech scholarship. Practical implications The findings guide fintech designers, Islamic financial institutions and Organisation of Islamic Cooperation regulators towards Sharīʿah-transparent product design, Sustainable Development Goals-aligned strategies and integrated regulatory sandboxes. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study offers one of the earliest TPB-anchored dual-database bibliometric mappings to jointly integrate Islamic fintech, ethical marketing and sustainability, advancing the field by treating Islamic constructs as more than contextual add-ons to TAM and UTAUT.

all.title: Economic Behavior and Fintech Usage Intention: The Moderating Role of Religiosity in Muslim Communities
all.venue: Journal of Economics Entrepreneurship Management Business and Accounting
all.abstract: Purpose: The objective of this research is to examine how perceived ease of use and perceived risk influence the intention to use fintech, and to analyze the function of religiosity as both a direct predictor and a moderating variable in the relationships under study among Muslim communities residing in Jambi City, Indonesia. Design/methodology/approach: The present research adopted a quantitative explanatory design. A convenience sample of 100 Muslim individuals who were familiar with fintech in Jambi City was selected, and the data were gathered by means of a structured five-point Likert questionnaire. Analyses were performed using the Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) approach in SmartPLS 4, which included two interaction terms for the moderation tests. Findings: The perceived ease of use was found to have a positive and statistically significant effect on fintech usage intention (β = 0.510, p < 0.001). In addition, religiosity also showed a significant positive direct effect (β = 0.414, p < 0.001). Perceived risk was observed to exert a negative but statistically insignificant effect on fintech usage intention (β = −0.100, p = 0.414). The results further indicated that religiosity did not moderate the effect of perceived ease of use (β = 0.054, p = 0.157) or of perceived risk (β = 0.103, p = 0.213) on fintech usage intention. Taken as a whole, this study demonstrated that 62.4% of the variance in fintech usage intention was accounted for by the theoretical model (R² = 0.624). Originality/value: This study contributes to the body of knowledge in the field of Islamic fintech by simultaneously examining the effect of religiosity as a direct predictor and as a moderator, and by providing empirical evidence of its limited role within this context. The findings underscore the importance of functional attributes, including ease of use, over religious attributes in shaping fintech adoption among Muslim customers, which constitutes useful information for Islamic fintech developers and regulators.

all.title: Financial Inclusion and Economic Development: The Role of Digital Banking and FinTech in Reducing Poverty
all.venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
all.abstract: Financial inclusion has become an important component of contemporary economic-development strategies because access to affordable, secure, and appropriate financial services can influence household welfare, entrepreneurship, savings, investment, employment, and resilience to economic shocks. The expansion of digital banking and financial technology (FinTech) has transformed the delivery of financial services by reducing transaction costs, overcoming geographical barriers, enabling mobile payments, facilitating digital credit and savings, and connecting previously underserved individuals and small enterprises to formal financial systems. This paper examines the relationship between financial inclusion and economic development, with particular emphasis on the role of digital banking and FinTech in poverty reduction. Using a conceptual and systematic literature-review approach, the study analyzes the mechanisms through which digital financial services can improve economic participation and household welfare. The analysis indicates that digital banking and FinTech can support poverty reduction by expanding payment access, facilitating savings, improving access to productive credit, supporting micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), enabling remittances, strengthening social-transfer delivery, and improving households' capacity to manage financial shocks. However, digital financial inclusion also presents challenges involving digital literacy, cybersecurity, fraud, consumer protection, data privacy, algorithmic discrimination, over-indebtedness, unequal digital infrastructure, and regulatory gaps. The paper concludes that digital finance can contribute significantly to inclusive economic development when technological innovation is supported by reliable digital infrastructure, appropriate regulation, financial and digital literacy, effective consumer protection, competition, cybersecurity, and policies ensuring that vulnerable populations can meaningfully use financial services rather than merely possess accounts. Keywords: Financial Inclusion, Economic Development, Digital Banking, FinTech, Poverty Reduction, Digital Payments, Financial Technology, Mobile Banking, MSMEs, Financial Literacy, Inclusive Growth

all.title: From Behavioral Intention to Islamic Fintech Use: An Extended Technology Acceptance Model
all.venue: Dalwa Islamic Economic Studies Jurnal Ekonomi Syariah
all.abstract: This study examines the determinants of Islamic fintech use by integrating Islamic Financial Literacy, Perceived Usefulness, Trust, and Technology-Use Intensity, with Behavioral Intention as a mediating variable. A quantitative approach was employed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyze data from 300 valid Generation Z respondents in Langsa City, Indonesia. Respondents were selected through purposive sampling based on their prior use of fintech facilities. Actual Use was measured through respondents’ self-reported use rather than independently verified transaction records. The results show that all four antecedents have positive and statistically significant relationships with both Behavioral Intention and Actual Use. Behavioral Intention also positively influences Actual Use (β = 0.269, p < 0.001). Furthermore, the specific indirect effects through Behavioral Intention are positive and significant for Islamic Financial Literacy (β = 0.057, p < 0.001), Perceived Usefulness (β = 0.087, p < 0.001), Trust (β = 0.057, p = 0.002), and Technology-Use Intensity (β = 0.060, p = 0.001). Together with the significant positive direct effects, these findings are consistent with complementary mediation. The model explains 51.3% of the variance in Behavioral Intention and 55.7% in Actual Use. This study extends the application of the Technology Acceptance Model by examining how financial literacy, perceived usefulness, trust, and technology-use intensity relate to both behavioral intention and reported fintech use. The findings suggest that initiatives to encourage Islamic fintech adoption should consider users’ financial literacy, perceived service benefits, trust, and technology engagement, while recognizing that self-reported use does not independently verify actual transactions.

all.title: Digital Platforms and Retail Participation in Climate Finance: Evidence from the Indian FinTech Ecosystem
all.abstract: In India, the Net Zero will be implemented by mobilising the private capital particularly the emerging retail industry. Although institutional climate finance is a well-studied issue, the contribution of digital FinTech to the democratization of sustainable investments is not a theme that has been studied in detail within the developing economies, including India. The other variables, which will be discussed in the paper, are the ones that determine the role of retail investors in climate finance via digital investment platforms, and the mediation of investment behaviour by the platform adoption and the age of the investor. The research design that was employed to investigate 450 retail investors in the metropolitan regions of India that are important was the quantitative research design and structured questionnaire. The theoretical model incorporates the incorporation of Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) of the variables Digital Financial Literacy, Perceived Transparency and Trust and the statistical data were modeled in Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) on the SmartPLS. The findings indicate that Digital Financial Literacy and Perceived Transparency are the most relevant predictors of trust in the platform and subsequent adoption. The perceived Ease of Use can be an early adopting factor, whereas Trust is the actual financial adopting factor of climate-consistent assets, including green bonds and ESG funds. Moreover, the age is also a mediator between the platform adoption and climate investment participation since the Generation Z is more pro-environmental and less capitalized than other generations. The research design is the quantitative and explanatory research design. The structured questionnaire was used to gather the data on the 5-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly Disagree to 5 = Strongly Agree). Convenience sampling technique was used to sample the 450 big cities in India with retail investors. The available literature assisted in revising the constructs in order to be valid. Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was applied to analyze the data with the help of SmartPLS. Cronbachs alpha, composite reliability, and average variance extracted (AVE) were used to measure reliability and validity.The paper concludes that FinTech platforms can bridge the climate financing gap, and advises providers to concentrate on how they can best report their effect and open participants to educational nudges are the most effective methods of boosting participation. These conclusions can provide viable recommendations to policymakers and developers of FinTech in an attempt to ensure that the retail wealth is geared towards the sustainability objectives of the entire India.

all.title: Mapping the FinTech–financial inclusion nexus in emerging economies: a conceptual synthesis and research agenda
all.abstract: The emergence of FinTech has brought about changes in accessing financial products and services in emerging economies. However, there is insufficient evidence regarding its influence on financial inclusion in the scholarly literature. This paper presents an integrative narrative review concerning FinTech and financial inclusion. It relies on peer-reviewed studies obtained through Scopus, supplemented by organizational and policy documents in emerging economies. The results have shown that FinTech adoption increases access and financial participation. The evidence found is mainly correlational at present. The efficiency of FinTech is dependent on institutional context, digital infrastructure, financial and technological literacy, regulation, trust, and adoption. Despite this effect, FinTech raises a number of risks such as algorithmic discrimination, cybercrime, invasion of data privacy, and consumer rights problems. Based on these results, the paper creates an integrated conceptual model that includes the following elements: structural antecedents, individual factors, financial inclusion, financial resilience, and sustainable development. In the model, financial inclusion is defined as financial access, availability, use, affordability, quality, and substantive inclusion. There are eight propositions describing when FinTech fosters or diminishes financial inclusion. The contribution of the paper is in synthesis of evidence concerning FinTech and its influence on financial inclusion.

all.title: Digital Divide and Fintech Literacy: UPI Challenges Among Women Vendors in Ranchi, Jharkhand
all.venue: Jharkhand Journal of Development and Management Studies
all.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital payment systems in India, particularly the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), has increased the visibility of cashless transactions in local markets. However, the visible uptake doesn’t necessarily imply women’s financial inclusion through it, especially for women workers in unorganized sector. This exploratory study investigates the factors related to digital divide, financial technology literacy and issues of technological adoption related to UPI among women vendors in selected markets in Ranchi, Jharkhand. The study is based on primary data collected through a structured questionnaire from 20 women vendors following convenience sampling method along with secondary literature review on issues of digital inclusion, gender and fintech. The study finds that though the respondents own smartphones and are willing to adopt QR code, their regular and independent usage of UPI is not consistent. The majority of the respondents reported network problems, fear of digital fraud, transaction related problems and lack of knowledge about digital security as barriers to frequent use. The study also indicates that access to digital payments does not always translate into financial autonomy, as control over UPI accounts and transaction credentials is often shared with or mediated by male household members. The paper, thus, concludes that vendor’s digital payment adoption is more of a technological penetration than inclusion and suggests context specific and gender sensitive policy initiatives to address the issue.

all.title: Impact of FinTech on Financial Inclusion: An Empirical Study of Rural Households in Agra District, Uttar Pradesh
institutions: Mangalmay Institute of Management and Technology
Greater Noida Institute of Technology (MBA Institute)
IIMT College of Engineering, Greater Noida
all.abstract: The new FinTech revolution has revolutionized the provision of formal financial services, especially in rural areas where traditional banking services may be underdeveloped. The study focuses on how FinTech can contribute to financial inclusion (FI) of the rural population of Agra District in the state of Uttar Pradesh. Primary household survey data and government financial-inclusion data from Pradhan Mantri Jan-Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) are used to analyze the adoption of FinTech and the link between financial inclusion and the adoption of FinTech. The study considers the use of digital financial instruments, financial awareness, perceived security, financial trust, financial education and access to formal financial services (FS). These factors are evaluated to check the relationship among these using descriptive, reliability, correlation and regression analysis. The results showed that the adoption of FinTech (FT) is positively associated with the improved financial access and usage and that the perceptions of digital literacy, awareness, trust and security have a significant impact on effective adoption. The results underscore the need for inclusive and safe digital financial services to ensure financial inclusion in rural areas.

all.title: Governance as an institutional amplifier: Fintech–ESG interactions and digital economic efficiency in selected advanced and emerging countries
institutions: Tashkent Institute of Irrigation and Agricultural Mechanization Engineers
all.abstract: The convergence of digital financial innovation and sustainability governance is a fundamental element of 21st-century economies, but its aggregate productive effects are unknown. Fintech adoption and ESG integration are extensively pursued as discrete policy goals despite theoretical evidence that their interplay conditioned by institutional quality may deliver efficiency improvements that neither channel alone can. Cross-country research has not verified the causal direction of the Fintech–efficiency relationship or found the governance channel through which ESG integration transmits macroeconomic productivity effects. This study addresses both gaps using a balanced panel of 68 countries over 2010–2022. Employing second-generation panel unit root tests, Westerlund cointegration, and fully modified and dynamic OLS estimators to establish long-run relationships, the study applies the Dumitrescu–Hurlin heterogeneous causality framework to identify causal direction and deploys Baron–Kenny panel mediation and interaction-term moderation analysis to decompose the institutional transmission mechanism. Fintech development exerts a positive, unidirectional, and Granger-causal long-run effect on digital economic efficiency (β ≈ 0.18), with no evidence of reverse causality. ESG integration mediates 40.8% of this relationship confirming a previously undocumented governance transmission channel while institutional quality amplifies both the Fintech and ESG efficiency returns by 77% and 72%, respectively, at high-governance relative to low-governance environments. Bidirectional causality between Fintech and ESG establishes a self-reinforcing co-evolutionary dynamic that compounds over time. These findings imply that governance investment is the highest-yield component of any digital economy strategy, and that joint Fintech–ESG co-financing architectures, differentiated by economy type, will outperform siloed policy approaches.

all.title: Beyond Digital Payments: A Systematic Literature Review of Fintech, Financial Inclusion, and Financial Well-Being in Emerging Economies
all.venue: Jurnal Arbitrase : Jurnal Ekonomi, Akuntansi, Manajemen dan Bisnis
all.abstract: Financial technology (fintech) has significantly expanded financial inclusion in emerging economies; however, greater access to digital financial services does not necessarily improve financial well-being. This study aims to systematically examine the relationship between fintech adoption, financial inclusion, and financial well-being by identifying underlying mechanisms, moderating factors, and potential adverse consequences. A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, synthesizing 64 peer-reviewed articles published between 2018 and 2026 and retrieved from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. The findings reveal a financial inclusion–well-being paradox, indicating that fintech adoption generates both positive and negative financial outcomes. Digital payments, automated micro-savings, productive digital credit, and insurtech contribute to consumption smoothing, financial resilience, and improved access to financial resources. Conversely, unrestricted digital lending and Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) services may increase over-indebtedness, impulsive consumption, and financial distress, particularly among individuals with limited financial literacy. Digital financial literacy, ethical product design, and effective consumer protection emerge as critical conditions shaping these outcomes. Integrating the Capability Approach and behavioral finance, this study proposes the Fintech-to-Financial Well-Being (F2FW) conceptual framework to explain how financial inclusion translates into sustainable financial well-being. These findings highlight the importance of shifting fintech strategies from transaction-driven growth toward consumer financial health and responsible financial innovation.

all.title: Re-Engineering Fintech Firms in Port Harcourt: Adopting Enterprise Resource Planning Systems for Enhancing Operational Output
all.venue: IIARD INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ECONOMICS AND BUSINESS MANAGEMENT
all.abstract: This study determined the relationship that existed between enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems and the operational output of fintech firms in Port Harcourt. The problem were based on the declining service output and increasing cost per unit of service in the sector studied. A cross-sectional survey design was used, for 20 fintech firms and a sample of 80 respondents that was selected using simple random sampling technique. Data used were derived with the use of structured questionnaire patterned after modified four-point Likert scale, which was validated by expert opinion and reliability was established using Cronbach’s alpha of 0.70. Pearson Product Moment Correlation Coefficient was used to analyze the relationship between variables. Findings revealed a positive and significant correlation existed between ERP system adoption and operational output. The study concludes that ERP systems is capable to re-engineer fintech operations by improving efficiency and sustainability. It recommended continuous investment in ERP as a solution for enhancing service output through automation and streamlined workflows.

all.title: Beyond direct effects: how digital leadership enables sustainability in SMEs through agile and FinTech capabilities – role of responsible innovation
institutions: King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals
all.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how digital leadership drives sustainability performance in SMEs across multiple countries, including Pakistan, Malaysia and Saudi Arabia. The research examines the sequential mediating roles of digital leadership (DL) on FinTech adoption (FTA) and organizational agility (OA), and the contingent governance role of responsible innovation (RI). Design/methodology/approach Grounded in the integration of “Upper Echelons” and “Dynamic Capabilities” theories, a two-wave longitudinal design was employed and analyzed via PLS-SEM. A total of 1039 senior officials responded to this study spanning over a year, comprising respondents, n = 472 from Pakistan; n = 303 from Malaysia and n = 264 from Saudi Arabia. Findings The findings presented interesting results, revealing that the underlying mechanism is not universal but context-dependent. In Pakistan, the pattern was inconsistent mediation (suppression), whereby a positive indirect effect through FinTech-driven pathways coexisted with a negative direct effect, yielding a non-significant total effect. In Malaysia and Saudi Arabia, the pattern was instead indirect-only mediation, with FTA and OA transmitting the relationship. RI significantly and negatively moderated the OA-SP pathway in Pakistan and positively moderated the DL-FTA pathway in Malaysia and Saudi Arabia; the DL-OA moderation was non-significant in all three countries, and the magnitude of the DL-FTA moderation did not differ significantly across them. Multi-group results indicated that several structural paths differed across countries, suggesting that national institutional architectures can reconfigure strategic pathways. Originality/value The study advances theory by specifying contingent capability-building routes from leadership to sustainability and offers nuanced practical guidance for leaders and policymakers navigating digital transformation in distinct institutional environments.

all.title: The Influence of Trust, Perceived Risk, and Level of Technology Anxiety on MSMEs’ Interest in Using Financial Technology (Fintech) (Case Study: MSMEs in Pangkalpinang City)
all.venue: International Journal of Economics Business and Innovation Research
all.abstract: Although Indonesia’s micro, small, and medium enterprise (MSME) sector is expanding rapidly, fintech adoption within these businesses continues to lag. This research investigates how trust, perceived risk, and technology anxiety shape MSMEs' intentions to adopt financial technology in Pangkalpinang City. Utilizing a quantitative associative-causal framework, primary data were gathered from 70 purposively sampled MSME operators via a 5-point Likert scale instrument. Data analysis was executed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) on SmartPLS software. The statistical evaluation demonstrates that adoption intention is positively driven by trust (β = 0.334; p = 0.000), whereas perceived risk (β = -0.386; p = 0.000) and technology anxiety (β = -0.273; p = 0.023) demonstrate significant negative effects. Overall, the proposed model explains roughly 48.3% of the variance in adoption intention, with perceived risk acting as the primary barrier to adoption. These findings suggest that accelerating MSME digitalization requires more than payment infrastructure provision; it demands cybersecurity education to reduce risk perception, consumer protection guarantees to build trust, and digital literacy training to lower technology anxiety among business operators.

all.title: Too Smart to List? AI Disruption, Financial Reporting, and Corporate Governance in the IPOs of Chinese Fintech Ventures: Evidence from an Agent-Based Computational Model
all.abstract: Chinese fintech ventures adopt artificial intelligence (AI) faster than almost any other entrepreneurial population, yet the ventures that adopt the most AI do not list most often. We develop an agent-based computational model in which 5,000 fintech ventures, underwriters, a securities regulator, and IPO investors interact from 2013 to 2025 under the institutional conditions of China's approval and registration regimes. The model treats AI as an entrepreneurial actor that raises productive capability but also creates algorithmic opacity and reshapes the discretion embedded in financial reporting. Estimating archival-style models on the simulated data, we find an inverted U-shaped relationship between AI adoption intensity and the annual hazard of listing. AI disruption exposure raises pre-IPO discretionary accruals, and strong corporate governance cuts this effect roughly in half. Accrual magnitude raises first-day returns, income-increasing accruals predict lower three-year buy-and-hold returns and higher distress, and reporting quality fully mediates the effect of disruption on regulatory approval. Monte Carlo replication, global sensitivity analysis, specification curves, and measurement-error experiments show which of these inferences an archival researcher could reliably recover. Counterfactual experiments indicate that governance upgrades and explainable AI raise listing rates and post-IPO performance more than AI-enabled regulatory review does.

all.title: Factors Influencing Adoption of Digital Wallet in Nepal
all.venue: Techspire Journal of Innovation Technology and Management
institutions: Asia Pacific University of Technology & Innovation
all.abstract: Digital wallets have emerged as a crucial part of modern financial systems because they allow for quicker, more comfortable and widespread transactions in everyday life. However, security and privacy issues still remain as major challenges for their mass adoption, especially in emerging countries. In this context, the present study studies the factors affecting the adoption of digital wallets in Nepal, considering the behavioral and technological factors which affect the acceptance of digital wallet by the users. This study uses the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and explanatory research design to analyze the influence of the independent variables selected on the behavior of adopting digital wallets. The data were acquired by using a non-probability sampling technique with the 320 respondents by using a structured questionnaire. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used in the empirical analysis to test the hypothesized relationships between constructs. The results show that Trust, Compatibility, Relative Advantage, and Perceived Behavioral Control have significant influence on digital wallet adoption in the Nepalese context while Perceived Risk does not show any statistically significant effect. The findings indicate the importance of trust-related and utility related factors in explaining adoption, and suggest that risk perception might not play as significant a role among those who have greater experience in the use of digital financial services. Overall, the study joins the growing body of literature on the adoption of fintech and brings context-specific evidence from Nepal, along with implications for policy makers, financial institutions, and fintech service providers seeking to boost adoption and promote financial inclusion in low- and middle-income countries.

all.title: Financial Technology Adoption and Sustainable Performance of SMES in Nigeria: A Literature Review of the Roles of Financial Inclusion and Financial Literacy
all.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
all.abstract: Financial technology is reshaping how small and medium-sized enterprises obtain finance, receive payments, manage transactions and interact with customers. In Nigeria, where SMEs frequently encounter restricted credit access, high transaction costs, weak financial records and infrastructural constraints, fintech offers potentially valuable routes to inclusion and improved business performance. This article critically reviews the extent and patterns of fintech adoption among Nigerian SMEs, evaluates its relationship with sustainable performance, and examines the roles of financial inclusion and financial literacy in this relationship. A critical narrative approach was adopted, with Nigerian empirical studies forming the primary evidence base and research from other emerging economies used for comparison. The literature indicates that adoption is concentrated in mobile transfers, digital banking and point-of-sale payments, while the uptake of digital credit, crowdfunding, insurance technology and integrated financial-management platforms remains uneven. Fintech can improve transaction efficiency, access to finance, customer reach, cash-flow management, resilience and business survival. However, access to technology does not automatically produce sustainable outcomes. Financial inclusion determines whether SMEs obtain useful and affordable financial services, while financial literacy influences product selection, responsible borrowing, risk management and the productive use of digital finance. Evidence remains limited by cross-sectional designs, inconsistent SME classifications and narrow performance measures. The article concludes that fintech supports sustainable SME performance when accompanied by meaningful financial inclusion, adequate financial literacy, reliable infrastructure, consumer protection and institutional support. It recommends capability-centred fintech policies, affordable digital finance and stronger longitudinal research.

all.title: Digital Loan Adoption Among Consumers: A Study on Awareness, Convenience and Borrowing Behaviour
all.venue: International Scientific Journal of Engineering and Management
all.abstract: Digital financial services have transformed the way consumers access credit by making borrowing faster, more convenient, and easily accessible through digital platforms. The increasing use of smartphones and internet-based financial services has led to the rapid growth of digital loan applications, enabling consumers to obtain loans with minimal documentation and quicker approval processes. Digital loan services have become an important alternative to traditional banking, particularly for individuals seeking immediate financial assistance. However, the adoption of digital loans depends on several factors, including consumer awareness, perceived convenience, and borrowing behavior. The present study examines the level of awareness among consumers regarding digital loan services, identifies the factors influencing the adoption of digital loans, and analyses the relationship between convenience and digital loan usage behaviour. In addition, the study explores the major challenges faced by consumers, such as concerns about interest rates, privacy, security, and lack of awareness. The study adopted a structured questionnaire, and a survey was conducted among 70 consumers in Kochi, Ernakulam District, Kerala. The findings reveal that consumer awareness and the convenience offered by digital loan platforms significantly influence the adoption of digital loans. The study also indicates that while consumers appreciate the speed and ease of digital borrowing, concerns regarding high interest rates, data security, and privacy continue to affect their borrowing decisions. The study concludes that enhancing consumer awareness and strengthening security measures can promote responsible adoption of digital loan services and improve users' confidence in digital lending platforms. Keywords: Digital Loans, Consumer Awareness, Convenience, Borrowing Behaviour, Digital Lending, Financial Technology (FinTech), Consumer Adoption.

all.title: Integrating Technology Acceptance Model and Theory of Planned Behavior on the Adoption of Financial Technology Among Generation Z in Lubuklinggau
all.venue: ECOMA Journal of Economics and Management
all.abstract: This study conceptually integrates the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to examine how Perceived Usefulness (PU) and Perceived Ease of Use (PEoU) affect Generation Z’s Behavioral Intention (BI) to adopt and continue using fintech in Lubuklinggau City, with Perceived Financial Risk (PFR) as a mediator. A quantitative explanatory design was applied to 398 active Generation Z e-wallet users aged 17–29, selected through purposive sampling (minimum required sample: 119). Data were collected using a Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed with PLS-SEM. The results show that PU and PEoU significantly and positively affected BI. PEoU had a larger coefficient than PU, although the difference between the two was not statistically significant. Neither PU nor PEoU significantly affected PFR, PFR did not significantly affect BI, and PFR did not mediate either relationship. The model’s explanatory power was low (R² = 0.144). Limitations include the single-city, and cross-sectional. Theoretically, the study offers a partial TAM–TPB integration in which perceived financial risk is treated as an inhibiting belief. Practically, the findings suggest that usefulness and ease of use are associated with continued fintech use, whereas risk perception was not shown to be a barrier. The effects of risk on non-users and the TPB antecedents remain for future research.

all.title: Instant Payments and Financial Inclusion: an analytical framework and research agenda
all.venue: Revista da Procuradoria-Geral do Banco Central
institutions: Escola de Administração de Empresas de São Paulo
all.abstract: This article examines how the academic and technical literature has addressed the relationship between instant payment systems and financial inclusion. Despite the rapid global expansion of these systems and their growing relevance in policy debates, their inclusive potential remains insufficiently systematized. The study conducts a structured literature review aimed at organizing the state of the art on this relationship. The analysis combines a systematic examination of academic publications with the review of institutional and technical documents, focusing on the main dimensions through which instant payments have been conceptualized. The findings indicate a predominant emphasis on institutional arrangements, system design, and adoption dynamics, while social and distributive impacts remain comparatively underexplored. Based on this synthesis, the article proposes an analytical framework that integrates these dimensions and identifies relevant gaps and avenues for future research on the role of instant payments in financial inclusion.

all.title: The Economics of Instant Payments: A Structured, Evidence-Graded Review of Financial Inclusion, Welfare, and Macro-Financial Effects across Global Fast-Payment Systems
all.abstract: Purpose: This article examines the economic consequences of instant payment systems (financial inclusion, welfare, growth and macro-financial stability) and seeks to separate the well-established effects from the projections and correlations that form the basis of much of the practitioner discussion. Methodology: This is a structured narrative review. The evidence is synthesized under an explicit four-tier scheme that gives primacy to peer-reviewed causal studies and central bank research over industry reports, separates out the observed from the forecasted, and places causal identification at the heart of the analysis. The review draws on 22 sources published between 2014 and 2026. The four systems under review are Brazil's Pix, India's UPI, the US FedNow and RTP and the EU's SEPA Instant. These are compared on design features. Findings: The best-evidenced finding is microeconomic: mobile-money access is estimated to have lifted around 2% of Kenyan households out of poverty and there are quasi-experimental findings on the impact of adoption in Mexico and India. The aggregate GDP and consumer savings data are all based on industry estimates and should be treated as indicative only. Differences in outcomes across the four systems are associated with system design (operator model, pricing, mandate and interoperability) rather than with the technology itself, although with four systems and no causal design this is a pattern, not an identified effect. The macro-financial risks are material, notably deposit-funding pressure and authorized-push-payment fraud (£450.7 million in the United Kingdom in 2024). Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The paper offers a five-channel transmission framework, an evidence-graded synthesis that distinguishes causal effects from projections, and a design-feature comparison that explains cross-country heterogeneity. It directs researchers toward credible identification and policymakers toward public, low-cost, interoperable and well-supervised designs on which inclusive outcomes depend.

all.title: A financial geography agenda for instant payment systems in Africa
all.abstract: The instant payment system (IPS) landscape in Africa is undergoing significant transformation due to technological advancements, regulatory changes and a growing drive for financial inclusion. This conceptual and agenda-setting study argues that IPSs are spatial projects structured by power geometries and develops a financial geography framework and research agenda for Africa’s IPS landscape. Despite technical and development rationales, the geographical nature of IPS infrastructures is often disregarded. For the African IPS landscape, four interlinked themes are highlighted: (i) the uneven geographies of financial inclusion, (ii) cross-border dynamics, (iii) regulatory geographies and (iv) data geographies, platform finance and algorithmic governance. This study proposes several questions, structured by the four interlinked themes, to guide future research on IPSs in Africa.

all.title: Pix por dentro: arquitetura, APIs públicas e segurança do sistema de pagamentos instantâneos do Banco Central
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: O Pix, arranjo de pagamentos instantâneos do Banco Central do Brasil, destoa de outras infraestruturas nacionais de pagamento pela quantidade de desenho que tornou pública: especificações de API sob licença Apache 2.0, metas de latência e disponibilidade expressas em percentis e regras contra a raspagem do diretório de contas. Este artigo lê esses documentos como artefatos de engenharia. Descrevemos o sistema de liquidação (SPI), o diretório (DICT) e o ciclo de mensagens, analisamos as defesas do diretório, discutimos incidentes no perímetro e sintetizamos a evidência econômica sobre competição e liquidez bancária. A revisão é narrativa, não sistemática, e não envolve experimentos nem dados novos. Pix, the instant payment scheme of the Central Bank of Brazil, is unusual among national payment infrastructures in how much of its design is public: API specifications under the Apache 2.0 license, latency and availability targets stated as percentiles, and anti-scraping rules for its account directory. This review reads those public documents as engineering artifacts. We describe the settlement system (SPI), the directory (DICT) and the message cycle, analyse the directory's defences, discuss security incidents at the perimeter and summarise the economic evidence on competition and bank liquidity. The review is narrative, not systematic, and involves no experiments or new data.

all.title: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI): Emerging Challenges and Issues in International Financial Law
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Digital public infrastructure is slowly becoming the base for many financial services. It includes systems such as digital identity, instant payments, and sharing of financial data with consent. These systems help people receive government benefits, make payments, and open bank accounts more easily. But they also bring legal problems, especially when personal data, private companies, and cross-border transactions are involved. This paper looks at the legal issues connected with digital public infrastructure in international financial law. At present, there is no one international law that covers DPI completely. Payments, data protection, cybersecurity, and digital identity are handled under different laws in different countries. Because of this, companies and users face confusion when a DPI-based service works across borders. The paper studies India, the European Union, and Brazil. These three examples show that countries are building DPI in different ways, but the law has not developed at the same speed. The paper points out problems such as weak cybersecurity, unclear liability when fraud or system failures happen, digital exclusion of people without documents or smartphones, and differences in data-protection rules. It argues that DPI should be treated as important financial infrastructure and should be regulated more clearly. Finally, the paper suggests that countries should follow common principles for DPI, improve cooperation between regulators, protect consumer rights, and provide offline or assisted options for people who cannot use digital systems. A balanced legal framework is needed so that DPI can support financial inclusion without putting users at risk.

all.title: Digital Infrastructure as an Engine of Economic Convergence
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Digital Infrastructure as an Engine of Economic Convergence (HH-2026-38) examines how high-speed telecommunications connectivity and open, interoperable Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI)—verifiable digital identity, instant low-cost payment rails, and consent-based data exchange—unlock productive opportunities, compress economy-wide transaction costs, formalize micro-enterprises, and accelerate long-run income convergence in emerging economies. Synthesizing ITU Facts & Figures 2024, World Bank Global Findex and ID4D baselines, BIS fast-payment panels, GovTech Maturity evaluations, and H Heuristics Integrated Digital Convergence Model (v3.8) simulations across 184 economies, the report shows that while +10 pp broadband penetration lifts annual per-capita GDP growth by +1.21% to +1.38%, synchronizing open Digital ID (+1.44%) and interoperable fast payments (+1.65%) generates a super-additive +2.45% annual growth dividend. Open DPI slashes cross-border remittances from 6.35% to 1.45%, merchant MDR from 2.40% to 0.15%, and G2P benefit leakage from 18.5% to 1.4%, propelling adult financial inclusion from 51.0% to 88.5%. In 2026–2050 scenarios across 184 economies, transitioning from fragmented telecom monopolies to a Coordinated Full-Stack DPI & Connectivity Compact doubles convergence velocity—lifting emerging-economy per-capita GDP from 24.2% of the OECD frontier in 2026 to 68.4% by 2050 versus 34.8% under persistent analog inertia.

all.title: Cashless Payment Activity: Banking Capacity, Income and Economic Structure in 25 Economies
all.abstract: Payment activity sits between the banks that supply payment services and the economy that uses them, yet most studies centre on one side. The present study asks how much of the cashless payment activity of an economy is associated with its banks, its income and its economic structure, for the 25 jurisdictions with a total cashless payment series in the statistics of the Bank for International Settlements, 2012 to 2024. Three hypotheses are tested and combined. Firstly, payment activity stands higher where banks had more capacity and payment infrastructure in place a year earlier: across economies, credit to the private sector is associated with more payments per adult with income held constant, and within economies payments track the terminals already deployed, though no single measure stands out beyond each economy's own trend. Secondly, a year of faster growth of real gross domestic product (GDP) per adult is a year of faster payment growth (1.10 points per point, p < 0.001), significantly so for card payments and more strongly in emerging economies; no association is detected for direct debits. Thirdly, economies with larger finance, real estate, business and public service sectors settle more payments by direct debit, with income held constant (ρ = 0.72, q = 0.010 over 72 tests). A Shapley decomposition shows that income and domestic sector shares exceed a placebo benchmark in every specification that includes them, while bank measures do so only under some measures. Hence the explained variation in payment activity is shared among banking measures, income and structure.

all.title: Analisis Perkembangan BI-FAST sebagai Bentuk Inovasi Jasa Perbankan dalam Mendukung Efisiensi Transaksi di Indonesia
all.abstract: The development of digital technology encourages banks to provide payment services that are faster, more accessible, and affordable. One of Indonesia’s payment system innovations is Bank Indonesia Fast Payment (BI-FAST), which is designed to support real-time retail transactions, operate 24 hours a day and seven days a week, and offer relatively affordable transfer fees. This study aims to analyze the development of BI-FAST as a banking service innovation and its contribution to supporting transaction efficiency in Indonesia. The study employs a descriptive qualitative approach using a literature review method. The secondary data are obtained from Bank Indonesia institutional reports published between 2022 and 2025 and relevant scholarly journal articles. The analysis involves classifying information, comparing previous research findings, and interpreting the evidence through Transaction Cost Economics (TCE), Diffusion of Innovations (DOI), and the PIECES evaluation framework. TCE is used to examine transaction costs and barriers, DOI helps explain the development and utilization of innovation, while PIECES provides an organizing framework for evaluating economic aspects, performance, efficiency, security, information, and service quality. The study focuses on identifying service developments and their potential contributions to transaction efficiency, particularly in terms of affordability, processing speed, service availability, and wider utilization. The analysis is expected to provide an overview of BI-FAST’s role in the development of Indonesia’s digital payment system. Since this study relies on secondary data and does not directly measure banks’ operating costs or survey customers, its assessment of efficiency is limited to the available evidence. Accordingly, potential contributions to transaction efficiency are discussed descriptively rather than treated as statistically established causal effects.

all.title: The Three Laws of Payment Physics: Speed-Finality Separation, Friction Relocation, and Multilateral Liquidity-Saving Netting Across Global Retail and Wholesale Rails
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Modern electronic checkouts complete contactless card authorizations and mobile QR scans in 150 to 400 milliseconds, sustaining the widespread illusion that sovereign purchasing power moves at fiber-optic speed. In reality, global financial plumbing separates fast cryptographic messaging from irrevocable balance-sheet extinction across commercial and central bank ledgers. Bridging monetary economics with protocol-level distributed systems engineering, this 8-page open-access working paper (Digbijoy Labs Working Paper WP-2026-03) formalizes The Three Laws of Payment Physics: Law I — The Speed–Finality Divide: Authorization messages record conditional intent at fiber-optic speed, whereas interbank debt extinguishes only when central-bank reserves (Tier 0 M0) or statutory settlement assets mutate across nested double-entry ledgers. Law II — The Conservation of Friction: Checkout simplicity never destroys verification complexity; it relocates protocol work into hardware cryptography (EMV ARQC, FIPS 140-3 HSMs), alias and Verification of Payee directories (NPCI VPA, BCB DICT, EU Reg. 2024/886 VoP), prefunded liquidity pools, or post-settlement dispute arbitration. Law III — The Conservation of Risk: Credit, intraday liquidity, fraud, foreign-exchange principal (Herstatt), and split-brain timeout exposures never vanish; Debit Pull vs. Credit Push rulebooks invert risk polarity and price exposure across balance sheets. Includes a unified 9-archetype comparative taxonomy and monochrome schematics contrasting Four-Corner ISO 8583 Pull Cards, Sovereign Instant Credit Push (India UPI, Brazil Pix, US FedNow and RTP, Eurozone SEPA Instant / TIPS), Wholesale RTGS and Liquidity-Saving Mechanisms (Fedwire Funds, Eurosystem T2, CHIPS 26:1 continuous multilateral netting), and CLS Bank 18-currency atomic FX Payment-versus-Payment (PvP). Companion Monograph (Releasing December 8, 2026): Jay Thorne, The Physics of Payments: A Practitioner's Guide to Cards, Instant Rails, B2B Treasury, Cross-Border FX, and Wholesale Settlement (Digbijoy Labs, 2026, 242 pp., 20 Chapters, 20 Monochrome Schematics; Paperback ISBN 979-8-1449-0879-5, Hardcover ISBN 979-8-1449-1281-5). Interactive Open-Source Simulators (MIT): https://digbijoylabs.github.io/anatomy-of-a-payment/ | Source & Free 23-Page Chapter 1 Sample: https://github.com/digbijoylabs/anatomy-of-a-payment

all.title: Macroeconomic volatility and the value of AI analytics in Nigerian digital lending
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence can help digital lenders assess borrowers, but its value for credit risk management may vary with economic conditions. This study examines whether perceived macroeconomic volatility weakens the relationship between AI-driven predictive analytics and credit risk management performance in Nigeria. Drawing on contingency theory, it analyses survey responses from 185 digital lending professionals in Lagos State using partial least squares structural equation modelling with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. AI analytics was positively associated with perceived performance (β = 0.382, p < 0.001), while its interaction with macroeconomic volatility was negative and statistically significant (β = −0.163, p = 0.006; f² = 0.063). Alternative data utilization and regulatory compliance also showed positive associations with performance. Together, the predictors explained 68.4 percent of the variance in the outcome. The findings suggest that the relationship between analytics and risk management performance becomes weaker as perceived economic instability increases. They support a contingency perspective in which the benefits of technology depend partly on its operating environment. For digital lenders, the findings highlight the importance of model validation, borrower affordability and timely adjustments to lending policy.

all.title: Business Intelligence and Analytics in U.S. Financial Services: Evidence on Lending Decisions, Risk, and Governance
all.venue: Cureus Journal of Business and Economics.
all.abstract: Banks, FinTech lenders, and other U.S. financial-service firms increasingly use analytics to screen borrowers, verify information, price risk, allocate credit, monitor conduct, and support operational decisions. This structured narrative review synthesizes 47 U.S. empirical studies published between 2010 and August 2026. The evidence is concentrated in mortgage, consumer, small-business, marketplace, and related lending, with additional studies of bank information technology, information-sharing systems, automated underwriting, application programming interfaces, regulatory technology, robo-advice, and artificial intelligence-related operational risk. Several studies associated digital verification, alternative data, and stronger information-processing capability with faster processing, wider credit access, better screening, or improved loan performance. Others reported higher default, mispriced risk, suspicious lending patterns, persistent pricing disparities, and operational losses. Findings varied by setting and research design. Across the settings represented in the evidence base, analytics contributed most to decision quality when information was credible and decision-relevant, useful complementary information was retained, analytical signals influenced institutional action, and incentives, governance, risk controls, and monitoring supported appropriate use.

all.title: Artificial Intelligence and Credit Scoring: Opportunities, Ethical Challenges, and Regulatory Implications
all.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) is changing credit scoring and to assess the opportunities, ethical concerns, and regulatory challenges associated with its use. It traces the shift from traditional statistical models to AI-based approaches, reviews machine learning, neural networks, and deep learning techniques, and compares their main characteristics with conventional scoring methods. It also considers the safeguards needed for responsible adoption. The study draws on a narrative review of academic literature and regulatory documents, including the European Union’s Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI and the AI Act, alongside a qualitative comparison of credit scoring approaches. The findings suggest that AI can help lenders capture nonlinear relationships, use alternative data, assess applications more quickly, and reach borrowers with limited credit histories. These benefits, however, depend on the quality of the data and how models are validated and used. The review highlights persistent concerns about algorithmic bias, the difficulty of explaining model decisions, data privacy, and regulatory compliance. More accurate predictions alone do not guarantee fair lending decisions. The study concludes that responsible AI adoption requires fairness checks, meaningful explanations, human oversight, and sound data governance. Its practical contribution is to help financial institutions and policymakers assess AI-based credit scoring in terms of both predictive performance and the transparency, accountability, and protection it offers borrowers.

all.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Financial Services Innovation
all.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are important elements of today’s technology landscape, generating significant hype and excitement. However, hype does not equal reality, and AI enables true innovation in only a limited number of areas. The financial services industry is experiencing AI-driven innovation, but in certain aspects, in a very different way than other industries, for example, consumer internet services. It is not always possible for banks to create truly unique and new market-leading products based on AI. Instead, most institutions are training whales’ and several use cases in the financial services sector focus on supporting functions such as risk management and compliance. A clear direction for the application of AI in financial innovation centers on significant improvements in personalized or tailored services, striking the right balance between personalization, relevance, and ethical use of customer data. What are the most important innovation areas influenced by AI? What are the main opportunities for value creation, and what are the associated risks and trade-offs? The introduction seeks to provide preliminary answers to these questions by analyzing the role of AI in the financial services-proximity and support-oriented innovation domains. AI in finance is most strongly associated with enhanced personalization and user experience—better product recommendations, improved customer support, and a wider monitoring of customer behaviors and needs. Segmentation models play an important part, enabling further differentiation of AI-friendly services by modifying the type of algorithm or logic used to reach an outcome, for example, recommendation systems or credit-scoring systems. However, ethical aspects are extremely important in these applications. AI is also widely used in risk and compliance functions and is probably more mature in these areas than in customer-facing functions. AI can enable a better and faster detection of abnormal behavior, thus limiting damages and enhancing the rapidity of incident-response operations. However, the increasing complexity of AI models may make risk management in itself more challenging.

all.title: A systematic review of quantum machine learning: algorithms, application domains, and emerging trends
all.abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) integrates the principles of quantum mechanics superposition, entanglement, and interference into mathematical and logical operations that classical computers cannot emulate. Despite the limitations of today’s noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ-ERA) devices, these platforms already sustain small- to medium-scale machine-learning workloads, catalyzing rapid expansion in QML research. Guided by PRISMA methodology, we systematically screened 5,463 publications published between January 2015 and June 2025 and identified 160 high-quality studies that implemented or evaluated QML algorithms on real or simulated quantum processors. The selected literature converges into four thematic categories: (i) quantum adaptations of classical algorithms, (ii) variational and hybrid quantum–classical models, (iii) quantum linear-algebra accelerators, and (iv) quantum-inspired generative and reinforcement techniques. Application domains span image and signal classification, cybersecurity, finance, chemistry, and healthcare, with benchmarks such as MNIST, CIC-IDS2019 and credit-risk corpora featuring prominently in the reviewed corpus. Separately from the reviewed literature, Sect. 6 reports our own five-seed benchmark of five quantum and two classical classifiers on five public tabular datasets (Breast Cancer, Diabetes, Iris, Sonar and Bank Marketing). Comparative analyses reveal that hybrid QML systems typically match or marginally exceed the performance of state-of-the-art classical baselines while employing fewer parameters. Nevertheless, a clear, reproducible quantum advantage remains elusive, hindered by data-encoding overheads, circuit-depth constraints, environmental noise, and barren-plateau training phenomena. By integrating algorithmic trends, empirical outcomes, and hardware considerations, this review delineates QML’s present capabilities and identifies critical technological milestones error mitigation, scalable qubit architectures, and efficient data-loading schemes needed to unlock its full potential.

all.title: Digital Transformation and Credit Risk Mitigation in Conflict-Affected Yemen: An Intelligent Decision Support System with Knowledge-Graph Augmented Explainable Boosting
all.venue: European Journal of Applied Science Engineering and Technology
all.abstract: This study investigates whether and how digital transformation affects the credit risk of commercial banks in Yemen, where protracted conflict, institutional fragmentation, and severe data constraints complicate the operation and evaluation of the banking system. Using a balanced branch-level panel of 42 branches from two representative Banks over 2013–2024, we construct a composite digital transformation index (DDT) covering digital management, digital business, and digital strategy, and measure credit risk primarily by the Z-score, with the non-performing loan (NPL) ratio as a robustness proxy. The Z-score is constructed in its conventional form, in which higher values denote a greater distance from insolvency and therefore lower credit risk; all regressions were re-estimated with the corrected measure and every reported sign has been reassessed accordingly. Fixed-effects regressions show that digital transformation significantly reduces credit risk, while model fit improves (R² from 0.209 to 0.303). This paper additionally presents the formal architecture, algorithmic pseudocode, and computer simulation of an Intelligent Decision Support System (IDSS). The IDSS introduces the Knowledge-Graph Augmented Explainable Boosting Model (KG-EBM). To rigorously evaluate the system under wartime data restrictions, we implement an in-silico computational simulation testbed strictly calibrated to the empirical panel moments alongside 10,000 Monte Carlo dynamic stress simulations. Machine learning experiments demonstrate that the proposed KG-EBM engine achieves superior predictive accuracy (R² = 0.7974, RMSE = 0.2812, F1 = 0.7192, and AUC-ROC = 0.8559), outperforming standard econometric OLS (R² = 0.6535), Multi-Layer Perceptron (R² = 0.6694), and standard Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (R² = 0.7872). A controlled ablation study isolates the marginal contribution of relational graph information, and complete mediation and ownership-heterogeneity tests report the corresponding indirect effects and interaction coefficients with bootstrap uncertainty estimates. Furthermore, Monte Carlo stress-testing reveals that adaptive IDSS deployment compresses 95% Value-at-Risk (VaR) from 6.339% down to 4.300%, containing catastrophic tail risk by 32.2%. The resulting framework bridges computational intelligence and empirical financial risk management for post-crisis economic reconstruction.

all.title: Controlled Synthesis of Imperfect Datasets for Machine Learning Education: A Variational Autoencoder, Wasserstein GAN, and Gaussian Mixture Model Framework with Domain-Aware Fraud and Error Injection
institutions: University of the West of England
all.abstract: Machine learning and data science education overwhelmingly relies on pre-cleaned, statically curated benchmark datasets from repositories such as the UCI ML Repository and Kaggle. These datasets are ill-suited to teaching the realities of production data pipelines, which invariably contain missing values arising from mixed mechanisms, domain-specific typographic errors, format inconsistencies, and embedded fraud of varying sophistication. This paper presents a configurable framework for generating synthetic imperfect datasets tailored to four United Kingdom financial domains: banking transactions, mortgage lending, insurance claims, and investment and trading. The framework offers three alternative generators, one selected per request: a $$\beta $$ -Variational Autoencoder ($$\beta $$ -VAE) with KL annealing, a Wasserstein GAN with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP) and their hybrid, with a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) fitted to the VAE latent space as an optional prior, all implemented entirely in pure NumPy so that every operation is an explicit array computation. A probabilistic error injection layer introduces nine distinct corruption types—covering MCAR, MAR, and structural errors—allocated via a Dirichlet prior over a user-specified global error budget. A domain-aware fraud injection layer encodes archetypes drawn from UK Finance, Payment Systems Regulator, Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and Association of British Insurers (ABI) taxonomies. Evaluation across the four domains, against external baselines fitted to the same training splits, shows that the $$\beta $$ -VAE attains a mean Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic of 0.104 against a held-out partition of the rule-based seed corpus, ahead of CTGAN and TVAE on the same target at 1/34 and 1/9 of their respective fitting times, and that a structureless independent-marginals generator matches every marginal while destroying the correlation structure, so marginal fidelity alone does not discriminate between generators. A zero-cost smoothed bootstrap of the seed corpus attains a better statistic still on both marginal fidelity and correlation error, and a Gaussian copula is ahead of the $$\beta $$ -VAE on categorical divergence and correlation error at a fifth of its fitting cost, so the case for the generative stage is not made on fidelity to the seed corpus and is not made here. Validation against real record-level data shows close agreement for bounded quantities and substantial disagreement in the tails, so the framework is characterised as generating plausible rather than realistic records. A detector transcribed from the documented fraud injection ranges and fitted to nothing attains AUROC 0.994 when archetypes overwrite records outright, which motivates an overlap-controlled injection scheme introduced here that makes archetype separability a declared continuous parameter; at its default expression coefficient $$\lambda = 0.25$$ the same detector falls to 0.609, while a trained classifier reaches 0.948. Error injection realises a stable and monotone but systematically low fraction of the requested rate, averaging 0.596 of it, and the missingness mechanisms are verified to be correctly instantiated when isolated from the default allocation. Generation scales to 100,000 records in 7.0 min on two commodity CPU cores without GPU acceleration. No evidence involving learners or instructors is presented; a protocol for the evaluation that would be required is specified in full.

all.title: Intelligent Mortgage and Housing Finance Through Predictive Analytics
all.abstract: Data-driven intelligence enabled by predictive analytics is transforming diverse aspects of the mortgage and housing ecosystem. Intelligent automation of decision making through predictive models helps mortgage lenders develop efficient, customer-centered underwriting strategies. In addition to credit scoring, open data sources and machine learning techniques are used to enhance forecasting of housing prices and borrower prepayment, default, and delinquency risk. Such advanced analytics should ultimately help lenders develop personalized mortgage offerings throughout the loan lifecycle. Predictive analytics in housing finance encompasses a wide range of techniques across multiple subdomains of the mortgage ecosystem. A systematic literature review reveals major categories and problems, as well as the principal sources and models. However, multiple dimensions of delivering data-driven intelligence in mortgage underwriting remain relatively unexplored.
