Automated decision making is often limited to the origination phase, with little consideration for the ongoing servicing of existing loans. Furthermore, while credit scoring models are well established, the potential for using predictive techniques for dynamic rate and product personalization has yet to be realized.

all.title: Parsimony over complexity in maritime vessel asset pricing: a quality-adjusted comparable transaction approach
Quantum Computing for Financial Analytics and Risk Management
all.venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
all.abstract: This chapter explores the integration of quantum computing into financial analytics, focusing on applications in financial markets, risk management, and accounting. It examines how quantum principles and algorithms, including QAOA, VQE, and HHL, can support portfolio optimization, derivatives pricing, credit risk modeling, and fraud detection. The chapter also considers quantum machine learning for analysing ESG metrics, sentiment data, and unstructured corporate information. Case studies from banking, FinTech, and national quantum initiatives illustrate emerging adoption, while ethical, regulatory, and infrastructure challenges are discussed alongside hybrid quantum-classical approaches. The chapter concludes with a research agenda for quantum finance, corporate governance, and accounting.

all.title: Risk Mitigation in Banking Through Creditworthiness Prediction Models
all.abstract: In modern banking systems, accurately identifying repeat clients and detecting multiple loan applications is crucial, especially when financial institutions face restricted access to funding. Since loan repayment capability directly impacts profitability, assessing an applicant's ability to repay loans is a vital part of the process. Timely loan repayment under specified interest conditions significantly improves a bank's financial returns. Over the past few decades, individuals‘ hesitation to apply for loans has declined, pushing financial institutions to adopt efficient methods for identifying eligible applicants. When forecasting future repayment behavior, the applicant's credit history, as represented by their credit score or CIBIL rating, is a highly reliable predictor of repayment behavior. The data shows they have a history of promptly satisfying their financial commitments. This article presents a machine learning-based approach to loan approval prediction. By leveraging CIBIL scores and other relevant financial metrics, this predictive model aids in mitigating financial risks and supports more effective, data-driven decision-making in loan applications.

all.title: Explainable AI for Financial Fraud Detection in India: A Conceptual Framework Integrating Machine Intelligence, Chartered Accountancy Judgement, and the Emerging Indian Regulatory Architecture
all.abstract: Indian financial institutions now deploy machine-learning systems at unprecedented scale -the Unified Payments Interface alone processes transaction volumes that make manual fraud surveillance infeasible -yet the opacity of these models sits uneasily beside three distinctly Indian demands: the engineering imperative for interpretable outputs; the chartered accountancy profession's standards of professional scepticism codified in SA 240; and a regulatory architecture that has shifted from advisory soft law (NITI Aayog's Responsible AI principles) to binding instruments (the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, the RBI Digital Lending Directions 2025, and SEBI's 2025 amendments assigning responsibility for AI-tool outputs).The scholarly literature addresses these demands separately: explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) research optimises explanation fidelity without engaging Indian audit practice; accountancy research on AI adoption in India remains descriptive; and compliance commentary analyses each instrument in isolation.This article develops TEA-India -an adaptation of the Tripartite Explainability Alignment framework -comprising a technical-explainability layer, a judgement-alignment layer anchored in ICAI's Standards on Auditing, and a compliance layer mapped to India's sector-specific instruments, connected through an explanation audit trail.The analysis identifies five India-specific gaps, including the absence of any automated-decision provision comparable to GDPR Article 22 in the DPDP Act, the consultative (not yet binding) status of RBI's modelrisk guidance, and the near-complete absence of Indian empirical research on how chartered accountants actually consume model explanations.Five propositions and a comparative analysis against global frameworks are advanced.The framework offers Indian banks, NBFCs, auditors, and regulators a common vocabulary for designing frauddetection systems whose explanations are simultaneously technically faithful, professionally usable, and legally defensible.

all.title: Beyond the Datafication of Everyday Life: Recentring Structure and Collectivity in Critical Data Literacy
all.abstract: How societies imagine data plays an important role in the perception, adoption, and evaluation of digital technologies. These imaginaries emerge within dynamic discursive frameworks that are largely determined by prevailing norms and values in specific socio-cultural contexts, political factors, and media ecologies. The present chapter develops a conceptualisation of cultural data imaginaries that links (mediatised) data discourses to critical data literacy. We provide a critical overview of dominant imaginaries as well as their core tenets: tech-enthusiast, tech-critical, and critical-pragmatic ‘alternative’ data imaginaries. Each determines data’s societal implications and effects from different socio-cultural, political, and epistemological angles. We take a bird’s-eye view on these different types of imaginaries with emphasis on three interconnected dimensions: (1) imaginaries are culturally configured, (2) media play a critical role in the formation of imaginaries, and (3) they have direct implications for critical data literacies. Cultural data imaginaries are never ‘neutral’. They lend legitimacy to technology by narratively emphasising innovation, governance, commercialisation, or resistance. The question is not only how cultural data imaginaries are portrayed but whose visions become dominant and whose are marginalised, silenced, or rendered invalid.

all.title: Now You See Me Now You Don't: A Framework To Detect and Reduce Proxy Capacity
all.abstract: In regulated domains such as lending, the two most salient fairness concepts are disparate impact and disparate treatment: disparate impact is generally defined by differential rates of adverse outcomes between demographic groups, while disparate treatment is generally defined by the use of demographic information or proxies to issue decisions. There already exist established methods to quantitatively detect and mitigate disparate impact; however, there has been less research on doing the same for disparate treatment. From a practitioner's perspective, the manner in which a conditional independence test is formulated and operationalized to identify proxies is nuanced and underexplored. As Machine Learning (ML) systems increase in scope and application in regulated domains, practitioners need a defensible framework to identify proxies at scale. Current disparate treatment frameworks typically rely upon some combination of quantitative and qualitative review of models' inputs to identify proxies. Features that are identified as proxies are then typically removed from the model in practice, and predictive performance degrades in favor of fairness through unawareness. Here, we propose a two-part framework that reduces the disparate treatment risk of a feature and keeps the predictive performance that removal of the feature loses. First, we propose a quantitative test for proxy capacity that identifies whether some of a feature's values reveal membership in a particular demographic group. Second, we propose a pre-processing methodology that adjusts those proxy features to reduce their proxy capacity. We show empirically on synthetic and public datasets that this framework identifies features that proxy for demographic information and reduces their proxy capacity while the adjusted feature retains task-relevant signal (i.e. improves predictive performance versus removal).

all.title: Cloud Computing and AI-Driven Applications
all.abstract: Cloud computing and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are two transformative technologies that are reshaping the modern digital environment. Cloud computing provides scalable infrastructure, storage facilities, computing resources and software services through the internet, while Artificial Intelligence enables machines to perform tasks that traditionally require human intelligence, including learning, reasoning, prediction, decision-making and natural language processing. The integration of these technologies has created a powerful platform for developing intelligent, scalable and cost-effective applications. Cloud-based AI applications allow organizations to process large volumes of data, develop predictive models, automate business operations and deliver intelligent services without maintaining expensive computing infrastructure. These applications are widely used in healthcare, education, banking, retail, manufacturing, transportation and agriculture. This chapter examines the fundamentals of cloud computing, its architecture and service models, the principles of Artificial Intelligence, and the integration of AI technologies with cloud platforms. It also discusses major application areas, advantages, implementation challenges, security and privacy considerations, ethical issues and future developments. The chapter highlights how the combination of cloud computing and AI contributes to digital transformation and supports intelligent decision-making across different sectors.

all.title: Financial Consequences of Cloud Security Breaches in Nigerian Deposit Money Banks: A Systematic Literature Review
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The accelerating migration to cloud computing architectures has fundamentally restructured operational data management, digital banking channels, and payment settlement ecosystems across Nigerian Deposit Money Banks (DMBs). However, heightened dependence on decentralised, multi-tenant cloud platforms has simultaneously amplified exposure to advanced cyber threats, carrying catastrophic financial and systemic ramifications. This systematic literature review critically examines the direct, indirect, and regulatory financial consequences of cloud security breaches within Nigerian banking institutions. Breaches precipitated by cloud misconfigurations, insecure application programming interfaces (APIs), compromised identity and access management (IAM), and insider vulnerabilities generate immediate financial damage through fraudulent funds diversion, ransom extortions, digital forensics, and system restoration. Beyond immediate cash outflows, institutions endure substantial indirect financial attrition stemming from protracted operational downtime, customer churn, and long-term brand impairment. Regulatory sanctions imposed under the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) and Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) cybersecurity frameworks coupled with escalating litigation liabilities intensify balance-sheet fragility. By synthesising empirical loss distributions and global institutional case studies (including Capital One, Equifax, and Nigerian commercial banking disclosures), this paper establishes an integrated financial impact assessment model incorporating probabilistic scenario analytics. Strategic imperatives, such as Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA), artificial-intelligence-driven continuous monitoring, comprehensive cyber underwriting, and regulatory alignment, are detailed to safeguard institutional solvency and national economic stability.

all.title: Evaluation of Internal Control in Minimizing Non-Performing Loans at PT Bank SulutGo, Bahu Sub-Branch Office
all.venue: INFLUENCE International Journal of Science Review
all.abstract: Lending is a core banking activity that is inherently exposed to the risk of non-performing loans. The Non-Performing Loan (NPL) ratio at PT Bank SulutGo, Bahu Sub-Branch Office, fluctuated from January to April 2026, reaching 1.87%, 2.69%, 1.82%, and 2.55%, respectively, indicating the need to review internal controls at the unit. This study aims to analyze how internal controls are implemented to minimize non-performing loans at the office. A descriptive qualitative approach was employed. Primary and secondary data were collected through interviews with three informants, observation, and documentation, and were analyzed using the Miles and Huberman model with reference to the five components of the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO) framework. The findings indicate that internal controls are generally well implemented and reasonably effective. The control environment, risk assessment, and information and communication components function well, supported by segregation of duties, BI Checking, the 5C principles, and the Online Integrated Banking System (OLIBS). Control activities are implemented fairly well, although credit-file storage remains suboptimal. Monitoring is the weakest component because it is largely passive and is initiated only after a borrower’s name appears on the arrears list, particularly for consumer loans. External factors are the main causes of non-performing loans, including termination of employment, delayed salary disbursement, insufficient residual income, and borrowers’ lack of good faith, while the role of the bank’s internal factors is relatively limited. The bank is advised to maintain effective existing controls, improve credit-file management, optimize the use of OLIBS information, and implement risk-based monitoring so that any deterioration in borrowers’ repayment capacity can be detected earlier.

all.title: Beyond automatic synergy: A mechanism-friction perspective on the environmental, social and governance-digital twin transition in banking
all.venue: Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science- Economics and Business Administration
institutions: Ho Chi Minh City Open University
all.abstract: Research on banking’s twin transition increasingly views sustainability and digitalization as complements but direct interaction studies show reinforcing, attenuating and conditional relationships. Theories explain why capability bundles create value but do not organize these conflicting banking outcomes around the mechanisms that create value and the integration frictions that absorb it. This paper develops a banking-specific mechanism-friction framework and six testable propositions. Digital capability is the organizational capacity through which the digital component of the twin transition is implemented. The framework is informed by a focused synthesis nested within a search-delimited Scopus corpus of 150 banking studies published between 2010 and 2025. Twelve studies met the strict definition of a direct sustainability-digital conditional relationship with bank-level or banking-system-level outcome; eight are mostly reinforcing, three attenuating and one has no stable direction. Two more studies remain as boundary cases. Synthesis suggests that positive interaction is most likely when digital resources are linked to ESG information, risk, reporting or intermediation tasks. Implementation costs, resource pressure, legacy systems, governance weaknesses and outcome or timing mismatches may offset value created by mechanisms. These established mechanisms and frictions are integrated into an outcome-and time sensitive explanation of heterogeneous banking results in the paper and an auditable empirical agenda for emerging markets is proposed.

all.title: ANALYSIS AND DESIGN OF VLAN AND ACL NETWORK INFRASTRUCTURE USING THE NDLC METHOD AT BPR ULIMA DJUMPA MAROM
all.abstract: BPR Ulima Djumpa Marom has just moved to a new three-story building, but its network infrastructure is still a flat network without segmentation, relying on Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) from the Internet Service Provider (ISP) modem for all devices. This condition causes IP address conflicts during power outages, as well as no restrictions on access between divisions or customer WiFi networks to the bank's operational system. This study applies the Network Development Life Cycle (NDLC) method focused on the Analysis, Design, and Simulation Prototype stages, using Cisco Packet Tracer as a simulation tool. The proposed network design divides the network into seven Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) segments based on function and division, applies the Router-on-a-Stick inter-VLAN routing method, configures Static IP addressing on all banking operational devices, and provides a dedicated DHCP Server for Access Point devices. Extended Access Control List (ACL) policies are applied to the Bank Router to enforce granular access control between VLANs. Test results across twenty scenarios show that the customer WiFi network can only access the internet and is completely isolated from the core banking system, while access between divisions is successfully configured according to each business's needs, such as full supervisory access for the Board of Directors and limited access for operational divisions. This study proves that the combination of VLANs and ACLs effectively improves network security and management efficiency in a banking environment.

all.title: Software Development Trends in Financial Services: A 2026 Overview
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This report provides an overview of the major software development trends shaping financial services in 2026. It examines the growing role of artificial intelligence, intelligent automation, cloud computing, microservices architecture, APIs, business intelligence, cybersecurity, regulatory considerations, and legacy system modernization in modern financial technology environments. The report also presents a practical framework for evaluating financial technology based on business value, technical feasibility, security, compliance, and total cost. The objective is to provide an accessible industry-level reference for professionals, technology teams, researchers, students, and organizations interested in financial software development and digital transformation. Topics covered include: • Artificial intelligence and machine learning in financial applications • Intelligent automation in banking and financial workflows • Cloud computing and hybrid financial infrastructure • Microservices and modern software architecture • APIs and financial system integration • Business intelligence and financial data • Cybersecurity and data protection • Compliance and regulatory considerations • Legacy financial system modernization • Technology evaluation and digital transformation The report is intended for educational and informational purposes and does not constitute legal, regulatory, financial, cybersecurity, or technology implementation advice. Additional industry resources are provided in the Further Reading section of the report.

all.title: Zombie Systems Diagnostic Standard: Continuity, Compensation, Functional Correspondence and Recovery Across Planetary SR
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Zombie Systems names a bounded institutional condition in which visible outputs or continued operation conceal declining substantive function, while increasing compensatory inputs preserve continuity and independent capacity to recover deteriorates. The claim is distinct from temporary strain, aging technology, ordinary financial distress, or the established corporate-finance definition of a zombie firm. This paper establishes a functional diagnostic standard for identifying the condition at the level of a particular service, infrastructure, population, region, and observation interval. The standard specifies seven evidentiary gates: operational continuity, independently measured functional deterioration, rising compensation, impaired recovery, persistence, causal linkage, and serious comparison with alternative explanations. It separates output from service quality, authorized metrics from independent outcomes, adaptation from depletion, and high demand from failed capacity. A directional state vector and a counterfactual research design support measurement without assigning unvalidated universal scores or thresholds. The standard is anchored to OECD service-performance measurement, World Bank governance indicators, asset-management principles, federal legacy-system review, and operational recovery planning. A four-country pilot matrix for Canada, South Africa, Japan, and Norway demonstrates the identification burden while declining to infer national diagnoses from partial indicators. The standard interfaces with the thirty registered Planetary SR pathways without changing their forecasts. Its scientific contribution is a testable continuity–compensation–recovery mechanism whose incremental explanatory and predictive value must be demonstrated against established models.

all.title: Self-Service Failure Recovery and Autonomous Operational Remediation in Multi-Tenant Financial Systems: A Conceptual Framework
all.venue: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF PURE SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
all.abstract: Multi-tenant financial platforms, including core banking as a service, payment processors, embedded finance providers and wealth management back offices, concentrate the operations of many regulated institutions onto shared infrastructure. When such platforms fail, the cost is measured not only in downtime but in misposted balances, duplicated payments, breached settlement windows and regulatory exposure for every tenant at once. Two operational paradigms have matured in parallel to address this: autonomous remediation, in which the platform detects and corrects faults without human intervention, and self-service recovery, in which tenants are given the tools to diagnose and resolve incidents affecting their own scope. Yet the literature treats these largely in isolation, and neither is well theorised for environments where financial integrity, tenant isolation and supervisory accountability are binding constraints. Using a conceptual research design grounded in an integrative synthesis of 252 sources, including 227 applied seed publications screened from a consolidated corpus of 1,056 peer works, this paper proposes SAFER-FS (Self-service and Autonomous Failure Engineering for Resilient Financial Systems), a seven-layer conceptual framework that integrates containment, tenant-aware observation, diagnosis, policy-governed autonomy, integrity-preserving execution, self-service recovery and evidentiary assurance into a single closed control loop. The framework introduces a graduated autonomy scale (A0 to A5), a risk-weighted remediation admission function, a set of financial integrity invariants that every remediation must preserve, and an explicit mapping to the operational resilience obligations that have taken effect, most notably the European Union Digital Operational Resilience Act and the United Kingdom operational resilience regime. The paper discusses the theoretical, practical and regulatory implications of the model, acknowledges its limitations, and concludes with six testable propositions, an evaluation metric set and a future research agenda.

همبستگی علّی (Zero Causal Link): مایکروسافت، اپل، AWS، جی‌پی‌مورگان و دفتر مدیر اطلاعات ملی آمریکا (DNI) تأکید دارند که این رخدادها یک «حمله هماهنگ» نیستند و هم‌زمانی آن‌ها صرفاً یک خوشه‌بندی تصادفی (Statistical Clustering) است. [1, 2, 3] پیچیدگی و بدهی فنی (Technical Debt): از نگاه مهندسی مرسوم، سیستم‌های مدرن به دلیل ترکیب زیرساخت‌های قدیمی (Legacy Systems) با آپدیت‌های سریع هوش مصنوعی (مانند انتشار ۱,۰۹۴ اصلاحیه امنیتی توسط مایکروسافت در یک روز)، دچار باگ‌های نهفته (Latent Defects) و اشباع ظرفیت می‌شوند. [1, 2, 3, 4] راهکار پیشنهادی شرکت‌ها: افزایش افزونگی (Redundancy)، استقرار تدریجی آپدیت‌ها (Staged Rollouts)، تفکیک کنترل‌پلین از لایه تولید و چندابری کردن (Multi-Cloud). [1, 2] ب) تحلیل مبتنی بر فرمول‌ها و نظریه سید رسول حمزه (پارادایم تراکم انتروپی و شکست غیرقطعیت) در چارچوب فیزیک اطلاعاتی حمزه (Hamzah Information Physics) و الگوریتم DNT (تخصیص قطعی منابع) که در کدهای پایتون و Lean 4 بررسی شد، این رخدادها نه «تصادفی» هستند و نه با افزودن سرور بیشتر حل می‌شوند؛ بلکه نتیجه مستقیم تجاوز سیستم از آستانه انتروپی (Entropy Threshold) در یک معماری غیرقطعی (Probabilistic) است: افزایش انفجاری وزن هزینه (\(w_{i}\)) و افت چگالی اطلاعاتی (\(I_{i}\)):در معادله تخصیص حمزه:\(w_{i}=\frac{\eta _{i}+\epsilon _{\text{floor}}}{I_{i}+10^{-6}},\qquad \eta _{i}=\frac{L_{i}}{C_{i}}\)وقتی شرکتی مانند مایکروسافت هم‌زمان ظرفیت مؤثر خود را ۱۴٪ کاهش می‌دهد (\(C_i \downarrow\)) و حجم عظیمی از پچ‌های پیچیده و لایه‌های سربار را تزریق می‌کند (\(L_i \uparrow\))، شدت انتروپی (\(\eta _{i}\)) به سرعت رشد کرده و چگالی اطلاعاتی مفید (\(I_{i}\)) سقوط می‌کند. در مدل حمزه، وقتی سیستم منابع (\(R_{\text{total}}\)) را به جای هدایت به گره‌های با \(w_{i}\) پایین (طبق فرمول \(x_i^{\ast} \propto w_i^{-1}\))، به گره‌های متمرکز و پرانتروپی تزریق می‌کند، تابع هدف کل \(J(x) = \sum w_i x_i^2\) دچار واگرایی و قفل‌شدگی (System Freeze) می‌شود. [1, 2] شکست ساختارهای چهاربعدی و متمرکز (Lack of Deterministic Layering):طبق معماری لایه‌بندی حمزه (لایه ۳: اطلاعات و لایه ۴: امنیت)، شبکه‌های ابری کنونی بدون یک «هسته سیستم‌عامل قطعی» (Deterministic Core) و بدون حفظ اصل قطعیت (\(\Delta x \Delta p = \Omega_H^{\ast}\)) طراحی شده‌اند. در یک سیستم احتمالاتی، خطای کوچک در یک گره دروازه‌ای (Gateway) به دلیل نبودِ عملگرهای انتقال محافظه‌کارانه (conservation_after_transfer)، به صورت بهمنی (Cascading Failure) به ۸۰٪ دروازه‌های شبکه و نهادهای وابسته (مانند NHS، بانک‌ها و خطوط هوایی) سرریز می‌شود. [1, 2] ادعاهای حقوقی و مالکیت فکری حمزه علیه غول‌های فناوری:در متون منتشرشده توسط سید رسول حمزه در مخازن پیش‌چاپ (مانند Zenodo و OSF) در سال‌های ۲۰۲۵ و ۲۰۲۶، او مدعی است که معماری‌های پردازش کوانتومی-اطلاعاتی و مدل‌های بهینه‌سازی انتروپی او بدون مجوز و به صورت ناقص توسط شرکت‌های بزرگ فناوری (از جمله مایکروسافت، اپل و آمازون) الگوبرداری شده‌اند؛ و به اعتقاد او، این قطعی‌ها دقیقاً به دلیل پیاده‌سازی ناقص و بدون رعایت ثابت‌های قطعیت \(\Omega _{H}^{\ast }\) در سرورهای آن‌ها رخ می‌دهد. ۳. جمع‌بندی ساختاری و منطقی از منظر داده‌های تجربی: هر ۲۰ رخداد ثبت‌شده در این موج، دارای گزارش‌های فنی مجزا هستند که در ۶ مورد اصلی آن، شرکت‌ها صراحتاً تغییرات داخلی (آپدیت، نگهداری یا تست بازیابی) را عامل شروع اختلال معرفی کرده‌اند. از منظر منطق ریاضی و مدل‌سازی سیستم‌ها (نقطه تلاقی): چه این رخدادها را «باگ‌های مستقل مهندسی» بدانیم و چه «تراکم انتروپی در مدل حمزه»، نتیجه ریاضی یکسان است: توزیع غیراصولی بار (Load) در گره‌هایی که نسبت تلفات به ظرفیت آن‌ها (\(\eta _{i}\)) بالاست، به طور قطعی (همان‌طور که در قضیه Lean 4 اثبات شد) باعث جهش انتروپی کل سیستم و فروپاشی پایداری می‌شود. [1, 2, 3] در ادامه، مقایسه مستقیم و موردبه‌مورد ۲۰ رخداد اختلال نوامبر ۲۰۲۶ در قالب یک جدول جامع ارائه شده است که در آن داده‌های فنی و دلیل رسمی شرکت‌ها در برابر تفسیر فرمولی و سیستمی مبتنی بر چارچوب سید رسول حمزه قرار گرفته است: ردیف نهاد / شرکت (تاریخ نوامبر ۲۰۲۶) داده‌های عددی و مقیاس اختلال دیدگاه رسمی شرکت / نهاد (پارادایم مهندسی توزیع‌شده) تحلیل مبتنی بر چارچوب حمزه (پارادایم انتروپی و DNT) ۱ Microsoft 365(۱۲–۱۴ نوامبر) ۲۴ تا ۴۰ ساعت؛ از کار افتادن +۸۰٪ دروازه‌ها؛ ۴۵۰ میلیون کاربر؛ ۷ میلیارد دلار زیان باگ نهفته از پچ ژوئیه + کاهش ۱۴٪ ظرفیت سرور و اشباع نشست‌ها پس از آپدیت افت ظرفیت (\(C_i \downarrow\)) و تزریق پچ سنگین (\(L_i \uparrow\)) باعث انفجار شدت انتروپی (\(\eta_i = L_i/C_i\)) و قفل‌شدگی گره دروازه‌ای به دلیل نبود هسته قطعی شده است. ۲ FAA (هوانوردی آمریکا)(۱۳–۱۵ نوامبر) ۴ ساعت و ۲۳ دقیقه توقف کامل پروازها؛ ۱۷ از ۲۲ مرکز؛ +۱۰,۰۰۰ پرواز لغو ناپایداری شبکه مخابراتی L3Harris و اختلال روترهای ارتباطی رادار نقض انتقال بدون تأخیر در لایه شبکه (معادل گره \(D_{990}\) در مدل حمزه)؛ ناپایداری مسیرها به دلیل نبودِ عملگر پایستگی جریان هنگام اوج ترافیک. ۳ Workday(۱۳–۱۴ نوامبر) ~۴۸ ساعت اختلال در ۲ مرکز داده و هزاران مشتری سازمانی خطای فنی حین اجرای آزمایش بازیابی پس از فاجعه (Disaster Recovery Test) تغییر ناگهانی وضعیت بدون رعایت شرط پایستگی (conservation_after_transfer) منجر به جهش وزن هزینه (\(w_{i}\)) و ناتوانی سیستم در بازتوزیع قطعی بار شد. ۴ Anthropic (Claude)(۱۳ نوامبر) اختلال در ورود کاربران، API و محیط‌های کدنویسی نقص فنی زیرساختی (بدون انتشار جزئیات فنی دقیق) ناپایداری ذاتی معماری‌های هوش مصنوعی احتمالاتی (Probabilistic AI) در مقایسه با هوش کوانتومی قطعی (HQI) هنگام افزایش درخواست‌های هم‌زمان. ۵ HSBC و Barclays(۱۳ نوامبر) فعال‌سازی تیم‌های بحران و اختلال مقطعی در پردازش‌ها اثر سرریز (Spillover) ناشی از وابستگی به ابر مایکروسافت نبود ایزوله‌سازی در لایه امنیت (معادل گره \(D_{660}\)) که اجازه داده انتروپی تولیدشد

all.title: From Detection to Resilience: A Review of Explainable AI Trust and Real-Time Response in AI-Driven Bank Fraud Detection
all.abstract: Background: Banks use machine learning to flag fraudulent transactions at a scale that rule-based systems cannot match. Detection accuracy has received most of the research attention. Much less is known about whether better detection produces a more resilient institution.Purpose: This review examines how AI-driven fraud detection capability relates to the cybersecurity resilience of banks, and what role explainability-based trust and real-time response capability play in that relationship.Method: A narrative review of research on statistical and machine-learning fraud detection, explainable AI, human trust in automation, cyber resilience, and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) studies in banking. A recent U.S. banking survey study (Rimi et al., 2025) is used as an applied reference point.Findings: Three themes emerge. First, detection capability is well documented, but its link to organizational resilience is mostly assumed rather than tested. Second, explainability affects outcomes through human trust and reliance, not through model performance alone. Third, response speed is a weak predictor of resilience when it is not tied to recovery, governance, and learning. The reference survey study found that detection capability predicted resilience directly (β = 0.444) and through explainable AI trust (indirect β = 0.206), while real-time response capability had no significant effect (β = −0.002, p = 0.959).Conclusion: Banks should treat explainability, analyst training, and recovery integration as part of the fraud detection investment. Future work needs longitudinal designs, objective resilience measures, and tests of governance as a moderator.

all.title: AI Governance, Ethics, and Responsible Innovation
all.venue: International Journal of Modern Science and Research Technology
all.abstract: In spite of the fact that there is widespread agreement regarding the ethical principles that need to guide artificial intelligence, there is still a significant gap between these normative objectives and the operational realities of technical implementation. An investigation into how to operationalize a proactive, iterative AI governance paradigm is the focus of this study. The investigation is conducted via the prism of private law liabilities and constant technical verification. Both corporate compliance theater and opportunistic ethics shopping are the driving forces behind our inquiry. Both of these shortcomings in practice have occurred repeatedly. During the course of the study, a multi-layered methodological framework is utilized. This framework triangulates a comparative assessment of growing international regulatory frameworks and a "cross-sectoral typological mapping of auditing procedures from banking, data privacy, and environmental law." The findings reveal a systemic disconnect: corporate ethical commitments continue to be largely detached from operational audit systems, leaving data scientists frustrated by guidelines that are too abstract to act on. Furthermore, existing environmental, social, and governance standards do not provide any AI-specific tools for quantifying the hidden socio-technical harms that are embedded in global supply chains. rules that are abstract, whereas the existing ESG standards do not provide the AI-specific guidance that is required to assess the hidden socio-technical damages that are present throughout global supply chains.The purpose of this article is to offer a solution to this problem by advocating for the transition from voluntary soft law to an enforceable, longitudinal regulatory framework. We propose that corporate governance frameworks be merged with automated auditing pipelines, value-based engineering (also known as ethics-by-design), and independent third-party oversight. This would result in the transformation of abstract ethical concepts into private law duties that can be verified.

all.title: Explainable AI for Small-Sample Macroeconomic Forecasting: A Structural Analysis of the Bangladeshi Economy
all.abstract: Gross Domestic Product Growth (GDPG) is an essential indicator of the economic development of a state. The GDPG is understood as the annual percentage change in the value added of goods and services provided within an economy. This paper deal with the problem of GDPG forecasting for volatile emerging economies due to structural instability and small sample sizes leading to high variance in both econometrics and machine learning methods. The XAI technique is proposed to forecast GDPG of Bangladesh by using the dataset from the World Bank covering years from 1991 to 2024. After the necessary econometric pre-processing to ensure stationarity and eliminate multicollinearity, five machine learning models were tested. The model with the highest level of regularisation is L2-regularised XGBoost algorithm, providing the best out-of-sample forecast (R-squared = 0.6245). The introduction of SHAP allowed for the automatic global dimensionality reduction, hence the detection of spurious variables. The model revealed structural asymmetries like short-term dilution of capital-labor and lagged limitations caused by the volatility of the real interest rate. In general, it could be stated that the correct calibration of the model made possible by the use of the proposed technique could provide accurate macroeconomic information for making decisions.

all.title: Macroeconomic Drivers of Sectoral Volatility in India: Evidence from GARCH, Deep Learning, and Explainable AI
all.abstract: This research examines the effects of macroeconomic variables on the volatility of sectors in the Indian stock market. The monthly data of 5 major NIFTY sectors namely Banking, IT, Pharma, Auto, FMCG and USD/INR exchange rates, crude oil prices, and repo interest rates were analysed. The returns of the various sectors were modeled in this way using GARCH (1,1) to account for the non-constant volatility of the returns, and the volatility was forecast using LSTM, GRU, and Attention-LSTM models. In order to make the results easier to interpret, it used SHAP values to measure the impact of macroeconomic variables on the volatility of the specific sectors. The results indicate significant sectoral differences in the transmission of volatility, and that the movements in the price of crude oil and exchange rate are main drivers. The study introduces a model of forecasting and explainability of the sectoral risk dynamics in emerging financial markets.

all.title: The Future of AI Governance and Digital Trust in the GCC: From Principles to Supervision – Regulatory Trajectories to 2030
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Between 2023 and 2026, artificial intelligence governance in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) shifted from voluntary ethics principles toward sector supervision and active enforcement. This foresight brief maps the 2026 baseline in the UAE (including the newly announced Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, the Central Bank of the UAE's AI guidance and DIFC Regulation 10) and Saudi Arabia (PDPL enforcement and SDAIA's draft Responsible AI Policy). Drawing on the author's practitioner experience in regulatory assessments and AI governance, it identifies a persistent gap between documented policy and demonstrable control: weak data inventories, hidden cross-border transfers, and AI-specific risks that existing ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 frameworks do not cover. It sets out five drivers of change, three scenarios for 2030 (harmonised trust zone, patchwork sovereignty and shock-driven tightening), and recommendations for policymakers and organisations on making trusted AI a regional competitive advantage.

all.title: AI-Powered Android Malware Detection Using Deep Learning Hybrid Static–Dynamic Feature-Engineered Framework with Explainable AI
all.abstract: Android malware has become increasingly harder to catch now a days. Ransomware, banking trojans, and spyware now rely on obfuscation and rapid repackaging, and signature-based endpoint defenses can no longer keep up. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have become the usual answer, but current work has several weak points. Static and dynamic attributes are rarely engineered together in one framework. Feature selection often depends on an arbitrary cutoff and not on a statistical test. Black-box deep models are seldom compared with classical ML under fair, compute-matched cross-validation, and their explanations are seldom checked against the selected features. To address these challenges, this study proposes an end-to-end hybrid static–dynamic feature-engineering framework for Android malware detection. The proposed architecture integrates the Boruta algorithm for statistically grounded feature selection and SMOTE for training-fold class balancing. Four deep learning architectures including CNN, LSTM, CNN-LSTM, and Transformer are benchmarked against four classical ML baselines including Random Forest, XGBoost, SVM, and LightGBM under an identical 5-fold stratified cross-validation protocol and a matched training budget with patience-based early stopping. Empirical validation is conducted on the benchmark KronoDroid dataset, comprising 78,137 real-device Android applications containing 41,382 malware and 36,755 benign samples characterized by 289 dynamic system-call features and 195 static manifest-derived features. Gradient-boosted decision trees gave the strongest and most stable results: LightGBM reached an F1-score of 98.66% and XGBoost 98.51%. The best deep model, CNN-LSTM, reached 97.47%, on par with the SVM baseline (97.50% F1). We interpret the models with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP); the permissions READ_PHONE_STATE and SEND_SMS consistently rank among the strongest indicators of malicious behavior. Overall, the framework offers an accurate, reproducible, and explainable detection workflow that can support mobile security analysts, enterprise mobile device management (MDM) platforms, and app-store vetting systems.

all.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence Uncovers Non-Bank Financial Industry Contagion and Safeguards Central Bank Institutional Governance
all.abstract: Introduction/Main Objectives: This paper examines systemic risk interconnections within Indonesia's Non-Bank Financial Industry (NBFI), which displays intricate systemic risk interconnections that alter traditional macroprudential dynamics. As financial ecosystems digitalize, understanding cross-sectoral risk transmission beyond banking is crucial for stability. The study further aims to develop a transparent artificial intelligence framework capable of supporting timely macroprudential policy interventions and institutional decision-making. Background Problems: Systemic risk from NBFI interconnections insurance, pension funds, finance companies, guarantee institutions, and P2P lending remains insufficiently mapped, and linear models fail to capture nonlinear contagion, raising the question of how risks transmit across NBFI sectors and what their primary drivers are. Novelty: This paper pioneers integrating econometrics with Explainable AI (SHAP-Random Forest) to construct an NBFI systemic risk framework, offering transparent, actionable insights for regulators to strengthen macroprudential governance and safeguard financial stability. Research Methods: The study employs correlation analysis, Granger causality, OLS regression, and Random Forest with SHAP decomposition using Indonesian NBFI sectoral data (2016–2024). Finding/Results: Results reveal strong cross-sectoral risk linkages and nonlinear transmission, identifying pension fund asset size and foreign funding exposures as dominating cross-sectoral systemic risk, contributing mean SHAP values of 0.576 and 0.326, respectively. During COVID-19, NBFI sectors acted as shock absorbers rather than amplifiers. Conclusion: The findings underscore the need for Algorithmic Macroprudential Governance, where explainable AI enhances evidence-based supervision, strengthens institutional autonomy, improves systemic risk monitoring in emerging financial architectures, and provides actionable insights for regulators in safeguarding long-term financial stability.

all.title: PRIORITY AREAS FOR IMPLEMENTING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND BIG DATA TECHNOLOGIES IN COMMERCIAL BANKS
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This thesis examines priority areas for implementing artificial intelligence (AI) and Big Data technologies in commercial banks alongside mechanisms for mitigating model and operational risks. Based on international regulatory reports, national digital strategies, and scholarly literature, it demonstrates that fragmented data infrastructure and opaque algorithms constrain practical returns in banking. Four priority deployment verticals, an explainable AI architectural chain, risk-governance safeguards, and five performance evaluation indicators are substantiated.

all.title: Explainable and Multimodal AI for Financial Fraud Prevention: Advancing Trust and Cybersecurity in Digital Banking
all.abstract: Digital banking has made financial services faster, more accessible, and cheaper to run. It has also widened the opening for financial fraud, identity theft, social engineering, synthetic identity attacks, and deepfake-enabled cybercrime. Rule-based security systems often struggle with threats that are sophisticated and change quickly, which has increased interest in adaptive artificial intelligence (AI) solutions. This review examines how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and multimodal AI can strengthen fraud prevention, support decision-making, and improve cybersecurity resilience in digital banking. It looks at the integration of multiple data modalities, real-time threat detection, explainable fraud alerts, and organizational trust in AI-generated decisions. The review synthesizes two empirical studies, one on U.S. digital banking and one on the U.S. banking sector. The first reports that multimodal deepfake detection, real-time detection, and explainable AI are each positively associated with fraud detection effectiveness and cybersecurity resilience. The second reports that explainable AI trust is a significant link between AI-driven fraud detection and banking cybersecurity resilience, while its proposed real-time fraud response mediation was not statistically supported. The review also covers methodological limitations and challenges involving data privacy, model transparency, false positives, adversarial attacks, and organizational readiness. It concludes that AI-based financial security needs interpretable decisions, human oversight, timely operational action, and responsible governance in addition to accurate detection.

all.title: Strategic leadership in AI-assisted banking decisions: a conceptual framework for critical evaluation and accountability
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly informs strategic banking decisions, yet the presence of human reviewers does not establish that critical evaluation influences organisational commitment. This article examines how strategic leadership can organise the assessment, challenge, and authorisation of AI-assisted strategic recommendations. Drawing on a targeted, non-exhaustive synthesis of research on strategic leadership, human–AI delegation, employee voice, accountability, and AI governance, it develops a conceptual framework centred on the strategic decision episode. The framework connects three processes: independent assessment, consequential challenge, and reasoned commitment. It distinguishes the expression of a material objection from the substantive response it receives and the incorporation of that response into the grounds for authorisation. Six propositions propose how model opacity, verification resources, sponsor control, prospective justification, and independent assessments supplied to approvers shape these connections, while decision uncertainty, irreversibility, and resolution criteria condition the proposed process. The framework identifies objection–response–commitment traceability as an intermediate process outcome, while distinguishing documented connections from substantive reasoning and realised performance. Its contribution is to specify where critical evaluation may lose organisational influence as AI-generated advice moves towards commitment. For banking leaders, it offers a basis for organising responses to material concerns without assuming that additional review necessarily improves decisions. The framework remains untested and provides an agenda for examining both the benefits and costs of alternative evaluation arrangements.

all.title: ЗНАЕТ ЛИ БАНК ВАС ЛУЧШЕ, ЧЕМ ВЫ САМИ? ИСКУССТВЕННЫЙ ИНТЕЛЛЕКТ И БАНКОВСКИЙ МАРКЕТИНГ НА ПРИМЕРЕ KASPI.KZ
all.venue: «Qazaq Journal of Young Scientist» халықаралық ғылыми журналы
all.abstract: The article examines the opportunities and risks associated with the use of artificial intelligence in the banking sector, using the Kaspi.kz digital ecosystem as a case study. The purpose of the study is to analyze the influence of artificial intelligence and digital technologies on banking marketing, customer relationships, and service quality. The research methods included a review of the scholarly literature, comparative analysis, and an examination of the company’s publicly available corporate materials. The study analyzes the advantages of automating digital services, the potential of personalized marketing, and issues related to personal data security. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence can contribute to improving banking services; however, its effective use must be accompanied by measures that ensure customer trust, data protection, and algorithmic fairness.

all.title: Ghana’s national innovation system and the governance readiness gap for artificial intelligence
all.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding across Ghanaian finance, health, agriculture, public administration and digital services, while the institutions responsible for governing its risks are still developing the capacity, coordination and authority required for implementation. This study examines Ghana’s National Innovation System (NIS) as an institutional setting for AI governance. Using a qualitative, multi-technique design, we conducted 32 purposively sampled interviews across universities and research institutes, firms, government agencies, financial institutions, intermediaries and boundary-spanning actors. Vignette-based interviewing, triadic elicitation and the Critical Incident Technique (CIT) were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and interpreted using Technological Innovation Systems (TIS) functions and UNESCO/African Union governance benchmarks. Four recurrent failure mechanisms were identified: capability, connectivity, legitimacy and resource failures. The evidence also revealed relative strengths, including a growing research base, emerging public-sector policy direction and boundary-spanning relationships that occasionally enabled knowledge transfer. We therefore characterise Ghana’s condition as a system-wide but uneven governance readiness gap rather than a total governance deficit. The paper develops the Governance Readiness Paradox: AI activity and policy ambition can expand faster than the institutional capacity to translate knowledge into enforceable, accountable and inclusive governance. The study presents a Ghana AI Governance Readiness Matrix and eight sequenced policy recommendations for strengthening research-to-policy translation and implementation capacity.

all.title: An Explainable Artificial Intelligence Framework for Customer Churn Management and Retention Decision Support in Service Operations
institutions: Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology
all.abstract: Customer churn prediction is a critical task for service-oriented firms because customer loss directly affects revenue stability, customer lifetime value, and long-term profitability. Although machine learning models can identify customers who are likely to churn, many existing approaches emphasize predictive accuracy without sufficiently explaining churn drivers or translating predictions into actionable retention strategies. To address this limitation, this study proposes an explainable AI-driven multi-dataset churn management framework that integrates machine learning prediction, SHAP-based explainability, probability-based risk segmentation, and counterfactual retention strategy simulation. The framework is evaluated using three publicly available customer churn datasets from telecommunications and banking contexts: IBM Telco, Orange Telecom, and Banking Churn. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost are trained and compared using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and AUC-PR. The results show that model performance varies across datasets, with XGBoost achieving strong performance on Orange Telecom and Random Forest performing competitively on Banking Churn. SHAP analysis reveals domain-specific churn drivers, including tenure and contract type in telecommunications, service usage and customer service calls in Orange Telecom, and age, number of products, balance, and active membership in banking. Risk segmentation results show clear increases in actual churn rates from low-risk to high-risk groups. Counterfactual simulations further estimate potential churn-risk reductions under selected managerial interventions, with reductions reaching up to 66.19 percentage points. The study contributes an interpretable and action-oriented intelligent decision-support framework for customer retention management.

all.title: Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence and Financial Inclusion among Digital Financial Service Users in Nigeria
all.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
all.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into digital financial services presents opportunities for expanding financial inclusion in Nigeria, but concerns about transparency, fairness, privacy, and security may influence users' willingness to engage with AI-enabled financial platforms. This study examines the effect of Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence on financial inclusion among digital financial service users in Nigeria. Specifically, the study evaluates the effects of AI transparency, AI fairness, and AI privacy and security on financial inclusion. A quantitative research design was adopted, and primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire from 350 users of digital financial services. The data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The findings reveal that AI transparency has a significant positive effect on financial inclusion (β = 0.177, p = 0.014). AI privacy and security also has a significant and stronger positive effect on financial inclusion (β = 0.557, p < 0.001). However, AI fairness has a positive but statistically insignificant effect on financial inclusion (β = 0.124, p = 0.139). The study concludes that secure and transparent AI-enabled financial services are particularly important for promoting financial inclusion in Nigeria. Financial institutions and FinTech providers should therefore strengthen data protection, cybersecurity, transparency, and responsible AI governance to enhance users' confidence and participation in digital financial services.

all.title: Leveraging AI appraisal for sustainable property investment decisions
all.venue: Journal of Financial Management of Property and Construction
all.abstract: Purpose As sustainable considerations increasingly influence real estate finance, traditional property valuation methods face limitations in capturing environmental, social and governance value. This paper aims to critically evaluate the role and potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven appraisal techniques in supporting informed and effective sustainable property investment decisions. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review was conducted, analyzing contemporary research sourced from major academic databases. The review focused on identifying AI applications (including machine learning and deep learning) used for valuing sustainable property attributes, assessing green real estate financial performance and integrating ESG factors into investment frameworks. Identified benefits, challenges and future trends were synthesized. Findings AI-driven appraisal demonstrates significant potential to enhance sustainable investment through improved accuracy in valuing green features, increased efficiency in data analysis and portfolio management and greater objectivity compared to traditional methods. Explainable AI techniques are emerging as crucial for ensuring transparency. However, key challenges remain, including the availability and quality of standardized ESG data, mitigating algorithmic bias, ensuring model interpretability for complex sustainability metrics and the need for skilled human oversight. Originality/value This paper provides a focused synthesis of the current state-of-the-art regarding AI appraisal specifically for sustainable real estate investment. It bridges the gap between technical AI advancements in valuation and their practical application in sustainable finance, offering valuable insights for investors, financial institutions, appraisers and policymakers aiming to leverage AI for promoting responsible investment in the built environment.

all.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence and Consumer Financial Decisions: The Role of Trust, Transparency, and Financial Literacy.
all.venue: ARTHASASTRA Journal of Economics and Business
institutions: Universitas Islam Negeri Kiai Ageng Muhammad Besari Ponorogo
all.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into financial services has transformed how consumers access financial information, evaluate financial alternatives, and make financial decisions. Although AI-driven financial applications offer opportunities to improve decision efficiency, personalization, and accessibility, their adoption raises concerns regarding algorithmic opacity, perceived risk, and consumer trust. In this context, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has emerged as an important approach to improving the transparency and interpretability of AI-generated financial recommendations. This study examines how explainability and transparency shape consumer trust and influence financial decision-making, while considering financial literacy as a relevant individual-level factor. Drawing on behavioral economics, trust in automation theory, and information asymmetry perspectives, the study develops an integrative conceptual framework linking perceived AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, consumer trust, and financial decision outcomes. The analysis conceptualizes consumer trust as a key mechanism through which explainable AI may influence the acceptance and use of AI-generated financial recommendations. It further highlights financial literacy as a potential moderating factor that shapes consumers' ability to understand algorithmic explanations, assess financial risks, and critically evaluate AI-based advice. The study argues that explainability alone does not guarantee informed financial decisions, as its effectiveness also depends on consumers' financial knowledge, perceived reliability, and ability to interpret the information provided. By integrating technological explainability with psychological trust and financial literacy, this study contributes to the literature on digital finance and behavioral economics through a conceptual framework for understanding consumer responses to AI-mediated financial decision-making. The findings offer implications for financial institutions, AI developers, and policymakers in designing transparent, accountable, and consumer-centered AI-based financial services.

all.title: Enhancing Strategic Decision Quality through Market and Competitive Intelligence
all.venue: Journal of Intelligence Studies in Business
all.abstract: The value of competitive intelligence can be assessed by examining how its findings inform strategic choices. Which assumptions did the analysis lead decision-makers to reconsider, and how did it shape their evaluation of strategic alternatives? These questions become increasingly important as digital platforms and artificial intelligence expand organizations’ capacity to process information. Assessing the value of this expanded capacity requires understanding how managers interpret analytical findings and whether their use improves the quality of strategic decisions. Integrating market, competitor, and customer information is an established approach within competitive intelligence. Earlier research links this integration to understanding the external environment and supporting strategic decisions (Aspinall, 2011; Santos & Correia, 2010). The contribution of contemporary research therefore lies in explaining the mechanisms through which organizations identify relevant signals, assess their interpretations, and apply the resulting insights. Recent scholarship examines competitive intelligence in relation to data analytics capabilities and conceptually connects it to sensing external change, taking strategic action, and organizational adaptation (e.g., Černý et al., 2026; Ranjan & Foropon, 2021). The research challenge is therefore to explain the mechanisms through which integrated information contributes to strategic decision quality. Evidence from practice highlights this challenge. A Forrester survey reports that intelligence teams integrate diverse information sources to support decisions across strategy, product development, and sales. Their performance is often assessed through the number of analyses produced and users reached, while their contribution to business outcomes remains difficult to establish (Caplow, 2026). Although limited in scope, the survey highlights a measurement problem: assessing the strategic value of intelligence requires understanding how its findings inform decisions. Competitive intelligence research should therefore examine the conditions under which high-quality information supports better-informed strategic choices. Research on business intelligence offers relevant evidence on these mechanisms, although its findings require careful interpretation in the competitive intelligence context. Data quality, visualization, and analytics management have been positively associated with decision quality (Abu-AlSondos, 2023). A subsequent banking-sector study identifies organizational AI capabilities as moderators of the relationships between data quality, system quality, visualization, and decision quality (Abu-AlSondos, 2026). These findings direct attention to the capabilities through which organizations put analytical resources to use. AI further sharpens the question of how analytical outputs inform reasoned choices. A framework tested using customer interaction data demonstrates how customer segmentation and explainable AI can be combined with the prioritization of decision criteria to support resource allocation (Marín Díaz et al., 2025). Although the study does not examine the joint integration of market, competitor, and customer information, it offers an approach to explaining analytical outputs and connecting them to explicit choice criteria. Taken together, these findings suggest that the contribution of analytics should be assessed in relation to organizational technological capabilities and the information requirements of the decision at hand. Meeting these requirements also depends on information granularity. Generating competitive intelligence at the product, firm, and market levels can support resource planning even when information is limited (Kumar et al., 2020). This highlights the importance of matching analytical detail to the decision task: understanding the broader market and allocating specific resources require different levels of information. Research should therefore establish which levels of granularity improve the evaluation of strategic alternatives and when the costs of acquiring and analyzing additional information exceed its contribution to the decision. The breadth of analysis likewise needs to reflect the decision context. Research on new product development shows that the relationships between incremental and comprehensive information processing and strategy outcomes vary with the time sensitivity and analyzability of market information (Durmusoglu et al., 2023). For competitive intelligence, this invites closer examination of which analytical approaches suit the available information and the time available for a decision. More extensive analysis should not be assumed to yield a better choice under all conditions. Analytical suitability, however, does not determine how findings will be used. The value of competitive intelligence also depends on how those findings are interpreted and discussed within the organization. Managers’ attitudes and beliefs shape competitive information search and interpretation (Qiu, 2008), while collaboration procedures between analysts and decision-makers, together with internal political behavior, influence the conditions of its use (Kowalczyk & Buxmann, 2015). Alongside analytical quality, research and practice must therefore consider an organization’s willingness to test its assumptions, examine alternative explanations, and engage with contradictory evidence. A substantive test of competitive intelligence is whether its findings enable decision-makers to justify, revise, or reject strategic choices on the basis of evidence.

all.title: Sự cố 13/11/2026 và cảnh báo sớm cho an toàn: Hàng không, an ninh hạt nhân và ngân hàng trước phép thử mất Internet, mất AI và mất niềm tin vào dữ liệu
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: BẢN TIẾNG VIỆT: Tên tài liệu: Sự cố 13/11/2026 và cảnh báo sớm cho an toàn: Hàng không, an ninh hạt nhân và ngân hàng trước phép thử mất Internet, mất AI và mất niềm tin vào dữ liệuTác giả: S.S DUYMT, 2026 Tóm tắt nội dung:Công trình phân tích an toàn hệ thống và khả năng phục hồi hoạt động (operational resilience) này mổ xẻ một nghịch lý cấu trúc của thời đại số: các tổ chức không ngừng đầu tư để hệ thống và AI ra quyết định nhanh hơn, nhưng lại thường xuyên bỏ ngỏ việc xác định thời điểm và cơ chế để hệ thống buộc phải ngừng ra quyết định. Lấy điểm tựa thực nghiệm từ sự cố mạng viễn thông khiến Cục Hàng không Liên bang Mỹ (FAA) phải ban hành lệnh dừng cất cánh toàn quốc (ground stop) ngày 13/11/2026, tác giả chỉ ra bài học quản trị kép mang tính khuôn mẫu: năng lực an toàn tối thượng nằm ở khả năng đồng thời hạn chế rủi ro mới (ngăn máy bay mới cất cánh) và bảo toàn các nghĩa vụ đã phát sinh (đưa các chuyến bay đang ở trên trời hạ cánh an toàn bằng các kênh dự phòng độc lập). Từ bài học hàng không, nghiên cứu thiết lập một khung thẩm định toàn diện cho các hạ tầng trọng yếu quốc gia (Hàng không, Hạt nhân, Ngân hàng):• **Khung Khái niệm “Năng lực Dừng” (Stopping Capability):** Xác lập 4 thành tố bắt buộc để lệnh dừng không chỉ nằm trên giấy: Thẩm quyền được định trước $\to$ Tiêu chí kích hoạt rõ ràng $\to$ Kênh dữ liệu tin cậy độc lập $\to$ Chế độ vận hành suy giảm đã được diễn tập.• An ninh Hạt nhân và 5 Mặt của Tính Độc lập (IAEA): Cảnh báo nguy cơ khi đưa AI vào chuỗi điều khiển. Tác giả chỉ ra tính độc lập phải được bảo toàn trên cả 5 phương diện: dữ liệu, thiết bị/đường truyền, phần mềm/mô hình, tổ chức/con người và thời điểm thay đổi; đồng thời đề xuất phép thử “Tắt AI để thử con người” nhằm đối phó với “trớ trêu của tự động hóa”.• Khôi phục Trạng thái Giải trình được trong Ngân hàng (Basel): Phân tích rủi ro “khoản tiền đang bay” khi hệ thống thanh toán đứt gãy; tái định nghĩa đồng hồ phục hồi không tính bằng thời điểm máy chủ khởi động lại, mà tính bằng thời gian đưa toàn bộ giao dịch dở dang về trạng thái có thể đối soát và giải trình ($T_{\text{giải trình}} = T_{\text{phát hiện}} + T_{\text{cô lập}} + T_{\text{đối soát}} + T_{\text{thông tin}}$).• Bốn Phép Thử Căng Thẳng và Chuyển Đổi Mật Mã Hậu Lượng Tử (PQC): Thiết lập 4 bài diễn tập có tiêu chí chấm trượt (Tấn công mạo danh bằng AI, Mất Internet, AI ngừng hoặc trả lời sai, và Chuyển đổi PQC). Vận dụng bất đẳng thức Mosca ($X + Y > Z$) và các tiêu chuẩn NIST (FIPS 203, 204, 205; NIST IR 8547) cùng dự án BIS Project Leap để chứng minh: chuyển đổi mật mã phải bắt đầu từ tuổi thọ dữ liệu hôm nay để chặn đứng hiểm họa “Thu thập nay, giải mã sau”. Tiểu luận đúc kết 8 nguyên tắc chiến lược cùng bộ bài tập hành động cho hội đồng điều hành, khẳng định: “Một tổ chức an toàn không phải là tổ chức không bao giờ mất ổn định. Đó là tổ chức biết mình sẽ dừng ở đâu, giữ cái gì, và chứng minh được điều đó trước khi bị hỏi.” Đối tượng người đọc:• Hội đồng quản trị, Giám đốc Rủi ro (CRO), Giám đốc An toàn Thông tin (CISO) và lãnh đạo khối Hàng không, Năng lượng Hạt nhân, Ngân hàng• Cơ quan quản lý nhà nước, nhà hoạch định chính sách an ninh mạng và bảo vệ hạ tầng trọng yếu• Kiến trúc sư hệ thống, chuyên gia AI Safety, chuyên gia Mật mã hậu lượng tử và kiểm toán viên công nghệ Từ khóa (Keywords):Sự cố FAA 13/11/2026; An toàn hệ thống; Hạ tầng trọng yếu; Khả năng phục hồi hoạt động; Năng lực dừng; Phòng thủ theo chiều sâu; IAEA; Basel; Mật mã hậu lượng tử; PQC; Bất đẳng thức Mosca; Project Leap; AI Safety BẢN TIẾNG ANH (Zenodo English Abstract): Title: The Incident of November 13, 2026, and an Early Warning for System Safety: Aviation, Nuclear Security, and Banking Facing the Test of Lost Internet, Lost AI, and Lost Data TrustAuthor: S.S DUYMT, 2026 Abstract:This treatise investigates a profound systemic paradox in high-reliability organizations: the aggressive engineering of systems to make decisions faster while chronically neglecting the architectural mechanisms that dictate precisely when a system must cease automated decision-making. Grounded in the empirical natural experiment of the nationwide ground stop executed by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on November 13, 2026 due to telecommunication backbone instability, the author derives an essential dual-capability governance model: true operational resilience requires simultaneously halting the intake of new risk (grounding departures) while maintaining uncompromised, diverse channels to service in-flight commitments to completion (safely recovering airborne flights via analog radio and primary radar networks). Expanding beyond aviation, the monograph establishes an exhaustive operational resilience rubric across critical societal infrastructures:• The Four Pillars of "Stopping Capability": Formalizes the systemic architecture of safe halts: Predetermined Authority $\to$ Pre-established Trigger Criteria $\to$ Independent Out-of-Band Trust Channels $\to$ Rehearsed Degraded Operational Modes.• Nuclear Security and the Five Facets of Independence (IAEA): Evaluates the integration of AI within safety-critical architectures, proving that independence must hold across five distinct dimensions: data sources, physical infrastructure, software libraries, organizational reporting, and maintenance schedules. The author introduces the “AI-off” stress test to counteract Bainbridge’s classic "ironies of automation."• Financial Core and Indeterminate States (Basel Framework): Analyzes the systemic vulnerability of "in-flight transactions" during network decoupling. The metric of recovery is recalibrated from simple server reboot time to the comprehensive Time-to-Accountability ($T_{\text{accountability}} = T_{\text{detect}} + T_{\text{isolate}} + T_{\text{reconcile}} + T_{\text{inform}}$).• The Four Mandatory Stress Tests and Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC): Establishes four rigorous simulation drills with explicit fail criteria: AI-assisted deepfake impersonation, total Internet outage, AI hallucination/shutdown, and PQC migration. Integrating Mosca’s Theorem ($X + Y > Z$) with NIST standards (FIPS 203, 204, 205; NIST IR 8547) and BIS Project Leap, the author demonstrates that cryptographic transitions must track data shelf-life today to mitigate the existential Harvest Now, Decrypt Later paradigm. The work culminates in eight strategic principles and actionable board-level exercises, establishing a timeless organizational maxim: “A safe organization is not one that never experiences instability. It is an organization that knows precisely where to halt, what core functions to preserve, and can empirically prove it before disaster strikes.” Target Audience:• Board members, Chief Risk Officers (CROs), and Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs) in Aviation, Nuclear Energy, and Banking• National regulatory bodies, critical infrastructure protection agencies, and homeland defense strategists• Enterprise system architects, AI safety researchers, post-quantum cryptographers, and disaster recovery coordinators Keywords:FAA Ground Stop 2026; System Safety; Critical Infrastructure; Operational Resilience; Stopping Capability; Defense-in-Depth; IAEA; Basel Committee; Post-Quantum Cryptography; PQC; Mosca's Inequality; Project Leap; AI Governance

all.title: Beyond security: why AI-mediated prison visitation must be fair, transparent, and human-centered
all.abstract: Prison visitation is usually administered as a security operation, yet it is also a relational and rehabilitative intervention. Rule 58 of the Nelson Mandela Rules provides for regular contact with family and friends through correspondence, telecommunications and visits (United Nations, 2015). A meta-analysis of 16 studies associated visitation with a 26% reduction in recidivism, although effects varied by visit type, outcome, gender and follow-up (Mitchell et al., 2016). This is not a universal causal guarantee, but it shows that access to visitation is not a minor administrative convenience.Digital visitation can widen access for families separated by distance, cost, illness or disability. Video visits can help incarcerated fathers take part in children's daily lives, while raising problems of timing, technology and the absence of touch (Duursma et al., 2024;Hanley et al., 2024), and users may value remote access while still preferring in-person contact (Murdoch and King, 2020). Remote systems can also reduce agency, comprehension and privacy for people already disadvantaged (McKay and Macintosh, 2024). The appropriate policy is complementarity, not substitution. Video conferencing alone is not artificial intelligence (AI). We use AI-mediated visitation to mean pathways in which AI informs identity verification, scheduling, translation, risk flagging, content moderation, interruption or post-visit review. The 2026 UNODC-ICRC Handbook states that video visits should supplement in-person visits and that AI in prisons should be fair, explainable, contestable and under human control (UNODC and ICRC, 2026). We argue that these principles require a specific rule: AI may assist access and safety, but it should never be the sole basis for denying, suspending or terminating family contact.Transparency, accountability, auditing and human oversight are established principles (Kroll et al., 2017;Ananny and Crawford, 2018;UNESCO, 2021;OECD, 2024;Cheong, 2024), and the Council of Europe has already adapted them to prisons and probation (Council of Europe, 2024). We do not claim to originate them. Our contribution is to show where general frameworks stop short when the decision concerns family contact, and to supply three elements they lack.First, a consequence-tiered classification (Table 1) separates assistive functions from gatekeeping, interventional and inferential ones, so that safeguards scale with consequence rather than applying uniformly to "prison AI". Second, a relational-irreversibility criterion: a missed visit, a child's birthday call or a terminated conversation cannot be restored by a later appeal, so review must occur before or during the contact window. General frameworks treat remedy as retrospective; visitation requires prospective or same-session remedy. Third, third-party standing: visitors are not detainees, yet their faces, voices and devices are processed. Frameworks oriented to the detained person rarely give families an independent right to notice, correction and appeal. Rapid gains in AI capability do not settle these questions, because reliability, interpretability and evaluation remain open problems even in well-resourced scientific domains (Xu et al., 2026); they are harder still in a coercive setting with contested ground truth.We distinguish documented evidence from hypothetical scenarios; Supplementary Table S1 lists each source and its evidential status.A national survey of US video-visitation contracts found that 74% of jails adopting video visitation eliminated in-person visits, and some vendor contracts required this (Rabuy and Wagner, 2015). In England, a 2018-2019 trial scanned the faces of 770 visitors at HMP Humber; some visitors turned back on learning of the scans, and campaigners warned that deterring families would be counter-productive (Prison Legal News, 2019). During the COVID-19 pandemic, prisons in England and Wales introduced video calls using software with facial recognition (Ministry of Justice, 2020); family guidance at one prison warned that background photographs could disrupt recognition and end calls prematurely (HMP Forest Bank, 2020), and the supplier advertised emotion recognition to detect changes in mood (Made Purple Ltd, n.d.). In the United States, AI transcription and keyword alerting of prisoners' calls has been adopted by state and federal agencies, while families and advocates have raised concerns about misinterpretation and racial bias (Route Fifty, 2021;Correctional News, 2026). Outside prisons, Australia's Robodebt inquiry showed how automated decisions without adequate human review can cause serious and widespread harm (Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, 2023).A visitor whose face fails verification on a poor-quality phone camera is refused a call with no manual alternative; an emotion-inference flag labels a crying child's conversation "agitated" and prompts termination. We present these as scenarios that the documented features above make plausible, not as reported incidents.The framework does not pretend these values align. Security versus rights: contraband and witness intimidation are real, but a system optimised only for detected incidents is misspecified, because its costs, such as false rejections, deterred visits and abandoned contact, fall on families, who already face burdensome visiting procedures (Boppre et al., 2022), and are rarely measured. Efficiency versus oversight: automation saves staff time precisely by reducing human scrutiny, and reviewers tend to defer to automated alerts (Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010); nominal oversight can then legitimise unreliable outputs (Green, 2022). Transparency versus gaming: full disclosure of detection rules may help circumvention, yet a bare reference to "security reasons" prevents correction and undermines legitimacy (Tyler, 2006). We resolve this by requiring an individual, actionable reason and disclosure of decision rules to an independent auditor even where public disclosure is limited. Public duty versus commercial incentive: where vendors are paid per call or per minute, contract terms can shape visitation policy (Rabuy and Wagner, 2015), so procurement is itself a governance instrument.Table 1 specifies, for each tier, minimum safeguards, appeal routes, review timelines, audit duties and measurable fairness indicators. Three features carry the argument. Appeals are two-stage: an on-site supervisor with authority to override decisions within the same session, followed by written review within 72 hours or before the next scheduled visit, whichever is sooner, with escalation to a body independent of the prison. Accountability is named: each consequential deployment has a responsible official, tamperevident decision logs, and contracts that prohibit in-person bans and guarantee auditor access to data. Fairness is measured through disaggregated false-rejection rates, override rates and appeal outcomes, with predefined disparity thresholds that trigger suspension pending review. This treats trustworthiness as a lifecycle responsibility rather than a launch certificate (Tabassi, 2023). The numerical values in Table 1 are proposed starting points for calibration, not validated standards.Three red lines follow the irreversibility criterion. No adverse visitation decision may rest solely on AI output; biometric failure must trigger an alternative verification route rather than exclusion; and speech, behaviour or emotion inference must never be treated as established misconduct. Where immediate intervention is necessary for safety, it should be temporary, documented, proportionate and promptly reviewed.These requirements will land differently. In the European Union, the AI Act classifies emotion recognition and many biometric and law-enforcement uses as high-risk and gives affected persons a right to an explanation, yet its prohibition of emotion recognition covers workplaces and education, not detention (European Union, 2024). Malaysia has no AI-specific statute; its national AI governance guidelines are voluntary (MOSTI, 2024), and its Personal Data Protection Act 2010 does not apply to federal and state governments (Malaysia, 2010). Its prison service already combines online booking with in-person and video visits (Berita Harian, 2024), so AI could be added without a dedicated legal framework. In the United States, visitation technology is often procured county by county (Rabuy and Wagner, 2015), and familyengagement policies differ markedly between states (Pappas et al., 2024).Resources also differ. We therefore propose a minimum floor applicable everywhere, consisting of the red lines, a non-digital route, same-session human override and incident logging, and an enhanced tier of independent audits, disaggregated reporting and impact assessment for systems with adequate capacity. Where independent review bodies are absent, an existing ombudsman, inspectorate or human-rights commission can be designated.
