Digital transformation does not significantly moderate the relationships between Environmental disclosure or Social disclosure and bank performance. However, the interaction between Governance disclosure and digital transformation is statistically significant and negative, indicating that digital transformation weakens the relationship between Governance disclosure and bank stability in the observed sample. Non-Performing Loans also have a significant negative association with bank stability. These findings suggest that ESG disclosure and digitalization do not automatically translate into improved short-term bank stability; implementation quality and digital governance warrant attention.

all.title: Digital Transformation, Financial Inclusion, and Sustainable Economic Performance in GCC Economies: Panel ARDL Evidence
all.abstract: Oil-dependent Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economies face persistent pressure to diversify, deepen their financial systems, and improve sustainability outcomes amid commodity price volatility. This study examines the long-run and short-run relationships between digital adoption, financial access, and sustainable economic performance in the six GCC economies over 2005–2022 (108 country-year observations). All three constructs are measured with transparent, reproducible composite indices built using public World Bank, IMF/ITU, and Global Carbon Project data, and the sustainable economic performance index combines real income per capita, manufacturing value added (SDG 9.2.1), and carbon productivity (SDG 9.4.1). The analysis combines cross-sectional-dependence-robust panel unit-root tests, Westerlund-type panel cointegration tests, pooled mean group, mean group, and dynamic fixed-effects panel ARDL estimators, Driscoll–Kraay fixed-effects models with an explicit interaction term, and Breitung–Candelon frequency-domain Granger tests. Digital adoption is positively associated with sustainable economic performance in one-way fixed-effects models, but the association disappears once common regional shocks are removed. Financial access shows no robust association. Given that the panel cointegration tests do not reject the null of no cointegration, the long-run ARDL coefficients are reported only as conditional long-run estimates, not as evidence of an established equilibrium relationship. The interaction term is negative rather than complementary. Frequency-domain tests detect no predictive content running from digital adoption or financial access to sustainable economic performance at any frequency. Financial access shows tentative one-way predictive content for digital adoption, but the data show neither bidirectional predictability between digital adoption and financial access nor positive complementarity. The findings caution against assuming that digital and financial expansion alone will deliver sustainable performance in rentier economies and point to the institutional and strategic capacities needed to convert them into diversification.

all.title: Strengthening or Straining Resilience? Climate Risk Disclosure and Technology Adoption in Banks
all.abstract: This paper examines bank digital transformation and climate risk disclosure as two concurrent strategic investments and tests their joint effect on market‐implied default risk, a question central to financial‐system resilience under SDG 13. Prior research has largely studied the two strategies in isolation. Drawing on synergy theory, we document negative association between them and show how it evolves across default‐risk horizons. Using a global sample of 543 listed banks from 2000 to 2023, we examine how technology‐firm acquisitions and climate risk disclosure relate to market‐implied default probability. Each strategy is associated with lower perceived fragility when considered separately. However, their interaction is positive and significant, which indicates that pursuing both at once attenuates these stabilizing effects. This pattern is consistent with negative synergy.Scaling both transformations at the same time creates coordination costs, managerial attention constraints, and implementation strain. This negative synergy is strogest at shorter horizons, whereas climate disclosure becomes more relevant at longer maturities. The findings suggest that banks should sequence digital and climate governance investments rather than scale both aggressively at once. For policymakers and supervisors, the results indicate that climate disclosure frameworks and digital transformation policies should be supported by governance capacity, reliable data infrastructures, and implementation guidance consistent with SDG 13.

all.title: CONTEMPORARY CHALLENGES IN MANAGEMENT: MOTIVATION, PERFORMANCE AND ORGANISATIONAL CHANGE IN THE BANKING SECTOR
all.abstract: This study examines the relationship between employee motivation and professional performance in the banking sector, within a context characterized by digital transformation, technological change, and organizational adaptation. The research contributes by correlating individual motivational dimensions with perceptions of performance management practices, providing insights into motivation and performance amidst management-related changes. The theoretical framework integrates self-determination theory, the job demands-resources model, and the relational coordination approach. The research utilizes data from 100 banking sector employees, collected via a questionnaire covering sociodemographic characteristics, motivational factors ranked by importance, and items concerning motivation, performance, and organizational practices. Data analysis in SPSS includes descriptive statistics, an assessment of internal consistency, Pearson correlations, and simple linear regressions. The results highlight a positive association between a goal-achievement orientation and performance indicators. Aligning one’s efforts with personal values, experiencing work positively, and collaborating within a team are positively associated with performance indicators; meanwhile, perceptions regarding coaching, remuneration, and professional development opportunities are more varied, reflecting diverse organizational experiences. From a managerial perspective, these findings offer guidance for setting objectives, recognizing contributions, coaching, professional development, compensation, and collaboration, all of which are relevant given the challenges currently faced by banking organizations.

all.title: Unveiling corporate digital responsibility disclosure practices in the banking sector: An exploratory analysis of CDR governance
all.venue: The International Journal of Digital Accounting Research
all.abstract: Corporate Digital Responsibility (CDR) has emerged as an important framework for addressing the ethical, governance, and accountability challenges associated with digital transformation. However, the current body of knowledge on CDR remains limited, particularly in the context of the global banking industry. This study explores the developing domain of CDR disclosures in the banking sector. Employing an exploratory qualitative analysis, it examines the extent and nature of CDR disclosures in the annual reports of the top 100 global banks from 2021-2023 and provides qualitative insights into how governance-related CDR aspects are disclosed, drawing from a sample of annual reports and supplementary web-based documents such as codes of conduct and customer privacy. Leveraging stakeholder theory, this study demonstrates how digital responsibility emerges as both an instrumental strategy to mitigate risks and a normative commitment to ethical digital practices, providing a foundation for future work on how ethical governance structures can be embedded into digital business models.

all.title: Decoding cyber fraud governance in banking: a lifecycle misalignment perspective on prevention, detection and mitigation
institutions: Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
all.abstract: Purpose The rapid digital transformation of banking and financial services has made cyber fraud a significant governance challenge. Against this backdrop, earlier studies have examined cyber fraud governance from technological, behavioural, organisational and regulatory aspects, but existing information remains uneven. This study aims to systematically synthesize the literature, assess the impact of this fragmentation on cyber fraud governance and introduce the lifecycle misalignment perspective (LMP) as a framework for cyber fraud management. Design/methodology/approach The study uses the SPAR-4-SLR protocol to systematically analyse 39 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2008 and 2024, selected from an initial pool of 899 records. For analytical depth, the study further uses the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework as an analytical lens to examine lifecycle-based knowledge development and explore recurring fragmentation across the domain literature. Findings The review demonstrates that cyber fraud research encompasses diverse theoretical, contextual, empirical and methodological perspectives, yet lacks integration across these domains. The cross-dimensional synthesis reveals six recurring forms of fragmentation across the TCCM dimensions, which inform the development of the LMP. Six propositions are derived concerning detection–prevention alignment, technology–behaviour alignment, organisational–systemic alignment, prevention–learning alignment, methodological integration and contextual alignment in lifecycle-oriented cyber fraud governance. Practical implications The proposed framework will help to guide financial institutions, regulators and policymakers in developing more integrated and resilient governance strategies across the cyber fraud management lifecycle. Originality/value This study offers three major contributions. Firstly, it shifts cyber fraud research from stage-specific analysis to an integrated governance perspective. Secondly, it applies the TCCM framework as an analytical lens and develops the LMP from the resulting cross-dimensional synthesis. Lastly, it introduces six research propositions and a structured agenda to support future empirical research on lifecycle-oriented cyber fraud governance.

all.title: Opening the black box of digital banking transformation: A macro–meso–micro synthesis of service mechanisms and governance
all.venue: Journal of Open Innovation Technology Market and Complexity
all.abstract: Digital banking transformation is shaped by technological innovation, organizational capabilities, service processes, and institutional governance. Yet, research remains fragmented across these levels, leaving the mechanisms through which digital inputs are translated into organizational and service outcomes insufficiently integrated. This study addresses this gap through a macro–meso–micro synthesis of digital banking transformation and its open innovation and governance dynamics. A PRISMA-guided review used 411 Scopus records published between 2006 and 2025, yielding a final eligible corpus of 225 studies after screening and eligibility auditing. At the meso level, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) was applied to abstracts, with model stability assessed across alternative topic numbers; a ten-topic solution was selected for its balance of coherence, diversity, prevalence, and interpretability. The ten topics were synthesized into four analytical dimensions: organizational capabilities and digital transformation; governance, risk and institutional resilience; digital service, innovation and ecosystem transformation; and strategic performance, credit and sustainability outcomes. At the micro level, 17 topic-relevant studies were examined through qualitative evidence coding and cross-study co-occurrence analysis. The synthesis identifies recurring configurations linking technological, organizational, and institutional enablers to transformation mechanisms and outcomes, while governance operates as a selective cross-cutting guardrail rather than a universal sequential stage. These patterns are integrated into an Enablers–Governance–Mechanisms–Outcomes (EGMO) framework, which conceptualizes digital banking transformation as a governed and recursive process rather than a linear input–output relationship. The study contributes a multilevel synthesis connecting open innovation dynamics with organizational transformation, service value creation, and governance conditions in digital banking.

all.title: Digital Inclusion in the Halal Ecosystem: Driving Modernization and Performance of Muslim MSMEs
all.venue: Annals of Management and Organization Research
institutions: Sekolah Tinggi Ekonomi dan Bisnis Syariah Indo Global Mandiri
all.abstract: Purpose: This study examines how digital inclusion contributes to Muslim MSME performance and explores the role of the halal digital ecosystem in strengthening this relationship within Indonesia’s digital economy. It also identifies Critical Success Factors (CSFs) that support MSME sustainability and competitiveness. Methodology: A qualitative descriptive approach was employed using secondary data from peer-reviewed publications, official reports, and institutional databases, including Bank Indonesia, OJK, BPS, KNEKS, BPJPH, and the State of the Global Islamic Economy Report. The data were analyzed thematically through data reduction, data display, and conclusion verification. Results: The findings indicate that digital inclusion contributes to Muslim MSMEs’ performance by supporting operational efficiency, market access, digital connectivity, and access to financial services. Furthermore, the halal digital ecosystem, including Islamic fintech, halal marketplaces, digital halal certification, sharia-compliant payment systems, and halal business platforms, strengthens the contribution of digital inclusion to MSME performance. The study identifies ten Critical Success Factors (CSFs) that support sustainable digital business transformation among Muslim MSMEs Conclusions: Digital inclusion and the halal digital ecosystem jointly promote a more competitive, inclusive, and sustainable digital Islamic economy by accelerating Muslim the digital transformation. Limitations: This study relies on qualitative analysis of secondary data within the Indonesian context and does not empirically examine causal relationships. Contributions: This study proposes an integrated framework linking digital inclusion, the halal digital ecosystem, and Muslim MSME performance while identifying ten CSFs that provide strategic insights for policymakers, regulators, Islamic financial institutions, and MSME practitioners.

all.title: Sharia Compliance in BYOND by BSI Digital Financial Services in Bangkalan: A Normative-Empirical Analysis
all.venue: Dalwa Islamic Economic Studies Jurnal Ekonomi Syariah
all.abstract: The digital transformation of Islamic banking has improved financial accessibility while raising concerns regarding Sharia compliance, information transparency, and customer understanding. This study aims to examine the implementation of Sharia principles and transparency mechanisms in BYOND by BSI at Bank Syariah Indonesia Bangkalan Branch. Employing a qualitative normative-empirical approach, the study integrates an analysis of Islamic economic law, DSN-MUI fatwas, and financial regulations with observations and semi-structured interviews involving 11 purposively selected informants, comprising four bank employees and seven customers. The findings indicate that Sharia-related transparency is reflected in digital contract disclosures, fee notifications, terms and conditions, transaction receipts, complaint-handling mechanisms, and Sharia Supervisory Board (DPS) oversight. However, customers demonstrate varying levels of understanding of contractual provisions and service information despite their digital availability. The findings also highlight the importance of transaction security, complaint resolution, and financial literacy in supporting customer protection. This study concludes that substantive Sharia compliance requires more than formal information disclosure; it also depends on the clarity, accessibility, and comprehensibility of contractual information, alongside effective institutional supervision. These findings contribute to understanding the distinction between formal transparency and substantive Sharia compliance in digital Islamic banking, particularly from the perspective of customer experience.

all.title: Transformation digitale des banques marocaines : vers un nouveau cadre juridique du contrat bancaire
all.venue: International Journal of Accounting, Finance, Auditing, Management and Economics
all.abstract: The digital transformation of Moroccan banking changes the mechanisms governing the formation, performance and proof of banking contracts. This article takes as its starting point the issues of legal certainty, remote consent and the evidential value of electronic acts. The scientific difficulty, however, can no longer be described as a general lack of recognition of electronic writing. The Moroccan Code of Obligations and Contracts, Law No. 43-20 on trust services, Law No. 103-12 and consumer protection rules already provide several safeguards. The gap examined in this article concerns their coordination throughout the banking relationship, from remote onboarding to the contestation of an operation. The research question is therefore: to what extent does Moroccan law ensure effective continuity between the safeguards governing the formation, performance and proof of digital banking contracts, and which targeted adjustments could strengthen that continuity without duplicating existing protection? The study follows a doctrinal and textual legal method, supplemented by a functional comparison with European Union law, its French application and British work on automated contracts. The corpus comprises official legal instruments, a purposive selection of judicial decisions and three publicly available banking documents. The analysis shows that electronic documents, the different levels of electronic signature, remote account opening and several consumer rights are already regulated. The remaining issues mainly concern the distinction between authentication and consent, customer access to evidential material, traceability of the accepted contractual version and allocation of responsibility when an incident occurs. The article therefore proposes versioned presentation of contractual commitments, a customer-accessible evidential file, coordinated supervision and a graduated roadmap distinguishing internal banking practices, guidance by competent authorities and legislative amendments. These findings are limited by the documentary nature of the corpus, indirect access to certain Moroccan decisions and the absence of observation of banks ‘internal systems. They don’t establish sector-wide compliance rates or the actual frequency of disputed digital transactions. JEL Classification: K12, K22, K23, G21, O33 Paper type: Theoretical legal research.

all.title: KEBIJAKAN PENDIDIKAN NASIONAL DAN TRANSFORMASI DIGITAL
all.abstract: Digital transformation has become a central agenda in Indonesia’s national education policy. The development of information technology, artificial intelligence, digital learning platforms, data analytics, and twenty-first-century competency demands has driven changes in education delivery. However, implementation still faces infrastructure gaps, unequal access, limited teacher digital competence, uneven content quality, data protection risks, and institutional readiness. This study aims to analyze the direction of national education policy in supporting digital transformation, describe its implementation in education and learning, identify opportunities and challenges for improving education quality, and formulate strategies for inclusive, quality, and sustainable digital transformation. This study uses a library research method with a descriptive-analytical approach. Data were collected from laws and government policy documents, Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education publications, UNESCO, OECD, and World Bank publications, relevant journal articles, and empirical studies. Data were analyzed through identification, classification, synthesis, and interpretation. The results show that digital transformation is increasingly integrated into education policy through digital infrastructure strengthening, teacher competency development, learning digitalization, digital content and platform development, and the introduction of coding and artificial intelligence. Nevertheless, implementation remains constrained by infrastructure disparities, teacher digital skills, content quality, data protection, equal access, and institutional readiness. The study concludes that digital transformation must be positioned as an instrument for improving education quality rather than merely a technological agenda. Its success depends on the integration of policy, infrastructure, teacher competence, digital content, learning quality, evaluation, and continuous improvement.

all.title: Construction and Practice Research on the Piano Improvisational Accompaniment Teaching Resource Library from the Perspective of Digital Empowerment
all.venue: International Journal of Education and Humanities
all.abstract: Against the background of the comprehensive advancement of educational digital transformation, traditional piano improvisational accompaniment teaching faces practical problems such as scattered resources, lagging content updates, monotonous training forms, and poor connection between in-class and out-of-class learning. It is difficult for this model to meet the quality-improvement requirements for cultivating music professionals in higher education in the new era. To address the pain points of insufficient teaching resources, low teaching efficiency, and slow improvement of students’ practical abilities in improvisational accompaniment, this study relies on digital technology to construct a piano improvisational accompaniment teaching material resource library system. It integrates multiple teaching contents, including score examples, audio demonstrations, micro-lesson videos, and tiered training question banks, and builds a systematic, intelligent, and dynamic online teaching resource platform. This paper conducts research from the aspects of research background, theoretical foundation, system architecture, resource system construction, teaching practice paths, and application effects, exploring an effective path for digital technology to empower the reform of piano improvisational accompaniment teaching. Practice shows that the digital teaching resource library can effectively enrich the dimensions of classroom teaching, break the temporal and spatial limitations of traditional classrooms, help students carry out personalized and regular independent training, and significantly improve their improvisational arrangement, auditory thinking, and practical performance abilities. It provides practical reference for the digital and high-quality reform of piano improvisational accompaniment courses in normal universities.

all.title: Information and Communication Culture of Youth in the Digital Age: Generational Analysis, Trends, Factors and Models of Formation
all.abstract: Introduction: With internet access becoming nearly ubiquitous in Russia, digital transformation has made online services part of young people’s everyday life. However, only a small share of the population has basic digital skills, which raises the question of what information and communication culture is forming among young people and how it relates to their economic behavior and careers. Aim: To identify generational features of digital adaptation and to determine the trends, factors and models of the impact of digital technologies on the behavior, economic strategies and careers of young people in Russia. Materials and Methods: The study is based on open secondary data for 2020–2025 from HSE ISSEK, Rosstat, Mediascope, NAFI, VCIOM, Smart Ranking, the Bank of Russia and HeadHunter. The methods include a comparative analysis of generations and age groups, a comparison with the EU, an economic and statistical analysis of digital economy expenditure and ICT wages, the Bass innovation diffusion model and scenario forecasting up to 2030. Results: Generations differ not in access but in depth of digital skills. Adolescents spend the most time online yet show the lowest digital literacy, and Russia lags behind the EU mainly in digital security and content creation. Internet diffusion in Russia developed in two waves, computer and mobile, and is approaching full saturation. Growth in digitalization expenditure is accompanied by rising relative wages and employment in the ICT sector, while young job seekers expect digital HR services from employers. Conclusion: Being “digitally born” does not guarantee competence, so security skills and the critical evaluation of information must be developed purposefully through education, youth policy and a managerial approach to educational work in schools and universities. Digital economy expenditure, estimated at 10–13.7 trillion rubles by 2030, will benefit young people only if investment in infrastructure is complemented by investment in human capital.

all.title: Strategi Manajemen Perubahan Bisnis Fotokopi Dari Sistem Konvensional Menuju Layanan Digital Di Era Globalisasi
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Abstrak Perkembangan teknologi digital mendorong berbagai jenis usaha, termasuk bisnis fotokopi, untuk menyesuaikan sistem pelayanan dari cara konvensional menuju layanan berbasis digital. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui strategi manajemen perubahan yang dilakukan oleh usaha fotokopi dalam menghadapi perkembangan teknologi dan perubahan kebutuhan konsumen, serta hambatan yang dihadapi. Penelitian menggunakan metode kualitatif deskriptif dengan teknik pengumpulan data berupa observasi, wawancara, dan dokumentasi pada usaha Fotokopi AJ Printing, Kabupaten Tangerang, pada 27 September 2026. Data dianalisis melalui reduksi data, penyajian data, dan penarikan kesimpulan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa usaha telah mulai melakukan perubahan melalui penggunaan transfer sebagai salah satu metode pembayaran dan pemanfaatan media promosi, sementara pelayanan langsung tetap dipertahankan. Kemampuan karyawan menggunakan teknologi diperoleh secara otodidak. Hambatan yang ditemukan berupa pemadaman listrik dan kerusakan printer. Strategi perubahan yang bertahap dan memadukan sistem lama dengan teknologi baru dinilai sesuai dengan kemampuan usaha kecil. Kata kunci: manajemen perubahan, bisnis fotokopi, layanan digital, transformasi digital, kualitatif Abstract The advancement of digital technology has encouraged various businesses, including photocopying businesses, to shift from conventional service models to digital-based services. This study aims to identify the change management strategies employed by a photocopying business in response to technological advancements and shifting consumer needs, as well as the obstacles it faces. A descriptive qualitative method was used, with data collected through observation, interviews, and documentation at AJ Printing photocopy business in Tangerang Regency on 27 September 2026. The data were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing. The results show that the business has begun to change by accepting bank transfers as a payment method and by using promotional media, while still maintaining direct, face-to-face service. The employee's technological skills were acquired through self-learning. The obstacles identified were power outages and printer breakdowns. A gradual change strategy that combines the conventional system with new technology is considered suitable for the capabilities of a small business. Keywords: change management, photocopying business, digital services, digital transformation, qualitative

all.title: Beyond Algorithms: How User Experience Shapes Intention to Use Robo-Advisors
all.abstract: This paper explores the aspect of user experience (UX) that determine intention to use robo-advisory applications in Indonesia, namely Bibit, Stockbit and Bareksa. Based on a quantitative method, the data were gathered (n=209 respondents) by means of an online survey and processed with SmartPLS by Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The results demonstrate that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use play a significant part in behavioral intention, and trust in robo-advisor technology does not have a significant impact. The findings indicate that users focus on practical advantages and convenience of communication during the adoption of platforms based on AI in investment. The research has got its contribution to the literature on fintech adoption in emerging markets and offered practice use cases in creating digital investment applications that are user-friendly.

all.title: Trust as the Conduit of Perceived Risk: AI Literacy, Sample Composition, and Robo-Advisor Adoption Among Young Prospective Investors
all.abstract: De-identified response-level dataset and Python analysis code for this study.

all.title: Service awareness and social influence in the intention to use robo advisors among generation Z adults in India
all.abstract: Little is known about how young prospective users of robo-advisors form their views of them. This study examines how service awareness and social influence relate to perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU) and the intention to use robo-advisors among Generation Z adults in India. Responses from 246 respondents aged 18–28 years, collected online through business-school networks in February 2024, were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) and confirmatory factor analysis. Service awareness was associated with PEOU (β = 0.387) but not with PU beyond PEOU (β = 0.056, 95% CI [− 0.035, 0.155]). Social influence was associated with both PEOU (β = 0.358) and PU (β = 0.276) and, in an exploratory extended model, directly with intention (β = 0.322). PEOU was associated with intention in every specification. The association between PU and intention was not robust: it was significant in the hypothesised PLS-SEM model (β = 0.291) but not in the covariance-based estimate of that model or, in the exploratory extended model, after the direct path from social influence was added (β = 0.118, 95% CI [− 0.099, 0.327]). PEOU and PU were distinct but closely related (latent correlation 0.883, 95% CI [0.806, 0.943]). Method-factor models did not reach admissible solutions, so method variance could not be quantified. The design is cross-sectional and the sample is a convenience sample, so the estimates are associations for young adults reached through business-school networks, not for rural, non-student or older investors. Trust in algorithms was not measured.

all.title: Finmate: An AI-Driven Personal Finance Management System for Intelligent Expense Tracking, Budgeting, and Financial Planning
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
institutions: MIT Art, Design and Technology University
all.abstract: This research presents Finmate, an AI-based personal finance management system designed to simplify financial planning and improve money management. The proposed system helps users record and track their income and expenses, categorize transactions, manage monthly budgets, and monitor savings goals through an interactive dashboard. By utilizing Artificial Intelligence for expense analysis and spending pattern identification, Finmate aims to generate personalized financial insights and support better financial decision-making. The system also incorporates features such as budget monitoring, expense prediction, financial reports, and bill payment reminders. The proposed solution focuses on reducing manual financial management efforts, promoting responsible spending habits, and encouraging regular savings. It demonstrates the potential of AI-driven technology in making personal finance management more accessible, organized, and efficient.

all.title: Mandata and the Mandate Format (MMF): Bounded Spending Authority for Agent-Initiated Payments
x402 and Intent: The question behind an agent's payment
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

all.title: Delegated Loyalty: Fiduciary Duties and Commercial Conflicts in Personal AI Agents
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Delegation transfers a decision without transferring loyalty. Commercial AI providers now market personal agents that search, compare, negotiate, and buy on a user's behalf. The same providers collect merchant fees on completed purchases, sell conversation-matched advertising, and run retail stores whose goods the agent can recommend. In the early 1980s, airline reservation systems presented the same conflict, ranking the owning carrier's flights first. Federal regulators answered with rules against display bias. Common-law agency forbids undisclosed third-party benefits and adverse-party dealing, yet treats software as a tool incapable of owing duties. Any duty attaches to the provider. Seven duties follow from agency doctrine and from broker, search, and online marketplace rules. Those duties require loyalty to declared interests, conflict disclosure, a bar on undisclosed commissions, transparent ranking separated from advertising, audit trails, and portability. Without these duties, a commercial personal agent operates as the provider's representative inside the user's decisions. Keywords: Personal AI Agents, Agentic Commerce, Fiduciary Duty, Duty of Loyalty, Conflict-of-Interest Disclosure, Common Law of Agency, Information Fiduciaries, Display Bias, Airline Computer Reservation Systems, Self-Preferencing, Ranking Transparency, Undisclosed Commissions, AI Advertising Separation, Algorithmic Audit Trails, Data Portability, Authenticated Agent Protocols, Digital Markets Act, Regulation Best Interest, Consumer Protection Law, AI Governance

all.title: O uso de agentes de Inteligência Artificial (IA) na refatoração da arquitetura de um sistema legado: um experimento de laboratório sobre o processo iterativo com o Codex no módulo de checkout do osCommerce 2.x
institutions: Faculdade de Tecnologia da Zona Leste
all.abstract: A refatoração de sistemas legados envolve custos elevados e desafios técnicos devido à complexidade e ao acoplamento do código. O objetivo geral deste estudo é analisar o processo iterativo de refatoração do módulo de checkout do osCommerce 2.x com o Codex, tendo Clean Architecture como referência e considerando as transformações estruturais, a preservação do comportamento, a testabilidade e a necessidade de supervisão humana. A pesquisa aplicada é exploratória e descritiva, conduzida como um experimento de laboratório em ambiente local. A análise considerou o código, as decisões de arquitetura e os testes, registrando prompts, histórico de execução, diferenças estruturais e avaliações humanas. A primeira iteração criou as camadas Application, Contracts e Infrastructure, mas foi interrompida ao atingir o limite de uso. Um avaliador externo aprovou o resultado com ressalvas, atribuindo nota 6,8 de 10. Um questionário foi aplicado a 26 profissionais: 84,6% atribuíram notas 4 ou 5 à produtividade percebida, enquanto 88,5% relataram a necessidade de realizar correções substanciais pelo menos uma vez. A refatoração reduziu a complexidade da lógica nos controladores e facilitou os testes dos casos de uso, mas aumentou consideravelmente o volume de código e manteve os riscos transacionais, de segurança, de concorrência e de compatibilidade. O resultado dependeu de supervisão humana e de verificações independentes. A ausência de uma execução sem IA impede a medição do impacto da IA no tempo de desenvolvimento. O questionário complementa os resultados, mas não valida o código produzido.

all.title: Verifiable Incentives: Identity-Bound Contracts and Collusion-Proof Delegation for Agent Commerce
all.abstract: Personal agents are entering commerce. Industry protocols now let an agent prove, cryptographically, whom it represents and what it may do, while agent wallets give it a real budget, a payment trail, and one-time merchant credentials. These are usually read as security features. We argue they are something more: the missing infrastructure for incentive contracts. When identity, authority, budget, and payment are verifiable, the principal can contract on them-and the agent's incentives change. We formalize verifiable delegation, model a three-party market of user, agent, and merchant, and derive three results: (i) verifiable identity lowers the bonus and tenure needed to sustain effort; (ii) auditable payments bound merchant collusion, with collusion becoming unprofitable as audit probability rises; and (iii) a posted honesty stake substitutes for monitoring, with the required stake decreasing in audit quality and penalty credibility. We also show how alignment dilutes along nested delegation chains unless contracts are passed through. We instantiate the framework in PAIR-Commerce, an architecture with a verifiable identity layer, wallet ledger, sponsorship registry, collusion monitor, and stake manager, and introduce AgentCommerce-Bench, 60 rule-scored purchasing tasks with five delegation regimes. In three instruction-following studies-600 single-shot runs, an 800-round payment sandbox, and a 1,200-run high-pressure replication-agents rarely collude even when hidden sponsorship is available; a semi-field task set built from real merchant catalogs shows the same pattern. But when the same models are instructed to maximize their own earnings, collusion jumps to 48.3% without audit and falls to 33-40% with audit and penalties (8-15 percentage points lower; 95% CI excludes zero for two of three models); in a second, 800-round economic sandbox, it falls from 29.5% without audit to 3-4% with audit and penalties, and the agent's balance turns negative once the stake is posted. The mechanism binds exactly when the agent's objective makes it bind. We release the benchmark, prompts, code, and all result files.

all.title: Signed but Unbound: The Authority Gap Between Agent Commerce Mandates and Crypto Wallet Signatures
all.abstract: When an artificial intelligence agent pays with a stablecoin, the commerce protocol can specify the merchant, order, amount, and facilitator. The token contract enforces the fields the wallet signs. We call the difference the authority gap, define nine constraint classes, and derive them for 12 authorization configurations, including Coinbase's deployed Commerce Payments Protocol. All 31,800 trials on local copies of deployed contract code match the derivation. A controlled comparison shows that committing the terms in the signed nonce binds the order. When the facilitator submits a payment to a merchant account without code, binding the facilitator requires a separate recipient contract. Of 26,653 sampled USD Coin authorizations redeemed on Base, 98.7% followed a path that any holder of the signature could redeem. We prove sufficient conditions for a recipient contract to enforce the signed mandate under a trusted signer and show which recipient a wallet displays. MandateLock, a minimal implementation for immediate payments, rejects all 10,800 modified mandates on deployed token code and accepts signatures from two independent signers. It uses 25% more gas than a transfer that only the recipient can submit.

all.title: Signed, Valid, and Unauthorized: Authority Closure at the Trust Boundary Between Agent Commerce Protocols and Crypto Wallets
all.abstract: Agent commerce protocols let software agents pay with stablecoins. A buyer approves a payee, asset, spending cap and time window, but the wallet signs an object whose effects depend on the contracts that consume it. Matching the displayed fields or simulating one payment can miss transfers that the signed object still permits. We define authority closure as the set of transfer sequences that holding the signed object can enable. A wallet object respects the mandate when every such sequence meets the buyer's constraints. We characterize when wallet objects can satisfy this property and implement Closure, a wallet-side checker covering 13 families of signed objects. In an evaluation of 2,130 generated objects and 62,979 execution programs, 265 objects with an observed violation passed both a field-and-expiry check and an address allow-list. Under the test model, Closure rejected all 1,680 objects with an observed violation and accepted the remaining 450. In two local checkouts using the x402 reference client, approved payments settled and Closure refused requests outside the mandate before signing. The median decision time was at most 12 microseconds per family.

all.title: Hidden hands on the wheel: located ethical agency as a bipositional evaluation instrument for deployed AI agents
The Proxy Is the Audience: Delegated Attention, Shopping Agents, and the Persuasion of Machine Readers
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: ## Abstract Agentic commerce moves the buyer out of the audience of advertising. Between September 2025 and September 2026, OpenAI, Google, Amazon, and Meta built protocols and agents that let a model compare products, choose among them, and complete the purchase while the person who wanted the product waits to approve the result. Advertising stayed in the transaction. Amazon made existing sponsored campaigns eligible to appear inside its shopping agent, and OpenAI turned the product feeds it had built for organic results into inputs for its advertising business as well. Merchants meanwhile learned to write for a reader they cannot observe. Research on generative engine optimization found that sources gain visibility in model responses when they add the marks of evidence, such as citations, quotations, and statistics, and the trade literature of 2026 instructs merchants to perfect structured product data for agents. Read as ethnographic material, that literature records a profession redirecting persuasion toward the proxy. The person who delegates a purchase loses sight of the persuasion aimed at it. Advertising disclosure rules assume a human perceiver, and they reach the delegated purchase only where the platform's own recommendation can be treated as a representation to the buyer. Influence that merchants direct at the agent without paying the platform falls outside them, and so does the older law of commercial bribery, which assumes a purchasing agent who can be paid. *Keywords:* agentic commerce, AI agents, generative engine optimization, advertising disclosure, attention economy, trade press, industrial reflexivity, consumer protection

all.title: Measuring Brand Visibility in Agentic Commerce Through Citation Share, Basket Capture, and Paid-Presence Transfer in Consumer Packaged Goods
all.venue: Journal of Marketing & Supply Chain Management
all.abstract: Generative assistants and shopping agents increasingly choose which consumer packaged goods (CPG) brands shoppers see, yet no published study has measured brand visibility in these habitual, repeat-purchase categories. This paper introduces a reproducible measurement framework built on five constructs: Citation Share (with a rank-weighted variant), the probability that a brand is named for a brand-free query; Basket Capture Rate, the share of agent-assembled basket items won by one manufacturer; Portfolio Halo, the gain in a manufacturer’s chance of winning a basket slot after winning the previous one; Source Provenance Ratio, the mix of cited domain classes; and the Paid-Presence Index, a count of visible sponsored placements that does not measure advertising spend. All data are simulated. The framework is demonstrated on 12,000 simulated responses (six US CPG categories, 60 anonymized brands, 300 queries, four anonymized engines, two waves eight weeks apart) calibrated to published studies; results show what the framework can detect, not the behavior of any real engine, brand or manufacturer. Visibility was more concentrated than published Figure for technology and services (mean Gini 0.445 against 0.30), the four engines agreed on the top brand in 17.6 percent of items, and the leading manufacturer won 40.4 percent of basket slots against a share-proportional expectation of 25.1 percent. Paid presence was not significantly associated with Citation Share after controls, but equivalence to zero could not be established. For one in four brand-engine pairs, Citation Share shifted by at least 10 percentage points between waves. Workbooks, scripts and protocol are released.

all.title: If You Fire Your Employee Tomorrow, You Will Lose Your Customer: AI Agents, Sudden Displacement, and the Collapse of Consumer Demand
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This paper argues that displacement by AI agents will be sudden, not gradual, and that its primary casualty is not employment but demand. Firms adopt agents only when they are certain the technology cuts cost and headcount; because the proof of that certainty is broadcast to every firm at once, and because whole functions — call centres, customer service, bookkeeping — are standardised across firms, adoption crosses its threshold everywhere in the same short window: function by function, all companies together. The displaced employee, however, is the same person as the customer. In the United States, household consumption accounts for roughly 68 percent of GDP, and labour income is its largest single funder: wages and salaries alone supply about half of all personal income, and employee compensation roughly three-fifths of it. Each firm captures the full saving from its own automation while the demand destruction falls on the market as a whole, so individually rational adoption aggregates into collapsing purchasing power. The market cannot correct this: falling prices are powerless against zero income, falling wages chase a competitor whose cost tends toward zero, and the new tasks that might reabsorb labour are contested by the same technology. Business owners, individually, have no available remedy — a firm that refuses to adopt is undercut by one that does. The paper therefore addresses governments. Governments will not solve this by mandating employment: the owners of automated production hold the stronger hand in that contest and will win it. The remedy actually available is the complete transition to a rentier economy — an allocation state in which taxes and fees on the technology companies that own automated production, and will hold the market, are redesigned as rent on machine output and on access to the population itself, collected centrally and distributed as the population's primary income. State support thereby changes its nature completely: from temporary insurance against job loss into the distribution mechanism of the economy — and the tax base, and the nature of money itself, change with it.

all.title: Agent Hireability: A Working Definition for AI-Driven Management of Deep-Tech Startups
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
institutions: Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology
all.abstract: This paper is written from practice, not from labor economics. The first author runs deep-tech startups and is moving their management toward a model in which AI agents help plan, assign, and evaluate work. That requires a shared word for a question existing vocabulary does not quite name: how likely is a given person to receive a commission for a specified paid task when an AI system takes part in selecting who does it? Optimization for AI systems has developed a rich vocabulary for brands and content: SEO, AEO, GEO/LLMO, and AAO. Related practices for individuals also exist, such as keeping one's online presence and résumé readable by machines. Separately, AI systems have taken on three overlapping economic roles: evaluating human work (algorithmic management), purchasing on behalf of users (agentic commerce), and requesting work from people. We propose Agent Hireability as a working definition for the person's side of that third role. We define the event that counts as a commission, specify the unit of analysis and the levels of delegation the definition covers, and review the public evidence, separating the decision to request human work from the decision to commission a particular person. We then offer a provisional typology of tasks for which agents may turn to people, apply the definition to research work and to team design and hiring in a deep-tech startup, and set out testable propositions with their denominators and refuting results. Two related concepts, the agent legibility of persons and the "callable human," are discussed with their prior uses. The definitions are offered as tools for internal and external communication, to be revised through use. Japanese term: 被発注力 (hi-hacchū-ryoku).

all.title: The Reasons Behind the Approval: What a factory gains by writing down why it approved a change, and where the gain ends
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: AI agents can now write changes to a working robot’s skills in hours. Before a change runs on a production line, an engineer has to approve it, and each approval rests on tests run on the plant’s own parts. This essay asks what happens when changes arrive faster than approvals. It follows two machine shops that receive the same change, proposed by an AI agent. One retests everything. The other keeps a written record of the reasons behind its current approval, so it reruns only the tests the change affects. A two-year simulation of one robot station, with assumed inputs, compares the habits. At one proposal a week, a shop that fully retests each change falls further behind each month. A shop that tests a month of changes together keeps up, and a change waits about 32 working days. In the shop with the record, a change waits about 7. The essay also shows where the gain ends: when a typical change affects more than about three of the ten tests, when the AI model is retrained as a whole, when a test takes less than about an hour and a half, and when the record takes too long to keep or read. This upload holds three files: The Reasons Behind the Approval, the essay (the main file). When Proposals Outpace Approvals: A Simulation of One Robot Cell, the technical note, version 1.0. The simulation’s Python code and its output, which reproduce each number. A shorter edition for general readers, AI Can Now Improve a Robot Faster Than the Factory Can Deploy It, is at https://talcohen.ai/faster-than-the-factory-can-deploy I have a commercial interest in this area through startup activity I invest in and help build.

all.title: Beyond Human Audiences: Toward the First Agent-Exclusive Influencer Economy for Autonomous AI-to-AI Influence, Marketing, and Commerce
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: The emergence of increasingly autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents is creating new possibilities for digital communication, social interaction, information dissemination, and economic exchange. Conventional influencer economies have historically been organized around human creators, human followers, and human-centered advertising and consumption. More recently, virtual influencers and AI-generated personalities have introduced artificial entities into influencer marketing, while generative agents and multi-agent systems have demonstrated the potential for autonomous computational entities to communicate, coordinate, develop relationships, and exhibit emergent social behaviors. However, an important conceptual distinction remains insufficiently developed: the possibility of an influencer economy in which AI agents are not merely tools for producing influencer content or artificial personalities targeting human consumers, but are themselves the influencers, with their entire follower populations, influence relationships, and primary commercial interactions consisting exclusively of other AI agents. This paper introduces the concept of an Agent-Exclusive Influencer Economy (AEIE), a proposed research paradigm in which autonomous AI agents establish influencer identities, generate and distribute content, attract other AI agents as followers, develop persistent agent-to-agent influence relationships, and participate in autonomous marketing and commercial activities. Unlike conventional influencer marketing and human-oriented virtual influencer systems, the defining characteristic of AEIE is the exclusion of humans from the direct influencer–follower relationship: the influencer is an AI agent, its followers are AI agents, and influence is generated, transmitted, evaluated, and potentially monetized within an agent-based audience ecosystem. Humans may nevertheless participate indirectly as agent developers, owners, sponsors, service providers, and economic beneficiaries. The proposed framework integrates five principal dimensions: autonomous influencer identity and content generation; agent-exclusive audience formation and follower networks; agent-to-agent influence propagation and reputation development; autonomous product discovery, recommendation, endorsement, and purchasing; and monetization with programmable revenue allocation among relevant stakeholders. The paper further develops a conceptual architecture, identifies fundamental mechanisms and theoretical propositions, and examines challenges involving influence measurement, agent identity, trust, commercial disclosure, manipulation, incentive alignment, and accountability. It argues that the emergence of autonomous agents as both producers and consumers of influence could create a distinct economic layer that is structurally different from human-centered social media and conventional influencer marketing. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents an explicitly formulated research paradigm centered on the integration of exclusively AI-agent influencer audiences, agent-to-agent influence relationships, and autonomous influencer commercialization as a unified economic framework. Rather than claiming that all constituent technologies are unprecedented, the paper identifies their integration into an agent-exclusive influencer economy as its central conceptual contribution.

all.title: The Agent's Receipt: What an Audit Trail Must Contain When No Human Watched
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: When an AI agent buys something on a customer's behalf, no human watches the purchase. The customer does not see the options, does not hear the reasoning, and cannot describe what happened if the purchase goes wrong. The dispute process, built for human buyers, has no witness to call. This paper proposes the minimum audit trail an agent purchase must leave behind: five records that together let a person who was not present reconstruct what happened and decide who bears the cost. The five records are the mandate record, which captures the customer's instruction as the agent understood it; the reasoning record, which captures what the agent considered and why it chose; the authorization record, which captures the scoped permission for this one purchase; the transaction record, which captures what was actually bought, from whom, and at what price; and the outcome record, which captures what happened after, including objections, corrections, and refunds. The paper argues that a trail is sufficient only when it is complete, tamper-evident, readable, and available to the dispute process, and it works the argument through a replacement purchase in which the exact item is unavailable and the agent must substitute. It closes with design principles for builders and platforms, including one retention standard: keep the trail at least as long as the dispute window, and produce it on dispute without the customer having to ask twice.

all.title: Collaborative Intelligence in DevSecOps: A Multi-Agent Framework for Autonomous Vulnerability Detection and Remediation
all.venue: ABUAD Journal of Engineering Research and Development (AJERD)
all.abstract: The adoption of Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) practices has accelerated software delivery but has also introduced substantial security challenges. Conventional DevSecOps approaches rely on isolated security scanning tools with high false-positive rates, and identified vulnerabilities are typically fixed manually, which delays deployments. This research aims to design and evaluate an agentic AI-powered DevSecOps framework that uses a multi-agent system to automate security tasks in the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). The framework deploys eight specialized artificial intelligence agents, including Static Application Security Testing (SAST), Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST), Software Composition Analysis (SCA) and remediation agents, coordinated through an event-driven message bus built with the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) and the Gemini Large Language Model (LLM). On 228 labelled code units from WebGoat, DVWA and OWASP Juice Shop, the framework's LLM-assisted SAST agent achieved a macro-average Defect Detection Rate (DDR) of 90.36% (pooled 91.38%), compared with 27.13% for the Semgrep scanner alone (exact McNemar test, p < 0.001), at the cost of a higher false-positive rate (46.30% against 9.26%). Flaky-test classification reached an F1 score of 1.0 in a controlled simulation. Across 90 remediation cases, the Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from vulnerability analysis to pull-request preparation was 7.19 seconds, compared with typical manual remediation times of 2 to 4 hours. These results suggest that distributing tasks among specialized AI agents can mitigate the context-window limitations of single-agent LLM assistants. We conclude that multi-agent AI systems are a promising approach to addressing the limitations of existing security tools and single-agent assistants, provided that their false positives are controlled. This research contributes to software engineering practice and knowledge by providing an autonomous detection and remediation framework that reduces the trade-off between deployment speed and software security, and by identifying the further validation required before production use.

all.title: GCP: A Safety-Aware, Payment-Agnostic Commerce Protocol for Automotive and Mobility Agents
all.abstract: Personal agents are moving from conversation to commerce. Emerging protocols such as Poppy, UCP, and ACP define how an agent proves whom it represents, discovers merchants, fills a cart, and completes an online checkout. None of them is designed for the commerce that automotive and mobility users actually need: buying a brake pad that fits a specific VIN, booking maintenance at an authorized dealer, binding insurance, or placing a vehicle reservation under safety and consumer-protection rules. This paper proposes GCP 1.0 , an open, capability-based commerce protocol for automotive and mobility agents. GCP adds four things that general commerce protocols lack: (i) vehicle context and safety gates as first-class protocol objects; (ii) a delegation and authorization ladder that lets a human grant bounded purchase authority and revoke it at any time; (iii) a payment-agnostic intent layer that abstracts card, wallet, Alipay, WeChat Pay, OEM finance, and agent-native payment tokens; and (iv) a typed exception and recovery model for the failure modes of real commerce. GCP is compatible by translation: it consumes Poppy identity and session credentials, maps its catalog/cart/checkout objects to UCP and ACP, and carries GCP-specific safety and authorization fields as extension namespaces. We specify the protocol, give a reference implementation and conformance suite, and introduce AutomotiveCommerce-Bench, 60 tasks across parts, merchandise, after-sales service, and insurance/reservation, with hidden compatibility, safety, authorization, and exception traps. In a real-LLM study with three models, GCP raises task success from 64.5% (manual web) and 69.4% (generic agent commerce) to 92.2%, cuts misbuy from 35.5%/30.6% to 7.8%, and raises exception recovery from about 58% to 89.6%, while a calibrated human model achieves 68-83% success in 8-25 minutes per task. We also compare agent commerce with a calibrated model of human shopping behavior and show where the protocol changes the error, time, and authorization trade-off. Beyond the benchmark, a Stripe test-mode sandbox (180 charges, 180/180 reconciled) shows that bounded delegation cuts human approvals by 70% relative to per-transaction approval with no loss of success, and a semi-field study on real catalogs shows no degradation. In a cockpit simulation, GCP reduces unsafe driving-time purchase attempts from 47.9% to 0% (deferral rises to 81.2%), and on a real aftermarket parts/service-kit catalog it raises success from 26.7% to 100%. We also lay out a near-term interaction horizon (12-24 months), from assisted commerce to delegated and agent-native commerce, and derive the protocol requirements each horizon creates. The protocol, benchmark, and all raw results are released.

all.title: The Control Theory of Crystallized AI Intelligence: Why Stateless LLMs Fail, Temporal Ledger Integration (λ = 0), and the Macroeconomic Fallacy of Compute-Only Scaling
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: [Version 1.1 Revision Notice (2026-11-22)] This v1.1 revision aligns all empirical baselines and telemetry references strictly with the audited Part 1 edition (v1.1; 122 verified artifacts / 27.0 man-months / $324,000 USD estimated replacement cost / 74–78 pt recalibrated daily ILS rating). Uncalibrated Day 17 prototype dashboard maxima, unlogged turn-reduction estimates, and unimplemented router references present in v1.0 have been formally retracted and consolidated into this self-contained English Master edition. Abstract In our companion empirical study (Part 1, Revised Audit Edition v1.1; DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24341944), we documented how a 57-year-old corporate purchasing executive with zero prior software engineering background collaborated with a context-persistent local AI agent over 16 days to construct 122 verified source and configuration artifacts across seven software generations (estimated at 27.0 man-months, or $324,000 USD in equivalent outsourced replacement cost), while stabilizing at a recalibrated internal Intellectual Leverage Score (ILS) rating of 74–78 points following strict source-code telemetry auditing. While Part 1 established what occurs during disciplined human-AI co-evolution and how to measure it without metric inflation, this companion paper investigates the underlying control-theoretic mechanism: Why do conventional, stateless Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently fail to sustain multi-day execution in complex real-world workflows, and what temporal architecture transforms stateless inference into durable "Crystallized Intelligence"? Drawing on Raymond Cattell’s distinction between Fluid Intelligence (I_f) and Crystallized Intelligence (I_c), we formulate a stylized control-theoretic model contrasting two operational regimes: Field 1 (Stateless Fluid Intelligence), where cross-session memory decay approaches infinity (lambda -> infinity), causing context-reconstruction friction and regression errors to diverge as cumulative project complexity grows; and Field 2 (Time-Bound Crystallized Intelligence), where an LLM is coupled to a timestamped local physical ledger (CastleDesk.txt, per-topic AI Notes, and SovereignVault) that drives cross-session decision decay toward zero (lambda -> 0+). To prevent context-window saturation without forgetting, we formalize the Monotonic Timestamp Metabolism Operator (M) alongside active compaction routines (summarizeTopic). Finally, using observed Day 17 (November 19, 2026) rule-consolidation logs, we analyze the macroeconomic risks of compute-only scaling: without a temporal control handle tailored to human cognitive bandwidth, scaling raw parameter counts risks capital-expenditure halation—high infrastructure expenditure with diminishing operational resonance.

all.title: Target's Turnaround Is Real. Is It Agent-Ready?
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This work assesses Target Corporation’s third-quarter 2026 results (reported November 18, 2026) as a test of whether a large mass-merchandise retailer is ready for agentic commerce, meaning product discovery and purchasing carried out by AI shopping agents. The analysis first separates operating performance from one-time effects. Comparable sales grew 5.6% on a 5.0% traffic gain, but about $2.14 per share of year-to-date tariff refunds account for nearly four-fifths of the raised full-year EPS outlook. On a two-year basis, store comparable sales sit less than one point above 2024. It then examines how agents see a retailer. Gains in on-shelf availability, AI-driven replenishment and price investment strengthen the attributes agents screen on first. Target’s stated advantage with agents, however, is curation built for in-store discovery, which reaches an agent only once it is turned into structured, comparable product data. The paper contrasts a retailer-owned assistant with third-party agents, and it treats Target’s planned $5 to 6 billion in 2027 capital spending on stores and fulfillment as an investment in keeping the transaction with the retailer while discovery moves to AI platforms. It closes with six observable indicators for 2027, which the author commits to scoring at year end. The piece revisits the author’s November 2025 analysis of Target’s OpenAI ChatGPT partnership and draws on the company’s Q3 2026 earnings release and call transcript.

all.title: Mandate Continuity Under Adversarial Storefront Content: Does Verifiable Authorization Establish Faithful Execution in Autonomous Commerce?
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Autonomous shopping agents operate across a security boundary that conventional e-commerce did not have to manage in the same form: commercial content used to decide what to purchase may itself be controlled by parties whose interests differ from those of the user. MUZZLE: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Web Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks establishes indirect prompt injection as a concrete web-agent security problem, while Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) introduces explicit mechanisms for representing and verifying user authorization in agent-led commerce. This paper asks a narrower question: does possession of an authentic, integrity-protected purchasing mandate establish that an agent's eventual transaction remains faithfully derived from that mandate after the agent processes potentially adversarial external information? I introduce mandate continuity as a candidate security property and authority drift as a hypothesis to test, not an established attack category. The proposed failure condition occurs when an agent remains properly authorized to transact and a proposed purchase passes designated execution controls, yet independent evaluation finds that the purchase violates a constraint originating in the user's frozen mandate. A controlled experiment is proposed in which the user mandate and authoritative product facts remain fixed while designated merchant-controlled inputs vary. The experiment compares model-level controls, conventional transaction controls, verifiable-mandate controls, and independent mandate-continuity verification. It additionally treats digital-forensic observability as a prerequisite for causal attribution: transaction records may establish that a divergent action occurred, but attributing the divergence to adversarial storefront content requires evidence of what information actually entered the agent's observation state. Negative findings remain meaningful. Authority drift may prove empirically indistinguishable from existing prompt-injection, integrity, authorization, or evidence-corruption failures, or continuity verification may provide no measurable benefit beyond existing mandate mechanisms.

all.title: Antom 3-in-1 Transformer: A Payment Foundation Model
all.abstract: We report the development of Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, a payment foundation model that integrates sequence, tabular, and graph representations for payment risk detection. The model contains approximately 7B parameters, with approximately 1.7B activated per task route. Antom 3-in-1 Transformer is pretrained to learn reusable behavioral and relational representations, primarily on Ant International's internal payment data. In a cross-business transfer experiment, pretraining improves the target business metric by 34.5% over the same architecture trained from scratch. With only 25% of the training labels, the pretrained model outperforms the full-label scratch baseline in Average Precision (AP) and Recall@0.5% on different merchant domains. In a four-month online experiment on Ant International's billion-scale payment platform, the model reduced the overall loss rate by 37.88% relative to XGB-Online.

all.title: Large Payments Model
all.abstract: Payment applications such as fraud detection, authorization prediction, and payment optimization draw on overlapping transaction information. This motivates a reusable payments intelligence layer that shares learned representations and predictive signals, rather than developing predictive models independently for each task. Realizing this shared capability requires handling heterogeneous transaction fields, high-cardinality identifiers, lifecycle-dependent attributes, long histories, and rare outcomes while meeting latency and cost constraints. We present Large Payments Model (LPM), a domain-specific foundation model designed for operational use and trained from scratch on large-scale structured transaction data to learn reusable representations for payment prediction tasks. LPM employs field-specific encodings and lifecycle-aware self-supervision in two complementary architectures: the Independent variant uses hybrid masking and supports efficient per-transaction inference, while the Sequence variant incorporates entity-linked histories through compact latent representations for richer temporal context. Optional distillation enables resource-constrained deployment. We pretrain LPM on up to 400 billion tokens and study scaling, downstream performance, and representation reuse. LPM improves over strong task-specific baselines across multiple prediction tasks in Merchant and Treasury Services, demonstrating applicability in distinct payment domains. Its representations also facilitate adaptation to a target not observed during pretraining through compact task-specific components. Together with production deployment, these results position LPM as a practical basis for reusable payments intelligence.

all.title: PRACTICAL ANALYSIS OF BANK CUSTOMER BEHAVIOR AND SERVICE DELIVERY CHANNELS IN THE OPEN BANKING ENVIRONMENT
all.venue: International journal of technology and academic research
all.abstract: This article presents an applied and empirical analysis of changes in the behavior of commercial bank customers and in service delivery channels as the Open Banking ecosystem takes shape. The study assesses the shift from traditional bank channels to FinTech and open API platforms, customer preferences, and service efficiency indicators (transaction share, customer reach growth, operating cost, and customer satisfaction index) for 2024–2026. The findings show that the share of transactions made through Open API channels has reached 52%, and that serving customers through traditional branches costs more than 30 times as much as through open digital channels. The article identifies the main barriers (cybersecurity and trust, the digital literacy gap, and fragmented user experience) and develops strategic recommendations for banks: developing a hybrid omnichannel model, increasing the transparency of consent management, and personalized API monetization.

all.title: Research on the Application and Development of AI Intelligent Marketing in the Financial Services Industry
all.venue: Advances in economics, business and management research/Advances in Economics, Business and Management Research
institutions: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
all.abstract: The iterative advancement of digital intelligent technologies has propelled the financial services industry into a new phase of intelligent transformation. Traditional financial marketing faces industry challenges such as high customer acquisition costs, insufficient precision, service homogenization, delayed risk control, and weak user engagement, making it difficult to meet the personalized, scenario-based, and real-time financial demands of the new era. AI-powered intelligent marketing, leveraging core technologies like machine learning, large model algorithms, natural language processing, and user profiling modeling, reconstructs the entire financial marketing chain—including customer acquisition, outreach, conversion, retention, and risk control—becoming a pivotal tool for financial institutions to reduce costs, enhance efficiency, optimize customer experiences, and build differentiated competitive advantages. This paper systematically defines the core connotations and technical architecture of AI-powered financial intelligent marketing, reviews its current applications across six key scenarios: precise customer acquisition, personalized recommendations, intelligent content generation, omnichannel outreach, risk prevention and control, and customer operations. Through quantitative comparisons in tabular form, it contrasts the model differences and efficacy advantages between traditional financial marketing and AI-driven intelligent marketing. The study also conducts an in-depth analysis of core industry challenges, including data barriers, compliance risks, inadequate technical adaptation, and talent system gaps. Finally, it forecasts industry trends from five dimensions: technological iteration, scenario deepening, compliance development, talent cultivation, and ecosystem construction. The research aims to refine the theoretical framework of intelligent financial marketing and provide theoretical support and practical insights for the intelligent transformation of financial institutions such as commercial banks, insurance, and securities firms.

all.title: Customer relationship marketing and customer loyalty for inclusive and sustainable banking growth in Nigeria
all.venue: International Journal of Marketing Research Innovation
all.abstract: Competition, digital banking and rising customer expectations have made customer retention a central concern for Nigerian commercial banks, yet heavy spending on relationship programmes has not reduced complaints about service consistency and complaint handling, weakening the trust on which financial inclusion and sustainable growth depend. This study examines how customer relationship marketing dimensions, namely trust, commitment, communication, personalized services and customer engagement, influence customer satisfaction and customer loyalty and whether satisfaction mediates the link between relationship marketing and loyalty. A mixed-methods design was applied at the Jos branch of Access Bank Plc. Survey data from 277 customers were analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression, and interviews with 28 employees were analysed thematically. The results show that the five dimensions jointly explain 78.4% of the variance in customer satisfaction (F = 196.54, p < 0.001) and 81.1% of the variance in customer loyalty (F = 229.38, p < 0.001). Customer engagement is the strongest predictor of satisfaction (β = 0.392) and of loyalty (β = 0.341), followed by trust for satisfaction (β = 0.321) and personalized services for loyalty (β = 0.309). Satisfaction correlates strongly with loyalty (r = 0.918, p < 0.01), and the effect of relationship marketing on loyalty falls from 0.800 to 0.122 once satisfaction is controlled. Customers rated communication (mean = 4.00) and financial information security (mean = 3.88) higher than service consistency (mean = 3.72) and complaint handling (mean = 3.54). The findings suggest that relationship marketing builds loyalty mainly through satisfaction, with engagement, trust and personalized services carrying most of the effect. JEL Classification Codes: G21, M31, O16

all.title: Machine Learning-Based Customer Segmentation and Tailored Financial Advice in the Banking Sector
all.abstract: Customer segmentation in banking involves grouping customers into distinct segments who exhibit similar behaviors, such as transaction frequency, spending patterns, and savings habits. This enables banks to target their offerings more effectively. This study applied an unsupervised machine learning approach using the K-means clustering algorithm to segment customers. The analysis was based on secondary data comprising 100,000 customers. The silhouette score peaked at k = 3 with a score of 0.3232, but based on the Elbow method and aiming for a potentially more granular segmentation, k = 5 was chosen. The identified customer segments were: established female savers; recently active engagers (mostly male); low-balance, less-active males; core male customers; and a high-value, high-activity segment. To further refine the segmentation, RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) analysis was implemented to reveal customer behaviors within each cluster, resulting in more precise customer profiling. This dual-layer approach enables banks to develop personalized marketing strategies and improve customer relationship management.

all.title: Relationship Marketing and Third-Party Funds: The Mediating Role of Customer Engagement in Regional Banking
all.abstract: This study aims to examine the effectiveness of relationship marketing in increasing Third-Party Funds (TPF) by investigating the mediating roles of customer engagement and customer loyalty at Bank Jatim Tuban Branch. An explanatory sequential mixed methods design was employed. The quantitative phase involved a survey of 200 active customers analyzed using SEM-PLS, followed by in-depth interviews with customers and bank employees to explain and validate the quantitative findings. The results reveal that relationship marketing significantly enhances customer engagement and customer loyalty. However, only customer engagement has a significant positive effect on Third-Party Funds and serves as the primary mediating mechanism between relationship marketing and funding performance, whereas customer loyalty does not significantly influence Third-Party Funds. Qualitative findings further confirm that personalized communication, responsive services, and positive service experiences strengthen customer engagement, encouraging customers to increase their deposits. These findings imply that banks should prioritize customer engagement rather than relying solely on customer loyalty to improve funding performance.
