The study is limited to a single regional development bank, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings.

all.title: Service quality in Islamic banking: a cross-model meta-analysis of SERVQUAL, PAKSERV and CARTER models
all.abstract: Purpose This study aims to analyze the relationship between service quality (SQ) and customer satisfaction (CSAT) within the context of Islamic banking using a meta-analytical approach, as well as to assess the variation of effects based on different measurement models through group analysis. Design/methodology/approach This study integrates findings from multiple empirical studies using a multilevel random-effects meta-analytic model in JASP software, complemented by heterogeneity testing and subgroup analyses based on SQ measurement models and SQ dimensions. Findings The findings indicate that PAKSERV has the strongest influence, underscoring the dominant role of sincerity, personalization and formality within value-based Islamic service contexts; SERVQUAL demonstrates a moderate effect, while CARTER shows the weakest effect, suggesting that Shariah compliance is perceived as a basic expectation rather than a differentiating factor in shaping satisfaction. At the dimension level, sincerity showed the largest point estimate, followed by personalization and formality, while Shariah compliance showed the smallest estimate. Research limitations/implications This study is limited to Scopus-indexed publications, which may exclude relevant nonindexed or local studies and introduce potential publication bias. The analysis focuses solely on the direct relationship between SQ and CSAT, without incorporating mediating or moderating variables such as trust, perceived value, religiosity or digital service experience. Future research should integrate broader databases, apply cross-context validation and use more comprehensive analytical frameworks to capture the multidimensional nature of CSAT in Islamic banking. Practical implications Islamic banks should prioritize interpersonal service attributes, particularly sincerity, personalization and formality, as these dimensions show the strongest association with CSAT. Shariah compliance remains essential, but it functions more as a basic expectation than as the main driver of satisfaction. Therefore, Islamic banks should complement compliance with ethical, relational and culturally responsive service practices. These findings can guide frontline training, service standards and customer engagement strategies. Originality/value To the best of authors’ knowledge, this research is among the first meta-analytic studies to systematically compare SQ measurement models within the Islamic banking context. It offers practical, evidence-based insights for Islamic banks in shaping CSAT and evaluating Shariah-compliant SQ.

all.title: Smooth Subband Entropy and Time-Domain Feature Fusion for Personalized Lower-Limb Movement Recognition
institutions: Nanjing University of Science and Technology
National Key Laboratory of Transient Physics
Southern University of Science and Technology
all.abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) supports personalized movement recognition, but feature utility must be interpreted together with preprocessing conditions. We evaluated a task-specific integration of a smooth fast Fourier transform (FFT) subband bank, nearest-neighbor entropy (NNE), time-domain (TD) descriptors, and participant-specific extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). Nine-channel recordings from 40 Shenzhen Institute of Advanced Technology Lower Limb Motion Dataset (SIAT-LLMD) participants were evaluated for 16-class recognition using repetition-grouped five-fold cross-validation. Under complete-record amplitude normalization, the 216-dimensional fusion achieved 95.63% accuracy and 94.54% macro-F1, exceeding TD-XGB by 1.043 percentage points; random and repeated-feature expansion did not reproduce this gain. With the classifier configurations held fixed, macro-F1 was 94.85% with record-specific references fitted to all eligible samples, 95.58% with record-specific training-only references, and 75.31% with shared participant-level training references. The record-specific controls require movement-associated recording identity and do not establish prospective unknown-action performance. This gain was accompanied by median single-thread CPU computation of 34.210 ms per conditioned window for Fusion-XGB, compared with 5.392 ms for TD-XGB (approximately sixfold). Across the evaluated amplitude-reference conditions, Fusion-XGB retained a macro-F1 improvement over TD-XGB, while absolute recognition performance varied with the reference definition.

all.title: Digital Banking Service Excellence and Its Impact on Customer Satisfaction and Customer Retention: A Structural Equation Modeling Approach
all.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
all.abstract: With the increasing number of digital banking platforms, how to deliver financial services has changed completely, requiring a greater understanding of service excellence and its effect on customer behavioral outcomes. This study aims to explore the impact of Digital Banking Service Excellence on customer satisfaction and customer retention in technology-based banking environment. Service excellence is manifested in several aspects such as, system reliability, information security and privacy, ease of use of the interface, responsiveness of the service, service personalization and service accessibility. The study also explores the mediation between S.E., C.S. and C.R. The approach used in the study is quantitative using a structured questionnaire with a five-point Likert scale and sample of active users of digital banking. The proposed conceptual framework is tested empirically using advanced statistical and machine learning-supported analytical techniques, such as Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) for dimensional validation, Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) for construct validation and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) for hypothesis testing and relationship assessment. Further, the reliability and validity are checked by Cronbach's alpha, Average Variance Extracted (AVE) and Composite Reliability (CR). The findings that are expected are that the level of service excellence provided by digital banking has a positive impact on the customer satisfaction, and in turn, the retention behaviour. Furthermore, it is expected that service excellence has both direct and indirect effects on customer retention via customer satisfaction. The study adds to the service quality and digital banking literature by bringing together the multidimensional constructs of service excellence so that they can be modeled together in one behavioral model. The results offer practical guidance for financial institutions to maximize delivery of digital services, enhance trust amongst users and facilitate the long term retention of users within a digital financial ecosystem.

all.title: Price and Non-price Instruments of Commercial Banks’ Deposit Policy with Regard to Individuals
all.abstract: Introduction. The purpose of the study is to identify specific impact of the Bank of Russia’s key rate and non-price factors on deposit rates for individuals of varying maturities — in the context of alternating macroeconomic stability and exogenous shocks — in order to clarify the mechanisms of price and non-price transmission and their subsequent use in forecasting the dynamics of deposit rates. Methods. The period under study for interest rates (2014–2025) is segmented into intervals defined by the boundaries of exogenous shocks, which were identified using statistical methods and expert evaluation. For each interval, a regression analysis was conducted, distinguishing between price-based and non-pricebased components of influence. Results. During crisis periods, the price factor exerted a dominant influence — particularly within the segment of short- and medium-term deposits — ensuring that changes in the key policy rate were rapidly transmitted to the deposit market. In more stable phases, the role of non-price factors — such as loyalty programs, digital services, personalized offers, and branding — grew in importance. Long-term deposits showed the lowest sensitivity to the key rate, with their dynamics being largely shaped by non-financial incentives. Overall, the role of non-price factors is growing, which enhances the significance of the non-price component within the product policy of commercial banks. Conclusion. The proposed methodology allows for the classification of periods based on the dominance of price and non-price factors, thereby improving the accuracy of interest rate forecasting and the effectiveness of scenario analysis. These results are of practical value to the Bank of Russia, commercial banks, investors, and regulators; they also hold theoretical significance as an example of integrating macroeconomic shocks into an econometric analysis of the deposit market.

all.title: Privacy-Preserving AI in Finance: Federated Learning, Secure Computation, and GDPR Compliance for Fraud Detection and Credit Scoring
all.abstract: Financial institutions need large datasets to build AI systems, yet they must protect sensitive customer information under regimes such as the GDPR. This review examines how federated learning, secure multi-party computation, homomorphic encryption, and differential privacy support privacy-preserving AI in financial services. It covers the principles of data sovereignty, federated architectures for enterprise systems, and applications in cross-institutional collaboration, fraud detection, credit scoring, and personalized banking. It also discusses regulatory compliance, auditability, adversarial robustness, and cyber resilience. The literature indicates that these techniques help institutions meet data minimization requirements, reduce legal risk, and collaborate across borders. Trade-offs remain in computational overhead, latency, non-IID data, and model bias. Future work should focus on standardized protocols, hybrid privacy models, and auditing frameworks.

all.title: Al Powered Personal Finance Tracker with Behavioral Analytics
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: Managing personal finances has grown ever more complicated especially as we witness the explosion of digital payments, online banking, e-commerce platforms and new consumer behaviors. Financial management systems have traditionally been very focused on recording financial transactions and keeping track of expenses without much help for users to understand their financial characteristics or get advice on how to spend their money wisely. This paper introduces the idea of developing an AI-Powered Personal Finance Tracker with Behavioral Analysis which is a smart and personalized way of dealing with financial transactions. The solution is a combination of the finance data manager with user behavior analytics, machine learning-generated finance reports, personalized suggestions, investment and stock advice, multi-person family financial planning, and monitoring in one single platform. Users can be allowed to provide bank account details via bank API in such a secure way so that the financial information is being accessed by only those users with a valid bank account and user permission. Behavioral analytics is able to detect the spending habits and financial habits of the users to generate the income, expenditure, and saving trends. Firebase Cloud Fire store database has been chosen by us as a very real-time, synchronized, and secure database. In addition, the system will implement Firebase authentication as only the authentic and verified users will be allowed to log in to a specified account. By making use of predictive analysis and customized advice, this innovative system will enable individuals to understand their personal money matters more thoroughly and ultimately, to make financially wise choices.

all.title: Individual Investment Account to Stimulate Long-Term Household Investments
all.abstract: Encouraging long-term household savings is a key objective in the development of the financial market. The relevance of the study is driven by the transformation of the individual investment account (IIS) mechanism and the introduction of IIS‑3 type in 2024. The subject of the study is the IIS as a tool for long-term household investment. The aim is to assess the stimulating potential of different types of IIS for the long-term investment of household savings. The specific objectives include identifying regulatory features, evaluating the returns provided by the IIS tax incentive, and identifying associated risks. The novelty lies in a comprehensive mathematical assessment of the effectiveness of IIS‑3 compared to its previous versions and bank deposits within current macroeconomic conditions. The study employs financial modeling of cash flows and sensitivity analysis. The results demonstrate the attractiveness of Type A IIS and IIS‑3 compared to Type B IIS. It has been established that, despite a negative yield spread between Individual Investment Accounts (IIAs) and bank deposits — a result of the Central Bank of Russia’s tight monetary policy — IIAs remain attractive due to their guaranteed tax benefits. The primary risks associated with this instrument are operational and price-related. The practical significance lies in the fact that the sensitivity analysis provides investors with the insights needed to develop personalized investment strategies. It is concluded that the IIA‑3 retains significant incentive potential, and growing interest in it is anticipated. The success of this instrument’s development depends on enhancing the financial literacy of the general population.

all.title: Improved K-Means-Based Learner Profiling and Adaptive Learning Intervention for College English Education
all.venue: Frontiers in artificial intelligence and applications
all.abstract: College English education increasingly relies on data-driven approaches to understand learner differences and provide personalized instructional support. However, existing adaptive learning strategies often fail to fully characterize heterogeneous learning behaviors, resulting in limited precision in learner profiling and intervention design. To address this issue, this paper proposes an improved K-Means-based learner profiling and adaptive learning intervention framework for College English education. First, ten multidimensional indicators are constructed from formative assessment records and Unit Test 1, including writing performance, practice accuracy, learning duration, learning progress, long conversation, passage listening, vocabulary, banked cloze, reading comprehension, and translation. Then, an improved K-Means clustering algorithm is employed to construct learner profiles by optimizing centroid initialization and incorporating feature weighting to enhance clustering stability and interpretability. Based on the clustering results, learners are categorized into different behavioral groups, such as highly active learners, performance-oriented learners, low-engagement learners, and learners requiring targeted support. Furthermore, differentiated adaptive intervention strategies are designed for each learner group, including personalized resource recommendation, learning task adjustment, feedback enhancement, and early academic risk warning. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively distinguish learner behavior patterns and provide reliable support for personalized College English instruction. Compared with conventional K-Means clustering, the improved method achieves better clustering performance and supports more accurate adaptive intervention. The proposed framework provides a practical reference for integrating machine learning, learning analytics, and intelligent instructional design in college English education.

all.title: Doc-to-LoRA Analysis: Query Conditioning, Wrong Facts, and Distractor Interference
all.abstract: Doc-to-LoRA (D2L) compiles documents into low-rank adapters, allowing language models to use their contents without repeatedly processing the original text. We investigate its suitability for internalizing user memories through factual question answering, controlled interventions, and a production MidBrain memory pipeline. Across Gemma-2-2B and Qwen3-4B, D2L loses accuracy relative to in-context learning, with additional documents introducing substantial interference. Single-document errors frequently match answers to other questions about the same passage, suggesting unreliable question-answer attribution. Layer-wise interventions show that interference accumulates across depth, with more concentrated early damage at larger bank sizes on Gemma. With eight documents, applying the full bank in the initial layers gives similar accuracy to withholding all document contributions there. Source membership is detectable in intermediate states, but trained readers do not reliably resolve the interference. On PersonaMem-v2, joint compilation and normalized adapter composition achieve accuracy close to consolidated text memory when retrieved episodes remain text, but the resulting token savings are modest. Measured throughput gains also depend on model and batch size despite substantial reductions in analytical compute. Together, these findings limit the practical case for D2L as a replacement for text-based memory and motivate investigating online-learning methods that acquire personalized behavior from interactions in which memory is used.

all.title: Geese with Golden Omelets
all.abstract: This chapter examines the complexities and potential of the Insight Economy, where data sharing for mutual benefit is essential yet often hindered by adversarial mindsets, misaligned incentives, and technological limitations. It argues that economic principles, not altruism, should govern data transactions, with direct, transparent exchanges benefiting both parties. Legal constraints, particularly around health data, and societal transformations impact data usage, but consumers are increasingly willing to share data for better services. The chapter highlights the paradox of Big Data, where overestimating predictive power and misidentifying privacy issues as greed or technocracy obscure the true costs of data handling. Value lies in the relational activation of data, with insights generated at the source, driving immediate mutual value and economic benefits. However, human identity is complex, and digital transformation risks eroding personal relationships. Asymmetric information in industries like banking and travel leads to missed opportunities, but insight algorithms can bridge gaps, driving personalization and market orientation. The perishability of insights discourages data hoarding, and AI's efficiency benefits local data models. The chapter advocates for decoupling data wallets from warehouses, reimagining data technology to focus on context and insights, not raw data, to restore market forces and ensure efficient, compliant transactions.

all.title: Enhancing Customer Experience Through Intelligent Financial and Travel Service Platforms
all.abstract: Customer experience within economy sectors such as financial services (FS) and travel and hospitality (TH) is often studied separately. FS firms have been investing significantly to improve customer experience through innovations in payment methods, risk management tools, and financial wellness tools, yet more than half of their customers indicate that they are not fully satisfied. Similarly, TH firms have also been investing in several customer experience-related innovations in their services, such as dynamic pricing, personalization, loyalty programs, and extended travel-as-a-service offerings, but customer satisfaction for many of them has remained unimproved. However, people tend to use services offered by both industries at roughly the same time. For someone who needs to make payments during travel, travel insurance and credit card options are two of the most popular FS products. Offering new FS and TH services independently and in silos can help create better customer experiences, and integrating the financial and travel service facilities offered by different providers can provide seamless interconnectivity among their offerings. Thus, the first research question emerges: How can the customer experience within economy sectors such as FS and TH be enhanced when a service platform integrates a group of intelligent services from different industries? Ignoring integration and interconnectivity from different industries can result in customers taking considerable time to search for, prepare for, and pay for these services in advance. Innovative intelligent tools can predict customers’ future needs before the trip starts and can act before it starts or during the trip. Comprehensive customer journey mapping along with information quality factors, such as completeness, relevance, accuracy, currency, and variety, can help design the FS and TH platforms with enhanced prediction and proactive capabilities. The next research question is, How can the customer experience be improved when the TH and FS platforms are connected in an intelligent manner, including adequate and comprehensive prediction and proactive mechanisms based on the customer journey mapping process? Evidence-based insights regarding both questions contribute to the body of knowledge related to customer experience analysis, design, and enhancement using intelligent innovation on an integrated FS and TH platform.

all.title: The Role of Local Microbiological Monitoring and Phage Therapy in Counteracting Antimicrobial Resistance: An Analytical Review
institutions: Ministry of Health of the Russian Federation
Regional Public Health Care Institution "City Hospital No. 5, Barnaul"
all.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major medical and social threat since it reduces the clinical eﬀectiveness of antimicrobial therapy, increases the risk of poor infectious disease outcomes, and requires coordinated action at the levels of health policy, laboratory services, and clinical practice. The aim of this review was to consider AMR control as an integrated system combining national policy, local microbiological monitoring, antimicrobial stewardship, and emerging anti-infective technologies, including phage therapy. A narrative analytical review of international and Russian guidelines, methodological papers, and scientiﬁc publications addressing AMR surveillance, local susceptibility data, cumulative antibiograms, clinically oriented monitoring, and bacteriophage-based treatment of infections caused by resistant Gram-negative pathogens was performed. The clinical value of local monitoring is determined not only by the volume of laboratory data but also by the quality of metadata, separation of diagnostic and screening isolates, deduplication of repeated cultures, expert assessment of results, as well as direct linkage between reports and local empirical treatment protocols. Phage therapy is considered a promising personalized and adjunctive approach for infections caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii, particularly when standard antibacterial therapy has limited eﬀectiveness. However, its broader implementation requires standardization of phage susceptibility testing, development of phage banks, regulatory solutions, quality control of preparations, and assessment of clinical eﬃcacy in controlled studies. Integration of epidemiological surveillance, clinical microbiology, digital platforms, antimicrobial stewardship, and phage technologies may be considered a promising model for AMR containment in routine clinical practice.

all.title: Modern tools for assessing quality of life in patients with cardiovascular diseases: clinical significance and application opportunities. A review
all.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain among the leading causes of disability and mortality. Their clinical significance is defined not only by the risk of adverse outcomes but also by their considerable impact on daily activities, emotional well-being, functional status, and subjective well-being. Quality of life is increasingly recognized as an independent, patient-centered outcome and a critical component of personalized management for individuals with CVD. This literature review organizes current tools for assessing quality of life in patients with CVDs and evaluates their clinical significance, psychometric properties, and applicability in clinical practice. The review draws on publications from PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, Google Scholar, and eLIBRARY, as well as documents from specialized organizations and questionnaire developers. The review primarily emphasizes studies published between 2020 and 2026, citing earlier work for the development and validation of specific instruments. General questionnaires applicable across disease categories are reviewed, including WHOQOL, WHOQOL-BREF, EQ-5D-3L/5L, SF-36 and its brief forms, as well as contemporary digital approaches utilizing question banks and computer-adaptive testing, particularly PROMIS. Disease-specific instruments addressing the unique features of individual clinical syndromes are also examined: Seattle Angina Questionnaire and SAQ-7 for coronary artery disease and angina pectoris, MacNew and HeartQoL for various forms of coronary artery disease, Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire for chronic heart failure, AFEQT for atrial fibrillation, CIVIQ-14 and VEINES-QOL/Sym for chronic venous diseases, and emPHasis-10 for pulmonary hypertension. The findings indicate that instrument selection should be determined by the assessment objective, clinical disease form, follow-up requirements, availability of a validated Russian-language version, sensitivity to clinically meaningful changes, and potential for use in research, medical rehabilitation, and health economic analysis. Incorporating validated questionnaires into cardiology practice expands assessment of treatment efficacy, improves communication between clinicians and patients, enhances adherence to therapy, and supports individualized management of patients with CVDs.

all.title: Competition in capital markets and its contribution to growth and innovation
all.venue: OECD competition law and policy working papers.
all.abstract: Financing conditions influence whether innovative firms can enter, expand and constrain established suppliers. Competition in capital markets can therefore affect innovation and productivity across the economy, as well as conditions in financial markets. This paper examines competition in equity investment in unlisted innovative firms, focussing on independent venture capital, corporate venture capital, private equity and equity crowdfunding. Bank finance, public equity markets, market infrastructure and intermediary services are covered where they offer workable alternatives or affect private financing or exit options. The paper assesses whether firms have credible alternatives that constrain capital providers on financial, governance and strategic terms, and how choice changes over the financing lifecycle. It distinguishes financing constraints arising from the risks of innovation from restrictions on competition among providers and intermediaries. It examines how later stage finance and exit conditions affect bargaining, investment incentives and the merger counterfactual. It considers how barriers to entry and expansion, anticompetitive conduct and mergers may restrict firms’ financing or exit options, including through investors’ ownership and contractual rights. Finally, it discusses how competition enforcement and advocacy, pro-competitive financial regulation, and co-operation between competition and financial authorities can address these risks while preserving investor protection and financial stability.

all.title: Intelligent Decision Automation for Saudi Government and Banking Services under Vision 2030: Integrating Robotic Process Automation, Business Process Management, and Human-in-the-Loop Decision Governance
all.abstract: Intelligent decision automation promises faster Saudi public and banking services, yet automating a task is not equivalent to governing a decision. This critical integrative review examines how robotic process automation, business process management and human oversight can be combined without weakening procedural fairness, operational resilience or accountability. Thirty peer reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025 are synthesised alongside the institutional context of Vision 2030, including digital government, regulated finance and electricity related service workflows. The analysis differentiates interface automation from process orchestration and consequential decision authority, and develops an original layered governance architecture with risk dependent human intervention, traceable rules and continuous process assurance. Applications considered include public licences, customer onboarding, banking exceptions, electricity connections, billing disputes and outage compensation. The review finds that automation benefits depend on prior process simplification, dependable data, documented decision rights and meaningful rather than symbolic human review. Machine predictions can inform routing and anomaly detection, but do not by themselves establish entitlement, legal compliance or equitable treatment. A proposed evaluation scorecard integrates throughput, accuracy, appeal outcomes, accessibility, cyber resilience and auditability rather than relying on labour savings alone. The paper identifies research gaps concerning Arabic language service design, cross agency interoperability, automation bias, electricity sector dependencies and longitudinal evidence in Saudi institutions. It proposes staged implementation and independent evaluation rather than claiming demonstrated national performance gains. The contribution is a context sensitive decision governance model that distinguishes technical execution, institutional responsibility and contestable public or financial outcomes.

all.title: Digital skills are no longer optional in the Asia Pacific
all.abstract: Listen to this article A 2026 Asian Development Bank study analysed six million online job postings from Indeed across Australia, India, South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore between 2019 and 2024. The study found that demand for digital skills is growing fastest in jobs long considered low-technology occupations, such as teaching, construction, retail and […]

all.title: MANAGEMENT MODEL FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF REGIONAL HUMAN CAPITAL AND DIGITAL SKILLS
all.abstract: This article proposes a management model for developing human capital and digital skills at the regional level. The model integrates a five-block indicator framework, a composite Regional Digital Human Capital Index (RDHCI), and a monitoring cycle linked to managerial decision-making. A review of international and national evidence identifies four areas requiring further improvement: fragmented measurement across education, labour, and digital agencies; national indices that do not fully reflect regional disparities; opportunities to strengthen alignment between training provision and local labour market demand; and the need to establish a clear link between measurement results and managerial action. Drawing on verified benchmarks (the World Bank Human Capital Index of 0.62 in 2020, the Human Capital Index Plus score of 170 out of 325, and the increase in Uzbekistan's UN E-Government Development Index from 0.6665 in 2020 to 0.7999 in 2024), the study establishes four design requirements and specifies the model's indicators, data sources, normalization procedure, weighting scheme, and managerial decision matrix. The index is calculated using min–max normalization and a weighted geometric mean, thereby maintaining a weakest-link approach.

all.title: DATA LITERACY CRÍTICA NA CIÊNCIA DA INFORMAÇÃO: PERSPECTIVA FREIREANA
all.abstract: Today’s vast amounts of data can impact various areas of society in different ways. Information Science programs that focus solely on the technical aspects of data processing may neglect the context surrounding the data, which is important for fostering critical thinking. This article aims to discuss how interpreting the world precedes interpreting data and how Information Science can benefit from Paulo Freire’s problem-posing pedagogy. A bibliographic research was adopted as the methodology, employing an exploratory and qualitative approach. An equivalence was found between the “banking education” identified by Paulo Freire and technical approaches to Data Literacy. Also, the importance of liberating education for the development of Data Literacy was observed, which can aid in the subject’s emancipation through the dimensions of dialogue, problematization, and conscientization. The study considers that Information Science can serve as a field of critical mediation between data, the individual, and the use of technologies, focusing on the training of critical professionals. This research aims to contribute to discussions on Data Literacy in the curricula of undergraduate programs in Information Science.

all.title: ACCOUNTING INFORMATION SYSTEM QUALITY AND EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE IN NIGERIAN COMMERCIAL BANKS: DIGITAL LITERACY, DECENT WORK AND INNOVATION
all.venue: International Journal of Accounting & Finance Review
all.abstract: Commercial banks depend on accounting information systems (AIS) to process transactions and sustain decent work, yet which system attributes improve bank employees' performance, and under what conditions, remains unsettled outside large urban centres. This study examines the effect of system quality, information quality, service quality, data quality and top management support on employee performance in commercial banks in Bauchi State, Nigeria, and whether employee digital literacy moderates the effects of data quality and service quality. The study employs survey data from 139 valid responses out of 192 employees with direct access to the ICT infrastructure of ten commercial banks, analysed with multiple regression and PROCESS Model 1 (5,000 bootstrap resamples). The results show that the five dimensions jointly explain 55.4% of the variation in employee performance (R = 0.744; F = 33.070; p < 0.001). System quality (β = 0.292; p = 0.010) and information quality (β = 0.265; p = 0.015) have positive and significant effects, whereas data quality (β = 0.144; p = 0.110), service quality (β = 0.030; p = 0.778) and top management support (β = 0.100; p = 0.293) are insignificant. Digital literacy significantly strengthens the effects of data quality (β = 0.182; p = 0.013) and service quality (β = 0.156; p = 0.037). The findings suggest that reliable systems and high-quality information are the core AIS drivers of employee performance. At the same time, the benefits of data and support quality depend on employees' digital skills, linking innovation, infrastru

all.title: Replication package for "Digital Skills, Unequal Market Participation: Explaining Cross-Country Differences in E-Commerce and Online Payment Activity in Germany and Russia"
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This study examines the relationship between operational digital capability and online participation in Germany and Russia using harmonised individual-level data from the EBRD Life in Transition Survey IV (LiTS IV). It distinguishes two outcome domains: online buying and selling, and payment-related activities, including sending or receiving payments and mobile banking. The analysis applies weighted logistic regression estimated through Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE), with robust standard errors clustered by primary sampling unit. The findings show that higher digital capability is positively associated with participation in both domains, while cross-country differences vary by outcome. The study contributes to research on digital inequality and electronic commerce by demonstrating the importance of distinguishing between different forms of online participation. The supplementary materials provide supporting research documentation and analytical materials.

all.title: Does Innovative Work Behavior Mediate the Relationship Between Dynamic Capability and Job Performance? Evidence from the Ethiopian Banking Sector
all.abstract: Employees’ dynamic capability (DC) is increasingly treated as a micro-foundation of organizational adaptation, yet little is known about how it translates into job performance (JP) in developing-country financial markets. This study tests whether innovative work behavior (IWB) mediates the effect of DC on JP among Ethiopian bank employees. Anchored in dynamic capability, social exchange, and self-determination theories, a cross-sectional survey was administered to permanent head-office employees of two large private commercial banks (Awash Bank S.C. and Dashen Bank S.C.). Bank-specific samples were drawn by random sampling using Yamane’s (1967) formula (450 targeted); 420 usable questionnaires (93.3%) were analyzed with PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4.0. DC positively predicted IWB (β = 0.445) and JP (β = 0.384), and IWB predicted JP (β = 0.360). IWB complemented and partially mediated the DC–JP relationship (indirect β = 0.160, 95% CI [0.118, 0.211]), carrying about 29% of the total effect; the model explained 19.8% of the variance in IWB and 40.1% in JP. Banks should build both pathways: structured cross-functional rotations and continuous digital-skill assessment to develop DC, and idea-to-pilot innovation laboratories, risk-tolerant appraisal criteria, and recognition systems to convert capability into innovation. Generalization is limited to head-office staff of large private banks. The study provides micro-foundational evidence on employee-level DC from an African regulated banking market.

all.title: A Methodological Framework for Developing a Managerial Decision-Making Instrument to Evaluate E-Banking Success: Integrating TAM, UTAUT and E-SERVQUAL
all.venue: Interdisciplinary Journal of Research and Development
all.abstract: The rapid digitalization of banking services has increased the strategic importance of e-banking, particularly in developing and transition economies. While existing research has extensively examined customer satisfaction and technology adoption, most studies rely on fragmented theoretical models and provide limited methodological support for evaluating e-banking success from a managerial perspective. The primary contribution of this paper is theoretical and methodological. It develops an integrated methodology for studying and evaluating e-banking success by proposing a comprehensive decision-making instrument that combines the core constructs of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), and E-SERVQUAL into a unified conceptual framework. The proposed methodology conceptualizes e-banking success as the combined effect of three interrelated dimensions: bank-related factors, environmental and institutional conditions, and consumer-related characteristics, while accounting for the moderating influence of demographic variables. These dimensions are operationalized through a structured measurement instrument designed to assess service quality, security, digital infrastructure, regulatory support, digital skills, customer attitudes, and perceptions of usefulness. E-banking success is measured through customer satisfaction, continued usage intention, recommendation, and perceived value. Using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), the proposed methodology enables the simultaneous assessment of latent constructs and their causal relationships, providing a rigorous framework for both academic research and managerial evaluation. Unlike previous studies that focus primarily on empirical testing of individual adoption models, this paper contributes a methodological framework that can be used as a theoretical basis for future empirical research and as a practical instrument for evaluating and improving e-banking success in developing and transition economies. Received: 12 April 2026 │ Accepted: 30 October 2026 │ Published: 20 November 2026

all.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Public Acceptance of AI Technologies among Adults in Iraq
all.abstract: This study investigated the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies among adults in Iraq. The role of AI in public services, healthcare, education, banking, and digital communication is growing, making it a key sociological and policy issue to understand what factors affect citizens' acceptance of AI. A quantitative cross sectional survey design was used and data were gathered from 420 adults living in Iraq. Artificial Intelligence literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies were measured by a structured questionnaire with a five-point Likert scale. The data were analysed by descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, exploratory factor analysis, Pearson correlation and regression analysis using IBM SPSS Statistics software. The results showed that the participants had a moderate to high level of AI literacy and moderate levels of public acceptance of AI technologies. The Pearson correlation analysis showed that there was a statistically significant positive correlation between the concepts of artificial intelligence literacy and public acceptance. The regression analysis also revealed that AI literacy was a significant predictor of public acceptance, accounting for 32.0% of the variance, and multiple regression analysis indicated that AI literacy is the most significant predictor, even after controlling for demographic and technology-related characteristics. The study is a significant contribution to the sociology of artificial intelligence, as it illustrates how AI literacy is a crucial social resource that influences citizens' receptivity to new technologies. The results highlight the need to encourage AI literacy initiatives to foster informed public acceptance and facilitate responsible digital transformation in Iraq.

all.title: Cognitive Asymmetry and Governance of Financial Data in Morocco: Institutionalizing Open Science to Safeguard Development Policy Autonomy
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This working paper examines the impact of cognitive asymmetry in financial data on the capacity of Moroccan national actors to design and evaluate autonomous development policies. Built on an institutional sociology and political economy framework, the study argues that limited local data transparency—compared to the epistemic authority of international financial institutions such as the IMF and the World Bank—generates knowledge dependency that constrains national policy space. By analyzing three levels of institutional dynamics (international, executive, and legislative), the paper highlights internal disparities between Bank Al-Maghrib’s statistical regularity and the executive constraints limiting raw data disclosure within the Ministry of Economy and Finance, alongside weak data literacy within Parliament. The study concludes that institutionalizing Open Science is not merely a technical reform, but a sovereign mechanism essential for reinforcing knowledge justice, democratic oversight, and developmental autonomy in Morocco. Keywords: Open Science; Financial Data Governance; Cognitive Asymmetry; Policy Autonomy; Knowledge Justice; Morocco.

all.title: Digital Technology and Gender-Differentiated Labour-Market Outcomes in the Mashreq
all.abstract: Technological change has often widened or preserved gender gaps in labour-market outcomes in favour of men. We examine whether digital capabilities are more strongly associated with women’s employment and earnings in low-female-employment settings. We analyse novel microdata from the World Bank’s 2023 Digital Gender Gap and Economic Opportunities Survey of 4,592 individuals in Iraq, Jordan, and Lebanon. In the pooled sample, self-assessed digital skills are positively associated with women’s employment. The association is more positive for women than for men across models, weights, and index constructions. With employment-calibrated weights, this gender difference is 6.1 percentage points per standard deviation of digital skills. Among workers reporting positive earnings in the combined administration, education, and health or social work group, a one-standard-deviation increase in skills is associated with approximately 13.7 per cent higher earnings for women, versus a negative but imprecise association for men. The gender difference is statistically significant in the primary analysis; the weighted estimate is similar, but the evidence is weaker. Complementary analyses show more positive skills associations for women in productive internet use and, under calibration, online safety. These cross-sectional findings identify digital skills as an important correlate of gender differences in employment and selected-earner earnings in the Mashreq.

all.title: Digital fluency and youth unemployment: a cross-national analysis of the moderating role of formal mentorship
Digital Infrastructure and Technology Diffusion: Building the Digital Foundations of Sustainable Economic Convergence in the Global South
all.abstract: A 30-page hybrid research report and academic paper (HH-2026-97) from H Heuristics' Global Outlook Optimization Series examining how digital infrastructure, technological adoption, and knowledge diffusion accelerate economic development, productivity growth, and long-term economic convergence across emerging and developing economies between 2027 and 2036. Covers affordable broadband, mobile internet, cloud computing, Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), applied AI diffusion, digital financial services, e-commerce, digital skills, technology transfer, physical-digital complementarity, and Polycrisis Resilience.

all.title: Examination of the nexus between Inclusive Growth, Financial Technology, and Poverty in Mauritius
all.venue: E-Journal of Humanities Arts and Social Sciences
all.abstract: This study thoroughly explored the complex triangle between inclusive growth, financial technology (FinTech), and poverty alleviation in Mauritius at a deeper level. It used a mixed-methods research design, a combination of qualitative and quantitative data. The research investigated the ways that FinTech innovations like mobile banking, digital payment systems, and peer-to-peer lending platforms help to expand financial inclusion and give power to marginalised groups. The results show that FinTech plays a vital role in providing cheaper financial services, unleashing entrepreneurship, and making the economy more efficient, thus leading to inclusive growth. However, the gains are not evenly shared amongst the different segments of the population. People living in remote areas, seniors, and those with low digital literacy are the most negatively affected since a lack of digital infrastructure and regulatory complexities are among the barriers they face. The article is a real eye-opener as to the crucial role that well-designed policy measures and capacity-building programs must play if these hurdles are to be overcome successfully. The policy suggestions revolve around equipping citizens with digital skills, enhancing regulatory frameworks, encouraging public-private partnerships, and adapting FinTech offerings to the local conditions of the socio-economic environment. Thus, the government of Mauritius can fully tap into the potential of FinTech as a powerful tool for poverty reduction sustainably and equitably. The study not only deepens the debate on technology-led inclusive economic growth in small island developing states but also stands as a manual with useful directions for stakeholders, policymakers, and practitioners involved in financial inclusion projects.

all.title: Economic Prospects of Georgia, DCFTA Obligations, and Labour Market Restructuring
all.abstract: This academic paper examines the theoretical foundations, structural challenges, and synergistic effects of digital transformation and European economic integration in developing economies, with a specific focus on Georgia. Drawing upon the World Bank’s "Digital Dividends" framework and the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) digital diffusion models, the study analyzes global digital asymmetry and Georgia’s transitional trajectory from basic digital adoption toward an advanced platform-based economy. Particular emphasis is placed on the implementation of regulatory commitments under the EU-Georgia Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area (DCFTA)—specifically harmonization with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), electronic identification and trust services (eIDAS), and cybersecurity standards (NIS2)—alongside the geo-economic significance of the EU Global Gateway initiative and the Black Sea submarine fiber-optic cable project. The research demonstrates that adopting a technological "leapfrogging" model, fostering remote online employment, digital freelancing, and cross-border e-commerce provide viable mechanisms for reducing structural unemployment, mitigating brain drain, and expanding high-value-added service exports. Finally, the paper outlines a three-pillar strategic roadmap centered on universal regional broadband connectivity, micro-credential-based workforce reskilling, and full institutional alignment with the European Union’s Digital Single Market.

all.title: Investment in Education As A Critical Factor in Realizing One-Trillion-Dollar Economy in Nigeria by 2030
all.abstract: Education is widely recognised as a major driver of human capital development, productivity, innovation and sustainable economic growth. Nigeria’s ambition to achieve a one-trillion-dollar economy by 2030 requires substantial improvements in the productive capacity of its population, diversification of the economy, technological advancement and the creation of employment opportunities. This paper examines investment in education as a critical factor in realising this economic ambition. It discusses the contribution of education to workforce development, technological innovation, entrepreneurship, poverty reduction, economic diversification, global competitiveness and effective governance. The paper adopts a conceptual review approach, drawing on relevant policy documents and reports from UNESCO, the World Bank and Nigerian government institutions. The discussion highlights the need for increased and more effective educational financing, improved teaching and learning facilities, strengthened technical and vocational education, digital skills development, research and innovation, and stronger partnerships between educational institutions and industry. It also emphasises that educational investment must be accompanied by effective governance, reliable infrastructure, economic stability and a favourable business environment. The paper concludes that although education alone cannot guarantee the achievement of Nigeria’s one-trillion-dollar economic target, sustained investment in quality, relevant and inclusive education is essential for building the skilled and productive workforce required to support economic transformation by 2030.

all.title: Self-Perceived Academic Artificial Intelligence Overreliance Associated with Academic Performance Among Nursing Students in a Resource-Limited Setting: A Multicentre, Cross- Sectional—Correlational Study
all.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is embedded in nursing students' routines, yet academic AI overreliance is rarely quantified, especially in resource-limited settings. Objective To examine the relationship between self-perceived academic AI overreliance and academic performance among nursing students in the West Bank, Palestine. Methods A multicentre, cross-sectional correlational study was conducted with 1213 second- to fourth-year nursing students from 11 Palestinian universities who completed the 22-item Academic AI Overreliance Scale (AAIO) and the 8-item Academic Performance Scale (AP). The relationship between self-perceived academic AI overreliance and academic performance was estimated using hierarchical regression analysis, with sociodemographic and academic characteristics being entered in the first step, and academic AI overreliance being added in the second step. Results The mean age of participants was 21.79 years (SD = 1.09; range 20–25 years), and 676 of them (55.7%) were female. The self-perceived academic AI overreliance in the study was moderate (mean = 2.42, SD = 0.49). Higher self-perceived academic AI overreliance was associated with higher self-reported academic performance (r = 0.34, p < 0.001); this self-perceived academic AI overreliance was the associated factor (β = 0.35, p < 0.001). Conclusions Self-perceived academic AI overreliance was common yet moderate; its positive association with academic performance underscores the need to shape AI engagement and safeguard unassisted learning. The findings give nurse educators a measurable target for AI-literacy curricula, assessment design and institutional policy in a resource-limited setting.

all.title: Challenges Encountered in Making Online Entries on the “Panchayat Darpan Portal” in Jabalpur District, Madhya Pradesh
all.venue: Jharkhand Journal of Development and Management Studies
all.abstract: In recent years, e-governance has emerged as a powerful tool for strengthening democracy by improving transparency, accountability, and service delivery. In India, the National e-Governance Plan (NeGP) paved the way for integrating digital systems into governance, with initiatives like Digital Panchayat playing a vital role in empowering local institutions. One such initiative is the Panchayat Darpan Portal, developed by the National Informatics Centre (NIC) for the Government of Madhya Pradesh. The portal provides real-time access to Panchayat-level information—such as financial transactions, development works, salaries, and bank details—thereby promoting transparency and encouraging citizen participation. However, the effectiveness of such platforms depends heavily on ground-level realities like infrastructure, digital skills, and institutional support. This study explores the challenges faced while making online entries on the Panchayat Darpan Portal in Jabalpur district. It is based on primary data from 105 Gram Panchayats across seven blocks, along with secondary data from Panchayat records. The findings show that while basic resources like staff, computers, and electricity are largely available, significant challenges remain. These include unreliable power backup, poor internet connectivity, limited training, and incomplete understanding of the portal’s features. The study highlights the need for stronger infrastructure and continuous capacity-building to ensure the success of digital governance at the grassroots level.

all.title: Digital Transformation and New Forms of Exclusion: Rural Peripheries, Gender and Income Inequality
all.abstract: Digital transformation can foster inclusive growth, but it may also deepen income and territorial inequalities. Using World Bank data for 155 countries over 2000–2023, we test three hypotheses derived from a stylised model of low-cost adoption and skill-complementary infrastructure. We combine pooled, fixed-effects, random-effects, between, weighted, dynamic and instrumental-variable panel models with six clustering algorithms and explainable and causal machine learning. Internet use reduces inequality: a ten-point increase in Internet users lowers the Gini index by 0.4–0.6 points within countries, and the fixed-effects estimate survives region-specific shocks, external instruments, spatial models and five alternative inequality measures. Fixed broadband is associated with lower inequality across countries and higher inequality within them, but the within-country association reflects regional trajectories rather than an established causal effect. Skill-based amplification is not supported, and no robust non-linearity emerges. A persistent rural digital periphery combines weak connectivity, incomplete electrification and low female financial inclusion; the few countries that leave it first expanded electrification and mobile access. Simulations suggest that closing the periphery's adoption gap would lower its Gini index by about 4 points. Policies should pair infrastructure with affordability, digital skills and gender-sensitive inclusion. JEL codes: D63; O33; R11; C23; C38

all.title: Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions Through Which Digital Financial Inclusion Affects the Urban–Rural Income Gap
all.venue: Advances in Economics Management and Political Sciences
all.abstract: Digital financial inclusion can reduce the cost of financial services in rural areas, but wider coverage does not necessarily narrow the urban–rural income gap. This thematic review examines evidence on credit access, entrepreneurship, industrial and employment change, vulnerability to poverty, and the digital divide. The studies suggest that digital financial inclusion can narrow the average gap by improving access to productive finance and income opportunities, while gains may be distributed unevenly within rural communities. Education, the ability to use digital services, local industrial conditions, and debt risk shape whether improved access translates into higher income. To reconcile these findings, the review organizes the evidence around three stages: access to services, effective use, and conversion into income. It distinguishes disparities between urban and rural residents from inequality within each group, and current income outcomes from the risk of future poverty. This framework identifies questions for household research and suggests that rural financial policy should pair wider access with digital skills, viable local production and employment, and safeguards against excessive debt.

all.title: Adoption of Digital Payment System Among Tribal Entrepreneurs in Ranchi District
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: This study examines the adoption of digital payment systems among tribal entrepreneurs in Ranchi district. Digital payments, such as UPI, mobile banking, and digital wallets, help make business transactions faster, safer, and more convenient. The study aims to understand the level of awareness and usage of digital payments among tribal entrepreneurs and identify the factors influencing their adoption. Challenges such as limited digital skills, poor internet connectivity, lack of awareness, and concerns about online fraud were also examined. Data were collected from 68 respondents through questionnaires and supported by information from books, journals, and previous studies. Statistical tools like regression, ANOVA, and coefficient analysis were used through SPSS software. The findings indicate that factors such as gender, education, income, and occupation influence the use of digital payment systems. The study concludes that digital payments are gradually gaining acceptance among tribal entrepreneurs and support business development. However, better training, awareness programs, improved internet access, and government support are needed to increase their adoption in tribal areas.

all.title: Third-party script defences of Nigerian financial institutions after the Optimizely compromise: a passive measurement of 63 bank, fintech and insurer homepages
all.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
all.abstract: On 16 November 2026, an attacker who had gained access to the Optimizely experimentation platform wrote malicious JavaScript into the projects of 178 organisations, and most of their websites served it to visitors for about 16 hours. The payload loaded a second-stage script from an attacker host, carried an obfuscated inline copy that executes through eval when that host is blocked, skimmed payment card data, swapped cryptocurrency addresses, and sent stolen data to the attacker host, card data through navigator.sendBeacon. Each of these steps can be blocked by the host site's Content Security Policy (CSP). We measured how far Nigerian financial institutions deploy that defence. We visited the public homepages of 63 banks, fintechs, insurers and pension managers once, recorded every script and the policies each site enforces, and scored each site against a threat model derived from the published payload. Of the 63 sites, 28 (44.4%) enforce a CSP, 17 (27.0%) restrict scripts, 4 (6.3%; 95% CI 2.5–15.2) forbid eval, and 3 (4.8%; 95% CI 1.6–13.1), all fintechs, would have blocked all three payload stages. Forty-seven (74.6%) block none. Differences between sectors are not statistically significant (two-sided Fisher exact tests, all p > 0.05). Google Tag Manager runs on 44 homepages (69.8%), a shared dependency that concentrates risk across the sector. No surveyed site loaded Optimizely when measured, and none of the institutions appears among the 178 affected organisations. We discuss low-cost changes, aligned with PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirements 6.4.3 and 11.6.1, that would contain a similar attack. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Results are reported at sector level only; no institution is named.

all.title: Information Design with Supplemental Investment
institutions: The University of Texas at Austin
all.abstract: This paper features a setting with two-dimensional information asymmetry on a firm’s fundamental (good or bad type) and the nature of its supplemental investment (improving upside potential, or mitigating downside risk). We examine the firm’s optimal design of the information system when the system can only address the dimension of fundamental. We show that, with only single-dimensional information asymmetry regarding the firm’s fundamental, greater informativeness on the firm’s fundamental type always improves efficiency. However, with two-dimensional information asymmetry, increasing informativeness about firm fundamental no longer guarantees higher efficiency and can be detrimental. The optimal information system trades off reducing information asymmetry and preserving firms’ incentives to invest, and it could be uninformative or optimistically biased, depending on the level of credit risk, which in our setting is higher when supplemental investment is more likely to improve upside rather than protect downside. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00524 .

all.title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
all.abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .

all.title: Product scope, product switching, and ownership structure
all.abstract: We use comprehensive trademark data to investigate how ownership structure relates to firm product scope and product-switching behavior. We find that higher institutional ownership is associated with more active resource reallocation within firms through more frequent product additions and removals. The net effect of these additions and removals expands overall product scope. The evidence is consistent with the career-concerns channel, in which institutional monitoring insulates managers from short-term performance fluctuations arising from product-market changes. We also examine common ownership across rival firms. The results indicate that common ownership facilitates technological-spillover internalization rather than anticompetitive product pruning.

all.title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?
all.abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. Another study shows that when women are overrepresented, the effect of descriptive feedback reverses in direction, increasing the subsequent selection of men (due to concerns about fairness), but this effect is significantly smaller in magnitude than the feedback effect produced when women are underrepresented. Practically, the effects of descriptive feedback were 45%–80% as large as simulating a strict quota requiring that at least one woman or racial minority be selected for a given opportunity, highlighting that descriptive feedback is a light-touch but potentially powerful intervention for promoting diversity. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01479 .

all.title: Bimodality everywhere: International evidence of Deep Momentum
Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
all.abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. We also find that unconditional model rankings closely mirror those in bull markets, overstating the superiority of the models identified as best performing in expansions by ignoring the performance convergence across models that emerges in downturns. This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04942 .

all.title: Insurer Capital and Organizational Forms in Market Equilibrium
all.venue: The Review of Corporate Finance Studies
all.abstract: We explain the coexistence of stock and mutual organizational forms and their relative dominance in different insurance markets in a market equilibrium model. Organizational forms endogenously reflect the benefits and costs of equity and the impact of insurer operating efficiencies. Stock insurers are larger and more efficient than mutual insurers. Mutualization (i) increases with taxes and agency costs, (ii) decreases with the mean and idiosyncratic variability of insuree losses, (iii) increases with aggregate insurer asset and liability risks, and (iv) increases (decreases) with the market return when insuree loss variance is low (high). Evidence from U.S. insurance data supports all our predictions. (JEL G12, G22, G32)

all.title: Technology-Mediated Services in Healthcare: Evaluating Telehealth Delivery Models for Underserved Populations
all.abstract: Telehealth is often promoted as a way to expand healthcare access, particularly for underserved populations, yet its benefits are far from uniform. Our research shows that how telehealth is delivered matters. Using data from U.S. Community Health Centers, we examine two common delivery models for mental healthcare: specialist-facilitated telehealth, in which health centers connect patients with external specialists, and remote telehealth, in which patients receive care virtually from their own locations. We find that specialist-facilitated telehealth expands access, increasing the number of mental health patients served and visits, with particularly strong benefits in areas where specialists are scarce and clinical need is high. Remote telehealth, by contrast, does not increase access on average but improves adherence to standardized depression screening and follow-up protocols. Its benefits also depend on local conditions; limited device access can constrain utilization gains, whereas transportation barriers increase the value of remote care. For healthcare organizations and policymakers, these findings suggest that the benefits of telehealth depend on how and where it is implemented. Different delivery models address different barriers. Effective telehealth strategies should, therefore, match the design of care delivery to the specific constraints facing the communities that they serve.

all.title: Does Private Equity Hurt or Improve Healthcare Value? New Evidence and Mechanisms
institutions: The University of Texas at Austin
all.abstract: Given the significant investments by private equity (PE) firms in healthcare, it is increasingly important for stakeholders, including policymakers, care providers, and patients, to understand how PE ownership affects healthcare value, defined as the quality of care delivered relative to clinical resources used. Using longitudinal data on U.S. hospitals from 2008 to 2020, we find that PE ownership reduces healthcare value. Reductions in clinical staffing following PE acquisition partly explain this pattern: lower staffing reduces operating costs but also weakens hospitals’ capacity to maintain care quality. However, hospitals with stronger health information sharing capabilities experience substantially smaller declines in healthcare value, as these capabilities support cost reduction while mitigating care quality deterioration. Our findings offer actionable insights for healthcare stakeholders including identifying the underlying mechanisms that explain the impact of health information sharing on care value. Policymakers should evaluate PE acquisitions using a comprehensive, value-based framework which measures both care quality and costs. Hospital administrators should prioritize IT investments that strengthen information sharing across providers, whereas policymakers should promote common health data interoperability standards. Together, these efforts can help PE-owned hospitals preserve care quality under financial pressure and better align PE firms’ financial objectives with the goals of value-based care.

all.title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
institutions: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China
all.abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we caution that a more efficient waste valorization process may lead to negative outcomes for both the manufacturer and the environment. This analysis not only sheds light on how waste valorization contributes to waste reduction and economic value, but also provides insights for production decision making. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Financial support from the National Science Foundation of China [Grants 72301055, 72322017, 72471244, and 72101102] is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08500 .

all.title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
all.abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge support from the FRIC Center for Financial Frictions [Grant DNRF102]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09038 .

all.title: Decision Considerations Influencing Information Systems Modularity: A Multimethod Study of LEGO
all.abstract: The maturing of concepts such as microservices and open application programming interfaces (APIs) has radically increased the practicality of fine-grained modularization in Information Systems (IS) architecture. These are critical technical advancements, given the central role of modularity in the ability of IS to transform and meet future organizational needs efficiently. Nevertheless, reports from practice suggest that, when presented with new opportunities for modularization, organizations face multifaceted decision criteria and do not necessarily embrace new approaches as may be expected. While emergent IS literature observes that organizations’ decisions on modularity in IS may involve competing concerns, understanding of the considerations involved and how they influence such decisions remains limited. To examine these considerations, we intensively study the experience of LEGO, a global toy company. Specifically, we sequentially apply multiple methods consisting of an exploratory inductive analysis of LEGO’s approach to IS modularity decisions over 36 months, which then informs a crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 31 episodes of LEGO’s situated decision-making on IS modularity. Through the analysis, we find the rationale for a purposeful choice between two forms of modularity that differ in granularity of decomposition, rather than a linear pursuit of maximizing decomposability in IS architecture. We bring to the fore a perspective of IS modularity as situated decisions reconciling competing demands in pursuit of the right type of modularity, in the right place to achieve the right effect. Our findings add nuance to modularity in the context of IS architecture and explain the complex causality of IS modularity decisions.

all.title: Populism, polarization and green investment
Learning from a Biased Sample
all.abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that this problem is equivalent to an augmented convex risk minimization problem. We give statistical guarantees for learning a model that is robust to sampling bias via the method of sieves, and propose a deep learning algorithm whose loss function captures our robust learning target.
