sample.title: Agent Money Benchmark: Can AI Agents Be Trusted to Spend Money?
sample.abstract: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.

sample.title: Fintech Expansion
sample.abstract: I study credit market outcomes with different competing lending technologies: a fintech lender that learns from data and can seize on-platform sales, and a banking sector that relies on physical collateral. Despite flexible information acquisition technology, endogenous fintech learning is surprisingly coarse, with a single threshold that screens out low-quality borrowers. As fintech lending technology improves, better enforcement harms, while better information technology benefits traditional banking sector profits. Big data technology enables the fintech to leverage data from its early-stage operations in unbanked markets to develop predictive models that support expansion into wealthier markets. (JEL G21, L13, L52, O33, O36)

sample.title: Impact of Data Privacy Regulations on Recommender Systems Performance
institutions: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
sample.abstract: Data protection regulations like GDPR and CCPA let consumers delete personal data or opt out of collection, but companies struggle to understand how these practices affect their recommendation systems. This matters because recommendations drive substantial revenue; according to industry reports, Netflix’s system saves more than $1 billion annually, and personalized suggestions generate 35% of Amazon purchases. We analyzed how different data privacy practices impact recommendation accuracy using large-scale simulations with real-world data. A critical finding: Context matters enormously. For services where user preferences are more stable (e.g., streaming platforms), opting out barely affects recommendation quality while deleting data cuts performance dramatically. However, for platforms where preferences and needs can change frequently (e.g., e-commerce), deleting old data can actually improve recommendations while opting out severely harms them. For policymakers, this means one-size-fits-all regulations may be counterproductive. For companies, we demonstrate that data privacy practices can be redesigned: users can protect their most revealing data while maintaining close-to-optimal recommendation quality. This challenges the tradeoff between privacy and personalization, showing both could be achievable through smarter design. Companies should offer context-appropriate privacy options; regulators should recognize different platforms need different approaches.

sample.title: Gatekeepers and Kingmakers: Do Superplatforms Distort Digital Competition?
institutions: The University of Texas at Dallas
sample.abstract: The rising dominance of superplatforms raises concerns about conflicts of interest and externalities on innovation, because they act as both marketplace gatekeepers and strategic investors. Studying Google’s dual role via Google Ventures (GV) and the Android marketplace, we find Google-backed startups receive 115% more reviews, 12% higher ratings, and 77% fewer bug complaints than their iOS counterparts—despite no major app updates. These gains are consistent with selective review removal and platform promotion. Using a difference-in-differences approach with iOS versions as controls, we isolate treatment from selection effects. Our findings challenge platform neutrality and highlight subtle mechanisms of competitive distortion. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The Online Appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03354 .

sample.title: Telemetry Blindness in LLM Agents: A Controlled Measurement of Valid-Format Semantic Errors at the Write Boundary
sample.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sample.abstract: An agent built on a large language model (LLM) can write a wrong value into a database while every signal reports success: the value has a valid format, the database accepts it, the write returns success, and the agent's explanation raises no flag. This paper measures how often this happens when the value is a computed financial amount. The reference is computed by deterministic code from Central Bank of Brazil series, and each value is read back from four database engines. The main experiment was specified and frozen in version control before its runs and uses one model, gpt-6-luna, with up to 100 instances per configuration. With reasoning effort none and no calculator, under the weekday calendar, the first answer was wrong in 82 of 100 compound-interest instances, 26 of 100 dated currency conversions and all 100 instances of a task that combines both. Of 532 wrong first answers, 384 were stored and passed every observer, with a median error of 0.15%. The database range rules caught only 9, each either about 5 to 10 times the correct value or about one-fifth to one-hundredth of it. Two pre-specified paired tests rejected their null hypotheses: raising reasoning effort to medium corrected 192 instances and made 3 wrong, and offering an exact calculator corrected 171 and made none wrong. One retry after a rejection that hides the value recovered fewer than 1 in 20 interest errors at effort none. A third pre-specified test, of a range check that needs no reference, could not be interpreted. Of the checks tested, only comparison with the reference, or recomputing it, separated every error. In exploratory runs on the same instances, outside those tests and on other dates, two other models gave far fewer and far more wrong answers (12 and 915 of 1,240, against 501). The pre-specified results hold for one model on numeric tasks. Code, data and evidence: https://github.com/estefano-ferreira/telemetry-blindness-agents/releases/tag/v1.0.0

sample.title: Is low-carbon transition risk affecting the market and credit ratings equally? Evidence for European companies
institutions: Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia
sample.abstract: This paper assesses the relationship between credit risk and different climate variables under a system of equations tested using seemingly unrelated regression. When considering both total emissions and Scope 1 emissions only, carbon intensity is found to be relevant to both the rating level credit risk and the market-implied distance-to-default. However, only the rating level credit risk has grown in importance since the Paris Agreement. With respect to mitigation variables, our findings indicate that the setting of emission targets is relevant in a similar way for both market and rating measures and that the Paris Agreement has had no impact. Furthermore, carbon pricing, a strategy that emerged after the Paris Agreement, was found to be significant for both market and rating agency measures. This finding suggests that markets and rating agencies do not value the same mitigation strategies more highly after the Paris Agreement, but they do value their greater definition and sophistication more highly. Overall, the results indicate that, after the Paris Agreement, rating agencies attribute greater importance to emissions in determining the distance-to-default, while the market assigns greater importance to carbon pricing strategies than the rating agencies do.

sample.title: Campaigns That Click: Unleashing the Power of Push Notifications on Mobile Apps
sample.abstract: Push notifications can do more than promote a single merchant: They can redirect attention across an entire mobile marketplace. Drawing on more than 200 campaigns, 60 million user-campaign observations, and two controlled experiments, this study shows that notifications substantially increase same-day engagement with advertised merchants while also generating meaningful spillovers to other merchants within and across categories. Effectiveness varies by merchant, user, message design, and delivery timing. Notifications tend to work especially well for less prominent merchants, newer users, Android users, deeper discounts, urgency cues, and carefully timed delivery. However, repeated exposure produces diminishing returns and can eventually reduce engagement as annoyance and attentional overload increase. For platform managers, the findings support managing notifications as a portfolio rather than evaluating campaigns in isolation: targeting, message design, timing, cross-merchant benefits, and cumulative frequency should be optimized jointly. Platforms should also incorporate spillover value into campaign pricing, performance reporting, and merchant communication. For policymakers and platform-governance leaders, the results underscore the importance of meaningful consent, frequency controls, and transparent notification practices that protect user attention while preserving the economic benefits of timely, relevant mobile communication.

sample.title: TrustBound: Mechanized Completeness for Payment Epochs Initiated by AI Agents
sample.abstract: Payment operations requested by an AI agent may remain executable, or their outcomes unresolved, after the agent has stopped. We study when a trusted payment service can account for every payment in an epoch and exclude further payments under earlier authority. We give a Lean model in which operations are recorded before they receive execution authority and both actions are serialized with an admission fence. We prove that fencing fixes a journal that covers every modeled effect and outstanding right; that discharging those rights prevents further effects; and that truthful outcomes for the recorded identities then give exact accounting. A provider-contract model, mapped to the admission model, makes created payment objects inert until registered. Premise-removal mutations confirm that each key premise is needed. We connect the models to an executable service: six service histories are checked against the model in Lean, and bounded schedules, scripted clients and concurrent workers exercise its reconciliation. The concurrent experiments uncovered a conflict caused by reordered provider reads, which serializing retrieval with journal updates removes in all tested cases. The result separates two obligations that are easily conflated in practice - preventing future payments and accounting for past ones - and states precisely which service guarantees establish each.

sample.title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
sample.abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.

sample.title: Human Capital Development in Emerging Economies: Education, Skills Formation, and the Foundations of Long-Term Productivity
sample.abstract: This report examines how the 93 middle-income economies holding 5.9 billion people, and the low-income countries behind them, can strengthen the human capital foundations of long-term productivity as digital infrastructure, automation, and artificial intelligence reshape labor demand. Built from public data on 172 countries covering 8.0 billion people (World Bank Human Capital Index and World Development Indicators) and situated within the H Heuristics Development Multiplier framework, it analyzes the learning crisis, early childhood foundations, secondary and TVET pathways, tertiary research, digital competencies, technology absorption, and ten sequenced priorities for 2026 to 2035.

sample.title: FinTech and European Bank Performance: A Machine-Learning Analysis of Greenwashing and Sustainability Channels
sample.abstract: The parallel diffusion of financial technology and the tightening of European sustainable-finance regulation have reshaped banking, yet how digitalisation affects financial performance remains unclear. Using a panel of 90 European banks over 2014–2025 (1080 bank-year observations) and a Fintech index built from annual-report text through a Dynamic Factor Model, we examine whether, and through which channels, Fintech adoption is associated with bank performance, focusing on two mechanisms usually treated as controls: greenwashing and substantive ESG practices. We combine causal mediation, a sensitivity analysis to hidden confounding, a doubly robust Double Machine Learning estimator, unconditional-quantile (RIF) regressions, Local Projections, a Causal Forest, and optimal policy learning. Four findings emerge. First, Fintech’s direct effect raises long-term soundness while depressing short-term profitability, though its total effect on profitability is insignificant. Second, both channels mediate the relationship in the baseline specification, but only the substantive-ESG channel is robust to alternative measurement: the greenwashing channel, significant in the baseline, does not survive a performance-free re-measurement of the disclosure–performance gap, so we read these as associations rather than established causal mechanisms. Third, effects are heterogeneous across the performance distribution and over time, with profitability turning positive from the second year. Fourth, the benefits concentrate among large, well-capitalised, high-ESG, low-greenwashing banks, a profile that an exploratory policy rule can target. These associations are specific to Europe’s sustainable-finance architecture; because the design is not experimental, they are interpreted as conditional on the identifying assumptions, and their external validity remains open.

sample.title: Understanding the Prompting Effects of Chain-of-Thought on Human Collaboration with Generative AI
sample.abstract: It is well established that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves model performance in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). Far less understood is whether presenting CoT reasoning in AI-enabled interfaces enhances users’ perceived trust in GenAI’s competence in performing tasks. Drawing on the Heuristic-Systematic Model, we develop a theoretical framework in which CoT presence and quality trigger either heuristic perceptions of transparency or systematic perceptions of diagnosticity and germane cognitive load, with distinct mechanisms across task-difficulty conditions. Across a series of online experiments, we identify two key findings. First, high-quality CoT consistently enhances perceived trust in GenAI’s ability to generate correct outputs, regardless of task difficulty. Notably, under high-difficulty conditions, users’ trust in GenAI is primarily driven by the greater germane cognitive load perceived from high-quality CoT, whereas under low-difficulty conditions, trust is primarily driven by perceived transparency or diagnosticity. Second, low-quality CoT reduces users’ competence trust in GenAI that generates incorrect outputs only under low-difficulty conditions and only when users engage in careful processing, operating through perceived diagnosticity. Yet, under high-difficulty conditions, low-quality CoT amplifies trust via perceived transparency. By disentangling the cognitive pathways through which CoT shapes competence trust in GenAI and by identifying task difficulty as a critical boundary condition, these findings deepen our understanding of transparent reasoning in AI interfaces and offer valuable insights for deploying CoT in GenAI systems.

sample.title: Add-in DSE Brain: A Domain-Specific Expertise Architecture for Governing LLM Reasoning via a Graph-Guided SEPath Framework and Causal AI
sample.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sample.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved widespread adoption across the financial sector, pure neural architectures still suffer from inherent stochasticity, creating severe bottlenecks in mission-critical, zero-tolerance operations such as corporate syndicated lending, cross-asset portfolio stress testing, and regulatory compliance. Currently, financial institutions rely heavily on costly frontier generalist LLMs, which are plagued by numerical hallucinations, black-box opacity, lack of auditability, and cloud data-leakage risks. Furthermore, because these models rely on surface-level statistical correlations, they are highly susceptible to spurious correlations and confounding biases. Conversely, on-premises compact open-weight LLMs offer superior data localization and cost efficiency, yet their constrained parameter scales prevent them from independently executing complex multi-hop financial logic and causal inference. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid neuro-symbolic architecture that decouples natural language representation from causal-logical governance by integrating an on-premises compact open-weight LLM, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and an add-in Domain-Specific Expertise Brain (DSE Brain). Functioning as a Cognitive Exocortex grounded in the five-layer Structured Expert Path (SEPath) control architecture, the DSE Brain upgrades static knowledge graphs into a universal, dual-regime Causal-Constrained Logic Graph (CC-LG), such as the Causal-Constrained Financial Logic Graph (CC-FLG) demonstrated in this financial setting, that distinguishes data-supported empirical variables from normative regulatory and procedural rules. Rather than forcing statistical estimation where observational data is unavailable, the system selectively invokes multi-paradigm Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) causal discovery (PC, GES, and DirectLiNGAM), dual-track back-door and Double Machine Learning (DML) estimation, and triple-robustness refutation diagnostics exclusively to calibrate empirical causal impact weights for data-supported DEPENDS_ON dependencies, while enforcing codified prerequisite and safety assertions over normative nodes. Executed through a five-layer CoT-CR-ReAct pipeline with dual compliance gates, external deterministic solvers, and closed-loop meta-learning, the architecture actively governs latent reasoning trajectories and agentic actions. Empirical validations across global financial market series, structural prompt auditing (achieving the maximum 5.00 audit score), and longitudinal FinQA benchmarks (\approx92.0% mean accuracy) demonstrate that equipping compact open-weight LLMs with the DSE Brain transforms them into deterministic, white-box auditable inference engines that surpass frontier generalist LLMs in reasoning depth, compliance fidelity, and cost efficiency.

sample.title: Gating the Internet
sample.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sample.abstract: More than half of the traffic on the internet now comes from machines, and the share grows every year. The gates that decide which machines get through can tell which company runs an agent, and that is all they can tell. They can't say whether the agent is cleared to fill out a form, move money, or act without a person watching, and they can't see how it has behaved before. So every website makes its own trust decision alone, with almost no information, and the agents that want to wreck things get the same answer as the agents that want to help. This paper argues that no AI agent should act online without a certificate being checked, and that the check should happen at the places every agent already passes through: the model APIs that give agents their brains, the content delivery networks in front of most websites, the browsers and operating systems that agents act through, the protocol that signs their requests, and the payment rails. A certificate, in the sense that Licensed to Act lays out, says what an agent is cleared to do and how it has behaved. An agent without one can read the web, but it can't act on it. An agent with one acts within its scope, and an agent whose record stays clean earns room to act on its own. The whole method rests on one principle: misalignment has to cost more than alignment, everywhere and at every moment, and the gates are where that price gets charged. Gating the whole internet can happen without anyone being in charge, because it has happened twice before, when email adopted sender authentication and the web went encrypted. The paper also faces what gating can't do: it won't stop a well-funded attacker on its own, it depends on telling people from agents, and it hands real power to whoever runs the gates. It argues the answer is an open standard, many certifiers, and a floor that nobody falls below. Humanity Systems working paper. Part of a series on one question: how do we trust AI, now and into the future?

sample.title: Analisis Komparatif Workforce Planning Berbasis Kapabilitas Pada Perbankan di Era AI
sample.abstract: Perkembangan artificial intelligence (AI) mengubah karakter pekerjaan dan kebutuhan kapabilitas organisasi perbankan sehingga menantang perencanaan tenaga kerja yang bertumpu pada jumlah dan posisi. Penelitian ini menganalisis workforce planning berbasis kapabilitas pada perbankan Indonesia dengan membandingkan praktik yang terdokumentasi secara publik pada Bank Jago, BTN, dan bank bjb. Penelitian menggunakan analisis dokumen komparatif kualitatif atas 12 sumber publik yang dapat ditelusuri, dengan literatur ilmiah sebagai landasan konseptual. Melalui analisis isi kualitatif terarah, bukti dikodekan ke dalam empat dimensi, yaitu capability sensing, capability development, capability deployment, dan workforce readiness, serta diinterpretasikan melalui Human Capital Theory dengan literatur kapabilitas dinamis sebagai pendukung. Setiap bukti dinilai pada dua sumbu terpisah, yaitu keterkaitannya dengan AI dan kekuatan bukti praktik. Bank Jago memperlihatkan bukti yang relatif lebih jelas pada capability sensing; BTN lebih konkret pada reskilling dan penyesuaian peran; sedangkan bank bjb menekankan infrastruktur pembelajaran dan hambatan adopsi yang terdokumentasi. Bukti workforce readiness paling tipis pada ketiga kasus dan hasil pelatihan jarang terdokumentasi, sehingga perbedaan yang tampak dapat mencerminkan perbedaan pelaporan, bukan semata perbedaan praktik. Penelitian ini menawarkan kerangka analitis empat dimensi beserta tiga proposisi yang dapat diuji, dan menyarankan agar bank menghubungkan identifikasi kesenjangan keterampilan, pelatihan, dan penempatan serta mengukur hasilnya. Temuan bersifat interpretatif, bukan kausal, dan tidak dimaksudkan memeringkat bank.

sample.title: What Do LLMs Use to Judge Synthesis Recipes? An Experimental Analysis on 240 Solid-State Syntheses
sample.abstract: Inorganic materials discovery is increasingly limited by synthesis rather than by material design. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted to propose synthesis conditions with little experimental evidence of their capabilities and biases. Here, we carry out an experimental synthesis benchmark of 240 experiments across eight known and unknown inorganic oxides and subsequently evaluate an LLM as a zero-shot ranker over fixed banks of solid-state synthesis recipes. For each pair of recipes for the same oxide target, `GPT-5.6-Sol` selects the recipe expected to yield higher target-phase purity. We aggregate these pairwise preferences using a regularized Bradley-Terry model to obtain a ranked list of synthesis recipes for a given target material. By comparison with the actual purity, obtained through X-ray diffraction, we measure `GPT-5.6-Sol`'s performance as a zero-shot ranker (0.72 pairwise accuracy). By selective removal of the information exposed to the model during this ranking, we conclude that ranking is driven predominantly by thermal features, with reaction chemistry modulating the effect. Ranking accuracy tracks the purity-temperature correlation by target (Spearman ρ= 0.91\), \(p = 0.002\), and on the six thermally-driven targets withholding all chemical identity hardly impacts performance (0.68) compared to withholding temperature (0.56). Ranking performance was higher on known than unknown targets, but the group-level difference was not statistically conclusive. The methodological choices highlight the need for more experimentally validated synthesis benchmarks and position LLMs as a thermally informed prior.

institutions: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique
Groupe d'Analyse et de Théorie Economique Lyon St Etienne
sample.abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by H2020 Future and Emerging Technologies [IBSEN Contract 662725]; the Keynes Fund, University of Cambridge; and the Creative-Pioneering Researchers Program, Seoul National University. S. Goyal acknowledges financial support from the Center of Behavioural Institutional Design and Tamkeen [New York University Abu Dhabi Research Institute Award CG005]. sample.title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning in Islamic banking: insights using lexicon and machine learning-based models
sample.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) within the Islamic banking sector, focusing on sentiment analysis of these technologies across annual reports from 71 full-fledged Islamic banks in 16 countries between 2015 and 2023. Design/methodology/approach The authors used five sentiment analysis models, TextBlob, valence aware dictionary and sentiment reasoner, AFINN, long short-term memory (LSTM) and bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT), to assess sentiment polarity and word frequency of AI and ML terms using Python. Sentiment distributions and trends were analysed across time, country and individual banks using visualisations from R Studio. Findings The results indicate a predominantly positive sentiment towards AI and ML in Islamic banking, with advanced models like LSTM and BERT capturing nuanced sentiment more accurately than traditional models. Regional differences emerged, with countries like Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE demonstrating notably higher positive sentiment levels. The findings reveal significant sentiment variations among models, countries and banks, emphasising AI and ML’s perceived value in enhancing efficiency, compliance and customer experience. Research limitations/implications The study’s reliance on annual reports may limit sentiment scope, suggesting future research could expand to other data sources for a comprehensive view. Practical implications The findings offer valuable insights for Islamic banks, regulators and stakeholders to inform responsible AI adoption and its application in enhancing service quality and regulatory compliance. Originality/value This research fills a notable gap by examining AI and ML sentiment in Islamic finance, providing new insights into stakeholder perspectives on these technologies’ role and impact.

sample.title: Who Moved the Frontier? Paying Open Frontier Challenges with Free Identities
sample.abstract: In an open frontier challenge, anyone, person or AI agent, submits changes to a shared problem, and a change that beats the best measured score becomes the public baseline. How should it pay when identities are free? Rank prizes can be gamed: on a replay of one track of a recent challenge, one solver's steps under two identities would have taken first and second prize. We consider a prediction-market rule, proposed for machine-learning contests, that pays each accepted step for the progress it adds; with exact scores, among rules that see only a step's start and end, only these resist splitting and merging, and extra identities gain nothing. With noisy scores and independent normal runs, we prove that any payment that never takes money back and pays real improvements also pays something, on average, to a change that does nothing. We propose a fee per submission, at least what luck pays per attempt, that removes each attempt's expected profit if verifiers are honest and no submission is noisier than planned; nothing enforces that bound, and under noise the rule does not cap the total paid. If crediting another and faking credit to one's second account look the same, a rule that neither rewards fakes nor punishes honesty pays for credit at most what lying costs. We introduce a royalty on how much a later gain falls without the earlier change, which needs no claims but needs removable changes. For five public challenges, we name the rule our results would support.

sample.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Public Acceptance of AI Technologies among Adults in Iraq
sample.abstract: This study investigated the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies among adults in Iraq. The role of AI in public services, healthcare, education, banking, and digital communication is growing, making it a key sociological and policy issue to understand what factors affect citizens' acceptance of AI. A quantitative cross sectional survey design was used and data were gathered from 420 adults living in Iraq. Artificial Intelligence literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies were measured by a structured questionnaire with a five-point Likert scale. The data were analysed by descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, exploratory factor analysis, Pearson correlation and regression analysis using IBM SPSS Statistics software. The results showed that the participants had a moderate to high level of AI literacy and moderate levels of public acceptance of AI technologies. The Pearson correlation analysis showed that there was a statistically significant positive correlation between the concepts of artificial intelligence literacy and public acceptance. The regression analysis also revealed that AI literacy was a significant predictor of public acceptance, accounting for 32.0% of the variance, and multiple regression analysis indicated that AI literacy is the most significant predictor, even after controlling for demographic and technology-related characteristics. The study is a significant contribution to the sociology of artificial intelligence, as it illustrates how AI literacy is a crucial social resource that influences citizens' receptivity to new technologies. The results highlight the need to encourage AI literacy initiatives to foster informed public acceptance and facilitate responsible digital transformation in Iraq.

sample.title: DATA LITERACY CRÍTICA NA CIÊNCIA DA INFORMAÇÃO: PERSPECTIVA FREIREANA
sample.abstract: Today’s vast amounts of data can impact various areas of society in different ways. Information Science programs that focus solely on the technical aspects of data processing may neglect the context surrounding the data, which is important for fostering critical thinking. This article aims to discuss how interpreting the world precedes interpreting data and how Information Science can benefit from Paulo Freire’s problem-posing pedagogy. A bibliographic research was adopted as the methodology, employing an exploratory and qualitative approach. An equivalence was found between the “banking education” identified by Paulo Freire and technical approaches to Data Literacy. Also, the importance of liberating education for the development of Data Literacy was observed, which can aid in the subject’s emancipation through the dimensions of dialogue, problematization, and conscientization. The study considers that Information Science can serve as a field of critical mediation between data, the individual, and the use of technologies, focusing on the training of critical professionals. This research aims to contribute to discussions on Data Literacy in the curricula of undergraduate programs in Information Science.

sample.title: Beyond Adoption: A Critical Analysis of Fintech and Sustainable Performance in Pakistan's SMEs
sample.venue: Kashmir Journal of Academic Research and Development
sample.abstract: Fintech solutions are considered highly beneficial for SMEs in developing economies. In Pakistan, millions of merchants can now access digital payment infrastructure, and several recent studies demonstrate positive effects of fintech on firms. This paper provides a critical review of this literature. While many benefits are presented it is argued that there is limited evidence for long-term sustainable benefits (economic, environmental and social) from fintech. Using recently published empirical studies alongside official data from the State Bank of Pakistan, we show how the literature has significant limitations. These include 1) theoretical assumptions around adoption stopping short of actual adoption, 2) Cross-sectional design and self-reporting, 3) A limited understanding of sustainability, often measured perceptually, and 4) Inconsistent statistical data based on context. We conclude that whilst digital payments are necessary, SMEs gaining credit, documentation and capacity will determine long-term performance through fintech. Longitudinal, mixed-method and comparative across sector research should be conducted.

sample.title: Evaluating human-like chatbot interaction in customer service: integrating anthropomorphism and conversational capability
sample.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence (AI)-based technology has driven the development of rule-based chatbots into AI-based chatbots. This development is used by various companies to use AI chatbots as the frontline of customer service. Meeting user expectations for AI chatbots requires an evaluation model to measure chatbot quality. Based on the literature, chatbot evaluation models still focus solely on technical quality, even as AI chatbots are evolving towards human-like services. This research will explore the integration of the technical dimensions of information system success with a new dimension, namely Human-Like Chatbot Interaction (HLCI) as a higher-order construct of anthropomorphism and conversational capability. This quantitative study uses an explanatory research approach. Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of users of the Veronika chatbot, owned by Telkomsel, an Indonesian telecommunications company. A total of 213 respondents had data ready for analysis using the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) method in SmartPLS 4, namely the measurement model and structural model tests. The analysis results show that service quality is not significantly related to user satisfaction but has a direct effect on trust. Meanwhile, information quality, system quality, and human-like chatbot interaction are positively related to trust and user satisfaction. Trust and user satisfaction are positively related to intention to continue using. The results of this study can contribute both theoretically and practically to modern AI chatbot quality evaluation models.

sample.title: THE CONZETIAN PROTOCOL LANDSCAPE: Ecosystem Alignment, The Evidence Root Vacancy, and the Five Moves
sample.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sample.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive strategic analysis of the global AI agent-protocol landscape as of November 2026, and maps the Conzetian Sovereign Architecture directly against it. By reverse-engineering the adoption metrics, security gaps, and structural failures of current industry protocols—including MCP, A2A, x402, and AP2—this paper reveals an "unseen pattern": the global industry has successfully built communication, coordination, and payment rails, but has entirely failed to build the **Trust Layer**. This paper identifies that vacancy not as a product category, but as a specific architectural role: the **Evidence Root**. It demonstrates how the Conzetian architecture (L0–L8) and the G0 Prime trust root directly solve the "Ephemeral-Identity Crisis" described in current academic literature. Finally, it outlines the Five Moves required to transition the architecture from a private design into a public, verifiable standard.

sample.title: Al Powered Personal Finance Tracker with Behavioral Analytics
sample.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sample.abstract: Managing personal finances has grown ever more complicated especially as we witness the explosion of digital payments, online banking, e-commerce platforms and new consumer behaviors. Financial management systems have traditionally been very focused on recording financial transactions and keeping track of expenses without much help for users to understand their financial characteristics or get advice on how to spend their money wisely. This paper introduces the idea of developing an AI-Powered Personal Finance Tracker with Behavioral Analysis which is a smart and personalized way of dealing with financial transactions. The solution is a combination of the finance data manager with user behavior analytics, machine learning-generated finance reports, personalized suggestions, investment and stock advice, multi-person family financial planning, and monitoring in one single platform. Users can be allowed to provide bank account details via bank API in such a secure way so that the financial information is being accessed by only those users with a valid bank account and user permission. Behavioral analytics is able to detect the spending habits and financial habits of the users to generate the income, expenditure, and saving trends. Firebase Cloud Fire store database has been chosen by us as a very real-time, synchronized, and secure database. In addition, the system will implement Firebase authentication as only the authentic and verified users will be allowed to log in to a specified account. By making use of predictive analysis and customized advice, this innovative system will enable individuals to understand their personal money matters more thoroughly and ultimately, to make financially wise choices.
